articles/audio/channels/Binaural-Audio.h.title: Binaural Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Binaural-Audio.h.keywords: Binaural Audio A sound on the left reaches the left ear earlier and often more strongly than the right. It is also filtered differently by the listener's head and outer ears. Binaural audio supplies the resulting ear signals , either by recording them or by calculating them for a modeled listener. Qualitative illustration. It does not prescribe a measured delay or an HRTF response for every direction. Three kinds of cue work together Cue Information it can supply Interaural timing difference The relative arrival times at the ears Interaural level difference The relative strength, influenced by head shadow Direction-dependent spectral shape The frequency changes caused by head, torso, and outer ears Level and timing differences help distinguish the two sides. Spectral structure is especially important for distinctions such as front/back and elevation, where a simple left/right balance can remain similar. For illustration, a 0.3 ms interaural delay corresponds to 14.4 sample intervals at 48 kHz. It need not be an integer shift. A directional filter can encode fractional timing and frequency response together. Generate the ear signals from one sound A renderer chooses a head-related transfer function (HRTF) for the sound's direction. In practice, the corresponding left/right filters describe how an incoming sound is transformed for each ear. It applies the left-ear filter to the sound for one output and the right-ear filter for the other. With several source components, it filters each component for its direction and sums the contributions into the two ear outputs. The final pair can therefore represent a complex scene even though the stored file or output is only two channels. A dummy-head recording captures a related effect physically: microphones positioned at the ears receive the acoustic transformations during recording. Why headphones and speakers behave differently Headphones deliver each intended signal mostly to its corresponding ear. A pair of loudspeakers sends both channels to both ears and adds the room response. Playing a headphone-oriented binaural recording through speakers therefore adds another acoustic mixing step to signals that were already prepared as ear feeds. A conventional stereo mix is usually created for a left/right soundstage rather than a particular pair of ear filters. It can use the same storage format as binaural audio while having a different intended presentation. Keep a virtual sound fixed while the head moves A live renderer with head tracking can update the direction relative to the listener. If a sound is directly in front in the virtual world and the listener turns 30 degrees to the right, that sound is now 30 degrees to the left relative to the head. The filters should change accordingly. A finished two-channel binaural file generally contains only the already rendered ear signals. It does not automatically include the scene components and position data needed for that re-rendering. Its apparent scene can move with the listener's head instead of remaining fixed in the virtual world. Why the same render differs among listeners HRTFs embody anatomy. A generic model can give one listener clear external positions while another hears front/back ambiguity or weaker elevation. Headphone response and playback processing also alter the cues. For a track described as binaural in an Emby collection, its two-channel label tells you how many signals are delivered, while its description explains their intended ear-based role. A second virtualizer can filter those signals again and change the prepared cues. Comparing the original pair directly with additional processing disabled helps reveal what that stored render supplies. See Also Stereo Audio Virtual Surround Object-Based Audio References W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Mono-Aud.title: Mono Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Mono-Aud.keywords: Mono Audio Mono is one complete sound signal. It can include an orchestra, dialogue, effects, and ambience, all mixed into that one channel. It is a spatial arrangement, not a measure of how simple the content is. Stored arrangement Presentation One mono channel One complete signal Two identical copies The same mono presentation duplicated Two independent mono programmes Different signals that should not necessarily be heard together A playback system can send the mono signal to one speaker, both stereo speakers, or another configured output. Two speakers reproducing the same signal do not add a left/right distinction to the source. Make mono from stereo A simple normalized stereo fold-down is M = (L + R)/2. The factor of one half gives headroom and keeps matching left/right values at their original level. Left value Right value Resulting mono value +0.4 +0.4 +0.4 +0.4 0 +0.2 +0.4 −0.4 0 The last row explains why phase relationships matter: opposing components cancel when combined. Taking only the left channel avoids that sum but omits anything present only on the right. Choosing a proper mono presentation and taking one side are different operations. A mono film soundtrack is also different from the center channel of a surround mix. The mono track contains the whole programme; a surround center is one component among several. For an archival mono programme selected in Emby, equal sound from two stereo speakers can be the intended reproduction of the original single signal. Its language, edition, and mix remain more useful selection criteria than the number of physical speakers playing it. See Also Stereo Audio Multichannel Audio The Audio Center Channel References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEX: Sample rate, channels, and data rate W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Stereo-A.title: Stereo Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Stereo-A.keywords: Stereo Audio A singer appears halfway between two loudspeakers, yet no speaker is there. The mix carries the singer in both left and right channels. When their level and arrival time are suitably balanced, the listener perceives a phantom center . Stereo uses these relationships to construct a soundstage from two signals. Move a sound using channel relationships Treatment of the same sound Typical effect near the intended speaker listening position Matching signal equally in left and right A centered image Stronger signal toward one side The apparent source shifts toward that side Different ambience in the channels The soundstage gains width and spatial character Delays or phase differences The apparent location or width can change A mix can contain many sounds with different relationships at once. A voice can be centered, an instrument farther left, and ambience spread across both sides. Stereo is not two independent mono performances that must keep every sound exclusively on one side. The channel amplitudes chosen while panning also affect total level. A common constant-power panning model uses gain coefficients whose squared sum is one. At its center, each side has gain 1/√2, approximately 0.707, rather than both receiving a full-gain copy. This is one panning convention, not a rule that all stereo recordings or acoustic listening positions use the same level law. The listener completes the arrangement With speakers, both ears hear both channels, along paths shaped by head position and the room. Sitting closer to the left speaker changes both relative level and arrival time. The phantom center can consequently move toward that speaker. A dedicated center channel solves a different problem: it provides a real front-center output for a multichannel mix and helps anchor dialogue over a wider seating area. It is not part of the two-channel stereo source. Headphones deliver left and right more directly to their respective ears. A conventional stereo mix can consequently feel located inside or near the head. A binaural render deliberately supplies ear-specific directional cues to create another spatial experience using the same number of stored channels. Preserve the relationships when changing playback A stereo downmix of a surround film can include center dialogue and surround ambience. Those two outputs are a new combined presentation, not simply the original front-left and front-right channels. Duplicating a mono signal into two channels gives no new stereo differences. Conversely, combining stereo into mono can cancel opposing components; the mono page shows the arithmetic. When a stereo track in an Emby session sounds lopsided, compare whether a centered voice remains centered and whether a one-sided event goes to the intended side. That uses the relationships the mix relies on, rather than expecting every channel to have equal activity throughout the recording. See Also Mono Audio Binaural Audio The Audio Center Channel References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones W3C Web Audio API: Equal-power panning

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.title: 5.1 Surround Sound | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.keywords: 5.1 Surround Sound A screen-centered voice, a vehicle moving across the front, and rain surrounding the listener can remain separate parts of a 5.1 mix . Five main channels carry the spatial presentation; one additional LFE channel carries band-limited effects. Schematic top view. The LFE label names a signal, not a prescribed subwoofer location. Read the five positions Main channel How it contributes Front left and right A front soundstage and movement across the screen Center A stable front-center output, commonly including dialogue Left surround and right surround Sound around the sides/rear and surrounding ambience The center avoids relying entirely on a stereo phantom center for screen dialogue. The surrounds let the mix place sound outside the front arc. A surround pair can carry different effects or shared ambience; neither channel must be continuously active. ITU-R BS.775's reference geometry places front left/right at ±30 degrees and surrounds in sectors 100–120 degrees from the center-front direction. This gives the listener a defined relationship between channel roles and physical directions. Room-specific installation guidance can adapt the arrangement. Account for the sixth signal The “.1” is the low-frequency effects channel . It identifies a limited-band signal, not one tenth of the volume of a main channel. There are six decoded channels altogether. The main channels can carry substantial bass too. A playback system's bass management can redirect their low-frequency portions to a subwoofer, where they may join LFE. A subwoofer sounding during stereo playback is therefore understandable even though the stereo source has no “.1.” The LFE page separates these paths. A smaller output needs a new combination If a 5.1 film is played on a stereo television, center and surround contributions have to be incorporated into two outputs. Simply selecting the original front-left/right signals can remove much of the dialogue and ambience. The downmix uses coefficients to combine the channels and manage level. Its left/right result is a useful two-channel presentation, while the original individual positions cease to be independently available at that output. In an Emby session, first identify which track was chosen; a film can have both surround and stereo versions. Then follow whether the six-channel track stayed multichannel or was downmixed during server/client processing. A 5.1 source description and a stereo output can both be correct descriptions of that route. Adding more playback speakers can distribute or derive sound differently, but the particular 5.1 mix remains organized around these five main roles and the separate LFE signal. See Also Multichannel Audio 7.1 Surround Sound The Audio Center Channel Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.title: 7.1 Surround Sound | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.keywords: 7.1 Surround Sound A sound moving along the listener's side and then behind can use separate side and rear surround channels in a common 7.1 home-theater mix. The front remains left, center, and right. With LFE, the presentation contains eight signals. Top-view schematic of three front channels, two side surrounds, two rear surrounds, and a separately labeled LFE signal. Group Roles Count Front Left, center, right 3 Side surround Left and right 2 Rear surround Left and right 2 Effects bass LFE 1 What the extra pair changes A 5.1 mix has one surround signal per side. Those can already reproduce sound behind or around the listener, but they provide fewer independently controlled positions than the separate side/rear pairs of this 7.1 arrangement. In a 7.1 mix, the producer can move an effect from left side toward left rear by changing its contribution between those signals. A room-filling ambience can use several surround channels simultaneously. The benefit is additional spatial control, not simply a larger count of active speakers. These surround positions remain around the listener's horizontal plane. A system described as 7.1.4 adds four height positions to its speaker arrangement; the 7.1 count alone does not specify those heights. Reproduce it on a different layout A 5.1 destination must combine or otherwise appropriately render the side/rear information into its available surrounds. Dropping the rear pair can remove an event deliberately mixed there. The conversion also manages summed levels. The reverse operation is different. A receiver with seven main speakers can upmix a 5.1 source and derive rear outputs from the available material. Those derived outputs are not two additional independently stored channels in the source. When an Emby report shows eight channels, use the layout as well as the count to identify this particular presentation. Other eight-signal arrangements exist. Then compare the decoder's output roles and the receiving system's configuration: preserving eight values is useful only when they remain associated with the intended front, side, rear, and LFE paths. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound Multichannel Audio Audio Channel Order Object-Based Audio References Dolby: 7.1.2 speaker placement, including side and rear surrounds Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/Matrix-Surround..title: Matrix Surround | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Matrix-Surround..keywords: Matrix Surround How can a two-channel recording produce center and surround outputs? Matrix surround deliberately combines spatial signals into a pair with recognizable level and phase relationships. A matching decoder uses those relationships to steer the presentation. The transmitted pair is commonly labeled Lt/Rt , left total/right total. It can be heard as stereo as well as passed to a compatible matrix decoder. Understand the cue before the decoder A deliberately simplified mathematical model can illustrate the idea: Lt = L + C + S Rt = R + C − S This is not the actual Dolby matrix . Real systems use defined coefficients and phase processing; the model only exposes the information relationships. If only C is active, Lt and Rt match. If only S is active, they oppose each other. A decoder examining sum and difference can respond to those two cases: Model input Lt + Rt Lt − Rt Center only, C 2C 0 Surround only, S 0 2S Left only, L L L Matching and opposing relationships provide cues. Dolby's encoder documentation likewise specifies out-of-phase Lt/Rt outputs for surround-channel test signals, using its actual encoding process. Why two signals cannot preserve every independent channel In the model, arbitrary L, R, C, and S are four independent unknown signals described by only two transmitted signals. There is no unique algebraic solution for all possible mixtures. A center-only input and an appropriate matching front-left/right input can produce the same Lt/Rt. A practical decoder uses analysis and steering to emphasize the likely dominant directions and manage the ambiguous contributions. This can produce an effective surround impression, especially for material prepared for the matrix. It does not provide the unrestricted channel separation of a discrete multichannel recording. Later matrix systems use more sophisticated relationships and output arrangements. The specific encoding/decoder pairing determines which cues and outputs are intended. Carry the intended stereo pair Lo/Ro , left only/right only, describes an ordinary stereo downmix without that intentional surround-matrix treatment. Both Lo/Ro and Lt/Rt have two stored channels, but they ask different things of a surround decoder. For an Lt/Rt soundtrack in an Emby file, preserving the pair's relative phase and level preserves its decoding cues. Taking only one side, independently altering phase, or making an unsuitable mono conversion can change those relationships. Applying an upmixer to arbitrary stereo derives extra outputs from whatever relationships are present. Decoding an intentionally encoded matrix uses relationships the producer prepared for that purpose. A virtualizer can then take the resulting surround positions and reproduce their cues over headphones or fewer speakers, performing a subsequent acoustic-rendering job. See Also Stereo Audio Multichannel Audio Virtual Surround References Dolby DP563 Pro Logic II and Surround Encoder: Quick start guide Dolby: A Guide to Dolby Metadata

articles/audio/channels/Multichannel-Aud.title: Multichannel Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Multichannel-Aud.keywords: Multichannel Audio A six-channel English soundtrack and a six-channel French soundtrack are two tracks, each containing a complete multichannel presentation . Channels are the separate signals within that presentation, such as front left, center, or surround right. Keeping those signals separate lets a mix place sound around the listener. It also gives playback software meaningful components to combine when the listening system has fewer outputs. Follow one sample frame In a conventional 5.1 presentation, a single time position contains six values. An illustrative frame might be: Channel role Sample value at this instant Front left +0.10 Front right +0.12 Center +0.60 LFE +0.05 Left surround −0.20 Right surround +0.25 The values do not have to match. At this moment, the center contains a stronger signal, but a different scene can use other channels more heavily. All six advance on the same sample timeline, keeping their combined presentation aligned. A compressed codec can exploit similarities between channels to store them efficiently. Separate decoded channels do not imply that the file stores six literal uncompressed arrays. The codec reconstructs their values and provides the layout describing their meaning. Count, layout, order, and routing each do a job Count says how many signals exist. Layout says which roles they represent. Order associates those roles with array positions or buffers. Routing sends those signals to the available outputs. Six arbitrary recording stems are not automatically a 5.1 soundtrack. Likewise, six properly decoded channel waveforms routed using the wrong order can place dialogue behind the listener. The channel-order page follows this mapping explicitly. Adapt the presentation to the listening system A surround receiver can keep the principal channels separate and route bass according to its speaker configuration. A stereo television needs a downmix . That operation combines center and surround contributions into the left/right result; it does more than discard unused array positions. This adaptation explains an Emby session that starts with a 5.1 source but reaches the output as stereo. The source description remains six-channel even though that particular listening presentation has two channels. For object-based audio , spatial descriptions can accompany a compatible channel presentation. A renderer uses that additional information to make an output for the system. Channel decoding, layout conversion, and object rendering therefore solve related but distinct parts of turning stored sound into a listening arrangement. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound 7.1 Surround Sound Audio Channel Order Object-Based Audio References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/object-based/Dol.title: Dolby Atmos | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/Dol.keywords: Dolby Atmos An Atmos soundtrack can report “5.1” in a media tool and still supply sound above the listener. The number can describe a compatible channel presentation inside the delivery format. The Atmos information adds what a renderer needs to produce the immersive presentation. To understand a session, follow that information from the mix to the listening system. From a scene to a delivery track An Atmos production uses sound components and spatial instructions. A moving effect can have position updates; channel-based beds can provide other parts of the mix. The consumer delivery encodes a representation of this material and the information required for supported playback. That delivery is not a census of every individual object used in the studio. Encoders can use spatial coding and component reconstruction to fit the presentation into the delivery system. Common delivery or transport Audio role Dolby Digital Plus with Atmos Lossy compressed audio with compatible channel playback and additional spatial information Dolby TrueHD with Atmos Lossless delivery of the encoded audio presentation with Atmos information Dolby MAT with Atmos A supported transport for audio and spatial information, including PCM-based Atmos delivery The rows answer different parts of the chain. The first two identify common encoded source forms. MAT is especially relevant to what is sent over an output connection after the player has received or decoded its source. Why Dolby Digital Plus can have two useful results ETSI TS 103 420 describes backwards-compatible object carriage using Enhanced AC-3. The delivery includes a compatible channel presentation together with information used for component recovery and object rendering. A conventional supported decoder can play the compatible channel mix. An object-aware decoder uses the additional information to prepare the immersive presentation. This allows the same delivered programme to remain audible on conventional systems while enabling more spatial rendering on capable ones. The difference is not merely adding height speakers to the conventional decode. The renderer must receive the relevant spatial representation. An upmixer can derive height activity from channel audio, but it is working from a different set of information. Follow a movie to a 5.1.4 system Suppose an Emby library contains a TrueHD-with-Atmos soundtrack, and the listening system has five main speakers, one bass output, and four height speakers. The selected source supplies the encoded audio and Atmos information. Emby's delivery path either retains a suitable source representation or makes another presentation where required. The player can pass the supported encoded presentation onward for decoding, or use an object-aware decode and suitable output such as MAT. The renderer uses the supplied spatial information and its known speaker configuration to generate outputs for the five main and four height positions. The system reproduces those outputs and handles bass according to its configuration. The 5.1.4 label describes the speaker arrangement, not five audio objects plus four more stored tracks. An effect between available positions can use contributions to several speakers; another moment can use a different combination. If stage 3 instead outputs an ordinary 7.1 channel render, the receiver can play that presentation, but it no longer has the source's original object metadata to render as Atmos. If the player has already rendered a binaural presentation for headphones, the ear signals are likewise a finished spatial result. Decoding and compression quality are separate An object-aware decoder can preserve the metadata needed for later rendering. Decoding therefore does not inevitably remove Atmos. Dolby MAT develops this route through a concrete session. Likewise, lossless PCM-based transport does not turn a lossy Dolby Digital Plus source into a lossless studio master. It can avoid another lossy encoding while still carrying that source's decoded approximation. TrueHD's lossless property applies to its encoded audio presentation. Interpret the receiver's displays A receiver may show both a detected input format and a selected processing mode. “Dolby Surround” upmixing on ordinary channel audio and an accepted Atmos input are different observations. Height-speaker activity alone cannot distinguish them. A more useful report records the selected source form, delivered audio, player's output, detected receiver input, and speaker/rendering arrangement. That identifies where the scene information was retained, rendered, or replaced by a conventional presentation. See Also Object-Based Audio 7.1 Surround Sound Binaural Audio References Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Technology and delivery Dolby Atmos Renderer guide ETSI TS 103 420 V1.2.1: Backwards-compatible object audio carriage using Enhanced AC-3

articles/audio/channels/object-based/DTS.title: DTS:X | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/DTS.keywords: DTS:X A Blu-ray soundtrack labeled DTS:X may remain audible through an older DTS decoder, yet lose its immersive presentation. The delivery contains compatible audio, while a DTS:X-capable route uses additional spatial information to render the scene. DTS:X connects a spatial description with an output renderer , rather than requiring every source sound to name one fixed customer speaker. Follow the disc-based presentation DTS:X Master Audio delivery in the DTS-HD family supports channel and object-based material. Its encoded audio and spatial information prepare a presentation that a supported renderer can distribute across the listening arrangement. The DTS production tools describe backwards compatibility with DTS-HD and DTS Digital Surround devices. The result depends on which portions the path uses: Decoder/output result Presentation available Compatible DTS core Conventional lossy channel audio where that core is supplied Supported DTS-HD Master Audio presentation Lossless channel presentation Full supported DTS:X rendering Spatial information used for the immersive output A receiver playing one of the compatible presentations has not necessarily encountered a broken file. It can be reproducing the part it understands. The important change is which information reached the active renderer. Render positions rather than count speakers For a moving effect, spatial metadata describes its intended position through time. The renderer maps that movement onto the supported outputs. A denser supported speaker arrangement offers more physical positions; a smaller arrangement supplies another rendering of the available scene. That flexibility does not mean every DTS:X implementation supports every theoretical speaker count. The renderer's supported layouts and delivery form are part of the format route. If the player outputs only ordinary channel PCM after decoding, a later device receives a completed channel presentation. It cannot recover the original object instructions merely by recognizing that those samples came from a DTS-family source. The delivery context identifies the decoder job Disc-based DTS:X Master Audio and DTS-UHD should not be treated as interchangeable bitstreams. ETSI TS 103 491 specifies DTS-UHD channel, object, and sound-field delivery for other contexts, including streaming and broadcast. A “DTS:X supported” statement needs that context to tell you what source it covers. This is a concrete parsing and rendering distinction: software must understand the encoded presentation before its renderer can use the spatial information. For an Emby session, compare the exact selected source and delivered audio with the downstream input. A core-extraction or ordinary channel conversion is a different route from retaining a supported DTS:X presentation. Headphone:X performs another job DTS Headphone:X is headphone spatial rendering. It can use conventional source material as well as spatial presentations. Its output consists of processed ear signals; its name does not establish that the stored file had DTS:X object information. Thus a conventional 5.1 input can produce virtual surround over headphones, while a DTS:X source can play as conventional channel audio on a fallback route. Content description, compatible decoding, and final rendering explain these different results. See Also Object-Based Audio Dolby Atmos 7.1 Surround Sound Virtual Surround References DTS: Object-based audio and DTS:X backward compatibility DTS:X Encoder Suite: Production tools and compatibility ETSI TS 103 491 V1.2.1: DTS-UHD delivery of channels, objects, and sound fields DTS Headphone:X

articles/audio/channels/object-based/Obj.title: Object-Based Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/Obj.keywords: Object-Based Audio A helicopter travels from the front of the scene to a position above and behind the listener. A channel mix can describe the event by placing changing waveforms in particular speaker channels. An object-based description instead pairs the helicopter's sound with instructions about where it belongs over time. A renderer translates those instructions into the outputs available for the listening system. Conceptual path. Delivery codecs can combine and reconstruct components; the drawing does not imply a separate transmitted track for every production object. Keep the sound and the instructions together The object's audio describes what the helicopter sounds like. Its metadata can describe position, gain, size or spread, and other rendering properties. Position updates have timing so that the movement matches the sound and picture. For an illustrative event: Time in the event Object description Renderer's task Beginning In front of the listener Generate an appropriate front image Middle Above the listener Use supported height outputs or ear cues End Behind the listener Move the presentation toward the supported rear image The metadata supplies a desired scene relationship; it is not a recording of a particular customer's ceiling speaker. The renderer knows the target arrangement and chooses suitable output contributions. Render the same description for different systems For speakers, rendering distributes the object among positions the supported system can reproduce. A sound between two speaker positions can be produced by contributions to both. With a denser supported layout, the renderer has more physical positions available. For headphones, it can filter the sound into left-ear and right-ear signals, using direction-dependent cues instead of a separate physical driver at each location. The binaural page explains this operation. A system with fewer outputs does not need to invent new source sounds. It produces another presentation of the same encoded scene, subject to the delivery format's capabilities and the renderer's supported output. Beds and objects can coexist Production workflows can use beds : channel-based elements that coexist with movable or separately described objects. A background layer might be convenient to mix as channels while a moving effect benefits from object positioning. Delivery can then encode, combine, or spatially simplify those production elements to meet its data budget. A consumer decoder need not receive one independent file for every object that existed in the studio. It reconstructs the delivered representation needed for the supported render. This explains why a basic report on an Emby track can show a compatible 5.1 or 7.1 channel presentation while the bitstream contains additional immersive information. Decide where the render is finished If a player renders the scene into ordinary speaker-channel PCM, those samples already express one chosen layout. They remain playable, but the next component cannot recover the original object positions from those channels alone. An object-aware transport can instead carry the audio and required metadata together to a downstream renderer. Dolby MAT is relevant to one such path. The useful distinction is between carrying a scene description onward and carrying an already rendered presentation. Both can produce spatial sound; only the former leaves the next renderer the supplied object instructions for adapting it again. See Also Dolby Atmos DTS:X Multichannel Audio Binaural Audio References ITU-R BS.2076-3: Audio Definition Model Dolby Atmos Renderer guide Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: The Audio Center Channel | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: The Audio Center Channel The effects are loud, but the actors seem almost silent. One plausible cause is that a surround mix's center signal is missing from the output . Many screen-centered voices live there, while substantial music and effects remain in left/right or surrounds. The center is a separate front-center channel, not a special filter that detects speech. A mix can place music, effects, and panned voices there as well. Why the channel exists Stereo can put matching dialogue in left and right to create a phantom center . That image is most stable near the intended listening position. Listeners sitting closer to one speaker hear different levels and arrival times, so the voice can appear to move toward that side. A dedicated center speaker supplies an actual source near the picture. Its placement helps anchor screen dialogue across a wider seating area. This is the physical reason for the channel, rather than a requirement that every spoken word be isolated into it. Preserve it when reducing the layout Consider an illustrative surround moment with front-left +0.10, front-right +0.10, and center +0.60. A stereo fold-down using a center contribution of 0.707 gives each front output: 0.10 + (0.707 × 0.60) ≈ 0.524 . Taking only front left and right instead yields +0.10 per side. It has lost the much stronger center contribution. Operation Center content in the two outputs Retain only the original front pair Omitted Proper fold-down Combined using the selected mixing matrix Use a separate supplied stereo track Present according to that track's own mix The coefficient is an illustration of a common contribution, not a complete universal downmix recipe. Other channels and simultaneous peaks require appropriate headroom. The downmixing page develops that combination. Separate missing content from poor intelligibility If the channel never arrives, changing the receiver's overall volume cannot restore it. The useful comparison is whether center material survives the selected track's decode, layout conversion, and output routing. If the channel does arrive, a different problem can make speech hard to understand: an incorrectly set center level, placement relative to the listener, room reflections, or the mix itself. A receiver's local channel test can verify its speaker route, while a known multichannel identification file can test more of the media path. In an Emby movie, a supplied stereo mix can be a useful comparison with the surround track's stereo conversion. If one retains clear dialogue and the other loses it, the specific fold-down or routing deserves attention. These tests distinguish an absent signal from a signal that is present but obscured. See Also Stereo Audio 5.1 Surround Sound Audio Channel Order References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: Audio Channel Order | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: Audio Channel Order The dialogue waveform can decode perfectly and still come from the wrong speaker. Channel order associates positions in an audio buffer with channel roles. Moving the bytes successfully is only half the job; their meaning must travel with them. Interpret one six-channel frame Suppose an interleaved frame has the following values and uses the WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE mask 0x60F: Array position Role defined by that mask Value 0 Front left +0.10 1 Front right +0.12 2 Front center +0.60 3 LFE +0.05 4 Side left −0.20 5 Side right +0.25 The next six values belong to the next time position in the same order. Sending position 2 to a surround output would move the center's +0.60 sample behind the listener. Misinterpreting position 3 as a full-range speaker signal also changes the purpose of that channel. A mask is a set of roles with a defined ordering rule WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE uses flags for speaker positions. Interleaved samples follow the ascending set-bit order, not the order in which names happen to appear in a user interface. Example mask Roles in sample order 0x3 Front left, front right 0x60F Front left, front right, center, LFE, side left, side right 0x63F Front left, front right, center, LFE, back left, back right, side left, side right For 0x60F, the flags are 0x1 + 0x2 + 0x4 + 0x8 + 0x200 + 0x400. Six flags identify six channels. The 7.1 mask adds the back-left and back-right flags before the side pair in numerical bit order. A 5.1 mask using back positions exists too. Those names can describe a different source layout even if a room uses similar physical speakers for its two surrounds. Map roles across each boundary Compressed codecs, containers, and playback APIs can describe their own conventions. A decoder often exposes an already labeled working layout that differs from the codec's internal packing. Software must translate by role across these boundaries. A reliable conversion follows this sequence: Read the source's layout and coding convention. Decode and identify each output channel by its role. Map those roles into the destination's required order. Supply the corresponding destination layout description. An arbitrary rearrangement based only on the codec name can undo a decoder's correct mapping. Changing the label without moving values, or moving values without updating the label, are reciprocal ways to create a routing error. Planar storage does not remove this requirement. It places each channel in a separate buffer, and those buffers still have ordered or explicitly identified roles. For an Emby session with repeatable misplaced dialogue or effects, compare the source layout, decoder output, and destination roles. A known channel-identification recording is more informative than a movie scene whose channels may deliberately be quiet or shared. The goal is to verify which named signal reaches which named output. See Also Multichannel Audio PCM Sample Formats 7.1 Surround Sound References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks FFmpeg: Audio sample formats

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) A subwoofer plays bass from stereo music, even though the track has no LFE channel. During a 5.1 film, it may play both the main channels' bass and a separate effects signal. The subwoofer is a playback device; LFE is a source channel. Follow the two paths The main left, right, center, and surround channels can contain low frequencies. Bass management removes some of that low-frequency material from speakers configured to need assistance and redirects it to the bass output. Low-frequency effects (LFE) is a separately mixed, band-limited signal. It supplies additional low-frequency energy, such as selected film effects. ITU-R BS.775 gives its nominal upper boundary as 120 Hz. For an illustrative setup with an 80 Hz main-speaker crossover: Source content Relevant route A 60 Hz component in a main channel Can be redirected toward the subwoofer A 200 Hz component in that main channel Primarily remains in its main-speaker output A 100 Hz component in LFE Can reach the subwoofer through the separate LFE path This table illustrates the routing concepts. Real filters have gradual transition regions, rather than switching each frequency abruptly between outputs. An 80 Hz crossover therefore does not redefine LFE as an 80 Hz source channel. Crossover processing and LFE low-pass processing perform different jobs. Why “.1” is not a speaker count or a volume fraction In 5.1 or 7.1, “.1” denotes the limited-band effects signal. It is not one tenth of a main channel's amplitude. There are six or eight source signals respectively. One LFE signal can feed several calibrated subwoofers. A system can also route low frequencies to capable main speakers. Counting physical bass speakers therefore does not count the source's LFE channels. Understand the reproduction level convention For the broadcast/film convention described by BS.775, LFE is recorded with a −10 dB level offset and reproduced with compensation. Equal-level test signals give the LFE path a +10 dB acoustic output relationship within its low-frequency passband. That does not mean an arbitrary wideband meter reading should be ten decibels higher, or that every digital LFE waveform should be boosted manually. Bandwidth, calibration, decoder processing, and the delivery format's convention determine the intended result. The recommendation also notes formats using other LFE-offset conventions. This arrangement gives extra low-frequency effects headroom. Mixing compensated LFE with redirected bass must still avoid overloading the combined output. What remains after a stereo conversion A stereo downmix may omit the separate LFE signal while retaining bass already present in the main channels. Its result can still contain substantial bass. If a receiver subsequently redirects that stereo bass, the subwoofer can play again without LFE having been recreated. For an Emby source, keep those three observations separate: the selected track's LFE channel, any bass-management processing, and the bass signal finally reproduced. This identifies whether a missing effect, a crossover decision, or an output-level problem is actually responsible for the difference you hear. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound The Audio Center Channel Multichannel Audio References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/Virtual-Surround.title: Virtual Surround | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Virtual-Surround.keywords: Virtual Surround A headset marked “7.1” can reproduce virtual surround using one main driver per ear. The source positions are translated into directional cues , then combined into the two signals the headphones actually play. Virtual surround is this rendering job. It can operate after a conventional multichannel decoder or after a supported spatial decoder. Turn several speaker positions into two ear signals Consider front-left, center, and rear-right signals from a soundtrack. A headphone virtualizer treats each as a source at its assigned position: Choose the left-ear and right-ear filters associated with front left; filter that channel. Repeat for the center and rear right. Add all left-ear contributions together and all right-ear contributions together. Deliver the two resulting ear signals. The filters provide timing, level, and spectral relationships rather than merely making one channel louder. Binaural audio explains the directional cues and listener model. What reaches the virtualizer Available starting information Discrete multichannel audio Separate signals with channel positions Supported objects and metadata Components with spatial instructions Ordinary stereo Two source signals, possibly used for derived spatial processing An existing binaural render Ear signals that have already been spatialized Virtualizing an existing rear channel and deriving a new rear impression from stereo are different tasks. An upmixer can perform the second before virtualization, but does not give the processor access to original channels that were previously combined. Speakers require another acoustic strategy A speaker-based virtualizer has to account for each loudspeaker being heard by both ears. Some approaches shape or partly cancel the cross-ear paths to suggest positions beyond the physical speakers. Reflections, seating position, and listener movement affect that acoustic relationship. A method that works through headphones therefore cannot simply be assumed to give the same result through a soundbar. The input-to-ear path is different. Put the rendering at the intended stage During Emby playback, the system might deliver multichannel audio to a headphone renderer in the player or operating system. A different path might downmix to stereo earlier, leaving headset software only that smaller presentation. If a rear-channel identification sound disappears as a distinct position, inspect what the spatializer received. Keeping the source multichannel until a suitable renderer uses it preserves more positional information than first collapsing it into ordinary stereo. Also identify whether the track itself already contains a binaural render. Filtering those ear signals again changes their prepared timing and spectral cues; adding another effect is not simply adding more original spatial detail. A useful comparison uses the same source, roughly matched listening level, and one identified spatial-processing stage at a time. Listen for specific front/rear transitions and stable dialogue placement. That reveals what the renderer does to the input positions rather than just whether its mode sounds wider. See Also Binaural Audio Multichannel Audio Matrix Surround References Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering DTS Headphone:X Dolby: Sound bar surround virtualization and crosstalk cancellation

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Des.title: Audio-Description Tracks | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Des.keywords: Audio-Description Tracks A character silently hides a key under a flowerpot. The main soundtrack offers a rustle but no words explaining the action. Audio description adds the missing visual information , helping a listener who is blind or has low vision follow why that action matters later. The description is authored as part of the listening presentation. Making dialogue louder or transcribing its words does not supply an unspoken visual event. Fit useful description into the programme Descriptions can identify actions, expressions, scene changes, on-screen text, and other important visual details. They are generally placed around dialogue and significant sound where possible. The aim is enough information to understand the programme, not narration of every visible object. A complete described mix balances that narration with dialogue, music, and effects so they remain usable together. Identify the role, not just the language Illustrative track title Intended content English — Main Ordinary English soundtrack English — Audio Description Programme with important visual details described English — Commentary Discussion by creators or other commentators All three can have the same language code. Descriptive track names or role signaling tell the listener which presentation to select. A commentary is not a substitute for audio description merely because it adds speech. In an Emby library, preserving useful language and track-role information makes these choices distinguishable without listening to each track to discover its purpose. Complete described mix versus narration component A movie file can contain a fully mixed alternative soundtrack. Selecting it supplies the description and programme together, regardless of whether that mix is stereo or surround. Broadcast systems can instead carry associated narration that a capable receiver combines with the main audio. This supports the defined balance or control behavior, but the narration component alone may lack the movie's dialogue, music, and effects. That structural difference matters during conversion: Identify whether the source provides a complete described track or a supplementary component. If supplementary, assemble the intended presentation using its mixing/signaling rules. Preserve the resulting accessible mix, or preserve the component structure for a reader that supports it. Retain labels that make the accessible choice discoverable. Simply extracting an associated narration component can create a recording of descriptions without a complete programme soundtrack. Copying only the main track can remove the accessibility option entirely. Check the option as content Verify a few places where description is expected, its balance with dialogue, and the full intended duration. Then verify track selection and names in the listening app. These checks answer different questions from successful codec decoding. A perfectly playable main mix may still be the wrong presentation for the listener, while a complete described mix preserves information that neither louder dialogue nor another codec can generate. See Also Streams and Tracks Track Language Metadata Audio Codecs Explained Dolby AC-4 Audio References W3C: Description of visual information W3C WCAG 2.2: Audio description of prerecorded video ETSI EN 300 468 V1.17.1: DVB service information and audio description signaling

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Pla.title: The Audio Playback Path | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Pla.keywords: The Audio Playback Path The library says Dolby Digital 5.1 , the server says Direct Play , and the receiver says Multichannel PCM . Those observations can describe one successful session: the source was delivered unchanged, then decoded in the player. Following the actual presentation through the stages resolves apparent contradictions. Logical-stage schematic. Several stages can share a physical device. Trace a retained channel presentation Consider a player that accepts the chosen AC-3 track and can output its six channels as PCM: Stage Representation or job Selected library track AC-3 5.1 with language and timing Server delivery The compatible stored audio is retained Player decoder Reconstructs six PCM channel signals Output path Supplies those signals in its declared layout/order Receiver Receives PCM and routes the presentation to the system The receiver no longer needs an AC-3 decoder for that input because the player already performed the reconstruction. Its PCM label is expected. The result can still use decoder metadata, output gain, or bass management. To determine whether those altered the presentation, identify the specific operation rather than treating the change of codec label as the operation itself. Trace an audio-only compatibility conversion Now consider a seven-main-channel/LFE soundtrack whose video fits the client, but whose audio needs a stereo-compatible delivery. The server reads the selected audio track and decodes its channel presentation. A downmix combines the center and surround contributions with the fronts to produce two channels. A suitable audio encoder creates a stereo delivery stream. Compatible video is copied into the delivery package with the audio and timing. The client decodes that new soundtrack for its output. Emby's Direct Stream description includes situations where compatible video is retained and audio is converted. The overall label therefore does not imply that every audio property stayed unchanged. Here the source's eight channels and the receiver's two channels describe different points in the trace. The causal changes are downmixing and re-encoding, not simply “the receiver shows stereo.” Place decoding and rendering independently With bitstream passthrough , a supported encoded presentation reaches another device that decodes it. With ordinary PCM output , decoding already happened earlier. For an immersive source, there is also a rendering job: spatial information becomes speaker or ear signals. A player can finish the render itself or carry suitable audio/metadata onward using an object-aware path such as MAT . This makes four separate questions: Which presentation was selected? What did the server deliver? Where was it decoded or rendered? What did the output system receive? Record changes at boundaries A useful session report is a trace, rather than a single preferred label: Observation Useful details Source Track role/language, codec, channel layout, rate, spatial form Delivery Copied/remuxed/encoded audio and resulting properties Player output Encoded passthrough, PCM, or metadata-bearing transport Receiver input Detected input, separate from listening mode Reproduction Speaker routing, bass handling, headphone/spatial processing If dialogue vanishes between a six-channel decode and stereo output, investigate that combination. If timing changes after switching output devices, investigate that boundary's delay. If object information is retained at delivery but a receiver gets ordinary PCM, identify where the render or metadata loss occurred. Each observation now points to a particular transformation, which is more useful than treating Direct Play, PCM, or a surround-mode name as a verdict on the whole session. See Also Audio Bitstream Passthrough Decoded PCM Output Audio Transcoding References Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Vid.title: Audio/Video Synchronization | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Vid.keywords: Audio/Video Synchronization A clap is easy to use as a synchronization check: the hands meet at a visible instant, and the matching sound has an identifiable attack. If those events are separated, first observe whether the gap stays constant or grows. Synchronization aligns presentations on a common timeline , then accounts for different processing and output delays. Convert each stream's time units Video frames and audio sample blocks need not arrive together or represent equal durations. Their timestamps say when the reconstructed results belong in the presentation. For an illustrative timebase conversion: Stream timestamp Unit duration Presentation time Audio: 960,000 1/48,000 second 20 seconds Video: 500 1/25 second 20 seconds The numbers differ by nearly three orders of magnitude but designate the same instant. Comparing raw timestamp integers without their units would be meaningless. The decoder also needs its input early enough to produce the output for that instant. Decode order, buffering, and presentation scheduling are related but distinct jobs. Schedule around different output delays Suppose a picture path takes 100 ms from submission to display, while a sound path takes 20 ms to the audible output. To present both at a chosen wall-clock instant of 20.000 seconds: Submit the picture at 19.900 seconds. Submit the audio at 19.980 seconds. Submitting both at 19.900 would make the sound arrive at 19.920, 80 ms before the picture. Adding 80 ms of audio delay could compensate for that fixed difference. These are hypothetical processing delays, not universal television or player values. They show why equal submission/packet-arrival time is not synchronization. Separate fixed offset from clock drift A fixed offset can come from unequal processing paths, an initial timestamp difference, or an uncompensated encoder/filter delay. Delaying the earlier presentation can address that particular constant gap. A rate mismatch accumulates instead. A hypothetical audio device consuming 48,002.4 frames per wall-clock second instead of 48,000 runs 50 parts per million fast. Over one hour it consumes 2.4 × 3,600 = 8,640 additional frames , representing 0.18 seconds at the intended rate. Changing the starting delay does not remove the rate difference. A player can need clock tracking, scheduling changes, or appropriate rate conversion to keep the presentations aligned over time. Preserve the timeline through a seek or conversion A seek jumps the desired media time, but decoder buffers can still contain data from the previous position. The player must flush/reinitialize appropriate state and establish the new audio/video relationship. A transcoded track also has its encoder delay and final padding. Timestamps and trimming must account for them rather than making them extra audible programme time. These mechanisms explain why a file can start aligned and change after a seek, or why one delivery/output route differs from another. Use the symptom to select a test Observation First useful comparison Same offset at beginning and end Compare fixed delays and starting presentation times Increasing mismatch Compare timebase interpretation, rates, and clocks Sudden change after seeking Compare seek/reset behavior Only one audio output affected Compare that output path's buffering and processing Same misplaced event on several paths Examine the source's timing/presentation For an Emby session, record the event, approximate gap, and whether it changes with time. A comparison through another client or output route then isolates a boundary. This is more useful than choosing an offset value before knowing whether the problem is an offset at all. See Also Packet Timestamps Time Bases Video Frame Rate The Audio Playback Path References ITU-R BT.1359: Relative timing of sound and vision RFC 3550: RTP timestamps and synchronization FFmpeg: Audio filters, mixing, and delay

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Downmixing | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Downmixing A 5.1 film has center dialogue and surround ambience, but the television accepts two output channels. Downmixing constructs a new two-channel presentation from those source signals. It must decide both which contributions go where and how their levels fit the output range. Selecting only the original front pair is not that operation. Follow one moment through a stereo matrix For a conventional illustrative fold-down, ignoring LFE in this example: Left output = FL + 0.707 × C + 0.707 × SL Right output = FR + 0.707 × C + 0.707 × SR Here FL/FR are front left/right, C is center, and SL/SR are the corresponding surrounds. Real downmix conventions, metadata, and target formats can choose other coefficients and phase relationships. Take this particular sample frame: Source Value FL +0.10 FR +0.10 C +0.60 SL +0.20 SR −0.10 The resulting left value is 0.10 + 0.4242 + 0.1414 = 0.6656 . The right is 0.10 + 0.4242 − 0.0707 = 0.4535 . The center has contributed to both sides; the different surround values retain different contributions. Taking FL and FR alone would instead output only +0.10 and +0.10, losing those stronger parts of the moment. Leave headroom for coincident signals With FL=C=SL=+1, that illustrative left sum is 1 + 0.707 + 0.707 = 2.414 . The individual inputs are in range, but their sum is not. A simple worst-case normalization for this particular matrix could scale the sum by 1/2.414, approximately 0.4143 . Other approaches can use different target levels, metadata-driven coefficients, or suitable overload protection. A single maximum-sum bound is safe but may leave extra headroom for ordinary material whose peaks do not coincide. This explains why a downmix can be quieter without changing codec quality, and why compensating with a later indiscriminate boost can reintroduce clipping . Phase and channel roles affect the result Opposing contributions can cancel. If the left front signal and a routed surround contribution oppose each other, their combination changes even though both source channels decoded correctly. Ordinary stereo and a matrix-surround Lt/Rt presentation can use different relationships, including phase treatment. The intended downstream presentation determines which matrix is appropriate. The input layout also must be correct. A center contribution cannot preserve dialogue if software mistakenly interprets that buffer as LFE or a rear channel. Apply the matrix to named roles, not guessed array positions. Handle LFE and main bass separately The worked matrix omits LFE deliberately. A real conversion chooses its LFE treatment according to the intended presentation. The main channels already contain bass; omitting an effects channel does not erase every low frequency. Bass management happens for playback speakers and is another job. It can redirect main-channel low frequencies to a subwoofer after the mix has been constructed. Know what can no longer be separated After five source signals become two outputs, arbitrary original channels cannot be uniquely recovered. For instance, additional center contribution can be indistinguishable from matching front contributions in the final pair. An upmixer can derive useful output directions from that pair, but it does not invert every original component. Retaining the multichannel master preserves those separate signals for a later different render. Locate the combination during playback An Emby session can downmix in server conversion, the client decoder/processor, or a later output stage. Record the source layout, where the matrix was applied, and the delivered/output layouts. For weak dialogue, compare whether center contributions survived. For overload, inspect the sum and its gain. For missing rear activity, determine whether an earlier stereo downmix replaced the discrete source. Each symptom follows a specific property of the combination. See Also The Audio Center Channel Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) Audio Clipping Audio Upmixing References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system W3C: Web Audio API channel interpretation FFmpeg: Audio resampler and rematrixing options

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Transcoding | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Transcoding A movie's video can fit a client while its soundtrack does not. A server can keep the video and construct a new audio presentation. Audio transcoding is the decode/process/encode part of that route. The operation is easier to assess when its intermediate representation is made visible. Follow a surround source into stereo delivery Consider a hypothetical 48 kHz 7.1 source and a client requiring stereo AAC: Stage Representation Source reading Coded eight-channel presentation and timestamps Audio decoding Reconstructed samples with eight named roles Layout conversion Two-channel result incorporating the appropriate source contributions AAC encoding New coded stereo approximation Delivery packaging Compatible video and new timed audio in the target package The audio decoder and encoder are different jobs. The decoder reconstructs what the source represents. The encoder analyzes its supplied PCM and chooses a new representation that meets its settings. Emby's Direct Stream description includes compatible video retained while audio or packaging changes. The overall delivery label does not imply the source soundtrack's layout or codec remained unchanged. Separate conversions inside the pipeline Downmixing changes spatial channels. Resampling calculates another time grid. Gain or dynamics processing changes amplitudes. The final encoder changes the coded representation. These can occur together, but each has its own preservation effect: Operation Consequence Exact supported lossless decode/re-encode, no intervening changes Can preserve the samples Downmix Combines independent channels Resample Changes sample positions/count while retaining intended time Lossy encode Adds its representation's approximation Ordinary channel encode of an immersive result Does not retain original objects merely by using the same codec family An encoder generally also introduces buffering, delay, and final padding. The delivery's timing must account for those so the new soundtrack remains aligned and has the intended audible boundaries. Distinguish a new encoding from remuxing A remux reads coded packets and writes another supported package, translating necessary configuration and timing. It can leave the coded audio intact. A transcode instead reconstructs the signal and invokes an encoder. Moving AAC from ADTS into a compatible MP4 arrangement may be a framing change; changing AAC into another codec is a reconstruction-and-encoding operation. Understand generation loss at the right boundary If the source is already lossy, the new encoder receives that reconstruction. A larger target budget can avoid adding much more error, but cannot recover the source details previously merged or discarded. A lossless source avoids that prior approximation, yet a subsequent lossy delivery still makes a new approximation. Keeping the source master allows future sessions to start from it rather than repeatedly converting intermediate copies. Verify what the destination received Compare source and delivered codec, layout, rate, and timeline. Then check whether the output added further processing. For missing dialogue, inspect the layout conversion; for a timing shift, inspect delay compensation; for altered texture, inspect coding generations and settings. This makes a transcoding report about identifiable operations and outcomes, rather than treating “conversion happened” as a complete explanation. See Also Lossy Audio Compression Audio Downmixing Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References FFmpeg: Stream copy and transcoding FFmpeg: Audio resampler and rematrixing options Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Upmixing | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Upmixing A stereo song sends a stable voice to the front center and ambience into the surrounds when a receiver's upmixer is enabled. The processor is deriving an expanded presentation from the relationships in its available inputs. It is useful to inspect what it derived, rather than treating every active output as a newly discovered source channel. Start with shared and differing content A simple mid/side analysis illustrates relationships an upmixer can exploit: M = (L + R)/2; S = (L − R)/2. Stereo pair Shared component M Difference component S L=0.6, R=0.6 0.6 0 L=0.8, R=0.2 0.5 0.3 L=0.4, R=−0.4 0 0.4 A shared component can be useful for deriving a central image. Differences and less-correlated content can help derive width or ambience. These are only analysis illustrations: commercial upmixers use more elaborate time/frequency analysis, steering, and decorrelation. The processor must also decide how much derived center to remove from or retain in the fronts, how to preserve level, and how to avoid distracting motion when several sounds coexist. Merely copying M into another speaker is not a complete natural-sounding upmix. Directional cues and independent signals are different resources With intentionally matrix-encoded material , a decoder has relationships prepared for surround recovery. With arbitrary stereo, the upmixer infers a useful presentation from relationships that may have many origins. Two matching channels can represent one centered voice, several centered instruments, or a mono recording duplicated into stereo. The same inputs do not uniquely identify separate studio stems. This is why a stereo downmix followed by upmixing need not match the original multichannel mix. The earlier combination removed independent signals that the analysis cannot always distinguish again. Expand a conventional surround presentation An upmixer can also start with 5.1 and derive rear or height activity for a larger system. Existing discrete positions remain more information than ordinary stereo, but the additional outputs still come from a chosen rendering/analysis method. Dolby Surround and DTS Neural:X are examples of such processing. Native object rendering instead has supplied spatial instructions where the source and path provide them. Compare the result as a presentation Use the same passage and a sensible level comparison. Listen for dialogue that stays anchored, movement that remains coherent, and ambience that surrounds without pulling a foreground voice behind the listener. For an Emby session, identify the receiver's detected source presentation separately from its upmix mode. A 2.0 input with expanded outputs is a legitimate upmix result; it is not evidence that the file secretly contained all those discrete channels. See Also Matrix Surround Object-Based Audio Audio Downmixing Virtual Surround References Dolby: Atmos installation guidelines, Dolby Surround upmixer miniDSP: Surround decoding and upmixing FFmpeg: Audio filters, mixing, and delay

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core The selected soundtrack says DTS-HD Master Audio, but an older receiver detects DTS. An existing compatible core can explain this result: the player delivered the part that the receiver understands while omitting the enhancement information. Core fallback uses already encoded data. It differs from making a new codec version during playback. Follow the components A common DTS-HD disc stream has a core and extensions. The core is independently decodable; the appropriate full decoder uses the additional information for its enhanced or lossless presentation. If the output needs conventional DTS, a supported extraction route can retain the core's coded data. That result has the losses already present in the core, but avoids another lossy encoding generation. Route Origin of the delivered audio Extract existing core Coded component from the selected stream Choose another soundtrack Separately stored track/presentation Decode and transcode New encoded data from reconstructed audio A source can remain fully intact in the library while only one compatible component is used in the session. Describe what the fallback omitted A core may have fewer channels or lack lossless correction and spatial information used by the full presentation. The receiver's successful DTS decode therefore establishes that a compatible soundtrack arrived, not that the original Master Audio or DTS:X result was reconstructed. The lossless-correction example in Master Audio shows why the core alone differs from the corrected result. Establish that a core actually exists DTS defines extension-only arrangements too. An extraction operation cannot manufacture a missing core from such a stream; it would need another source presentation or a conversion. The Dolby cases also have different structure. TrueHD can be accompanied by separate/packaged AC-3 compatibility audio, but it does not contain the common DTS-HD-style lossy core. An E-AC-3 independent substream is independent within E-AC-3, not automatically an AC-3 component. For an Emby playback report, identify the selected source's actual components and the delivered codec. If a decoder/encoder created new AC-3 from the full source, call that transcoding , even if its final label resembles a familiar fallback. Naming the operation accurately explains both the preserved source and the presentation heard. See Also DTS Core Audio DTS-HD Master Audio Dolby TrueHD Audio Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Production tools and backwards compatibility Dolby: TrueHD lossless audio Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus audio coding

articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.title: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.keywords: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata A moving sound needs both its audio and instructions about its position through time. If the goal is letting the receiver render the original immersive scene , the required spatial information must remain available until that receiver's renderer uses it. Preservation depends on where the scene is decoded, transformed, and finally rendered. Make a boundary ledger For an illustrative Atmos source: Boundary or operation Information carried onward Copy compatible encoded source data Audio and relevant spatial information in that bitstream Object-aware decode to a suitable metadata-bearing output Reconstructed audio plus required spatial information Render to a chosen speaker layout The generated speaker-channel presentation Render to binaural headphones The generated ear signals Ordinary channel transcode A new channel presentation, without automatically retaining source objects The first two routes can leave a downstream renderer the scene description. The next two have already completed a render. The final route creates another coded channel result from the signal it was supplied. Rendering can be the intended end of preservation A headphone player can use the original object directions to generate convincing ear cues. Once those cues are delivered to the headphones, there is no need for the headphones to receive and render the original objects again. Likewise, a renderer can generate the supported speaker layout's PCM channels. That presentation can be correct for its target even though the metadata is no longer traveling onward. The distinction is therefore the intended renderer boundary , not whether the word PCM appeared anywhere in the chain. Use an object-aware decoded route when required A conventional PCM decoder/output can supply the compatible channel presentation of an immersive track. Its array of 5.1 or 7.1 values does not by itself encode the original object's position updates. An object-aware decoder can retain the appropriate reconstructed components and metadata. Supported Dolby MAT output can carry such information onward. The downstream system then applies the scene information to its own supported arrangement. The compressed source form still matters: Dolby Digital Plus object carriage and TrueHD delivery require different parsing/reconstruction before reaching that boundary. Identify irreversible combinations A downmix or ordinary channel render combines source components for a chosen output. A later processor cannot uniquely infer the original objects and paths from those sums. A generic E-AC-3 encoder also does not recreate an Atmos scene merely because the input came from Atmos. It needs the relevant scene representation and a supported encoding workflow; ordinary channel PCM is a different input. An existing compatible core can keep a soundtrack audible while leaving the immersive extension unused. That is a particular component-selection result, not proof that the file's spatial information vanished from storage. Verify the route using the active renderer For an Emby session, record the source form, delivered presentation, decoder's output type, and where rendering occurs. If the receiver is intended to render, confirm its detected immersive input instead of only its upmix/listening mode. If the player renders headphones, evaluate that output as the finished ear presentation. A basic channel-count report and height-speaker activity are insufficient evidence because a compatible channel mix and an upmixer can produce those observations. The boundary ledger establishes which spatial instructions actually remained available to the renderer making the final listening presentation. See Also Dolby Atmos DTS:X Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 103 420 V1.2.1: Backwards-compatible object audio carriage using Enhanced AC-3 Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering Dolby: Atmos Renderer guide Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Audio Bitstream Passthrough | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Audio Bitstream Passthrough A receiver can decode a movie soundtrack only if it receives a compatible encoded presentation . Bitstream passthrough arranges that delivery, leaving audio reconstruction to the downstream decoder rather than producing ordinary PCM in the player. The server's Direct Play decision happens earlier. It can retain a file that the player either decodes locally or passes onward. Follow the coded payload to the receiver The player reads the selected track and its codec configuration. It then supplies the encoded audio using the output API and transport convention required for that format. IEC 61937 defines transport of encoded audio in a digital-audio framework. Transport data includes framing and format identification so the receiver knows that it contains a coded payload to unpack, not ordinary amplitude samples to play directly. A declared carrier rate or channel arrangement can consequently describe the transport , while the encoded content has its own audio rate and presentation. Microsoft's transport documentation explicitly distinguishes those fields. Boundary What must happen File to player Find the correct coded track and configuration Player to output API Request the proper encoded format Driver/link Carry the required framing without treating it as normal mixed PCM Intermediate device Forward a compatible presentation where present Receiver Recognize, unpack, and decode that presentation This is why receiver capability alone cannot fix a player/output route that never supplied the encoded format. Why normal sample processing changes the route A volume multiplier acts on decoded sample amplitudes. Multiplying bytes in a compressed packet would instead alter coding symbols or headers, corrupting their meaning. Likewise, mixing a notification into a soundtrack requires sample-domain combination or a specially supported codec-aware path. An ordinary PCM mixer cannot simply combine arbitrary encoded packets and expect a valid soundtrack. A player may therefore disable some local effects during passthrough, choose PCM when processing is needed, or control downstream volume separately. Those are consequences of where the reconstruction happens, not inherently defects in the source. Confirm the input before interpreting a listening mode If a compatible receiver detects the intended encoded format, its decoder can reconstruct that presentation. It may afterward apply an upmixer, bass management, or other listening mode. The processing-mode name and detected input answer different questions. A height-speaker mode on a conventional input is not the same observation as receiving the original immersive bitstream. For an Emby immersive track, retaining the suitable encoded payload is one way to keep its spatial information available downstream. An object-aware decoded MAT path can perform a different supported route; ordinary channel PCM does not carry original objects just because it has many channels. Use these distinctions to locate a failed boundary: did the player request the format, did the link forward it, and did the decoder accept it?
