That trace is more informative than changing unrelated codec or speaker settings together. See Also Decoded PCM Output Dolby MAT Audio Transport The Audio Playback Path Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Decoded PCM Output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Decoded PCM Output After a decoder reconstructs audio, its output is usually PCM sample values for the next processing stage. A receiver that detects PCM is being given those values rather than the original compressed soundtrack to decode. Follow a lossless music example to see where preservation can change. Trace the samples, not just the output label Consider 24-bit stereo FLAC at 44.1 kHz, a player with a volume setting of one half, and an output fixed at 48 kHz: Stage Audio representation or operation FLAC source Compressed description of the original integer samples Decode Restore those samples into a working representation Volume Multiply their amplitudes by 0.5 Rate conversion Calculate the signal at 48,000 positions per second Output formatting Pack the result for the device's PCM interface Lossless decoding restores the source values. The next steps intentionally make another output representation. The PCM label alone cannot tell you whether those steps occurred. A source sample of +0.6 becomes +0.3 under half gain. If a fractional result cannot fit the final integer grid exactly, rounding/dither becomes another conversion decision. Rate conversion also changes the sequence's positions and count while preserving its intended duration. Read the complete output format Output property Why it is needed Sample rate Defines when each frame is presented Channel layout/order Associates values with intended positions Number representation Specifies integer or float interpretation Storage size and valid precision Defines how meaningful bits occupy sample words A 24-bit presentation can occupy 32-bit words. A six-channel output also needs named roles; an array size of six is insufficient to establish where the center belongs. For a block of 480 sample frames at 48 kHz, playback time is 10 ms, regardless of how many channels the frame contains. A device consumes complete frames on that timeline. Lossy decoders produce PCM too MP3 and other lossy codecs reconstruct their encoded approximation as PCM. Sending those samples uncompressed to an amplifier does not restore the missing original data, but it can avoid another lossy encoding. The decoded representation describes the current signal. Its source history must be obtained earlier in the path. Place an immersive render deliberately An object-aware player can render spatial content into speaker-channel PCM or binaural ear signals. Those can be useful finished spatial outputs. They no longer give a later receiver the source's original object instructions to adapt again. A supported metadata-bearing path such as Dolby MAT can instead carry the relevant audio and spatial information onward. It should not be confused with ordinary channel PCM. For an Emby session, record which source was reconstructed and which gain, layout, rate, or spatial operation followed. That explains a PCM result as a sequence of decisions rather than as a verdict that compression quality or immersive content must have been lost. See Also Linear PCM (LPCM) Audio Bitstream Passthrough Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Downmixing References Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Dolby MAT Audio Transport | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Dolby MAT Audio Transport The library file says Dolby Digital Plus with Atmos . The receiver says Dolby MAT . Follow one playback session, and those two labels can fit together: Point in the session What is present Job performed here Library file Dolby Digital Plus with an Atmos presentation Stores the compressed soundtrack Emby Server delivery The selected audio track, supplied without conversion Delivers the source presentation to the app Player processing Decoded audio with the required spatial information retained Decodes the compressed presentation Supported HDMI output A PCM-based Dolby MAT presentation Transports audio and associated Atmos information Receiver The received presentation and the configured speaker layout Renders the audio for those speakers This example assumes a player with the appropriate decoder and a supported PCM-based Atmos output route. Dolby MAT , Metadata-enhanced Audio Transmission, is the transport in the fourth row. The receiver names what arrived there; the file names what was stored in the first row. Read the chain at each boundary 1. Server to player. Supplying the selected compressed track unchanged leaves decoding to the player. A receiver indication farther downstream cannot establish whether the server changed the audio; check the actual server delivery path for that part of the chain. 2. Decoder to output. Decoding reconstructs audio, while rendering determines how a channel or object presentation becomes signals for speakers. An object-aware player can decode a compressed Atmos presentation and retain the information needed for downstream rendering. These are separate jobs, which is what makes a decoded Atmos transport useful. 3. HDMI to receiver. In the PCM-based MAT 2.0 use, the link carries audio together with the associated Atmos metadata. The receiver can use that presentation with its speaker arrangement. It receives more information than an ordinary set of completed 5.1 or 7.1 channel samples. 4. Receiver to speakers. Detected input information and the selected listening mode answer different questions. The former describes what arrived; an upmixer or other listening mode describes processing after receipt. Read the input-format report when tracing the source-to-receiver path. Change one part of the session Keep the same source track and server delivery, but select ordinary channel PCM output in the player. The receiver might now receive a completed 7.1 presentation: eight channels that it can play or further process. Those channels describe that particular rendering. They do not carry the original object presentation simply because the connection has room for multichannel PCM. Select encoded passthrough instead, where the whole path supports it. The downstream device then performs decoding as well as rendering. The placement of the decoder has changed, while the selected source may stay the same. Now change server delivery to an ordinary audio transcode. The app may receive a new channel-based presentation before it makes any output decision. A later MAT-capable output cannot reconstruct spatial information that the earlier conversion omitted. These changes explain why “where was it decoded?” is only part of the investigation. Follow what information survived each boundary , and the audible result becomes easier to account for. The audio playback path describes the surrounding stages. Why TrueHD playback also uses the MAT name MAT originally provided carriage for a variable-rate TrueHD bitstream over the HDMI audio transport arrangement. In that use, the source packs encoded TrueHD data into the transport and the receiving device unpacks and decodes it. PCM-based MAT 2.0 extends the possible route by carrying a decoded Atmos presentation with its metadata. The shared MAT name consequently does not locate the decoder by itself: identify the actual use and the source and output information. A media inspector examines the stored track. It can correctly identify TrueHD in an MKV even though the receiver describes its transport using MAT. There need not be a stored MAT track in the library file. Record the session in terms that can be compared For an Emby playback investigation, collect the selected source track, server delivery mode, player output choice, receiver input report, and speaker/rendering configuration. Together they describe a path. Reading just the file label or just the receiver's listening mode leaves several operations unexplained. Transport also preserves the compression history of the audio it carries. A decoded lossy source already contains the reconstruction from that lossy encode. Sending it onward without another lossy encoding step preserves that result; it does not turn the source into a lossless recording. A lossless TrueHD source can retain its recovered samples through a supported output path that preserves them. The file and receiver labels then have precise roles in the record: one identifies the retained source, and the other identifies the presentation delivered across the audio connection. See Also Dolby TrueHD Audio Dolby Atmos Decoded PCM Output Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.title: Audio Codecs Explained | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.keywords: Audio Codecs Explained A player opens a movie, displays the picture, and cannot reproduce its soundtrack. The file reader has located the audio track, but the audio still needs a decoder that understands its coded representation . An audio codec defines that representation and its reconstruction. The same word also commonly names an encoder or decoder implementation. Follow the data into a decoder For compressed audio, a stream consists of coded information rather than a literal number for every sample. Depending on the codec, it can describe frequency components, predictions, remaining errors, or other signal parameters. The decoder first needs configuration: which coding tools are used, the sample-rate arrangement, channel structure, and other format-specific details. It then interprets successive coded units and produces audio on a sample timeline. Information or component Job Container reader Locates track data and timing Codec configuration Describes how the coded audio should be interpreted Decoder Reconstructs the audio presentation Output processing Maps it to the listening system A container can provide configuration outside the individual audio packets. That is why copying one packet from a file does not necessarily make a complete independently playable recording. The encoder has decisions the decoder does not repeat A standard fixes what valid coded information means. Encoders can nevertheless differ in how they choose that information. They may spend more computation searching for a better prediction or allocate bits differently to minimize audible error. Two encoders can therefore produce different bitstreams from the same recording while one conforming decoder can reconstruct both. Improving an encoder does not necessarily require a new decoder if the encoded format remains within the same supported tools and constraints. With lossless compression , the choices affect storage efficiency and processing while preserving the represented source samples. With lossy compression , they also affect the approximation the decoder reconstructs. Identify the supported presentation precisely Codec families can contain variants requiring different tools. A basic AAC-LC decoder and an xHE-AAC decoder do different reconstruction jobs. Channel count, sample rate, and a supported profile can impose further implementation requirements. The surrounding package is another independent boundary. An M4A file can carry AAC or ALAC. Changing its extension does not change the coded audio, while changing the wrapper can sometimes solve an input-reader problem without making a new audio encoding. Use the distinction to choose the operation For an Emby session: If the audio codec is compatible but the wrapper is unsuitable, repackaging can preserve the coded sound. If the required reconstruction tools are unsupported, a decoder elsewhere in the path can reconstruct and re-encode a compatible presentation. If decoding succeeds but the listening system has fewer channels, layout conversion addresses the output arrangement. These solve different failures. A playback-path trace identifies which boundary changed, and whether the receiver gets coded audio for its own decoder or already reconstructed PCM. See Also Containers and Codecs Audio Bitrate The Audio Playback Path References Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ Xiph.Org: Vorbis I decoder specification and encoder freedom

articles/audio/formats/DSD.html.title: Direct Stream Digital (DSD) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/DSD.html.keywords: Direct Stream Digital (DSD) How can a recording with only one bit per sample represent a quiet voice and a loud orchestra? Direct Stream Digital uses a very fast one-bit sequence whose behavior over time represents the waveform. An individual bit is not a miniature multibit PCM amplitude measurement. DSD is associated with Super Audio CD and downloadable music. Its usual DSD64 rate is 2,822,400 bits per second per channel: 64 × 44,100. Read density as the starting idea In a simple illustration, map one to +1 and zero to −1. The average of a short bit group then changes with the balance: Eight illustrative bits Ones / zeros Average of the mapped levels 11110000 4 / 4 0 11111100 6 / 2 +0.5 11000000 2 / 6 −0.5 This is a teaching model of pulse density, not a DSD encoding algorithm . The actual order of bits and the feedback process matter. Two sequences with the same count in one group can have different high-frequency behavior. A DSD modulator uses a rapidly running quantizer and feedback. Noise shaping arranges much of the quantization error outside the desired audio band, where subsequent filtering can attenuate it. This lets useful low-frequency amplitude information emerge from a stream whose instantaneous values have only two states. The very high rate serves the representation Common label, 44.1 kHz rate family One-bit rate per channel DSD64 2.8224 MHz DSD128 5.6448 MHz DSD256 11.2896 MHz The rate and one-bit representation belong together. Comparing “2.8 MHz” with “96 kHz PCM” as if they measured one identical precision system discards the most important part of the description. For raw stereo DSD64, the data rate is 2,822,400 × 1 × 2 = 5.6448 Mbit/s . One minute uses 5,644,800 / 8 × 60 = 42.336 MB before file overhead. This is four times the raw data rate of 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo PCM, despite the one-bit samples. Those arithmetic relationships describe storage demand, not an audible ranking of music releases. Filtering turns the stream into a usable output The desired audio and shaped high-frequency error coexist in the sequence. Playback needs suitable reconstruction/filtering so that unwanted high-frequency energy is not simply sent onward as part of the audible signal. A DSD-to-PCM conversion also filters, then produces multibit values on a new time grid. For an illustrative 88.2 kHz target, DSD64 has 32 input bit positions per output sample interval. A proper converter uses a designed filter and rate conversion; merely counting ones in successive isolated 32-bit groups is not a complete high-quality converter. The result is a PCM representation of the available audio band. It is not byte-preserving restoration of the original DSD sequence. The filter, target rate, and numerical precision become part of that conversion. Keep packaging and compression separate DSF and DSDIFF are containers for DSD-related data. They have different channel-block, bit-packing, and metadata conventions. DST and WavPack can losslessly compress DSD: after unpacking, the original one-bit sequence can be restored. That operation differs from converting the audio to PCM. A useful source-to-output trace is therefore: DSF/DFF reader → any required lossless decompression → DSD sequence → native supported output or filtered PCM conversion → playback. For a DSD item in Emby, these stages explain why a file remains labeled DSD in the library while the client receives PCM. The stored representation, delivery representation, and DAC input are distinct observations. A DAC can additionally use its own internal processing; “DSD input” describes the accepted signal, not every internal circuit stage. See Also Linear PCM (LPCM) DSF: DSD Stream File DSDIFF: DFF Container WavPack Audio References Sony: DSF file format specification WavPack 5 porting guide: DSD compression and decoding Sony and Philips: Super Audio Compact Disc technical proposal

articles/audio/formats/lossless/ALAC.htm.title: Apple Lossless (ALAC) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/ALAC.htm.keywords: Apple Lossless (ALAC) An M4A file can contain Apple Lossless (ALAC) instead of AAC. Its audio remains reversibly compressed PCM; the shared extension supplies an audio-file convention, while the track's “alac” identifier selects the actual codec. Apple publishes its reference implementation and configuration description. Read the decoder's configuration Configuration item Purpose Sample rate Places decoded sample frames on the timeline Bit depth Defines the preserved integer sample precision Channel count and layout Identify the presentation's signals and roles Frame length Describes the coding packet's sample-frame arrangement Other codec parameters Supply the decoder's defined reconstruction setup The reference codec supports 16-, 20-, 24-, and 32-bit integer precision and supported layouts from one to eight channels. Apple's example conversion utility accepts a narrower selection of inputs than the full codec. Connect packet size to audio time For illustration, an ALAC configuration can use a 4,096-sample-frame packet length. At 44.1 kHz, a full packet spans 4,096/44,100 ≈ 92.88 ms . The uncompressed payload for 24-bit stereo over that span would be 4,096 × 2 × 3 = 24,576 bytes . ALAC's actual encoded packet size depends on the audio and compression; its duration comes from sample frames, not from dividing by an assumed compressed bitrate. A final packet can contain fewer frames. The decoder uses the configuration and coded packet information to restore the intended values and count. That makes both codec setup and packet timing relevant when moving ALAC between M4A and CAF arrangements. Convert the represented audio A supported FLAC-to-ALAC conversion can reconstruct the same integer PCM and encode it reversibly again. Compare decoded sample values, count, rate, and channel order when verifying preservation; the compressed bytes and outer tags will differ. An AAC-to-ALAC conversion instead preserves AAC's decoded approximation. The source entering the lossless encoder determines what can be restored. For an Emby M4A collection, the alac versus AAC identification consequently answers a real decoder and preservation question. It is more useful than interpreting the filename suffix as one fixed compression type. See Also Lossless Audio Compression M4A and M4B File Conventions FLAC Audio CAF: Core Audio Format References Apple: ALAC reference implementation and format features Apple: ALAC configuration and container mapping

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Audio-Lo.title: Lossless Audio Compression | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Audio-Lo.keywords: Lossless Audio Compression The samples 100, 104, 107, 109 can be stored directly, or described as a starting value followed by differences. Both descriptions contain the same information. Lossless audio compression searches for a description that uses fewer bits without merging distinguishable source values. Reconstruct the differences exactly Stored item Decoder operation Restored sample Starting sample: 100 Retain 100 100 Difference: +4 100 + 4 104 Difference: +3 104 + 3 107 Difference: +2 107 + 2 109 The decoder needs both the prediction rule and its initial values. It then follows the same arithmetic as the encoder. Even when the prediction is poor, keeping the entire difference allows exact reconstruction. A better predictor can make the remaining numbers smaller. Suppose the rule predicts the next sample as twice the preceding sample minus the one before it. Start with 100 and 104: Prediction for the third sample: 2 × 104 − 100 = 108. Store the residual −1 to restore 107. Prediction for the fourth: 2 × 107 − 104 = 110. Store another −1 to restore 109. These are illustrative predictors, not a complete implementation of a particular codec. Smaller numbers are useful only if they are coded efficiently A residual array alone is not compressed merely because its numbers are smaller. The next step assigns compact bit representations to likely residual values and sufficient representations to larger ones. The encoder also stores the predictor description, initial samples, and framing. If an elaborate predictor saves too few bits to repay its description, a simpler one is better. A nearly unpredictable or already noisy passage may compress less efficiently; a format can use a direct representation where that is appropriate. This accounts for variable lossless bitrate: different source passages have different redundancy. The encoder is changing the size of a reversible description, not the accuracy of the reconstruction. Compression levels change the search A stronger compression preset can spend more effort finding predictors, partitions, or coding parameters. If two valid lossless encodes preserve the same supported input samples, decoding either returns those samples. Their different file sizes are a measure of representation efficiency. Decoding cost and random-access structure also matter. A music archive and a constrained player can prefer different compromises among size, encoding time, and reading requirements without choosing different audio fidelity. Decide which equality to verify Two files using different lossless codecs cannot have identical compressed bytes. Their decoded audio can nevertheless be identical when sample representation, order, rate, and count are preserved. Comparison Question answered Whole-file checksum Are these exact files unchanged? Decoded sample comparison Do they represent the same audio values? Metadata comparison Did tags, artwork, and other descriptions survive? Actual output-path check Did playback later alter the decoded presentation? A lossless encode preserves its input . If that input was an MP3 reconstruction, the restored samples match that reconstruction, not an unavailable earlier master. Likewise, an Emby session can decode a lossless source exactly and then downmix or resample it. The source-codec promise has been fulfilled at decoding; preservation beyond that point is a separate question about the subsequent operations. See Also Lossy Audio Compression FLAC Audio Apple Lossless (ALAC) Linear PCM (LPCM) References RFC 9639: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) Xiph.Org: FLAC format overview Monkey's Audio: Lossless compression theory

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Dolby-Tr.title: Dolby TrueHD Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Dolby-Tr.keywords: Dolby TrueHD Audio A receiver changes from “TrueHD” to “PCM” when a player decodes the soundtrack locally. The lossless representation has not necessarily been lost: TrueHD decoding restores its encoded audio presentation, and PCM is the form of those reconstructed samples. The important questions are what was decoded and what processing happened afterward. A lossless description can have a changing bitrate TrueHD uses Meridian Lossless Packing-related technology to describe audio reversibly. Like other lossless coding, it can exploit predictable signal relationships and retain the exact information needed to reconstruct the encoded presentation. Simple passages can require fewer bits than difficult ones. The source's sample rate and precision remain fixed while its compressed data rate can vary. For example, eight channels of 48 kHz, 24-bit PCM require 48,000 × 24 × 8 = 9.216 Mbit/s before compression. TrueHD's encoded rate depends on how efficiently that particular audio can be described; it is not the PCM calculation repeated with a fixed reduction ratio. Blu-ray capability described by Dolby Context Up to eight full-range channels at 96 kHz/24-bit A supported source configuration Up to six full-range channels at 192 kHz/24-bit Another supported source configuration Encoded data rates up to 18 Mbit/s A format/application capacity, not every track's average MLP-related labels in an inspection report reflect the coding heritage. They do not mean every earlier MLP-based delivery format is interchangeable with TrueHD. Compare two decode placements Receiver decode: a supported path carries the encoded TrueHD presentation onward, using suitable HDMI/MAT transport, and the receiver reconstructs it. Player decode: the player reconstructs the supported presentation and outputs PCM. If it keeps the intended sample values and channel roles, moving decoding into the player does not add lossy encoding. Subsequent downmixing, resampling, gain changes, or another codec conversion are additional operations. They should be recorded separately from the successful lossless decode. Atmos adds a spatial-information boundary A TrueHD track can carry Atmos information . Ordinary channel PCM supplies a fixed channel presentation; an object-aware path can carry the required spatial information onward, including supported MAT output. Lossless channel reconstruction and retaining a scene for later immersive rendering are thus different preservation questions. A player-rendered spatial output can still be useful even after the original metadata is no longer carried to the receiver. Where a conventional fallback comes from A disc arrangement may provide companion AC-3 audio for compatibility. TrueHD does not contain the DTS-HD-style embedded lossy core that can be extracted from common core-plus-extension soundtracks. For an Emby item with a TrueHD and separate AC-3 track, selecting the latter chooses another encoded presentation. If the server decodes TrueHD and encodes a compatible codec instead, that creates a new presentation. Comparing the selected track and route resolves which of these occurred. See Also Dolby MAT Audio Transport Dolby Atmos Decoded PCM Output Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core References Dolby: TrueHD (MLP) high-level bitstream description — February 2018 archived specification IETF CELLAR codec draft-18: TrueHD bibliography (work in progress) Dolby: TrueHD lossless audio Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/formats/lossless/DTS-HD-M.title: DTS-HD Master Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/DTS-HD-M.keywords: DTS-HD Master Audio How can a soundtrack with a lossy DTS core give a lossless result? DTS-HD Master Audio includes the information needed to correct or reconstruct what the compatible core alone does not preserve. In a common core-plus-lossless-extension arrangement, the full decoder combines the required components. A core-only decoder plays a different, compatible result. Reconstruct the exact difference Use an illustrative pair of samples: Source Core reconstruction Exact correction Full result 1,020 1,001 +19 1,020 1,025 1,028 −3 1,025 The core's errors do not remain in the final result when the additional information restores the exact source values. This table models the lossless-correction principle; DTS's XLL processing and channel/frequency organization are more elaborate than two literal correction numbers. A lossy enhancement that quantizes its correction can merely reduce an error. The full Master Audio reconstruction must retain the information required for the exact encoded audio result. That is the distinction from DTS-HD High Resolution Audio . Choose the component set Components decoded Audio result Existing core alone Lossy compatible presentation Required core and lossless extension information Full lossless presentation Supported extension-only lossless stream Lossless presentation without a legacy core fallback The standard allows lossless streams without a backward-compatible core. For those, an older destination cannot obtain a missing core simply by asking to “strip HD.” The actual stream structure controls the available fallback. A core and extensions can also appear as one container soundtrack. They need not be separately selectable language tracks. Place output after reconstruction Once the full presentation has been decoded, the player can output PCM. The receiver sees sample values rather than a request to decode Master Audio, so its input label can change to PCM without a lossy conversion. If a receiver instead gets an extracted core, it decodes the lossy compatible presentation. If the server decodes and re-encodes another codec, there is a new encoding generation. Those three routes can be distinguished by their actual delivered components. For an Emby source, this explains why “DTS-HD Master Audio” in the library and “DTS” or “PCM” downstream require a route trace rather than a verdict based on either label alone. DTS:X can add immersive information in a compatible delivery context. Preserving the lossless audio values and passing the required spatial instructions to an immersive renderer are additional, distinct jobs in that trace. See Also DTS Core Audio DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS:X Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Decoded PCM Output References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Digital Surround and DTS-HD Master Audio DTS: Production tools and backwards compatibility

articles/audio/formats/lossless/FLAC.htm.title: FLAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/FLAC.htm.keywords: FLAC Audio A FLAC frame can describe a waveform with a predictor and exact residuals rather than storing every PCM sample literally. The decoder reconstructs those samples exactly. RFC 9639 defines the format, including integer PCM precision from 4 to 32 bits and one to eight channels. The residual coding makes its lossless promise easier to understand. Follow four illustrative values Consider the sequence 100, 104, 108, 112 within a channel. A previous-sample predictor stores the initial value 100 and residuals +4, +4, +4. Decoder state Residual Restored next sample 100 +4 104 104 +4 108 108 +4 112 FLAC can use fixed predictors, transmitted linear-predictor coefficients, constant subframes, or direct sample storage. The encoder chooses an efficient representation for the data; every valid choice still supplies what the decoder needs to restore it. Give the residuals compact codes FLAC's Rice coding first maps signed residuals to nonnegative integers. Under its folding rule, 0 becomes 0, −1 becomes 1, +1 becomes 2, and +4 becomes 8. For an illustrative Rice parameter k=2, split 8 into quotient 2 and a two-bit remainder 0. Encode the quotient as two zero bits followed by one, then the remainder as 00. The code is 00100 , five bits. A decoder reads the zero run, obtains quotient 2, reads remainder 0, reconstructs 2 × 4 + 0 = 8, and unfolds that to +4. The initial 8-bit sample plus three five-bit residual codes would use 23 bits, compared with 32 bits for four direct 8-bit samples. This is only the illustrated payload arithmetic within an excerpt. Real subframe/frame headers, parameters, block sizing, and checks also take space; it is not a claimed four-sample FLAC file. Frames make the audio readable and checkable Frame information identifies sample/block properties and position. Checks help detect corrupted frame data. File-level metadata describes stream properties and can contain tags, artwork, seek information, and an MD5 for the decoded audio. A seek table assists finding an audio position; it is separate from the prediction that makes the audio smaller. Tags can change while the audio frames remain the same. The reference tool's verification/test facilities decode and validate the stream. A stored audio MD5, when present, is useful for comparing the reconstruction to the encoded signature. It confirms consistency with that signature, not the accuracy of the original recording or disc rip. Choose compression effort without choosing audio quality FLAC's usual presets 0 through 8 select groups of encoding decisions. Greater search effort can find a smaller reversible description. The restored samples are unchanged by choosing another valid lossless preset. A dense or noisy passage can have a higher encoded bitrate than a simpler passage from the same recording. Both remain exact descriptions; the difference is how predictable the samples were. During playback, those samples normally become PCM for processing/output. An Emby receiver displaying PCM can therefore be showing a correctly decoded FLAC. Any subsequent rate or layout conversion is another stage, rather than a quality setting inside FLAC. See Also Lossless Audio Compression Linear PCM (LPCM) Apple Lossless (ALAC) Audio Resampling References RFC 9639: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) Xiph.Org: FLAC FAQ Xiph.Org: FLAC compression presets and verification

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Monkeys-.title: Monkey's Audio (APE) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Monkeys-.keywords: Monkey's Audio (APE) An APE album may be one long audio stream with a separate CUE sheet identifying track boundaries. Monkey's Audio compresses the audio losslessly; the CUE sheet describes navigation through it. Moving one without the other can therefore preserve the music while changing how the album is presented. Keep the three pieces distinct Piece Role APE audio Reversibly encoded sample data APE tags Descriptions such as artist and album CUE sheet, if used Track positions in the album audio APE tags are a metadata convention and can occur beyond Monkey's Audio files. Their presence alone does not identify the audio codec. Why compression levels do not change the sound The codec predicts sample relationships and compactly codes the remaining information. More demanding compression settings can spend more processing work finding a smaller reversible description. After successful decoding, the original supported audio is restored at every setting. “High” or “Insane” compression is consequently a size/processing decision, not an extra audio-quality grade. This matters for a constrained reader: a setting's decoding work or seeking behavior can be relevant even when the restored sound is identical. The project's SDK and source are the implementation reference. Verify an album conversion as an album The tool's verification mode checks encoded integrity. For a conversion, also compare decoded audio count/rate/channels and preserve the intended CUE boundaries and tags. A single stream can be split into tracks at the declared positions without making those boundaries part of the compression algorithm. A copy of the audio with missing boundaries can play continuously while losing useful album navigation. For an Emby collection using such material, this distinction identifies which component needs attention: audio decode, navigation description, or library metadata. The codec's lossless guarantee answers the first preservation question, not all three at once. See Also Lossless Audio Compression FLAC Audio WavPack Audio CUE Sheets References Monkey's Audio: SDK and source code Monkey's Audio: Help and verification Monkey's Audio: Lossless compression theory

articles/audio/formats/lossless/WavPack..title: WavPack Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/WavPack..keywords: WavPack Audio You have a small WV music file and a larger matching WVC file. Playing the WV works by itself. WavPack hybrid mode deliberately provides a lossy stand-alone file plus correction information for lossless restoration. WavPack also has ordinary lossless and lossy modes, so identifying the actual arrangement is the first step. Arrangement used by the decoder Result Lossless-mode WV Restored supported source data Lossy/hybrid WV alone Its lossy reconstruction Hybrid WV plus matching WVC, used by a capable decoder Lossless restoration of that source Why the correction file changes the result An illustrative source sequence is 1,000, 1,001, 1,004. Suppose the stand-alone representation reconstructs 1,000, 1,000, 1,008. Correction values of 0, +1, and −4 supply the missing differences. Stand-alone reconstruction Exact correction Combined result 1,000 0 1,000 1,000 +1 1,001 1,008 −4 1,004 This is a model of exact correction, not WavPack's literal packet coding. It explains why the pair can restore data that the WV alone cannot identify. A player must actually locate, validate, and use the matching correction information. A WVC kept in an unrelated folder or ignored by the decoder contributes nothing to that listening result. Prediction and noise management perform different jobs WavPack uses reversible prediction/decorrelation and compact coding for lossless operation. The exact residual information is sufficient to undo those transformations. Hybrid/lossy operation makes a controlled approximation in the independently playable part. Noise-shaping choices can affect that part's error spectrum. The correction information restores what is needed for the lossless result rather than asking the listener to infer it from the approximation. The two modes therefore answer different storage/delivery needs without requiring the source to be separately encoded into two unrelated music files. Preserve the actual sample representation WavPack can store integer PCM, floating-point PCM, and losslessly compressed DSD. DSD support uses lossless storage rather than the PCM hybrid arrangement. Those distinctions matter when converting. A target supporting the same integer data can preserve it. A target designed for integer PCM cannot automatically preserve every float value or a DSD bit sequence unchanged. Converting DSD to PCM filters and changes representation; unpacking lossless DSD restores its original one-bit data. WavPack can also retain wrapper information for restoration, depending on the operation and settings. Audio equality, original-file reconstruction, and tag preservation are separate verification goals. For a WavPack item delivered through Emby, identify whether the decoder used a lossless WV or a hybrid pair, and what sample representation it reconstructed. That establishes the source result before any subsequent delivery or output conversion. See Also Lossless Audio Compression Direct Stream Digital (DSD) FLAC Audio Media File Extensions References WavPack: Audio compression modes WavPack 4 and 5: Binary file and block format WavPack: User documentation

articles/audio/formats/lossless/WMA-Loss.title: WMA Lossless Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/WMA-Loss.keywords: WMA Lossless Audio WMA Lossless is Microsoft's reversibly compressed audio member , identified separately from lossy WMA Standard and Professional. Its format identifier is 0x0163. Property to record What it establishes Lossless member/identifier Which decoder and reconstruction promise apply Sample rate and precision The represented PCM format Channel layout Roles of the reconstructed signals Sample count/duration Whether the whole presentation is retained Convert a legacy lossless collection A useful conversion follows three independently checked results: Decode the WMA Lossless audio to its supported PCM representation. Encode those unchanged samples with the chosen compatible lossless codec. Transfer and verify the collection's tags, artwork, and organization. For example, a 44.1 kHz stereo source with 44,100,000 sample frames represents 1,000 seconds. A destination that retains the same values, order, rate, and count retains that audio even though its compressed bytes and size differ. Metadata preservation needs its own check. Comparing whole-file checksums between different codecs cannot establish sample equality, because the packages are intentionally different. If the source was WMA Standard instead, the first step produces its lossy reconstruction. The new lossless file would preserve that reconstruction rather than restore an earlier master. The member identification at the start is therefore decisive. An Emby client may also receive a temporary lossy delivery version of a retained WMA Lossless master. That changes the session's encoded presentation while leaving the library source available. Record those as source and delivery results separately. See Also Windows Media Audio (WMA) Lossless Audio Compression FLAC Audio Audio Transcoding References Microsoft: Windows Media Audio encoder and format identifiers Microsoft: Configuring Standard, Professional, or Lossless audio encoding Microsoft: About the Windows Media codecs

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: AAC-LC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: AAC-LC Audio “Low Complexity” in AAC-LC names a coding configuration, not a low-quality music grade. Advanced Audio Coding's LC form can represent mono, stereo, and multichannel material using a transform-based lossy codec. Consider a music passage containing a sustained note followed by a sharp drum hit. Those two events illustrate why its tools are useful. Sustained detail and sudden attacks ask different things of a window A transform represents a section of waveform through frequency components. A longer analysis window helps describe frequency detail over that section. A shorter window localizes changes more closely in time. For a steady tone, a longer window can be efficient. At the drum attack, spreading the section's coding error across a long window can make error audible before or around the hit. AAC supports switching to shorter windows to handle that transient. The encoder selects the window sequence and sends the information the decoder needs to reconstruct it. This is not switching sample rate or making the music play faster. Several shorter transforms describe the corresponding span of samples within the same timeline. Encode the representation, then reconstruct it The encoder selects precision for the frequency representation and codes the resulting values and side information. The decoder reconstructs those values, performs the defined inverse processing, and combines the overlapping sections into PCM. Stage What it contributes Window and transform A timed frequency-domain description Precision allocation and quantization The main lossy approximation Symbol and side-information coding An efficient description of the chosen representation Inverse processing and overlap A continuous decoded sample sequence Other AAC tools manage relationships between components or channels. Encoders can make different decisions while producing streams conforming to the same supported LC tools. Place LC in the AAC family HE-AAC adds spectral-band replication to an AAC core; HE-AAC v2 can add parametric stereo. Those names identify additional reconstruction jobs. HE-AAC explains why its core and output sample-rate reports can differ. AAC-LC reconstruction does not perform those extra tasks. A profile or audio-object-type description therefore tells you more than the bare “AAC” family label when comparing sources. Supply the decoder configuration An AAC track needs coding configuration such as its audio object type, sample-rate arrangement, and channel configuration. MP4/M4A can store that information with its track description, while other AAC framing formats provide it through their own structures. For an Emby source, this separates two operations. Repackaging compatible LC audio can preserve the coded sound while translating its framing/configuration. Re-encoding changes the audio representation itself. The useful choice follows whether the obstacle is supplying the existing LC bitstream correctly or reconstructing a format the destination does not support. See Also HE-AAC Audio AAC Stream Packaging M4A and M4B File Conventions Lossy Audio Compression References ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: AAC-LC Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: HE-AAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: HE-AAC Audio A report of AAC at 24 kHz and a completed output at 48 kHz can describe the same HE-AAC track. Why does one HE-AAC track report both 24 kHz and 48 kHz? In a recorded broadcast, the two rate fields can describe different stages of the encoded track. HE-AAC , High Efficiency AAC, combines an AAC-LC core with Spectral Band Replication (SBR) . The core supplies directly coded audio; SBR reconstructs an upper-frequency region using additional information. In a common dual-rate configuration, the core runs at 24 kHz and the completed output runs at 48 kHz. Field in this example What it describes Core rate: 24 kHz The directly coded AAC-LC signal Output rate: 48 kHz The signal after SBR reconstruction HE-AAC profile The combination of core coding and SBR To interpret a report, identify which field the tool is showing. Neither rate field establishes the sample rate of the original studio recording; each describes a stage in this coded presentation. What was stored instead of the missing upper-frequency detail? An encoder with a small data budget has to decide where those bits do the most useful work. Independently coding a wide frequency range at very low bitrate can leave too little precision for important parts of the sound. HE-AAC devotes much of its data to the AAC-LC core and represents the upper region more compactly. At the decoder, SBR takes patterns from the decoded lower-frequency content and uses them to generate candidate higher-frequency content. Transmitted information then shapes that result across time and frequency: how much energy belongs in different regions, how noise-like the content should be, and other reconstruction parameters. The generated upper region therefore has both a source of structure and a description of how it should sound. It is not another independently coded copy of every original upper-band detail. This is where the data saving comes from. A 24 kHz core can represent frequencies below 12 kHz, but that theoretical limit does not specify the encoder's chosen crossover between directly coded and reconstructed regions. The configuration and encoder decisions determine the actual division. Why an equalizer cannot do the same job. An equalizer raises or lowers frequency content already present. SBR generates upper-band content and controls its behavior. Turning up treble on a core-only decode cannot provide the reconstruction information that an SBR-capable decoder uses. Why ordinary upsampling is also different. Upsampling creates more sample positions. It does not, by itself, recreate the intended missing upper-band sound. SBR combines the higher-rate output with additional content-generation and shaping operations. The result can retain a convincing sense of bandwidth with relatively few bits. Rapid changes and difficult sound textures can reveal the approximation more readily, because their upper-frequency behavior is harder to represent using the compact reconstruction description. Do twice as many output samples make the track play more slowly? The rates and sample counts change together. For the usual 1,024-sample AAC-LC core block in this dual-rate example: Core duration: 1,024 / 24,000 = about 42.67 ms . Completed output duration: 2,048 / 48,000 = about 42.67 ms . The output has twice as many samples for the same interval. It supplies a higher-rate representation of that interval rather than doubling its duration. This calculation uses one common configuration; MPEG-4 audio also defines other block lengths and SBR modes. What happens if the player understands AAC-LC but not SBR? Where the stream's signaling permits backward-compatible core decoding, an AAC-LC-only decoder can reconstruct the core. It lacks the intended upper-band reconstruction, so the sound can have a narrower bandwidth than a complete HE-AAC decode. An SBR-capable decoder can produce the completed presentation. The player must also identify the configuration and pass the right information to the decoder. ADTS , LATM , and an MP4 track carry or signal that information differently. A decoder capability and a usable packaged stream are both needed for the expected result. For an Emby broadcast recording that sounds unexpectedly dull, follow the selected track through playback. Check the identified profile and core/output fields, whether the server delivers the audio unchanged or converts it, and which decoder handles the delivered stream. Server conversion and local decoding place the reconstruction in different parts of that path. HE-AAC v2 adds Parametric Stereo for low-bitrate stereo delivery. If that is the detected profile, SBR explains its bandwidth reconstruction while Parametric Stereo accounts for an additional part of its spatial presentation. See Also AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC v2 Audio AAC Stream Packaging Audio Sample Rate References FFmpeg 8.1: SBR generation and envelope processing ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2 Fraunhofer: The AAC audio coding family for broadcast and cable TV

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: HE-AAC v2 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: HE-AAC v2 Audio A stereo radio programme is delivered with a mono core, yet a full decoder produces stereo. HE-AAC v2's Parametric Stereo (PS) tool describes the stereo relationship alongside a coded mono downmix. The output channels are reconstructed using both. A mono combination alone is insufficient If a downmix contains the average of L and R, the pairs (0.8,0.2) and (0.5,0.5) both give 0.5. Their stereo impressions differ, but the combined value does not identify which pair existed. PS sends information about the relationships that matter for reconstructing the stereo image. Its parameters describe properties such as relative channel energy and correlation in time/frequency regions. A decoder uses these descriptions to distribute and shape the reconstructed signal into two outputs. What survives in the delivery What the decoder can do Mono downmix alone Reproduce the combined signal Downmix plus stereo parameters Reconstruct the described stereo relationships Original separate sample sequences Preserve more independent channel detail, at a different coding cost The PS representation is lossy. Parameters describe aspects of the relationship rather than carrying a second complete waveform that uniquely restores every original left/right sample. Follow the reconstruction stages For a stereo presentation, the chain combines three jobs: The AAC core reconstructs its coded lower-band signal. Spectral Band Replication reconstructs the intended wider audio band. Parametric Stereo produces the stereo image from that signal and the PS information. The HE-AAC article explains the first two jobs and their possible core/output-rate difference. PS adds a channel-reconstruction task, not a different meaning for the sample timeline. A suitably compatible core-only decode can produce narrower-band audio. SBR without PS can restore the wider band but leave the mono presentation. Full stereo reconstruction requires the PS information to be used. A report showing a mono core is therefore consistent with a correctly reconstructed stereo programme. Spend a small budget on useful relationships At restricted stereo bitrates, coding one main signal plus parameters can be more efficient than coding two complete HE-AAC signals. That can retain a useful stereo impression in broadcasts. The compromise becomes important when independent or rapidly changing channel detail is difficult to describe parametrically. A stereo result can be recognizable without matching every original spatial nuance. The HE-AAC v2 profile also permits multichannel configurations where PS is not used; those use the relevant HE-AAC tools instead. For an Emby recording, read its actual presentation and tool use rather than turning the profile label into a claim that every v2 track was encoded as mono-plus-PS. See Also HE-AAC Audio Stereo Audio AAC Stream Packaging References ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2 Fraunhofer: The AAC audio coding family for broadcast and cable TV

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: xHE-AAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: xHE-AAC Audio A podcast alternates spoken narration, music, and both together. At a tight delivery bitrate, a codec needs to handle the changes without the music collapsing when speech-oriented assumptions stop fitting. xHE-AAC combines Extended HE-AAC based on Unified Speech and Audio Coding (USAC) with MPEG-D loudness and dynamic-range control. Its parts address the coded sound, switching among delivery versions, and playback level. Match the signal's character Speech has predictable pitch and short-term spectral structure. Music and mixed content can require a broader representation of transients, tones, and textures. USAC includes predictive speech-oriented and transform-based coding tools. The encoder chooses an appropriate representation and signals what the decoder must reconstruct. This unification lets a programme move between voices and general audio within the format rather than requiring the listener to select a different codec for every segment. The reconstruction still represents a lossy approximation. Its efficiency is useful because a limited budget can be distributed using tools suited to different signal behavior. Adapt delivery without changing the timeline An adaptive service can prepare several encoded representations of the same programme, then select among them as the connection permits. xHE-AAC's bitstream tools support suitable switching points and continuous reconstruction across prepared changes. Delivery condition Service action More data budget available Select a higher-rate prepared version A restricted connection Select a lower-rate prepared version A switch point Continue the same programme timeline with the selected representation The decoder must initialize or update its coding state appropriately at a switch. The service must also align versions and supply the needed configuration. “Adaptive” therefore describes a complete prepared delivery process, not a stored file rewriting its own audio. Use metadata to control the listening level MPEG-D loudness and dynamic-range control supplies information for consistent loudness and suitable level-dependent processing. For an illustrative normalization calculation, if a programme's measured loudness is 5 dB below a chosen playback target, a simple gain correction is +5 dB. The amplitude multiplier is 10^(5/20), about 1.778 . That also raises peaks, so loudness gain, available headroom, and dynamic-range processing need to cooperate. The purpose is to make programmes usable across listening situations without treating each encoded sample value as if it directly specified room volume. The loudness/control system is a defined part of xHE-AAC delivery, rather than a promise that any app reading an audio file will apply identical gain. Identify the actual bitstream USAC content is not an ordinary AAC-LC stream with some new tags. It requires its own reconstruction tools. The xHE-AAC profile also provides earlier AAC-family decoding capability, but an older LC or HE-AAC decoder does not thereby gain USAC support. For an Emby item containing xHE-AAC, distinguish whether the client receives that source representation or a server-made compatible version. This identifies which decoder job is being performed, while the actual player's loudness/output processing determines how the decoded programme reaches the listening system. See Also AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC v2 Audio Speech Coding Audio Codecs Explained References ISO/IEC 23003-4:2025: Dynamic range control ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio ISO/IEC 23003-3: Unified speech and audio coding Fraunhofer: xHE-AAC Fraunhofer: xHE-AAC technical paper

articles/audio/formats/lossy/Audio-Lossy.title: Lossy Audio Compression | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Audio-Lossy.keywords: Lossy Audio Compression A compact audio file can contain an excellent-sounding approximation of a recording while having very different sample values from the master. Lossy compression spends a limited data budget on a representation intended to preserve what matters perceptually. To see where the approximation enters, follow a short section of sound through encoding and reconstruction. 1. Describe a section of the signal Many general-audio codecs divide the waveform into overlapping sections and transform them into a representation of frequency content. The transform itself need not discard information. It provides components that the encoder can handle differently. Other coding tools can exploit prediction, shared information between channels, or models of suitable sound types. The essential distinction remains: the encoder chooses what information will describe the section, and the decoder reconstructs from that information. 2. Decide where precision is useful A psychoacoustic model estimates which errors are likely to be noticed. A strong sound can mask weaker sound or error in nearby frequency/time regions. The encoder can permit more error there while spending precision elsewhere. That does not mean it simply deletes everything above a fixed frequency, or selects a list of inaudible instruments. Audibility depends on the current signal and the type of error. A quiet tone in isolation can need careful treatment even when it costs few total bits; a dense passage can have useful masking but many components to describe. The model is an estimate. A difficult signal or inadequate data budget can expose its compromise. 3. Quantize the chosen representation Consider two illustrative transform-component values, +0.83 and +0.12. Suppose the encoder rounds them onto steps of 0.25: Component Source value Stored grid value Difference A +0.83 +0.75 −0.08 B +0.12 0 −0.12 This is a toy quantizer, not the exact operation of MP3, AAC, or Opus. It shows the point where multiple possible source values become one stored value. The decoder can recover +0.75 and 0 from the coded information. It cannot know whether the first originally was +0.83, +0.78, or another value in that quantization interval. Using finer steps reduces those errors but usually requires more information. Real encoders allocate steps or other precision controls according to their tools and data budget. Encoding the resulting symbols efficiently can reduce file size further without adding another approximation; lossless entropy coding and lossy quantization can coexist inside one codec. 4. Reconstruct and join the sections The decoder reverses the defined coding operations, reconstructs the signal representation, and combines overlapping sections into an output waveform. The reconstructed waveform reflects the stored quantized values. Replaying this existing bitstream does not normally create another lossy encoding generation: it reconstructs the same represented signal each time. A later output stage can still change gain, layout, or sample rate for other reasons. Why transients and textures are difficult A sudden attack contains energy concentrated in time. If an encoder uses an unsuitable long window or insufficient precision, quantization error associated with that section can spread around the attack, including before it. Short-window tools help localize the problem, with their own coding tradeoffs. Noise-like textures such as cymbals or applause distribute energy over many components. They can require substantial detail to retain a stable texture. Inadequate coding can produce fluctuating, metallic, or watery impressions. Audible change Relevant kind of coding compromise Smearing around a sharp attack Time localization and quantization of the transient Fluctuating texture Representation of dense or noise-like content Reduced upper-frequency detail Bandwidth/precision allocation Altered stereo impression Shared or simplified channel representation These are mechanisms to investigate, not a rule that all tracks using a particular bitrate will exhibit the same artifact. What another generation does If decoded audio is passed to a new lossy encoder, that encoder receives the first reconstruction. It applies its own analysis and approximation to that signal. The new errors can combine with or change the first generation's artifacts. Encoding the result at a high bitrate can avoid making it much worse, but it cannot identify the original information that the earlier quantizer merged together. Saving the decoded result as FLAC preserves that reconstruction exactly; it does not restore the pre-compression source. This distinction matters in an Emby audio-transcoding session . A second encoding is a real generation change, while decoding an unchanged delivered track is not. Compare versions for the listening job Use the same source passage and matched listening level. Include the kinds of material that matter: quiet tones, attacks, ambience, or dialogue over music. A louder version can seem more detailed even when coding is not better. Bitrate is a useful size/delivery constraint, but quality depends on the codec tools, encoder decisions, channels, and signal. The best master for making further versions retains the source information, so each new listening copy begins from that master rather than from an already compromised intermediate. See Also Lossless Audio Compression MP3 Audio AAC-LC Audio Opus Audio Audio Transcoding References Fraunhofer: Psychoacoustic models for perceptual audio coding Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby AC-4 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby AC-4 Audio One AC-4 programme can offer several listening choices without storing a separate complete soundtrack for every choice. The decoder selects a presentation : the relevant audio components and the information needed to combine and render them. This is a central reason AC-4 is more than a newly named AC-3 bitstream. Assemble a hypothetical programme Suppose a programme supplies music/effects, English dialogue, French dialogue, and associated description narration. It can define presentations using different combinations: Presentation Illustrative selected components English main Music/effects + English dialogue French main Music/effects + French dialogue English described Music/effects + English dialogue + description The table illustrates a permitted component-oriented approach, not a rule that all AC-4 programmes use this exact structure. A programme can also use a complete main mix or other defined component types. Sharing music/effects avoids duplicating that content in every language combination. The presentation metadata tells the decoder which components belong together and how the available controls should affect them. Follow selection into sound Read the available presentation information. Select an appropriate language/accessibility presentation. Find and decode its required substreams. Apply the supplied mixing, gain, loudness, and rendering information. Produce the supported channel or spatial output. If description narration is an associated component, the decoder may also need instructions for balancing it with the main material. A standalone narration component is not necessarily the whole film soundtrack. This also explains why one container audio-stream entry can expose several meaningful choices. A conventional track list and an AC-4 presentation list describe different layers. Channel and object components support different render jobs Channel-based material has defined output roles. Object-based material supplies sound with spatial information for rendering. AC-4's standards cover both traditional channel coding and immersive/personalized uses. Dialogue enhancement depends on what the delivery provides. Separate dialogue or suitable enhancement information can enable a controlled change; a decoder cannot assume an arbitrary mixed recording contains an independently adjustable voice merely because the codec is AC-4. Preserve a selected result or the selectable structure AC-4 is specified in the ATSC 3.0 AC-4 audio system and other delivery contexts. An Emby recording can therefore contain picture that is readily decoded while the soundtrack needs AC-4-specific presentation handling. Converting a selected presentation to ordinary stereo or surround creates a useful listening result. It generally flattens the selected components into that mix, so the output no longer contains all the original language/accessibility choices as separately selectable AC-4 presentations. Preserving the encoded structure and creating a compatible listening copy are different goals. The distinction follows directly from which components and presentation instructions survived the operation. See Also Audio Codecs Explained Audio-Description Tracks Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) References ETSI TS 103 190-1 V1.4.1: AC-4 channel-based coding ETSI TS 103 190-2 V1.3.1: AC-4 immersive and personalized audio ATSC A/342 Part 2: AC-4 system

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby Digital (AC-3) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby Digital (AC-3) A 5.1 Dolby Digital track carries five main signals and LFE inside a lossy coded stream. AC-3 and Dolby Digital name this same format. Its frame structure describes the sound, while metadata helps a decoder present it for the listening situation. Read a frame as a timed unit A standard AC-3 synchronization frame represents 1,536 samples per channel. At 48 kHz, that is 1,536/48,000 = 32 ms of sound. For three selected encoded rates: Bitrate Bytes for a 32 ms frame at 48 kHz 384 kbit/s 1,536 448 kbit/s 1,792 640 kbit/s 2,560 The samples represented by a frame and the bytes storing it are different quantities. More encoded data gives the codec a different budget for describing the same timed sound. The format supports mono, stereo, and surround modes. Common coded rates include 32, 44.1, and 48 kHz. The standard maximum bitrate is 640 kbit/s, while DVD-Video applies a 448 kbit/s limit. An application's constraint is narrower than a format capability. Reconstruct audio using its coding choices AC-3 represents audio in transformed blocks and uses allocated precision and related coding tools to fit its rate. The decoder reads those choices, reconstructs the frequency-domain data, and returns timed channel samples. That approximation is the lossy part. The receiver's later volume or speaker processing is another stage and can change what the listener hears without changing the stored AC-3 bitstream. Metadata changes the presentation, not the source recording Three useful metadata roles are: Role Decoder use Dialogue normalization Align programme playback level to the relevant reference Dynamic-range information Supply level-dependent adjustments for supported listening modes Downmix information Guide combining channels for fewer outputs For an illustrative dialogue-normalization report of −27 dB, compensation toward a −31 dB reference is −4 dB . Its amplitude factor is 10^(−4/20), approximately 0.631. This is a decoder-level adjustment, not a claim that every piece of spoken audio occupies one isolated channel. A decoder applying dynamic-range information can reduce loud/quiet contrast for a chosen mode. A downmix can incorporate center dialogue and surrounds into stereo instead of losing them by taking only the front pair. Place the decoder in the session An Emby player receiving a compatible AC-3 track can decode and output PCM, or pass a supported encoded presentation to a receiver's decoder. In either case, source coding and selected decoder processing explain the output. If two AC-3 paths sound different in level or dynamics, inspect which decoder and metadata/listening mode were used before attributing the difference to compressed bitrate. The related E-AC-3 format requires its own bitstream handling; it is not obtained by changing the AC-3 name. See Also Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) Audio Bitstream Passthrough Audio Downmixing 5.1 Surround Sound References ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 standard Dolby: Dolby Digital 5.1

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) A Dolby Digital Plus programme can provide a conventional channel mix and a richer presentation using related substreams. Enhanced AC-3 (E-AC-3) extends AC-3's coding and presentation structure, while remaining a lossy audio format. Names such as E-AC-3, EC-3, and Dolby Digital Plus identify that encoded family. Build a presentation from substreams An independent substream supplies a decodable presentation without requiring its dependent substreams. A dependent substream is used with an associated independent one and can contribute additional or replacement channel information. This allows a compatible smaller channel presentation to coexist with information for a larger one. For example, a 7.1 arrangement can use a 5.1 independent presentation whose surround signals are partial combinations, plus dependent information that reconstructs the separate side/rear arrangement. The dependent information is not necessarily just “two more tracks.” The full decoder follows the specified channel mapping and replacement relationships to produce the intended presentation. Decoder uses Available result Independent E-AC-3 presentation Its compatible channel mix Independent plus required dependent information The complete associated channel presentation Supported object-carriage information too An immersive rendering input where supplied The exact structure belongs to the particular track. Consumer delivery commonly uses stereo, 5.1, and 7.1 presentations. Independence does not mean an AC-3 core An independent E-AC-3 substream is independent of other E-AC-3 substreams. It is not thereby a bitstream an AC-3-only decoder can reconstruct. Some disc arrangements include a compatible AC-3 component. A playback system can also produce AC-3 through a supported conversion. Those routes should be distinguished from extracting a pre-existing core from an arbitrary E-AC-3 file. This distinction explains why “backward compatible” needs its system context: compatibility can be supplied by packaging or an active conversion, rather than by the older decoder understanding the newer stream directly. Add Atmos as another reconstruction job Dolby Digital Plus can carry Atmos through backwards-compatible object audio carriage. The conventional channel presentation remains useful, while extra information supports recovery and rendering of the immersive representation. A decoder using only the compatible channel path produces ordinary channel audio. An object-aware route uses the spatial information too. The Atmos article follows that difference to a listening system. For an Emby source, a meaningful trace identifies which E-AC-3 presentation was delivered, whether it remained encoded or was decoded/converted, and what reached the renderer. This locates a specific substream or spatial-information boundary rather than treating a successful 5.1 output as proof of the whole source's feature set. See Also Dolby Digital (AC-3) Dolby Atmos Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Audio Bitstream Passthrough References ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 standard Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus audio coding

articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-Core.ht.title: DTS Core Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-Core.ht.keywords: DTS Core Audio A DTS-HD file can produce ordinary DTS at a receiver because the player delivered its compatible core . That core is an existing coded presentation, not a fresh low-quality version invented during playback. The independently decodable DTS core supplies conventional DTS Digital Surround and forms the foundation of many core-plus-extension streams. Separate the two decoding jobs Data handled Reconstruction job Core Reconstruct the compatible lossy channel presentation Relevant extensions Enhance that presentation, add information, or supply lossless reconstruction where defined The core does not depend on its extensions to be interpreted. A core decoder can reconstruct its own channels while leaving extension information unused. A full decoder reads the appropriate extension structure and performs the additional jobs. Conventional DTS Digital Surround commonly supplies up to 5.1 channels at an encoded rate up to about 1.5 Mbit/s. The exact source layout and rate are still properties of the selected track. Core extraction avoids a new encoding generation Suppose a soundtrack contains a core and DTS-HD Master Audio information. A player can select or extract the existing core component for a destination that accepts it. The sound then has the approximation already encoded in that core. It lacks the full lossless reconstruction, but no second lossy encoder had to analyze the audio and add another approximation. By contrast, decoding the whole soundtrack and encoding AC-3 or AAC is transcoding . That creates a different coded representation, even if its final speaker count resembles the core. The core can be inside one selectable track A container often lists one DTS-HD soundtrack, while the decoder handles the core/extensions within it. The core is not necessarily another language-track choice in the UI. This is why an Emby source report can say DTS-HD while the receiver detects DTS. Locate the delivered component and output path before treating the two labels as contradictory. DTS also defines extension-only arrangements. For such a stream, there is no supplied legacy core to extract. The actual substream structure determines whether core fallback is available; the family name alone does not create that component. See Also DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS-HD Master Audio Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Audio Bitstream Passthrough References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Digital Surround and DTS-HD Master Audio

articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-HD-High.title: DTS-HD High Resolution Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-HD-High.keywords: DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS-HD High Resolution Audio is the lossy enhanced DTS-HD presentation. It is different from lossless DTS-HD Master Audio. Consumer descriptions include up to 7.1 channels and 96 kHz capability, providing more presentation scope than conventional core-only playback. The important word “lossy” remains compatible with improvements over a core. Additional information can reduce an error without eliminating it The DTS extension family includes XBR, which can encode quantized residual information describing what a core representation did not retain. Its decoder adds the reconstructed residual to the corresponding core representation. A numerical illustration makes the distinction clear: Step Illustrative value Source component +0.83 Core reconstruction +0.75 Difference to be corrected +0.08 Quantized extension correction +0.05 Enhanced reconstruction +0.80 The enhancement moved the result closer to +0.83 but did not restore it exactly. These values illustrate quantized correction; they are not a DTS packet example or a complete specification of every High Resolution stream's extension combination. Lossless correction must preserve the necessary difference exactly. That is a different reconstruction promise, developed in DTS-HD Master Audio . Follow the selected presentation A compatible core-only route uses the existing lossy core and misses the supported enhanced result. A full High Resolution decoder uses the appropriate extensions. Either decoder can then output ordinary PCM. A receiver's PCM label consequently identifies where decoding finished, not which DTS presentation was reconstructed. To distinguish the routes, identify the player's selected decoder/result and output layout. High-rate or 24-bit descriptions concern supported sample representation. They do not make the quantized correction in a lossy coding process reversible. The useful distinction is the reconstructed presentation and its codec profile, rather than treating every “DTS-HD” display abbreviation as Master Audio.
