articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP2.html.title: MPEG Audio Layer II (MP2) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP2.html.keywords: MPEG Audio Layer II (MP2) A television recording can contain MPEG-2 video and MPEG Audio Layer II , commonly abbreviated MP2. The names share a standards history, but the video and audio are separate coded streams. Layer II is a lossy subband audio codec used in broadcast systems and older media. Conventional DAB uses Layer II; DAB+ instead uses the AAC family. Allocate precision across subbands Layer II divides the signal through a filter bank into frequency subbands. The encoder estimates how much precision each needs, then describes their sampled values with the selected quantization and scaling information. The decoder reads those choices, reconstructs the subband values, and combines them through the synthesis filter bank into the audio waveform. Giving one subband more precision can reduce its coding error, while the total bitrate constrains the available allocation. The subbands are frequency regions within audio channels. They are not separately selectable language tracks or physical surround speakers. Decode the channel mode as well as the samples Layer II mode Intended relationship Mono One presentation signal Stereo A related left/right presentation Joint stereo Shared coding treatment for suitable channel information Dual channel Two independently intended channel signals Dual-channel material can carry two language programmes. Treating those as left and right of one stereo soundstage can make both languages play simultaneously. Track selection and channel interpretation are therefore different operations. Keep the broadcast context while converting A transport-stream recording supplies programme selection and timestamps around the coded audio. The MP2 decoder reconstructs the sound; the systems reader keeps it associated with the correct programme and timeline. If an Emby client accepts the recorded video but needs a different audio codec, a Direct Stream path can retain compatible video and create a suitable soundtrack. That operation must preserve the selected programme, intended channel presentation, and timing. The converted audio starts from the Layer II reconstruction. Repackaging the original MP2 into another supported wrapper instead retains its coded representation. The choice follows whether the target needs another wrapper or another audio decoder. See Also MP3 Audio Lossy Audio Compression Streams and Tracks Audio Transcoding References ISO/IEC 11172-3: MPEG-1 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-3: MPEG-2 Audio Fraunhofer: DAB and DAB+ codec definitions Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP3.html.title: MP3 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP3.html.keywords: MP3 Audio MP3's compact music files made a large collection practical on limited storage. Its name means MPEG Audio Layer III : “III” is an audio layer, not MPEG-3 video. The format combines time/frequency analysis, perceptual precision allocation, and efficient symbol coding. Understanding a few of its tools makes the labels in a media report useful. Follow what the encoder spends bits on The encoder analyzes sections of the waveform, estimates where coding error is likely to be audible, and quantizes the signal representation. The decoder reconstructs sound from those coded values. The reconstructed PCM is an approximation of the input. More data can permit finer precision or retain difficult details, but the choice of encoder tools and material also matters. Lossy compression follows the general process through a numerical example. Joint stereo shares information rather than removing a side Left and right can contain substantial common content. A mid/side model illustrates a reversible way to describe that relationship: M = (L + R)/2; S = (L − R)/2. L = M + S; R = M − S. Example input Mid Side L=+0.8, R=+0.6 +0.7 +0.1 L=+0.4, R=+0.4 +0.4 0 L=+0.4, R=−0.4 0 +0.4 MP3's tools have their specified normalization and coding behavior; this algebra shows why shared stereo information can be described efficiently without turning everything into mono. Joint-stereo modes can choose suitable shared representations, and MP3 also has intensity-stereo tools that make a different perceptual tradeoff. The label is consequently a family of coding choices, not proof that a channel disappeared. Read CBR and VBR as budgets CBR selects a nominal frame bitrate. VBR allows the encoder's frame-bitrate choices to vary with the material. MP3 also has a bit reservoir: data associated with one frame can use space carried earlier. Even a CBR stream therefore has more flexibility than “every passage receives exactly the same coding treatment.” At an average 192 kbit/s, four minutes contain about 5.76 MB of encoded data before tags and overhead. At an average 320 kbit/s, the same duration uses 9.6 MB. These are size calculations, not thresholds of guaranteed transparency. Audio frames and file metadata answer different questions The MPEG audio frames carry sound. ID3 metadata can carry titles, artists, and artwork. Optional navigation or trimming information assists duration, seeking, and presentation boundaries. The MP3 packaging article develops those structures. A file can therefore have correct audio but incorrect artwork, or valid tags while suffering an audio/frame problem. A frame boundary is also not automatically an independent clean decoding start when reservoir dependencies exist. When an Emby music path converts MP3 to another lossy codec, the new encoder starts from the MP3 reconstruction. Keeping the master or the original delivered MP3 avoids making future versions from a chain of converted copies. See Also Lossy Audio Compression MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames Audio Bitrate Audio Transcoding References ISO/IEC 11172-3: MPEG-1 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-3: MPEG-2 Audio Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/Opus.html.title: Opus Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Opus.html.keywords: Opus Audio One Opus stream can carry an intelligible low-rate voice, music, or a mixture. Its design joins predictive speech coding and transform coding , allowing the encoder to use the tools appropriate to the material and operating mode. The format is defined in RFC 6716. Its decode rules, coded-frame durations, and supported mode transitions make the relationship between data, delay, and output explicit. Follow the operating modes Mode Main representation SILK-based predictive mode Speech-oriented linear prediction and excitation CELT-based transform mode Frequency-domain coding suited to music and other audio Hybrid mode Predictive lower-band speech plus transform-coded higher-band content Prediction describes recurring speech structure efficiently. Transform coding handles general audio and higher frequencies without forcing all content into a voice model. In the hybrid arrangement, the two parts cover their intended bands rather than redundantly encoding the same whole signal twice. Mode, audio bandwidth, and bitrate are related encoder choices. The output sample-rate number is another property: a decoder can put a narrower-band reconstruction on a 48 kHz time grid. Count a 20 ms frame At a 48 kHz output rate, 20 ms represents 960 sample frames per channel . Uncompressed 16-bit stereo needs 960 × 2 × 2 = 3,840 bytes for that span. At a nominal 96 kbit/s encoded data budget, 20 ms corresponds to 96,000 × 0.020 / 8 = 240 bytes , before external transport overhead. This calculation illustrates the scale of compression, not a fixed packet size for every Opus mode or VBR frame. Shorter coded durations can reduce one contribution to latency, but increase framing overhead and change coding tradeoffs. Codec look-ahead, packet accumulation, network buffering, and output buffering are additional delays. A low-delay codec is only one component of a low-delay route. For suitable communication modes, optional packet-loss tools can provide concealment or forward-error-recovery information. They address missing data during transport; they do not make the stored lossy representation lossless. Why an Ogg Opus file uses a 48 kHz clock RFC 7845 defines Ogg Opus timing in 48,000 sample positions per second regardless of the original capture rate or a decoder's chosen output rate. The header's input-rate field describes source information; it does not redefine that clock. The mapping also describes pre-skip and final trimming so codec delay and padding do not become unwanted audible boundaries. For an illustrative one-second file: Quantity Sample frames on the 48 kHz clock 51 decoded packets, each representing 20 ms 48,960 Initial pre-skip 240 Final discarded padding 720 Audible duration 48,000 The final retained granule position is 48,240; subtracting the pre-skip gives 48,000, or one second. These selected values demonstrate the accounting, not universal Opus encoder delay settings. Keep channel mapping with the stream A multichannel Opus presentation can use several coded streams and a mapping describing how their outputs become presentation channels. A packet reader must preserve that setup as well as the payloads and timing. For an Opus recording in Emby, inspect its container mapping and the delivered presentation when a duration or channel problem occurs. A bare 48 kHz label cannot diagnose a lost pre-skip instruction or an incorrectly applied channel map. Following those concrete structures explains the symptom. articles/audio/formats/lossy/Vorbis.html.title: Vorbis Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Vorbis.html.keywords: Vorbis Audio A Vorbis decoder begins with three header packets, then reconstructs successive audio packets using the configuration they supplied. This structure explains both how its sound is represented and why extracting packets without the setup can fail. Vorbis is a lossy general-audio codec. Ogg is a common wrapper, but it is not part of the audio-compression algorithm itself. Set up the decoder before the music starts Header What it supplies Identification Codec identity, channel count, sample rate, and basic properties Comment Textual metadata Setup Codebooks, floor/residue configurations, mappings, and modes The setup information gives meaning to the encoded symbols in later packets. Its codebooks are the dictionaries used for compact value descriptions; mappings and modes identify how those descriptions assemble the channels and transforms. A seek-capable reader retains this initialization, then locates appropriate audio packets and handles overlap/timing. Moving to a later byte position without the header state is not the same as seeking through a properly initialized Vorbis stream. Rebuild one audio section Vorbis describes a section using a spectral floor and residue . The floor captures a coarser spectral envelope; the residue carries detail relative to that envelope. A simplified numerical model illustrates the relationship: if the floor magnitude for a frequency region is 0.4 and a relative detail factor is 1.2, their product is 0.48. This is not a Vorbis packet decoder or a claim about exact quantized values; it shows how envelope and relative detail work together instead of storing unrelated full magnitudes everywhere. The specified decoder reconstructs these parts, reverses any channel coupling, combines the channel spectra, performs the inverse transform, and joins overlapping output sections. The resulting samples are the signal represented by the bitstream. Share channel relationships efficiently Stereo channels often have related content. Vorbis coupling can describe those relationships more compactly, then decouple them during reconstruction. The format supports different coding choices, including tradeoffs in the stereo image. A lossless channel-coupling step inside the decoder does not make the whole codec lossless: earlier quantization of the audio representation still determines its approximation. Let the encoder's budget follow the material Vorbis encoders commonly offer a quality-oriented variable-rate mode. A difficult attack or dense texture can use more data than a simpler passage at that selected quality policy. The header's nominal bitrate can be a hint, while a measured track average comes from actual bytes and duration. For an Emby music file, this distinguishes an expected bitrate change from an audio fault. Its metadata, initialization, packet timing, and coded sound remain separate preservation tasks when it is repackaged. A compatible remux can retain those coded packets; a conversion to another codec reconstructs them and creates a new audio representation. See Also Lossy Audio Compression What Is a Media Container? articles/audio/formats/lossy/WMA.html.title: Windows Media Audio (WMA) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/WMA.html.keywords: Windows Media Audio (WMA) Windows Media Audio member Intended coding role Microsoft format identifier Standard General-purpose lossy audio 0x0161 Professional Lossy audio including multichannel/high-resolution configurations 0x0162 Lossless Preserve supported source audio data 0x0163 Voice Separately implemented speech-focused coding A distinct codec family member Use this table when one old WMA file plays and another does not. WMA names a family ; the reader's format identifier selects a particular decoder job. Read the package, then the member A WMA extension commonly names an audio-only ASF file. The ASF stream description identifies the encoded audio. A reader can recognize the outer container while lacking the decoder for its specific WMA member. For example, a stereo music file using Standard and a multichannel recording using Professional can share the extension but need different codec capabilities. The latter also needs the appropriate channel-layout handling after decoding. A high bitrate or sample rate is not a substitute for that identification. Lossless is distinguished by its format, not by a file happening to be large. Match the conversion to the identified source If a WMA Lossless collection is moved to a suitable lossless PCM codec, preserving its decoded samples can preserve the audio exactly. A Standard or Professional source instead supplies its lossy reconstruction, even when the destination is FLAC. For Emby, this identification informs whether the source can be delivered to the client as it stands, whether its wrapper needs changing, or whether another decoder/encoder must create a compatible version. A useful inventory records the family member, sample rate, channels/layout, and any protection requirements. It explains a collection's different handling more directly than grouping every file under one WMA filename category. articles/audio/formats/LPCM.html.title: Linear PCM (LPCM) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/LPCM.html.keywords: Linear PCM (LPCM) A signed integer LPCM sample is a direct amplitude value. If the stored code is twice as large, its represented amplitude is twice as large. Linear pulse-code modulation uses this linear relationship, unlike companded formats that assign finer and coarser amplitude spacing in different parts of their range. There is no compressed-audio prediction or transform to undo before interpreting the sample values. Read a tiny stereo sequence Assume signed 16-bit samples, little-endian storage, and interleaved left/right channels. Two sample frames contain: Time position Left Right Four stored bytes 0 +1,000 −1,000 E8 03 18 FC 1 +2,000 −2,000 D0 07 30 F8 Each two-byte signed code is the amplitude for one channel at that time. To turn the eight bytes into correctly timed samples, the reader still needs the format description: sample rate, signedness, precision/storage size, byte order, and channel layout. A WAV or AIFF supplies such a description with its sample data. Their different wrappers do not inherently change the represented sound. Count the uncompressed payload At 48 kHz, each channel advances through 48,000 samples every second. With tightly packed 24-bit samples and six channels, each frame uses 144 bits: 48,000 × 24 × 6 = 6.912 Mbit/s . The rate follows directly from the sample representation. Unlike compressed bitrate, it does not decrease during a simple or quiet passage. All sample positions still occupy their storage. LPCM example Raw audio payload 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo 1.4112 Mbit/s 48 kHz, 24-bit, 5.1 6.912 Mbit/s 96 kHz, 24-bit, 7.1 18.432 Mbit/s A wider storage word changes the payload calculation. For example, 24 valid bits carried in 32-bit words occupy more space without increasing recorded precision. Sample formats develops that distinction. The samples can come from several earlier representations A lossless decoder can restore the PCM values that its encoder preserved. A lossy decoder produces its encoded approximation as PCM. Both results can enter an ordinary sample-processing/output stage, where gain, mixing, or resampling operate on numbers. Thus a receiver's PCM indication describes the delivered representation. The original library track may have been FLAC, a movie codec, or LPCM itself. To assess preservation, follow what happened before those values reached the output, rather than treating direct sample representation as evidence of a particular recording history. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Bitrate Decoded PCM Output WAV and RIFF References ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE

articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-NB.htm.title: AMR-NB Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-NB.htm.keywords: AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-NB property Value PCM sample rate 8 kHz Coded speech-frame duration 20 ms Reconstructed samples per channel/frame 160 Speech coding modes Eight, from 4.75 to 12.2 kbit/s Narrowband Adaptive Multi-Rate is a speech codec used in mobile voice and stored voice recordings. Its modes allocate different amounts of coded information to the same 20 ms speech interval. Count what a mode actually stores At 4.75 kbit/s, one 20 ms speech frame contains 4,750 × 0.020 = 95 coded bits . At 12.2 kbit/s, it contains 244 coded bits . The decoder reconstructs 160 speech samples in either case. The difference is the amount of information describing the voice model and excitation, not playback speed. The speech-coding article explains that reconstruction. RFC 4867's octet-aligned file storage adds a frame-header octet and packs the coded bits into whole bytes: Active-speech mode Coded bits Padded payload bytes Bytes with one frame header 4.75 kbit/s 95 12 13 12.2 kbit/s 244 31 32 With 50 active frames per second, the second case uses 1,600 bytes/s, or 12.8 kbit/s , before the initial file header. That explains why a stored-file data rate can exceed the nominal speech-mode rate. Silence-related frames and other containers change the overall accounting. Interpret the narrowband sound The 8 kHz grid supports the narrowband speech system. Its restricted frequency range and voice-model approximation can give an intelligible recording a telephone-like character. A 48 kHz output version can reproduce that signal on another grid, but the original coded bandwidth remains the source of its tonal character. AMR-WB is a different wideband codec with different reconstruction, not a setting that expands the old narrowband recording. AMR frames can be stored directly or inside 3GP media. For an Emby phone recording, identify that wrapper and channel presentation alongside the speech mode. It tells the reader how to retrieve the correctly timed coded frames without treating the nominal bitrate as the exact file-size rate. See Also Speech Coding AMR-WB Speech Audio Audio Sample Rate Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 126 090 V18.0.0: AMR transcoding functions RFC 4867: AMR and AMR-WB RTP payload and file storage

articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-WB.htm.title: AMR-WB Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-WB.htm.keywords: AMR-WB Speech Audio The “wideband” in AMR-WB means that its speech representation retains a broader voice spectrum than AMR-NB. It is also standardized as ITU-T G.722.2 , a distinct codec from G.722. At 16 kHz, each 20 ms frame corresponds to 320 sample positions. That greater time-grid capacity helps preserve upper-frequency speech cues, while the codec still uses a lossy voice-model reconstruction. Use more coded bits for the same speech duration AMR-WB mode endpoint Bits per 20 ms active-speech frame 6.60 kbit/s 132 23.85 kbit/s 477 There are nine speech modes between those endpoints. The algebraic CELP reconstruction uses the selected parameters/excitation to create the frame's speech samples. A higher mode supplies more information within the same time interval; it does not make the speech play more slowly. The sample rate's 8 kHz Nyquist boundary is a property of the grid. The codec's defined filtering and coding determine its actual preserved band. Grid capacity and recording bandwidth should therefore be read separately. Account for a stored AWB file RFC 4867 stores active-speech frame data in whole bytes, with a frame-header octet. At the 23.85 kbit/s mode, 477 bits need 60 bytes when padded. The frame occupies 61 bytes including its header. At 50 such frames per second: 61 × 50 × 8 = 24,400 bit/s . That is above the nominal 23,850 bit/s because of padding and framing. The initial file header adds a small further amount; silence modes or 3GP packaging can change the complete file rate. Compare speech representations meaningfully An older narrowband recording can sound dull next to a genuine AMR-WB source because frequency cues were never retained in the older source. Merely converting that old recording to an AMR-WB or high-rate PCM file cannot supply them. Conversely, an AMR-WB source can legitimately reach an Emby player as resampled PCM after decoding. The output label describes its current representation; the actual source's codec and coded band explain what was available to reconstruct. For an AWB or 3GP recording, keep those observations with the active mode, channel count, and full duration. They distinguish a storage-rate calculation, a decoder-format issue, and the expected character of a compressed voice recording. See Also AMR-NB Speech Audio Speech Coding Audio Sample Rate References ETSI TS 126 190 V18.0.0: AMR-WB transcoding functions ITU-T G.722.2: AMR-WB speech coding RFC 4867: AMR and AMR-WB RTP payload and file storage

articles/audio/formats/speech/Speech-Cod.title: Speech Coding | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/Speech-Cod.keywords: Speech Coding A spoken vowel is not a random collection of samples. The vocal source supplies excitation, and the vocal tract shapes its spectrum. Speech coding exploits these relationships to describe a voice with fewer bits than a literal waveform requires. Many speech codecs use a signal model that resembles these two jobs: an excitation signal drives a filter whose parameters change with the speech. Separate pitch from the spectral shape For voiced sound, recurring excitation contributes a pitch pattern. At an illustrative 100 Hz pitch, a period lasts 10 ms. On an 8 kHz sample grid, that is 80 sample intervals. The mouth and vocal tract also create resonances. Changing those resonances changes the vowel's character without requiring the same change in pitch. A coding model can therefore describe pitch-related repetition and the shorter-term spectral envelope separately. Unvoiced consonants need noise-like excitation rather than a simple periodic pulse. Real speech mixes and changes these behaviors, so a codec sends updated parameters as it progresses. Model information Reconstruction role Short-term predictor/filter parameters Shape the spectrum Pitch-related information Describe useful longer-term repetition Excitation information Supply remaining signal detail Gains Set the contributions' levels Choose a coded excitation by trying reconstructions In code-excited linear prediction (CELP) , the encoder searches for excitation information that produces a good reconstruction through the synthesis filter. A perceptually weighted error comparison helps choose the candidate and its gains. The decoder does not repeat the encoder's whole search. It reads the selected information, reconstructs the excitation, and applies the specified filter/state updates. Compact parameter coding thus describes a time-varying approximation of the recording. Algebraic CELP can define excitation patterns through compact rules and pulse positions rather than a large stored waveform dictionary. The result remains driven by the recorded speech's analyzed parameters. It is not text-to-speech and does not require recognizing the words. Give the model a sequence of frames The codec updates its description over short intervals. A frame must contain enough information for useful analysis, and some encoders need additional look-ahead. Those contribute latency before transport or playback buffering is considered. A format can offer several bitrate modes. More coded information can describe excitation or other parameters with greater accuracy, while the decoder follows the selected mode's defined reconstruction. Handle pauses without confusing silence and time Voice-activity detection identifies periods that can use another coding treatment. In a discontinuous-transmission system, less data can be sent during inactivity while comfort-noise information represents the background. The programme timeline still progresses. The receiver uses the format and transport's timing/state rules; absence of a voice packet is not an instruction to join the next word immediately onto the previous one. Noise suppression and automatic gain control before encoding are separate processing operations. They change the input the codec receives, whereas the codec describes that input. Why a speech model can struggle with music An isolated voice often fits prediction and excitation assumptions well. Dense music, applause, or several competing sounds have different structures and may require tools or data the speech-focused model does not provide. A narrowband recording also lacks some frequency content before or during encoding. Decoding it onto a 48 kHz output grid cannot recreate those missing frequencies. For a voice recording in an Emby collection, intelligibility, encoded bandwidth, model artifacts, and source fidelity answer different questions. Opus illustrates a codec that joins speech-oriented and general-audio tools for programmes whose character changes. See Also AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-WB Speech Audio Speex Speech Audio Opus Audio Lossy Audio Compression References Speex: Codec manual ETSI TS 126 090 V18.0.0: AMR transcoding functions RFC 6716: Definition of the Opus audio codec

articles/audio/formats/speech/Speex.html.title: Speex Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/Speex.html.keywords: Speex Speech Audio Speex wideband audio contains a low-band speech representation with additional upper-band information. This embedded-band structure makes its three sampling modes more meaningful than a list of rate numbers. Speex is an open lossy speech codec based on CELP. Mode Nominal input/output sample rate Narrowband 8 kHz Wideband 16 kHz Ultra-wideband 32 kHz Build the wideband representation For 16 kHz wideband input, a quadrature-mirror filter bank separates lower and upper frequency regions. The lower band is encoded using the narrowband structure. Additional information describes the higher band. The full decoder reconstructs both and recombines them. A supported embedded narrowband decode can use the low-band representation without recreating the high-band result. This is a coding-layer relationship, not a command to relabel an 8 kHz source as 16 kHz. A true wideband encoding contains the additional band information. Control bitrate and coding effort separately Speex offers bitrate/quality decisions and a complexity control. Bitrate changes the coded data budget, while complexity changes how much work the encoder spends selecting its representation. Voice-activity detection and discontinuous-transmission options can reduce data use during inactivity. Their state and framing affect how the timeline and background are reproduced. In packet communication, buffering and packet-loss handling add another layer around the codec. Keep preprocessing outside the format definition A Speex application may use the library's noise suppression, gain control, or echo cancellation before encoding. Those operations change the signal handed to the codec; a quiet background is not proof of a particular encoded mode. Stored Speex commonly uses Ogg, while RFC 5574 defines its RTP carriage. Headers, framing, and timing tell the decoder how to obtain the coded representation. The project's current guidance prefers Opus for new codec uses. Existing Speex recordings still need their own compatible decoding. In a legacy Emby voice collection, preserve the coded mode and full timing when making a listening copy; the embedded structure explains which frequency information that copy started with. See Also Speech Coding Opus Audio AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-WB Speech Audio References Speex: Codec manual RFC 5574: RTP payload format for the Speex codec Speex: Project status and technology Speex author manual: Wideband sub-band CELP

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Bitrat.title: Audio Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Bitrat.keywords: Audio Bitrate Bitrate is a data-flow measurement: how many bits of audio are carried in one second. Use it to estimate storage or delivery demand. For a compressed track, the encoder and signal determine that flow; for tightly packed integer PCM, it follows directly from the sample format. Calculate PCM from one sample frame A 48 kHz stereo track has 48,000 time positions each second. With 24 bits for each of its two channel samples, one sample frame contains 48 bits. 48,000 × 24 × 2 = 2,304,000 bit/s , or 2.304 Mbit/s . PCM representation Audio payload rate 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, 2 channels 1.4112 Mbit/s 48 kHz, 24-bit, 2 channels 2.304 Mbit/s 48 kHz, 24-bit, 6 channels 6.912 Mbit/s Decimal units are used here. File headers and transport overhead are excluded, and the samples are assumed to occupy exactly their stated integer precision. To find storage, divide by eight and multiply by duration. Ten minutes of the 48 kHz, 24-bit stereo example contain: 2,304,000 / 8 × 600 = 172,800,000 bytes , or 172.8 MB . If those 24-bit values occupy 32-bit storage words, the calculation uses 32 instead of 24. The stored sample data then occupy 230.4 MB for ten minutes. Precision and storage rate can change independently. Count compressed data over time A compressed codec represents the signal using coded blocks rather than storing every PCM value. Its encoded rate must be measured or supplied by the encoder configuration. Suppose three consecutive one-second intervals contain 16,000, 24,000, and 20,000 bytes of encoded audio. Their instantaneous interval rates are 128, 192, and 160 kbit/s. The three-second average is: (16,000 + 24,000 + 20,000) × 8 / 3 = 160 kbit/s . A header's nominal rate, an average for the whole track, and a rate measured over a short interval can therefore describe different observations. Variable-rate delivery needs enough buffering to handle the intervals, even when the long-term average is comfortably below the connection's throughput. Use the rate for the question you are answering For a lossless track, successful decoding restores the encoded samples regardless of how efficiently the encoder compressed them. For lossy encoding, a data budget constrains how accurately the signal can be represented; comparison also depends on codec, channel count, and material. An Emby movie's total delivery demand includes video, selected audio, and packaging overhead. Use the audio rate to compare soundtrack contributions, and the total media rate when sizing the complete stream's delivery. articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Clippi.title: Audio Clipping | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Clippi.keywords: Audio Clipping The dotted waveform asks for a peak of 1.3. The solid waveform reaches the available limit, +1, and stays there until the requested signal returns within range. That flat top is hard clipping . Calculated illustration: a 1.3-peak sine limited to [−1,+1]. It shows a mathematical limiter, not measured Emby output. A level change should multiply every sample by the same factor. Clipping stops doing that for the samples beyond the limit, so it changes the shape and creates distortion. Repeatedly reshaping a sine also introduces frequency components absent from the original sine. Put the volume adjustment before the failure Take an overloaded sample of +1.3 and a second sample of +0.6. Compare reducing gain by half before and after the clipping stage: Original value Half gain, then clipping Clipping, then half gain +1.3 +0.65 +0.50 +0.6 +0.30 +0.30 −1.3 −0.65 −0.50 The first route keeps the waveform's proportions. The second makes an already altered waveform quieter. Once +1.3 has become +1, the output no longer distinguishes it from +1.1 or +1.8. This explains why lowering a receiver's volume can leave distortion audible: the overloaded stage may have been the recording, a decoder-side boost, or an earlier mixer. How a valid input becomes too large Each channel in a soundtrack can fit its own range. Summing two simultaneous +0.8 values at full gain nevertheless requests +1.6. A downmix needs coefficients, output attenuation, or appropriate overload management to handle such combinations. An equalizer boost can similarly raise part of a waveform. A float processor may retain +1.6 successfully as an intermediate value; a later integer output converter must either bring it within range or lose the excess. The allowed working number range and the final output's usable range are different boundaries. Clipping can also occur in analog equipment when a circuit runs out of voltage or current capacity. Its overload shape need not match the flat limiter pictured here. Samples below full scale can have larger reconstructed peaks Sample peak measurement examines the stored or decoded values. A reconstructed waveform also exists between those sample positions. An idealized example has two adjacent values of +0.8, with all other values zero. At their halfway point, ideal sinc interpolation gives: 0.8 × sinc(0.5) + 0.8 × sinc(−0.5) = 0.8 × 2/π + 0.8 × 2/π ≈ 1.0186 . The samples are below +1, but this mathematical reconstructed waveform exceeds it. Real reconstruction and true-peak measurement use practical filters; the example explains why checking only the largest sample can miss an output peak. Locate the overloaded stage If an Emby soundtrack distorts after a boost or downmix, compare the same passage with that operation removed. If the source itself contains clipped peaks, changing the delivery bitrate will not recover them. A useful level trace records the input peak, processing gains, summed output, and final converter range. Reducing gain before the first overloaded boundary preserves the shape; reducing it later preserves the distortion at a lower listening level. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Dynamic Range Audio Quantization Noise References FFmpeg: Audio sample formats FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation Julius O. Smith: Bandlimited interpolation and between-sample overshoot

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dither.title: Audio Dithering | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dither.keywords: Audio Dithering A quiet fade can become rough when rounded to an integer grid. Its amplitude may move smoothly through small values, but the output jumps repeatedly between a few available levels. The pattern of those jumps can follow the waveform, producing distortion rather than an innocuous background noise. Dither deliberately randomizes the rounding decision. The added noise is small and controlled; its purpose is to stop quantization error from tracing the signal's structure. Start with a value the grid cannot hold Use a deliberately coarse grid with steps of one unit. Ordinary rounding sends +0.2 to 0 every time. A waveform whose samples stay between −0.5 and +0.5 can collapse entirely to zeros on that grid. Now add a random value before rounding. Occasionally, +0.2 plus the noise crosses a threshold and becomes another output level. The individual output remains an integer; over repeated trials its behavior can preserve information about where +0.2 lay between the levels. One common non-subtractive choice is triangular-probability-density dither (TPDF) . It can be formed from the sum of two independent uniform random values, each between −0.5 and +0.5 quantizer steps. Their sum spans −1 to +1 step, with values near zero more likely than values near the extremes. For the +0.2 input on our unit-step grid, ideal TPDF and round-to-nearest give: Quantized output Probability −1 4.5% 0 71.0% +1 24.5% The expected output is (−1 × 0.045) + (0 × 0.71) + (1 × 0.245) = +0.2 . This follows from the triangular distribution's areas beyond the rounding thresholds. The table is a statistical demonstration, not an instruction to average adjacent audio samples or use such coarse precision for playback. Audio samples vary with time. Proper dither controls the quantizer's error statistics at those successive values, allowing very quiet signal behavior to remain encoded among the noise. The trade is distortion for a controlled noise floor Dither does not make every rounded sample accurate. The added noise and quantization still produce error. What improves is the relationship between that error and the signal: quiet tones and fades stop controlling a repeating rounding pattern. The distribution, level, and quantizer behavior matter. Arbitrary hiss added at an unrelated level is not equivalent to a designed dither process. The usual TPDF choice removes input-dependent behavior in the first two error moments for an ideal non-overloading uniform quantizer. Other choices make other tradeoffs. At normal 16-bit or 24-bit steps, the demonstration's one-unit excursions become correspondingly small. That is why the mechanism can improve low-level behavior without intentionally adding a loud sound. Put it at the precision reduction Suppose a processor has mixed audio and adjusted gain using float. Its output can contain fractional values between 16-bit integer levels even if the input originally came from a 16-bit recording. Reducing this processed result to a 16-bit output creates a new quantization step; that is a useful place to consider dither. Copying unchanged integer samples to another file does not perform such a rounding operation. Adding dither to that copy would alter samples unnecessarily. Likewise, widening integer storage while retaining all original values does not need dither. Repeated processing and integer reduction can repeatedly add noise or distortion. A sensible pipeline preserves working precision during the operations, then chooses the necessary final conversion. The actual Emby player, server conversion, or operating-system output decides where those stages occur; a resampler's list of available dither methods does not tell us which was selected for a session. Noise shaping changes where error lies Noise shaping uses feedback around quantization to redistribute error energy across frequency. It can reduce error in one band while raising it elsewhere. It is a separate design choice from creating suitable dither statistics, and it does not remove all error. This helps interpret a comparison between output methods: listen for both quiet-signal distortion and noise character. A smooth fade, a lower in-band noise level, and unchanged individual samples are different outcomes. Dither is aimed at the first; lossless copying at the last. See Also Audio Quantization Noise Audio Bit Depth PCM Sample Formats References Wannamaker: The Theory of Dithered Quantization University of Waterloo: Digital audio and dither research by Stan Lipshitz FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dynami.title: Audio Dynamic Range | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dynami.keywords: Audio Dynamic Range You turn up a film to hear a whispered sentence, then turn it down when the next scene explodes. The soundtrack spans a wide range of programme levels. A device specification describing “dynamic range” asks a related but different question: how much usable level fits between its noise floor and its largest clean signal? Follow a listening example Suppose a loud event peaks at −2 dBFS and a quiet passage has a representative level of −42 dBFS. Those two selected levels are 40 dB apart. The quiet passage's amplitude is one hundredth of the peak amplitude, because 20 × log10(100) = 40 dB. If both are lowered by 10 dB, they move to −12 and −52 dBFS. Their difference remains 40 dB. A volume control shifts the range; it does not narrow it. A listener in a noisy room can therefore lose the quiet passage under the ambient sound while the peaks still sound loud. Playback gain, loudspeaker capacity, room noise, and the recording's dynamics all participate. Change Effect on the selected levels Lower overall gain by 10 dB Both move down by 10 dB Reduce loud sections more than quiet sections The range narrows Lower the system's noise floor Quieter details can remain distinguishable Add clean output headroom Larger peaks can fit without overload A dialogue boost or dynamic-range processor can change the relationship between the chosen programme levels. That is the relevant mechanism for a night-listening option, rather than merely selecting another file bitrate. Capacity and actual use An integer PCM representation supplies a finite amplitude grid. Its quantization error sets one theoretical limit on usable low-level detail. More bit depth makes that grid finer; a real recording can encounter microphone or room noise before reaching that limit. A soundtrack need not use all the available range. A heavily compressed mix can be stored at 24-bit precision, while another 24-bit mix may retain large contrasts. Bit depth describes capacity; the mix's level behavior describes its use. A device's dynamic range is measured with a specified bandwidth, weighting, and test method. Those conditions belong with the quoted number. They differ from selecting two scenes and comparing their programme levels. Peak-to-average behavior is another measurement Crest factor compares peak amplitude with RMS amplitude over the same interval. A pure sine with peak 1 has RMS 1/√2, giving a crest factor of about 3.01 dB. A brief transient over a quiet background can have a much larger crest factor. That does not by itself measure the contrast between an entire whisper scene and an explosion scene. Results change with the interval used, and a silence-heavy passage can produce a very different ratio from a dense one. When interpreting a “DR” figure for music, identify its measurement method and selected time windows. For playback, decide whether the problem is background noise masking quiet material, overload at peaks, or an inconvenient contrast in the mix. Those lead respectively toward a quieter listening environment or noise floor, more clean headroom, or level-dependent processing. See Also Audio Bit Depth Audio Clipping Audio Quantization Noise References Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Quanti.title: Audio Quantization Noise | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Quanti.keywords: Audio Quantization Noise Quantization rounds a value onto a set of available levels. The difference between the value you wanted and the level you stored is quantization error . That error exists even in an ideal numerical conversion with no microphone noise or analog electronics. It becomes especially interesting near the bottom of the available precision, where a small signal may cross very few levels. Follow a few values through rounding Use a deliberately coarse uniform step of 0.125, with no clipping. Rounding to the nearest level produces: Input amplitude Stored amplitude Error: stored minus input 0.10 0.125 +0.025 0.19 0.250 +0.060 0.31 0.250 −0.060 0.49 0.500 +0.010 An input can move while the stored level stays fixed. At the next boundary, the stored value jumps. Within the unclipped range, nearest-level rounding keeps the error within half a step: 0.0625 here. Calculated example: a sine with peak amplitude 0.6 and a quantizer step of 0.125. The exaggerated step makes rounding visible. The lower panel is the actual error, not an unrelated noise recording. More integer bits provide smaller steps across the same full-scale range. Each additional bit doubles the number of levels, which is why precision can improve without raising the maximum allowed signal. Why the error may repeat with the sound The rounding operation is deterministic. A periodic input that visits the same positions relative to the levels can produce a repeating error. For a sufficiently small signal, the quantized output may spend much of its time on only a few values. Its shape can then differ from the smooth waveform in a systematic way. Heard as audio, that error can contain distortion components related to the original signal, rather than behaving like a steady unrelated hiss. Calling all of it “quantization noise” can obscure this distinction. The waveform itself tells you why: when the input determines the rounding error, the error is correlated with the input. What dither changes Dither introduces a controlled random signal before the final rounding. Appropriate dither changes how the input crosses level boundaries, allowing the quantizer to behave more consistently for very small signals. It does not make the output numerically identical to the original. It exchanges unwanted signal-dependent behavior for a controlled noise contribution. For a low-level tone or a fade, that can be preferable to periodic distortion or an abrupt disappearance. This is why the order matters. Dither applied after the value has already been rounded cannot change which level that earlier rounding selected. Interpreting the familiar SNR estimate The ideal estimate 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB compares a full-scale sine with a particular model of uncorrelated uniform quantization error. For 16 bits, the result is about 98.08 dB. Reducing the sine's level reduces its signal-to-error ratio under that fixed noise model. Changing dither, noise shaping, or the assumptions about error changes the analysis too. The formula describes a model, not the whole noise performance of a recording. In playback and conversion, the useful place to apply this understanding is a precision-reduction step. If decoded audio is adjusted and then stored at a lower integer precision, values need rounding again. The source recording's noise and earlier compression remain separate parts of that signal. A higher-precision working format provides room for processing between conversions. The final rounding and its treatment determine what happens when the result must fit a lower-precision output. See Also Audio Bit Depth Audio Dithering Audio Dynamic Range References Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR Wannamaker: The Theory of Dithered Quantization

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Resamp.title: Audio Resampling | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Resamp.keywords: Audio Resampling A music track contains 44,100 sample frames for one second, but the output device consumes 48,000 per second. Sending the old frames faster would shorten the second. Resampling instead computes the signal at 48,000 new time positions , keeping its intended duration and pitch. That makes sample-rate conversion a signal-processing problem, not a header edit. Separate time from the array index For input sample index n at 44.1 kHz, time is n/44,100 seconds. Output index m at 48 kHz refers to m/48,000 seconds. The desired output is the value of the same signal at that new time. Treatment of one second of 44.1 kHz input Output sample frames Playback duration Retain 44.1 kHz 44,100 1 second Convert correctly to 48 kHz 48,000 1 second Relabel existing frames as 48 kHz 44,100 0.91875 seconds Relabeling also multiplies every frequency by 48,000/44,100, approximately 1.0884. A 1 kHz tone becomes about 1,088.4 Hz. A correct converter supplies more values for the same original 1 kHz tone. Work out a new value between two old ones Consider a simpler rate doubling: the existing figure on the sampling page represents a 1 kHz sine sampled at 8 kHz. Its first two values are: At 0 ms: 0. At 0.125 ms: approximately +0.7071. A 16 kHz output needs another sample at 0.0625 ms. Because we know the example's exact sine, its correct amplitude is sin(π/8), approximately +0.3827 . Simply averaging the neighbors gives (0 + 0.7071)/2 = +0.3536 . That is an interpolation, but it does not give the correct sine value. The error becomes more consequential for frequencies closer to the sampling limit. A high-quality resampler uses a suitable interpolation filter and a neighborhood of input samples. The values before and after the desired time jointly inform the result. Ideal bandlimited reconstruction uses sinc-shaped contributions from the whole sequence; practical filters approximate that operation using a finite number of samples. The converter does not discover new information in the recording. It evaluates the available, bandlimited signal on another grid. Upsampling to 96 kHz can be useful for a processing or hardware stage without extending the original recording's captured frequency range. Rate reduction needs a narrower signal first Downsampling must satisfy the new sampling condition. Suppose 48 kHz input includes a 23 kHz component and is converted to 44.1 kHz output. The new Nyquist boundary is 22.05 kHz. Retaining that component while sampling at the lower rate can turn it into an alias at 44.1 − 23 = 21.1 kHz . A low-pass filter attenuates such content before the reduced grid is taken. This preserves the wanted lower-frequency band and prevents unsuitable input frequencies from masquerading as different output frequencies. Real filters need a transition region between a passband that they preserve and a stopband that they attenuate. The engineering tradeoff includes how close the passband approaches the limit, residual unwanted energy, computational work, and transient behavior. “Keeps every frequency right up to Nyquist” is not an adequate practical filter description. Increasing the rate also needs filtering to avoid spectral images of the original sampled signal. In both directions, interpolation and filtering are parts of one conversion, rather than optional cleanup afterward. How a converter implements a fractional ratio 48,000/44,100 simplifies to 160/147 . A conceptual rational-rate converter can increase the internal grid by 160, filter, and keep every 147th position. This produces the correct relationship between input and output counts. Inserting zeros during the conceptual increase is a way to prepare a sequence for filtering; those zeros are not supposed to become silent samples in the finished signal. Filtering fills in the values appropriate to the new time positions. A practical polyphase implementation reorganizes the filter into phases so it computes the samples it actually needs. It does not have to construct an enormous intermediate array. That implementation detail explains how an apparently complicated fractional conversion can run efficiently during playback. Account for filter delay and boundaries A filter that uses neighboring samples needs stored input and may require future samples before it can produce the intended output. This creates latency. For illustration, a symmetric 64-tap linear-phase FIR filter has a group delay of (64−1)/2 = 31.5 sample intervals. At a 48 kHz filter rate that is about 0.656 ms. A complete resampler's buffering and boundary handling can add further delay. At the start and end of a finite file, the implementation must handle missing neighbors and flush delayed results. Correct timestamps and output length keep this implementation delay from becoming a missing ending or a permanent audio/video offset. A low-latency filter and one optimized for stronger rejection can therefore differ in more than CPU use. Their choices affect delay and transients as well as frequency response. Follow the conversion in an actual session For an Emby session that changes 44.1 kHz input to 48 kHz output, inspect the stages that require that change: server encoding, the player's decoder/output, or an operating-system mixer. An output fixed at 48 kHz naturally needs a conversion for a 44.1 kHz source. Then distinguish three observed problems: Observation Relevant part of the conversion Pitch and duration both change Samples may have been interpreted at a different rate instead of resampled An unwanted high-frequency tone appears Anti-alias filtering and rate interpretation deserve investigation The sound is aligned differently from picture Filter/buffer delay and timestamp handling are relevant Reducing integer precision during the same operation introduces quantization too. Dither addresses that amplitude-grid conversion; it is a separate operation from calculating the new time grid. See Also Audio Sample Rate Digital Audio Sampling Audio Dithering References FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion Julius O. Smith: Windowed sinc interpolation and sample-rate conversion

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Audio Bit Depth | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Audio Bit Depth Imagine measuring the height of a waveform with a ruler. A finer ruler gives more possible amplitude values over the same range. Integer PCM bit depth is that amplitude precision ; it changes the numerical grid, while sample rate changes the time grid. With N bits there are 2^N bit patterns. For signed integer PCM, these normally represent values from −2^(N−1) through 2^(N−1)−1. Sixteen bits therefore provide −32,768 through +32,767: 65,536 levels. Compare the steps, not just the labels Using a nominal normalized range of −1 to +1, the integer step is 2/2^N. The positive endpoint falls one step below +1 in this convention. Integer precision Levels Normalized step 8-bit 256 0.0078125 16-bit 65,536 About 0.00003052 24-bit 16,777,216 About 0.0000001192 Adding one bit doubles the levels and halves the step. Moving from 16 to 24 bits supplies 256 times as many levels, not merely eight more measurements. Suppose a signal sample should have amplitude 0.001. On the signed 16-bit grid, 0.001 × 32,768 = 32.768, so rounding selects code 33. Reconstructing that code gives 33/32,768 ≈ 0.00100708, an error of about +0.00000708. On the 24-bit grid, the calculation is 0.001 × 8,388,608 = 8,388.608. Rounding selects 8,389 and gives approximately 0.0010000467. The much smaller step allows a closer result. See quantization error for how such errors behave over a waveform. Why processing uses extra precision Even simple volume adjustment can produce values between integer levels. Halving code 33 gives 16.5. If a processor immediately rounds this back to the same integer grid, it loses the fractional part; if it keeps a wider or floating-point working representation, later operations can use it. Mixing, equalization, and repeated level changes create many such intermediate values. Keeping more precision during processing and rounding at the appropriate final conversion limits avoidable cumulative error. Dither controls the behavior of that last rounding rather than making every sample exact. Bit depth and the noise floor Smaller steps can make quantization error smaller relative to the permitted signal range. The often quoted ideal SNR formula, 6.02N + 1.76 dB, describes a full-scale sine and an ideal quantizer with a particular noise model over the full Nyquist bandwidth. It is not a measured dynamic-range guarantee for a microphone, music release, or sound card. A noisy room, microphone electronics, or earlier processing can dominate long before the numerical limit. A 24-bit recording is useful because it can accommodate precision and recording headroom; it need not contain 24 bits of clean musical detail. Recognize precision in a media report A 24-bit sample may occupy a 32-bit storage word. Those spare positions are a storage arrangement, not extra recorded detail. Likewise, 32-bit float uses a significand and exponent, allowing a wide numerical range with different precision behavior from 32-bit integer PCM. A lossless codec can preserve the encoded integer precision. A lossy codec instead reconstructs an approximation, and its decoder must still choose a working sample format. Consequently, a decoder's float or 32-bit output label and the source's original bit depth describe different stages. PCM sample formats shows how to read those working-format names. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Quantization Noise Audio Dithering References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Audio Sample Rate | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Audio Sample Rate Sample rate Samples per channel in one second Time between samples Nyquist frequency 8 kHz 8,000 125 microseconds 4 kHz 44.1 kHz 44,100 22.68 microseconds 22.05 kHz 48 kHz 48,000 20.83 microseconds 24 kHz 96 kHz 96,000 10.42 microseconds 48 kHz Sample rate sets the audio time grid. The interval is 1 divided by the rate. Every channel has the full grid: a 48 kHz six-channel track has 48,000 sample positions per second in each of its six channels. For a sine wave, the number of sample intervals per cycle is sample rate divided by frequency. At 48 kHz, a 1 kHz tone has 48 intervals per cycle; a 10 kHz tone has 4.8. That fractional result is normal: the tone need not complete an integer number of cycles between sample positions. Why half the rate matters The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate. For ordinary audio around zero frequency, ideal reconstruction needs the signal's frequency content restricted below that boundary. The significance is ambiguity , not a rule that high-frequency sound needs a prettier staircase. Calculated example at a deliberately low 1 kHz rate: a 700 Hz sine and an inverted 300 Hz sine give identical samples. The continuous curves differ; the measured dots do not. At sample index n, the first signal is sin(2π × 700 × n/1,000). The second is −sin(2π × 300 × n/1,000). Their phases differ by whole cycles at these instants, giving the same values: Sample index Time Either sampled amplitude 0 0 ms 0 1 1 ms About −0.951 2 2 ms About +0.588 3 3 ms About +0.588 A receiver given only that sequence cannot decide which original sine existed. Recording systems filter before sampling to prevent such ambiguity. Practical filters also require a transition band, so the Nyquist number is an ideal boundary rather than a guaranteed flat recording bandwidth. The rate also gives the samples their duration 44,100 sample frames played at 44,100 per second last one second. Played at 48,000 per second, those same frames last 0.91875 seconds, with every frequency multiplied by 48,000/44,100. That is what changing the declared rate without resampling does: it changes speed and pitch. Proper resampling instead calculates 48,000 values for the same one-second signal, preserving its intended timeline. Read an output rate in the right place A 48 kHz output can carry music originally stored at 44.1 kHz after conversion, or an encoded low-bandwidth voice recording decoded onto that grid. The output rate identifies how fast values are presented, not the frequencies the source actually contains. For an Emby audio report, use the rate to interpret duration, decoder configuration, and conversion. Use bitrate for compressed data demand and bit depth for PCM amplitude precision. Together they describe different parts of the representation. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Resampling Audio Bitrate References Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios Microsoft WAVEFORMATEX: Sample rate, channels, and data rate

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Digital Audio Sampling | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Digital Audio Sampling The dots in this figure are enough to describe the smooth sine wave because we know what kind of waveform is allowed between them . Sampling becomes easier to understand when that condition is made explicit. Calculated example: a 1 kHz sine wave sampled at 8 kHz over two milliseconds. The line is the mathematical signal; the dots are its sampled values. This deliberately low rate makes the positions visible. A microphone first produces a continuously changing electrical signal. Sampling measures its amplitude at regular instants. A digitally generated sound can supply the same sort of sequence directly, without a microphone. Build one cycle For the illustrated signal, one cycle takes 1/1,000 second: one millisecond. An 8 kHz sampler measures every 1/8,000 second: 0.125 ms. There are therefore eight sample intervals in a cycle. Time Fraction of a cycle Sine amplitude 0 ms 0 0 0.125 ms 1/8 About +0.707 0.250 ms 1/4 +1 0.375 ms 3/8 About +0.707 0.500 ms 1/2 0 0.750 ms 3/4 −1 1.000 ms 1 0; the next cycle begins These numbers describe the waveform at particular times. Bit depth determines how accurately each value can be stored; sample rate determines the times. Measuring twice as often and storing each measurement more precisely are independent changes. Why the spaces between dots are not holes in the sound Infinitely many arbitrary curves could pass through a set of dots. To reconstruct a particular continuous signal, we limit its frequency content. For ordinary baseband audio, a signal restricted below half the sample rate can, ideally, be reconstructed from the complete sample sequence. Reconstruction is a filtering operation using the sequence together, not a command to join neighboring dots with straight lines. Each sample contributes to the resulting continuous waveform. In a DAC, practical interpolation and reconstruction filtering perform the corresponding job before the analog signal drives the next stage. The familiar staircase drawing of a held sample voltage is a useful illustration of one intermediate circuit signal. It is not the intended final sound waveform. Protect the condition before measuring If a recording contains frequencies beyond the sampling limit, different signals can produce the same samples. A high-frequency component can then appear as a lower-frequency alias . Once only those ambiguous samples remain, a decoder has no label telling it which of the possible original frequencies was present. An anti-alias filter therefore attenuates unsuitable frequencies before sampling. Real filters need a transition region, so engineering a usable recording bandwidth involves more than choosing a sample-rate number. The alias demonstration on the sample-rate page shows two different sine waves passing through exactly the same sample positions. Apply the time grid to several channels At each stereo time position, a sample frame contains one left value and one right value. A 48 kHz stereo signal has 48,000 sample frames per second: 48,000 values per channel, or 96,000 individual channel values altogether. A compressed soundtrack in an Emby file need not store those values literally. It stores coded information from which a decoder produces them. The resulting sample timeline is what lets sound duration, channel alignment, and picture synchronization remain well defined. See Also Audio Sample Rate Audio Bit Depth PCM Sample Formats References Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: PCM Sample Formats | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: PCM Sample Formats A transcoding log changes from an AAC track to fltp . The sound has not acquired a new compression codec: the decoder has produced floating-point samples for processing, arranged in separate channel planes. A sample format specifies how numbers are represented and laid out . A codec specifies how encoded information reconstructs sound. Keeping those two jobs separate makes a processing log readable. FFmpeg working format Number representation Channel storage s16 Signed 16-bit integers Interleaved s32 Signed 32-bit integer words Interleaved flt 32-bit floating point Interleaved fltp 32-bit floating point Planar dblp 64-bit floating point Planar FFmpeg's native working sample formats use the host machine's byte order. Stored PCM codec names and container properties can additionally specify a particular byte order. Repack the same stereo samples Consider three stereo time positions: Time position Left Right 0 0.10 −0.10 1 0.20 −0.20 2 0.30 −0.30 An interleaved array stores 0.10, −0.10, 0.20, −0.20, 0.30, −0.30 . A planar arrangement stores a left plane 0.10, 0.20, 0.30 and a right plane −0.10, −0.20, −0.30 . Every value and its time/channel association remain the same. Correctly repacking these arrays changes memory organization without changing audio. Misreading the planar arrays as interleaved would instead assign values to the wrong channel and time. Planar processing is convenient for algorithms that operate on one channel at a time. Interleaving is convenient for interfaces that consume complete multichannel sample frames. A pipeline can legitimately convert between them several times. Convert integer values to float For signed 16-bit PCM, dividing a code by 32,768 maps it to the customary nominal floating-point range. Code +16,384 becomes +0.5; −32,768 becomes −1; +32,767 becomes approximately +0.9999695. The integer format has an asymmetric positive endpoint. It is normal for its largest positive code to map slightly below +1. A reverse conversion must handle the endpoints, rounding, and any values beyond the permitted integer range. Floating-point numbers combine a significand with an exponent. This allows processing results such as +1.2 to remain representable even though they exceed nominal audio full scale. A later stage can reduce gain before converting them to a bounded output format. If instead +1.2 reaches a stage that clips at +1, the numerical convenience of float has not prevented output distortion. Float processing also supplies fractional precision for mixing or gain operations. It is not a claim that the original recording contained 32 useful integer bits. Read valid bits and byte order separately A system can store 24 valid bits inside a 32-bit word. For example, WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE describes valid precision independently from its storage container. The unused positions are not new recorded detail. A working-format label such as s32 can therefore describe the storage of decoded 24-bit audio. Byte order is another axis. The 16-bit value 0x1234 has bytes 34 12 in little-endian order and 12 34 in big-endian order. Reading the wrong order turns 0x1234, decimal 4,660, into 0x3412, decimal 13,330. Every byte can arrive intact while the sample value is wrong. Channel roles are independently described by the channel layout and order . Correct byte order and storage format do not identify which samples belong to the center or surrounds. When following an Emby processing log, read a chain such as encoded AAC → planar float → downmix → integer PCM output as successive representations and operations. The working format explains the arithmetic at that stage; the input codec and output presentation tell you where those values came from and how they will be played. See Also Audio Bit Depth Digital Audio Sampling Audio Channel Order References FFmpeg: Audio sample formats Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.title: Understanding Audio in Media | Emby Learn
articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.keywords: Understanding Audio in Media A movie has three English soundtracks: 7.1 surround, stereo commentary, and audio description. Which one should you select? Start with what the track contains , then consider how it will play on your listening system. The most impressive channel count is irrelevant if you have selected the director discussing the film instead of the film's dialogue. Read a track as a presentation Each audio track is a separate timed stream in the media file. Its language, title, and accessibility role help identify the intended presentation. Its codec and channel layout describe how that presentation is represented. Part of an example track The question it answers English — Main Is this the language and presentation I want? E-AC-3 Which decoding format is required? 5.1 Which channel roles are in the compatible channel presentation? 48 kHz What sample timeline does decoded audio use? 640 kbit/s How much encoded audio data is carried per second? Those numbers are not different ways of expressing one quality setting. Changing 5.1 to stereo combines spatial channels. Changing 48 kHz to another sample rate changes the time grid. Changing the encoded bitrate gives a compressed-audio encoder a different data budget. Each operation solves a different problem. A container keeps the tracks together with timing and metadata. That is how a viewer can switch language or commentary while the video remains the same. The selected soundtrack must stay aligned with the picture even when its packets and video packets represent different amounts of time. Follow one soundtrack to the speakers Suppose you choose the 5.1 film track and listen on a stereo television: Emby selects that track for delivery. If its codec and packaging fit the app, the server may send the stored audio. A decoder reconstructs audio samples for the track's channels. This might happen in the player or during server conversion. A downmix combines those channels into two outputs, including center-channel dialogue that would be lost by simply discarding all but front left and right. The television converts the final signal into sound. On a compatible surround system, the same track can instead keep its separate channel presentation. An object-based soundtrack can additionally supply spatial information that a renderer uses for the connected speaker or headphone arrangement. This is why the source format, Emby's delivery method , and a receiver's input display can have different labels. “PCM” at the receiver can mean that decoding already happened in the player. “Stereo” can describe the final output even though the stored soundtrack has six channels. Use sampling to understand the numbers representing sound, channels to understand its spatial arrangement, or the playback path to locate a conversion between the file and what you hear. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Bitrate Multichannel Audio References ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.title: ASF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.keywords: ASF Container The Windows Media file extensions WMV and WMA often sit above an ASF package. Advanced Systems Format stores descriptions, timed media packets, and optional navigation as identified objects. ASF objects begin with a GUID identifying their kind and a size indicating their extent. A reader can recognize the descriptions it implements and use the object size to navigate through the structure. Top-level object What the reader obtains Header File properties, stream descriptions, and optional metadata Data Encoded media in packets Index objects Time-based access to packet positions Initialize, then deliver packets The Header appears first and describes the source and its streams. The stream properties identify the media representations and setup needed to decode them. Global properties include information such as packet counts, size conventions, and duration. The Data object follows. Its packets have parsing information and payloads associated with one or more streams. Packet presentation timing helps organize their delivery. A reader routes the appropriate payloads to video or audio decoding rather than asking a decoder to consume ASF object headers. This separation explains a readable Windows Media file whose picture still needs conversion for an Emby app: the server can identify the ASF structure and its codec, while the receiving framework may need a different encoded representation or package. How a later position is found An index can map a requested time to a useful packet position. Without appropriate index information, finding that time can involve more reading or scanning. Sequential playback and fast random access consequently exercise different parts of the same package. A new mux can change the packet organization, timing description, and navigation while copying suitable encoded media. Descriptive tags require their own destination representation. The copied codec name describes the media branch, not every ASF object retained by the output. Recognized content and protected content ASF can also describe content-protection information. Recognition lets software explain what kind of resource it has encountered; obtaining usable media may additionally require an authorized decryption path. An object parser or a new filename does not supply that authorization. For an older collection, follow this sequence: Header interpretation, Data reading, source decoding, and the particular output needed. It places a failure at an actual boundary instead of attributing it broadly to “Windows Media.” See Also Containers and Codecs Packet Timestamps Container Indexes and Seeking References Microsoft: ASF file structure Microsoft ASF Specification 1.20.06: archived download catalogue

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: AIFF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: AIFF Container An AIFF stores sample descriptions and sound data in separate chunks. Its outer FORM structure identifies the format; COMM describes the audio, and SSND holds its sound data and positioning fields. Chunk Reader use COMM Obtain channels, sample-frame count, precision, and sample rate SSND Locate the actual sound samples, accounting for its offset information MARK, where present Read named positions in the recording Descriptive/instrument chunks Interpret additional recording or instrument information The reader follows sizes through the chunk structure. It does not infer where samples begin solely from the filename or one assumed header length. Interpret the bytes in the declared order Original AIFF PCM stores multibyte values in big-endian order: the most significant byte comes first. For a positive 16-bit value of 291, hexadecimal 0123, the stored bytes are 01 followed by 23. Swapping their interpretation produces hexadecimal 2301, or 8,961, a very different sample. This does not give big-endian audio a sound-quality advantage. It specifies how bytes represent the same numbers. A proper conversion into a little-endian PCM arrangement swaps storage order as required while preserving the decoded values. For stereo, one sample frame contains a value for each channel. If COMM reports 44,100 sample frames at 44.1 kHz, the audio lasts one second. At 16 bits per channel, the uncompressed sample data occupies 44,100 × 2 × 2 = 176,400 bytes, before container structures. AIFF-C describes more encodings AIFF-C extends the description with an encoding identifier, allowing compressed audio and further representations. The extra letter therefore changes what the reader must interpret, rather than simply naming a smaller version of the same original PCM layout. To compare an AIFF master with a WAV listening copy in an Emby collection, compare decoded format, rate, channel layout, and complete duration. A conversion preserving those samples can still write different bytes and different tags because the destination structures differ. An accurate sample comparison begins after each container and byte arrangement has been interpreted. Comparing the raw file bytes would conflate the sample values with their storage order, headers, and descriptive chunks. See Also WAV and RIFF PCM Sample Formats CAF: Core Audio Format References Apple Audio Interchange File Format 1.2: original specification mirror Apple: AIFF file type

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: CAF: Core Audio Format | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: CAF: Core Audio Format A recording can outgrow a classic 32-bit chunk length, and compressed audio can contain packets whose byte sizes vary. Core Audio Format (CAF) describes both the large-file storage and the packet information needed to interpret such audio. CAF uses 64-bit chunk size fields. The Audio Description identifies the encoding, sample rate, channel count, and packet/sample conventions. The Audio Data holds the actual content. Other chunks can supply layout, markers, metadata, and a Packet Table. When a fixed calculation is enough For ordinary PCM with a known number of bytes per sample frame, the reader can translate a frame index into a data offset by multiplication. The same logic works for packets when their byte length and frame count are fixed and known. Variable packets require more information. Suppose three invented encoded packets occupy 180, 240, and 190 bytes. Their data offsets from the start of this packet sequence are 0, 180, and 420 bytes. A reader cannot locate packet 3 by multiplying one assumed length by two; it needs the intervening sizes or equivalent indexing information. Packet Bytes Start offset 1 180 0 2 240 180 3 190 420 CAF's Packet Table provides packet descriptions as needed for variable-size or variable-duration arrangements. The description and table together let the reader locate and count the audio it will decode. Decoded frames and valid frames A compressed codec can produce initial priming frames and trailing remainder frames beyond the intended recording. CAF can describe those alongside the number of valid frames. For an illustrative 48 kHz case, suppose three packets decode 1,024 frames each, with 256 priming frames and 256 remainder frames. The valid recording contains 3,072 − 256 − 256 = 2,560 frames, lasting approximately 53.333 ms. The encoded packet count alone would instead suggest 64 ms. These fields describe which reconstructed samples belong to the presentation. They are not another codec compressing the audio a second time. The production file and its listening copy CAF's size and packet conventions are useful in capture or editing workflows, including arrangements where data continues to be written. Its description can carry different encodings, so the playback requirements come from the actual encoding and layout inside. If a CAF production source is to be used in an Emby collection, preserve its intended valid audio interval when making a more convenient listening copy.
