The syntax associates fields through a shared entry number: [playlist] File1=Music/Opening.mp3 Title1=Opening song Length1=180 File2=Music/Second.mp3 Title2=Second song Length2=240 NumberOfEntries=2 Version=2 File1, Title1, and Length1 describe one entry. The second group describes another. Length values conventionally use seconds; −1 commonly represents an unknown duration, such as a continuing radio source. Reading an entry The reader obtains the location from FileN and uses TitleN for its description. Replacing “Opening song” with a new title changes how the entry is displayed, not what plays. Replacing File1 changes its destination even if the visible title remains unchanged. For a local relative path, the playlist's location supplies the base relationship. Keeping the playlist and its referenced Music folder together preserves that relationship when the collection moves. A remote location instead needs the relevant network access each time playback obtains it. A conversion to M3U writes the locations in that format's sequence and translates useful titles or lengths. Renaming .pls to .m3u does not perform this parse-and-write operation. PLS is useful to recognize when a media shortcut opens in a desktop player but is mistaken for a saved song. The contents of FileN identify the actual source; its availability and format can then be examined separately from the playlist text. See Also M3U Playlists Media Pointer Files: STRM References VideoLAN: PLS playlist reader implementation

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: Media Pointer Files: STRM | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: Media Pointer Files: STRM A STRM file lets an Emby library item point to media stored elsewhere. The pointer is small because it stores a location; the movie's encoded tracks remain at that destination. The library description, the pointer, and the media are three different objects. Follow the address through the system. Emby recognizes the named library item and reads its text pointer. The media-opening path obtains the referenced source. That source is then examined for its tracks and delivered through an appropriate playback route. The STRM documentation defines the supported pointer contents and organization. Two addresses that look similar can return different data A website's video page supplies HTML and player code. The player can make another request for the actual movie or a streaming playlist. A pointer needs the media location supported by the opening path, rather than an arbitrary webpage that happens to display a video. Similarly, a shared-file path is interpreted from the environment that opens it. A drive letter visible on an administrator's desktop may not exist for a server service. A network path can identify the same source more clearly, but access still depends on that process's credentials and connectivity. This is a location-resolution question before any codec is decoded. What is preserved when the library is copied? Copying the STRM file preserves its text address. Copying local library descriptions can preserve the displayed item. Neither operation copies the distant recording. The pointer's storage size therefore does not represent the movie's size, and an offline copy of the pointer does not provide offline movie bytes. If the destination changes or an expiring address stops granting access, the item can remain visible while playback can no longer obtain its source. Update the address relationship or source availability; the library's retained title is not evidence that the media was fetched. A useful failure trace follows the same boundaries: recognized item, readable pointer, resolved address, returned media rather than HTML, then source initialization . Once the actual media is obtained, its container and selected tracks determine the playback work just as they do for an ordinary local source. See Also What Is a Media File? M3U Playlists References RFC 3986: URI syntax

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.264 / AVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.264 / AVC Video H.264 , AVC , and MPEG-4 Part 10 name the same video coding standard. It defines the instructions a decoder follows to reconstruct compressed pictures, rather than a particular encoder's recipe for choosing those instructions. A film in an MP4 file, a camera clip in another container, and a television stream can all carry AVC. Their packaging supplies the coded track to the same kind of reconstruction process. An Emby session can show AVC at both input and output when the server has decoded and encoded a new AVC representation. The reconstruction steps below explain what differs from copying the encoded track. The coded data comes in units AVC's Network Abstraction Layer units , or NAL units, organize the bitstream. Some carry coded picture regions called slices. Others supply configuration or additional information. A coded picture can contain several slice units. The media packet or container sample that carries them is a packaging boundary; the AVC units describe the coding boundary. Before reconstructing a slice, the decoder needs the applicable sequence parameter set (SPS) and picture parameter set (PPS) . These describe such things as the coded grid, permitted sample format, picture-order behavior, and relevant coding options. A slice identifies the parameters and coding decisions it uses. This is why extracting one piece of picture data without its configuration does not necessarily provide a complete decoder input. Divide the picture into reconstruction work AVC's basic macroblock footprint covers 16 × 16 brightness positions . The picture is divided into those regions, with further partitions for prediction and transforms. For a progressive 1920 × 1080 presentation, the coded macroblock grid is 120 columns by 68 rows: 8,160 macroblocks , representing a 1920 × 1088 grid before display cropping. The crop describes the visible picture boundary; the coding grid determines this part of the decoder's work. Different regions can use different prediction choices. An edge, a flat area, and a moving object need not receive the same description. Construct a predictor An intra-coded region predicts from available reconstructed samples in the same picture. For example, values along an upper boundary can be extended in a chosen direction to form a candidate block. An inter-coded region identifies a decoded reference picture and motion information telling the decoder where to sample it. Fractional positions use the interpolation rules specified by AVC. A region can combine permitted reference information according to its coding type and mode. The encoder searches for a useful predictor. The decoder instead follows the predictor encoded in the syntax. Its task is deterministic reconstruction from the supplied information. Reconstruct the correction The source region usually differs from its predictor. The encoder represents that difference as a residual and can transform it into coefficients describing patterns within blocks. The decoder entropy-decodes those coefficients, reconstructs their scale from the quantization parameters, and applies the specified inverse transform. It then adds the resulting correction to the predictor. AVC uses integer transform operations for common 4×4 residual blocks; selected profiles permit additional tools such as an 8×8 transform. Quantization can discard precision, so the decoded correction need not equal the original source difference. The compression walkthrough demonstrates that approximation numerically. The entropy-coding mode is another syntax choice. CAVLC and CABAC use different coding procedures, so the decoder needs the selected mode even when both ultimately reconstruct the same kind of sample array. Filter and retain the reconstructed picture AVC can apply its in-loop deblocking filter to reduce selected discontinuities between coded regions. “In-loop” matters: the appropriately filtered reconstruction can become a reference for later pictures. The encoder reconstructs the same result locally when preparing those later predictions. Otherwise it would predict from samples the decoder does not have. The decoded-picture buffer retains references and pictures waiting for their display times. An anchor can be decoded before a B-picture that will appear earlier on screen. Picture-order information and presentation timing restore the intended viewing sequence after the dependency work. Read the profile and the names you encounter Profiles restrict this tool/sample set. Baseline, Main, High, and High 10 are different permitted AVC representations. Levels constrain picture size, throughput, buffering, and other resources. Label Place in the process H.264 / AVC The bitstream and reconstruction standard x264 One encoder implementation choosing valid AVC instructions High / High 10 Profile constraints on tools and sample formats A container's AVC track identifier The wrapper's description of its coded video An x264-made track can be decoded by another conforming AVC implementation. The encoder's search effort and quality settings change which valid representation it creates, while the decoder follows that representation. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles H.265 / HEVC Video Video Encoder Presets References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.265 / HEVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.265 / HEVC Video H.265 , or High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) , represents pictures with a flexible block structure and prediction/correction tools designed to use data efficiently. A common place to encounter it is a UHD film or recording, where there are many picture positions to describe. The way a picture is divided helps explain that efficiency. Start with a coding tree A stream can organize the picture in 64 × 64 coding-tree blocks . An encoder does not have to give every part of such a region the same small-block description. It can subdivide where detail or movement makes a smaller region useful. Imagine a 64 × 64 region with mostly smooth background and a detailed lower-right corner. One illustrative tree splits it into four 32 × 32 regions, then splits only the lower-right one into four 16 × 16 regions: 64 × 64 ├─ 32 × 32, retained ├─ 32 × 32, retained ├─ 32 × 32, retained └─ 32 × 32 ├─ 16 × 16 ├─ 16 × 16 ├─ 16 × 16 └─ 16 × 16 There are seven leaf coding blocks. Their areas still total the original region: 3 × 32² + 4 × 16² = 4,096 = 64². This is a possible partition illustration, not the mandatory layout of every HEVC picture. The stream's coding parameters and rules determine its allowed tree choices. The larger flat regions can use fewer region descriptions, while the detailed corner gets more local choices. Subdivision therefore follows the information the encoder is trying to represent rather than a single grid size chosen for every scene. Prediction and transform divisions have different jobs A coding block's prediction describes what reconstructed scene information can be reused. Intra modes use same-picture boundaries, including directional or smoothly varying predictions. Inter modes use decoded reference pictures and motion information. The transform division describes how the remaining correction is represented. A coding region and its residual transform blocks are related but do not have to be one identical subdivision. The decoder follows the supplied tree and modes to form predictions and reconstruct corrections. Quantization selects the precision of those corrections. Extra partition choices can help an encoder describe a region effectively, while the rate-control settings decide how much data it is allowed to spend. A good tree choice does not remove the need to encode changed or unpredictable content. Grain, newly revealed scenery, and complicated movement still require information. Finish the reconstruction inside the coding loop HEVC includes in-loop deblocking and sample-adaptive offset (SAO) tools. Deblocking addresses selected discontinuities around coded block boundaries. SAO can apply signaled corrections to categories of reconstructed samples, such as brightness bands or local edge relationships. These operations help form the reconstruction that later prediction references. The decoder must apply the applicable signaled behavior, and the encoder's reconstruction loop must make corresponding reference samples available for its next decisions. The decoded picture then participates in reference storage and presentation ordering, much as the dependency principles described in the reference-picture and GOP articles. Identify the sample representation Common HEVC profile Sample depth Sampling Main 8-bit 4:2:0 Main 10 8-bit or 10-bit 4:2:0 These are selected profiles. Additional HEVC profiles define other permitted sample/tool sets. Main 10 is common for HDR delivery, but its name describes sample precision and coding permissions. The transfer/color information establishes how those values represent SDR or HDR light. HDR10 combines the relevant HDR interpretation and metadata in common HEVC delivery workflows. x265 is one encoder that chooses an HEVC representation. A hardware encoder is another implementation of that job. Their effort and rate-control decisions can produce different pictures and sizes within the standard. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Video Codec Profiles HDR10 How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-2 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-2 Video An older television recording or disc-derived film often carries MPEG-2 Video , standardized as ITU-T H.262 and ISO/IEC 13818-2. Its compressed track describes how to build pictures; a transport or program stream supplies the packaging around that track. To understand the format, follow one of its coded pictures. Read the sequence and picture information Sequence information establishes the picture grid and relevant timing/format parameters. Picture information identifies the coding type and applicable reconstruction choices. In common 8-bit 4:2:0 material, a macroblock covers a 16 × 16 brightness region . Its brightness corrections are represented in four 8 × 8 blocks , with corresponding color-difference blocks. The encoder uses a discrete cosine transform (DCT) to represent correction patterns as coefficients. Quantization reduces their precision. The decoder reconstructs those coefficients, applies the inverse transform, and adds the correction to the picture's predictor. The block representation explains familiar low-bitrate artifacts: lost fine patterns or disagreeing coded regions can reveal softened texture and block-shaped boundaries. Follow the I, P, and B pictures An I-picture reconstructs its picture content without a temporal sample reference. A P-picture can predict from an available anchor and encode what changed. A B-picture can use the permitted prediction from surrounding anchors, which have to be decoded first. For a visible sequence I0, B1, B2, P3 , the decoder can reconstruct I0 and P3 before B1 and B2. It then shows them in their original viewing order. MPEG-2's I/P anchor structure differs from modern structures that can use B-pictures as references. The GOP explanation gives the general dependency trace; the specific codec's rules determine the legal graph. An entry at a GOP boundary also needs appropriate access handling if picture dependencies extend across it. Interpret a broadcast picture's time MPEG-2 can represent progressive and interlaced material. A reported 25 fps recording can mean 25 field pairs containing 50 native field times/s , rather than 25 complete progressive camera moments. Its picture and sequence signaling guide field presentation. Film transfers can instead use repeated-field timing to place a progressive source on a television cadence. The reconstruction task is then cadence recovery , while native interlaced movement calls for deinterlacing if the output is progressive. These differences matter when creating a new playback version: preserving a film's picture sequence and preserving a sport recording's field movement are different jobs. Identify the surrounding names Name Place in the recording MPEG-2 Video / H.262 Picture compression MPEG Transport Stream Packetized carriage of the video and other streams MPEG Program Stream Another systems packaging form MPEG Audio Separate soundtrack coding A TS file can carry video codecs other than MPEG-2, and a MPEG-2 picture track can be carried in other supported packaging. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References ITU-T H.262: MPEG-2 Video

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid Label on an older video What it identifies MPEG-4 Part 2 / MPEG-4 Visual The video coding standard Xvid An implementation of MPEG-4 Visual, commonly Advanced Simple Profile Classic MPEG-4-based DivX A branded implementation of this coding family AVI A possible container carrying the coded track H.264 / AVC / MPEG-4 Part 10 A different video standard These distinctions make a legacy AVI collection easier to interpret. “MPEG-4” names a standards family; Part 2 identifies this visual format. The DivX brand also covers other formats, including AVC in DivX Plus. Picture coding in the common rectangular form Common Simple/Advanced Simple video represents rectangular pictures with block-based prediction and corrections. Independently coded pictures establish scene content, while inter-predicted pictures reuse reconstructed references. The residual correction is transformed into block coefficients and quantized before coding. The decoder reverses the coded operations and adds the correction to the selected predictor. A newer encoder library does not change the decoder's job into a different standard: it chooses another permitted representation of the same format. The profile determines which tool set is available. Advanced Simple Profile (ASP) adds useful choices beyond the simpler form, including B-picture coding and enhanced motion tools. Two motion options with concrete meanings Quarter-pixel motion compensation allows finer reference positioning. An integer displacement selects an existing sample location; a quarter-position displacement requires the codec's interpolation to form a predictor between grid points. This can better follow movement that falls between whole positions. Global motion compensation (GMC) can describe a shared transformation across a larger portion of a scene. A camera pan or related movement can make many block displacements follow one common relationship, instead of describing every region solely as an unrelated local shift. Those modes change the encoded instructions. The Xvid project documents ASP support for them, but a particular file can use a narrower selection. A decoder must implement the modes actually present. Read the track rather than its filename FourCC labels such as XVID and DX50 help identify a container's track and its intended format association. They do not contain the prediction and transform operations themselves. A classic MPEG-4 Visual track moved into another supported wrapper still contains MPEG-4 Visual instructions. Turning it into AVC requires source decoding and a new encoding process; changing “Part 2” to “Part 10” in a label does not perform those operations. For an Emby library migration, inspect the actual codec, profile and coding features before deciding whether the work is repackaging or video conversion. The name table establishes the family, and the tool descriptions establish what its decoder needs to do. articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.266 / VVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.266 / VVC Video H.266 , also called Versatile Video Coding (VVC) , extends block-based picture coding with additional ways to divide, predict, and reconstruct regions. Its aim is to give encoders useful choices for different scenes and delivery uses. The “versatile” part becomes concrete when looking at a region's shape. Fit the coding regions to the picture A VVC picture can use a 128 × 128 coding-tree footprint and subdivide it into smaller coding regions. Alongside a four-way square split, its multi-type tree can use binary and ternary splits. For an illustrative 64 × 64 region: Split Resulting regions Quad Four 32 × 32 squares Vertical binary Two 32 × 64 rectangles Vertical ternary 16 × 64, 32 × 64, and 16 × 64 rectangles The ternary regions cover the same area: 16 × 64 + 32 × 64 + 16 × 64 = 4,096 = 64². The middle region can receive one coding description while narrower regions around it use others. A tall moving subject, a sharp vertical boundary, and broad flat surroundings can benefit from different region shapes. These are coding possibilities, not a compulsory layout. The stream's tree-size, depth, and split restrictions determine which choice is permitted at a particular point. The decoder reads the selected structure and reconstructs its leaves. Describe more than a uniform shift A basic motion vector translates a reference region by one displacement. Real camera movement can also rotate or zoom a region, making the displacement vary across it. VVC includes motion tools that can describe such varying relationships, including affine prediction. Rather than assuming every point in a region moves identically, a motion model can determine related displacements at different locations. Other prediction choices and coded residuals still provide the information needed to reconstruct the target. The benefit is a potentially better predictor for that region. A better predictor leaves less correction to describe. A poor model still needs larger corrections or another coding choice. The encoder explores; the decoder follows More region shapes and prediction tools give an encoder a larger set of candidates to evaluate. Its search must balance reconstructed-picture error against the bits needed for tree decisions, motion information, and corrections. The decoder does not repeat that entire search. It follows the signaled candidates, but it must implement their syntax, interpolation, transforms, filtering, and reference rules. This is why a HEVC decoder cannot simply treat VVC as another HEVC profile. Compression efficiency comes from the selected representation and settings. To measure a particular saving, compare encodes of the same source under an appropriate picture-quality evaluation; the standard's name does not supply a fixed percentage. Put the format into a playback path For direct playback, a receiving app needs a usable VVC decoder and compatible extraction/presentation of that stream. For conversion into another codec, the server needs the VVC input decoder first: VVC source → VVC reconstruction → processing → target encoder → target playback decoder. The target encoder cannot bypass the source reconstruction. The source's profile, workload, and packaging determine that input job, while the output format determines the client's job. For a VVC file in an Emby library, inspect the actual server and app implementations at those boundaries. The format explanation describes the work that needs to exist; it does not declare a particular Emby version or device to implement it. See Also H.265 / HEVC Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.266: Versatile video coding

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHD Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHD Video A legacy DNxHD name often includes a number such as 115, 120, or 145. Read it with the recording's picture format and frame rate. Those are nominal rate-oriented mode names, rather than a quality score that can be transferred unchanged to any raster. DNxHD is the established HD production use of the VC-3 coding family. Its independently coded pictures support editing and exchange without a long temporal prediction chain. A picture rate changes the data rate Avid's published HD bandwidth table gives a 1920 ×1080 SQ example with 602,112 coded bytes per frame . Using that fixed frame size: Picture rate Calculation Video rate 24000/1001 fps 602,112 ×24000/1001 ×8 Approximately 115.490 Mb/s 25 fps 602,112 ×25 ×8 120.4224 Mb/s 30000/1001 fps 602,112 ×30000/1001 ×8 Approximately 144.363 Mb/s Calculated from this published frame-size example, not a rule that every historical file carrying a115/120/145 label has exactly that payload. The per-picture representation is unchanged in the calculation. More pictures per second require more data each second. This explains why legacy nominal rates need the frame-rate context. For 25 fps, the byte rate is 15,052,800 bytes/s , or 15.0528 decimal MB/s, approximately 14.36 MiB/s. Avid's current naming table explicitly uses the binary MiB/s convention. Data units matter when comparing that number with a network or storage description. The coded mode is more than its rate name A decoder needs the applicable picture dimensions, sampling/precision and coding-mode information. VC-3 picture coding transforms and quantizes within-picture regions, then codes their coefficient information. Its mode identifiers and frame structure select the reconstruction behavior. The result is a lossy production picture with convenient independent access. Its quality depends on the source and chosen coding representation, while its nominal rate helps plan storage and transfer. A metadata inspector's broad codec name is only one field in that description. For example, FFmpeg groups DNxHD and DNxHR profiles within its dnxhd implementation. Inspecting the profile and raster distinguishes the actual representation even if that implementation family name is shared. Read legacy and current names in context Avid's newer naming scheme uses Avid DNx , removing the HD, HR and GX suffixes. It retains familiar quality-level names and adds broader capabilities and customizable rates. An older DNxHD file still contains its original mode. The current name does not rewrite its bits. The related DNxHR label identifies resolution-independent production workflows, while the newer unified codec should be read with its applicable specification and implementation. When using a legacy production copy as a source for an Emby viewing encode, keep its complete raster/rate/profile description attached to the file. That records the actual reconstruction input, while the delivery copy can have its own codec and data allocation. See Also Avid DNxHR Video Apple ProRes Video Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Generation Loss References SMPTE ST 2019-1: VC-3 picture compression and data stream format (2016) Avid: DNx naming scheme and data rates Avid: DNx SDK and specification overview Avid: DNxHR and HD coded-frame bandwidth table

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHR Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHR Video A production needs to edit pictures larger or differently shaped than traditional fixed HD modes. DNxHR supplies resolution-independent production workflows in the VC-3 family, retaining independently coded pictures while extending the useful raster choices. That does not give one fixed data rate to the letters “HR.” The chosen picture size, quality representation and picture rate determine how much data the source supplies. Follow a UHD frame-size example Avid's published legacy UHD table gives 3,641,344 coded bytes per frame for its 3840 ×2160 HQ/HQX example. At 25 fps: 3,641,344 ×25 =91,033,600 bytes/s. At 50 fps: 3,641,344 ×50 =182,067,200 bytes/s. Declared example Decimal byte rate Binary byte rate UHD example at 25 fps 91.0336 MB/s Approximately 86.8164 MiB/s Same coded frame size at 50 fps 182.0672 MB/s Approximately 173.6328 MiB/s The 25 fps case is 728.2688 Mb/s when expressed in decimal bits per second. This is a calculated production-data example from the published frame size, excluding additional wrapper/audio traffic. It is not the rate of every DNxHR file. Avid's current data-rate table uses MiB/s explicitly. Multiplying the published byte count first makes the unit conversion transparent and helps compare it with other storage or delivery numbers. Select a production representation Familiar level Role suggested by its name LB Low-bandwidth production/proxy representation SQ Standard quality HQ High quality HQX High quality extended 444 Higher-fidelity color representation A smaller proxy can make an editing session easier to handle, while finishing can return to the retained higher-quality source. Independent pictures provide direct frame access in both roles; quantization and coding choices determine the picture information retained. The sample-format permissions belong to the actual codec generation and mode. The names alone should not be used to impose historical 8-/10-bit restrictions on newer Avid DNx output. The newer name is Avid DNx Avid now uses Avid DNx without the HD, HR orGX suffixes, with its updated quality-level and capability scheme. Its newer implementation offers broader precision/alpha options and adjustable rates within the defined levels. The old DNxHR label remains useful for existing files, older exports and the historical specification. Record the actual raster, rate, profile and sample format when distinguishing those sources. A conversion for Emby viewing begins by reconstructing that production source. A delivery codec can exploit temporal relationships between its pictures and choose a much smaller viewing-data budget. The independently coded source remains the finishing input, while that output is a separate presentation designed for delivery. articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: DV Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: DV Video When a digital tape transfer copies DV data , it can preserve the tape's existing compressed representation. The computer is receiving the encoded video, audio, and associated recording data rather than necessarily making a new picture encode. That distinction explains both the value of a copied transfer and its familiar large file rate. What DV25 counts Common consumer SD DV has roughly 25 Mb/s of coded video . A complete DV data stream includes more than the video payload. Common consumer system Stored picture grid Frame rate 525/60 720 × 480 30000/1001, approximately 29.97 fps 625/50 720 × 576 25 fps Selected SD forms, not every professional or HD member of the DV family. The system's 525/625 line designation includes lines beyond the active stored picture. Its complete DV frame is organized in Digital Interface (DIF) blocks , which provide the transferable structure. Count a complete frame A DIF block has 80 bytes . A sequence contains 150 blocks , allocated as: Section Blocks in one sequence Header 1 Subcode 2 Video auxiliary 3 Audio 9 Video 135 The total is 150 . The 25-Mb/s structure has ten such sequences per 525/60 frame or twelve per 625/50 frame: 525/60: 80 × 150 × 10 = 120,000 bytes/frame . 625/50: 80 × 150 × 12 = 144,000 bytes/frame . For the 25 fps form, that is 144,000 × 25 = 3,600,000 bytes/s , or 28.8 Mb/s , for the complete stream. One hour is 12.96 decimal GB before an additional file wrapper's overhead. The apparent disagreement with “DV25” is thus a difference in what is being counted. The complete representation carries audio and structural/auxiliary data alongside its coded picture information. Reconstruct the independently coded picture DV picture compression works within a frame rather than relying on a long picture-to-picture prediction chain. This gives editing software direct access to individual recorded pictures once their data is located. The ordinary picture coding is lossy. Copying the DV bytes avoids another video-encoding generation; it preserves the camera's encoded result rather than changing that result into an uncompressed original. An export that decodes DV and then makes H.264 is a new representation. The two jobs can be useful for different purposes: retaining the transferred source and creating a delivery copy. Present the source picture correctly The reconstructed raster also needs its display interpretation. Standard-definition DV often uses nonsquare pixel presentation, and the same stored dimensions can describe different intended aspect ratios. Aspect information supplies that geometry. Native interlaced recordings contain two field capture times in each frame. For progressive presentation, field order and the chosen reconstruction cadence determine how their motion is retained. This is the information a playback or conversion stage needs from the transferred recording. A correctly copied DV source preserves that data for an Emby playback version whose picture shape and field motion can then be interpreted deliberately. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Video Field Order Deinterlacing References SMPTE ST 314: DV-based audio, data, and video at 25 and 50 Mb/s IEC 61834-2: Consumer DV standard-definition recording format

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: FFV1 Lossless Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: FFV1 Lossless Video FFV1 preserves the sample values supplied to its encoder. Its compression comes from prediction and compact coding of exact corrections, rather than rounding away the parts that require more bits. The equality is between codec input and reconstructed output in the same sample representation. Calculate the specified predictor For an ordinary 8-bit sample example, let: l , the reconstructed left neighbor, be 40. t , the reconstructed upper neighbor, be 42. tl , the upper-left neighbor, be 41. FFV1's median predictor is: median(l, t, l + t − tl). Here the three candidates are 40,42,41 , so the median is 41 . If the actual sample is 44, the encoded residual is 44 −41 =3 . Decode that exact residual and add it to the same predictor: 41 +3 =44 . The local difference estimate can adapt to edges. With left 40, top 70 and upper-left 30, the extrapolated candidate is 80. The median of 40, 70 and 80 is 70, so the predictor stays within the range supplied by the two immediate neighbors. The values demonstrate the specified ordinary-sample rule. The RFC defines separate handling for certain 16-bit coding cases and for slice borders. Use context to code the residual Nearby sample differences describe whether a region is smooth, changing gradually, or crossing an edge. FFV1 uses such context information to select coding behavior for residuals. A smooth area can contain many predictable small corrections. The coder can describe those common events compactly. Grain or noise leaves less predictable residual data and may require more bits. Either way, the correction is retained exactly. A different compression result does not select a different decoded picture quality. The lossless coding example illustrates this principle with a small reversible prefix rule. FFV1's actual range/Golomb coding and context rules are defined in its specification rather than by that toy code. Slices and coding state Version 3 organizes a frame into slices with relevant headers, sample content and footer information. Dividing the picture provides independent regional work and a useful boundary for error checking. The decoder also needs configuration and entropy-coder state. An FFV1 keyframe initializes the applicable coding states. In this format, “no temporal sample prediction” should not be confused with “any packet can be decoded without its coding configuration or state.” RFC 9043 defines versions 0, 1 and 3, including how version 3 configuration is carried by supporting containers such as Matroska. That supplies the information needed to interpret each coded frame's samples. Verify reconstruction and integrity separately Check Question it answers Compare decoded samples with the encoder input Did this round trip preserve the same values? Validate the configuration CRC Is the stored configuration consistent with its checksum? Validate enabled version 3 slice CRCs Are the coded slice bytes consistent with their checksums? A CRC detects corruption; it does not contain the missing sample information needed to repair an arbitrary damaged slice. If a source was resized before FFV1 encoding, the exact round trip preserves the resized array. Place the sample comparison at the encoder's actual input to verify that intended preservation boundary. This makes an FFV1 master useful as a stable source for future viewing conversions: its decoder restores the retained samples, and each derivative begins from that defined input rather than from an earlier lossy delivery copy. See Also Lossless Video Compression Video Generation Loss Lossy and Lossless Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References RFC 9043: FFV1 video coding format versions 0, 1, and 3

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Motion JPEG Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Motion JPEG Video Motion JPEG (MJPEG) builds moving video from independently JPEG-compressed pictures. The usual frame-based form does not use another picture's samples to predict the next one. The diagram shows a frame-based form. Some implementations code the two interlaced fields separately. An independent picture can still be highly compressed Common MJPEG uses JPEG's lossy DCT-based picture coding. Within a picture, blocks are transformed into coefficients representing spatial patterns. Quantization approximates those coefficients, and entropy coding describes their values compactly. The decoder reconstructs each picture from its JPEG coding information. The neighboring video pictures do not supply its temporal predictor. Its JPEG tables and the applicable sample/container description still have to be available. This combines compressed picture storage with straightforward frame access. Once the reader locates picture C and supplies its coding information, it does not first need to reconstruct A and B as scene references. The independence also determines what gets repeated. A wall unchanged between A, B, and C is described within each new JPEG picture again. An inter-predicted codec can instead reuse an earlier reconstructed wall and describe mainly its changes. Assign pictures to the timeline The surrounding video format supplies the sequence and timing. At 25 fps, each picture spans 40 ms. Let three independently encoded pictures have these illustrative sizes: Picture Duration JPEG payload A 40 ms 40,000 bytes B 40 ms 30,000 bytes C 40 ms 50,000 bytes Their total is 120,000 bytes across 0.120 second: 120,000 × 8 ÷ 0.120 = 8,000,000 bit/s , or 8 Mb/s . Constructed sizes, excluding container and audio overhead; no encoder benchmark or recommended setting is implied. C can contain more difficult texture than B and need a larger JPEG even though both have the same dimensions and duration. Independence does not require identical frame sizes. A frame can contain two coded fields Some MJPEG representations encode interlaced fields separately and carry their JPEG bitstreams together in one video frame. The decoder must recover both field images and interpret their order and times correctly. QuickTime's documented Motion-JPEG A and B forms differ in marker and header conventions, including where required compression tables and field information are supplied. Other containers can use other conventions. The JPEG image standard therefore supplies the underlying picture coding, while the particular MJPEG representation supplies its video organization. Those two pieces determine how to locate, decode, and schedule the images in an older camera clip or capture. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Compression Artifacts Apple ProRes Video References ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding Apple: QuickTime video sample data and Motion-JPEG variants

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Apple ProRes Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Apple ProRes Video An editor needs to jump to arbitrary frames, make cuts, combine layers, and render repeatedly. A streaming copy instead aims to deliver an acceptable finished picture with an economical data rate. Apple ProRes is designed around the production job, which explains why a ProRes export can be much larger than its playback derivative. Access one picture without a long prediction chain Conventional ProRes video encodes each picture independently. The decoder does not need earlier picture samples to predict a selected frame. It reconstructs that frame's block-coded data using the stream and frame information. This is useful for scrubbing and distributing complete pictures among processing tasks. Its within-picture transforms and quantization still compress the data; “independent” describes temporal dependence, rather than uncompressed storage. Keeping more picture information through a production workflow leaves later rendering and delivery encoders a useful source. A smaller proxy can serve the editing job when responsiveness or storage is more important, with finishing performed from the retained higher-quality media. Selected 422 variants and their data budgets Apple gives these approximate target rates for 1920 × 1080 at 29.97 fps : Variant Approximate target video rate Two-hour picture-only estimate ProRes 422 Proxy 45 Mb/s 40.5 GB ProRes 422 LT 102 Mb/s 91.8 GB ProRes 422 147 Mb/s 132.3 GB ProRes 422 HQ 220 Mb/s 198 GB The size estimate uses rate × 7,200 seconds ÷ 8 . It assumes the listed target is the exact average for that example and excludes audio and container overhead. Actual ProRes rate varies with source characteristics, raster, rate, and encoding choices; the table is not a measurement of every export. The profile names select different coding-quality/data-rate priorities within the 422 family. They do not mean that a Proxy converted into HQ acquires source detail that the Proxy discarded. Color and alpha are separately represented The 422 variants support 10-bit source picture workflows with 4:2:2 sampling. ProRes 4444 and 4444 XQ provide higher-fidelity color representation and optional alpha, the transparency information used when compositing layers. Conventional 422/4444 color-picture coding is lossy . The 4444 variants can encode their alpha losslessly, up to the supported alpha precision. A graphic's transparency can therefore be preserved exactly while its color picture uses another reconstruction guarantee. This separation matters when inspecting a production asset: sample depth, color sampling, and alpha presence describe different parts of its usefulness in a composite. RAW follows another input path ProRes RAW and RAW HQ represent a separate sensor-data workflow. Their input is intended for RAW processing rather than the conventional already formed video picture described by the 422/4444 coding family. A file using a logarithmic camera transfer is not automatically RAW. Its codec variant and its color/transfer description identify different stages of representation. Retain the source for finishing A ProRes production copy can supply an Emby viewing version after the relevant decoder and processing stages reconstruct it. That viewing version can use temporal prediction and another rate allocation suited to delivery, while the production source remains available for later work. The useful choice is the role of each copy: proxy for efficient editing, retained production media for finishing, and delivery encode for viewing. The format and variant make those roles explicit. articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.title: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.keywords: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Consider a playback target with this illustrative usable video capability: H.264 High, 8-bit 4:2:0. Up to a suitable 1080p30 workload and its supported level/buffer limits. MP4 packaging accepted by the selected player. Compatible audio, no subtitle rendering requirement, and adequate delivery bandwidth. This is a declared example, not an Emby device support table . It lets us follow why three similar-looking files take different paths. Source Video decision Packaging decision H.264 High, 8-bit 1080p24, in MP4 Matches the declared video target Matches The same encoded video, in an unsupported wrapper Video still matches Repackage if a compatible mapping is available H.264 High 10, 10-bit 1080p24, in MP4 Sample/profile requirement differs Already acceptable The first source can be delivered without video conversion. The second may only need the video packets placed into compatible packaging. The third needs a new video representation even though “H.264,” “1080p,” and “MP4” all appear in both descriptions. Locate the boundary that failed The container reader first needs to identify and extract the track correctly. It supplies the codec configuration and coded data to a decoder. Repackaging changes this outer representation while preserving video coding when the new mapping supports it. The decoder then needs the stream's actual tools and sample format . A 10-bit High 10 stream asks for different processing from an 8-bit High stream. A profile conversion requires reconstructing the source and encoding pictures using the target's permitted format and tools. Next come resource requirements . The same codec and profile at a higher rate or larger raster can exceed the target's throughput or decoded-buffer limits. The level calculations show how those demands are assessed. Finally, the player must present the decoded pictures with their timing, aspect, and color information. A successful decode is a necessary stage, while display processing gives the samples their intended presentation. A hardware capability has to be usable by the app A chip's media engine, the operating-system API that exposes it, and the playback framework selected by the app are separate components. The app needs a working route through them for the requested format. A software decoder can provide another route. Its required picture processing still has to finish quickly enough for playback. Whether a given source uses hardware, software, or another conversion therefore depends on the active implementation, rather than simply on the codec's name. Put the server decoder into a conversion path Video transcoding contains two decoder boundaries: Source file → server input decoder → processing and output encoder → client decoder → display. For the High 10 example, the server must first understand the source's 10-bit AVC. It can then construct the required 8-bit target representation and encode it for the client. The client only decodes that new stream. The source and delivered video may both be labeled H.264 because their codec family is the same. The profile, precision, bitrate, or other properties changed. Conversely, a server that can encode a target codec still needs an input decoder for the source before it can perform that conversion. In an Emby session, compare the selected source track with the delivered stream and the reported conversion reason. If the video already matches but audio, subtitles, or a delivery limit needs work, those requirements can choose another route. The case analysis locates the operation instead of treating every change as a missing codec. See Also Containers and Codecs Video Codec Profiles Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.title: VC-1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.keywords: VC-1 Video VC-1 is the video coding format standardized in SMPTE ST 421. It is associated with the Windows Media video ecosystem and older movie collections. The useful source description includes its Simple, Main, or Advanced profile , rather than only the broader Windows Media name. The standard reconstructs 8-bit 4:2:0 picture samples. Its coding tools determine how the compressed track turns into those samples. Reconstruct an inter-coded region The decoder selects the available reference information and applies the coded motion description to form a predictor. A correction block describes how the target region differs from that predictor. VC-1 can use different transform shapes for inter-coded corrections: Transform shape Region it represents 8 × 8 A square correction block 8 × 4 A horizontally extended sub-block 4 × 8 A vertically extended sub-block 4 × 4 A smaller square sub-block Transform signaling and sub-block patterns tell the decoder which structure to apply. Different shapes can describe a localized correction more effectively than one fixed square basis for every region. The coded coefficients are inverse-quantized and inverse-transformed. The decoder adds the resulting samples to the predictor. Applicable overlap-smoothing and loop-filter operations complete the specified reconstruction behavior. As in other predictive codecs, the encoder chooses a representation, while the decoder follows its syntax. Quantization controls reconstruction precision; selecting a transform shape is a way to represent the correction, rather than a new display resolution. Interpret the picture's scan structure Advanced profile includes interlaced picture coding. The picture structure tells decoding and motion handling how its line sets relate. For a native interlaced scene, alternating rows come from successive field times. Frame-shaped and field-shaped coding decisions have to preserve that relationship. A final progressive presentation then needs the appropriate field reconstruction . For a film transfer, repeated or related field presentation can instead reflect a progressive source cadence. The picture's format and timing information help identify that case, with inverse telecine providing the corresponding recovery process. This makes interlaced VC-1 more than a progressive picture with an “i” label: its decoder needs the relevant prediction and picture-structure operations. Keep reconstruction and display interpretation together ST 421 specifies coded reconstruction, while a complete player also interprets sample aspect, color, and timing information for presentation. Reconstructed samples with the wrong display shape are still being interpreted incorrectly. In an Emby library inspection, record the actual VC-1 profile and scan structure along with its raster and rate. That identifies the reconstruction job before a playback route either presents the decoded source or supplies it to another encoder. The format's standard reference is SMPTE ST 421:2013, VC-1 Compressed Video Bitstream Format and Decoding Process . It supplies the profile-specific syntax and reconstruction rules behind those observations. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References SMPTE ST 421: VC-1 bitstream format and decoding process

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: AV1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: AV1 Video AV1 is the video coding format defined by the Alliance for Open Media. Its bitstream contains instructions for reconstructing picture samples, maintaining reference state, and preparing visible output. One useful AV1 distinction is that the picture retained for later prediction and the picture prepared for display can pass through different operations. Read the sequence and frame instructions AV1 organizes coded data into Open Bitstream Units (OBUs) . Sequence information establishes the applicable profile, sample format, and other stream parameters. Frame information describes the picture's reconstruction choices, reference updates, and output behavior. Tile data supplies the coded regional information. A decoder needs the relevant headers as well as the block payloads. The picture isn't described by an isolated list of pixel values. Its block organization can start with 64 × 64 or 128 × 128 superblocks . Regions are partitioned further to fit the picture structure. The chosen partitions define where prediction and correction decisions apply. Construct the scene and its correction Intra modes use reconstructed information within the picture. Inter modes use retained decoded pictures with motion information, including permitted compound predictions from multiple views. A compound predictor can combine corresponding estimates of a region. Masks or weights can give different contributions where the coding mode permits them. The aim is to leave a correction that can be described efficiently. Transform and quantization operations represent that remaining correction. The decoder recovers coefficients, constructs the correction, and adds it to the predictor. Quantization settings control the approximation in ordinary lossy AV1, while the partition and prediction choices control how effectively the input is represented. Filter the reconstructed picture inside the coding loop AV1 includes several reconstruction-filtering stages. Deblocking addresses selected block-boundary behavior. CDEF , the Constrained Directional Enhancement Filter, identifies a local direction and constrains its filtering so the operation can address artifacts while respecting that structure. Loop restoration supplies additional signaled processing of reconstructed regions. The result used for reference updates is the applicable loop-restored picture. Later prediction needs these samples, so the encoder must locally reconstruct corresponding reference state. This separates coding-loop work from optional presentation processing. A filter used outside the reference loop can change what is shown without changing the samples later blocks predict from. Add grain to output when it is signaled Some AV1 streams describe film grain with parameters rather than coding every original grain sample as picture texture. An encoder can represent a cleaner scene and supply information for synthesizing grain in output processing. Those parameters describe such things as how grain strength varies with brightness, how nearby grain samples relate, and the generation seed. The decoder uses the specified process to produce the intended grain-like appearance. Grain is applied to output samples; the loop-restored reference picture remains the predictor state. Keeping the newly synthesized pattern outside that reference avoids making future scene prediction depend on that particular display grain realization. The film-grain explanation follows the preservation and modeling tradeoff. The metadata describes an appearance model, rather than an exact archive of every grain sample captured in the source. Decoded pictures and visible pictures AV1 can decode a hidden reference picture and later show a retained picture through its output instructions. A coded unit count therefore need not equal the number of new visible camera moments. The container's timeline and the format's picture/output instructions cooperate to schedule the visible result. In an Emby conversion, the chosen decoded output needs to include the applicable grain and presentation interpretation for the result being encoded or displayed. Reference details for the format Detail Meaning Main profile, sequence profile 0 8-bit or 10-bit, 4:2:0 or monochrome sample permissions Other profiles Additional permitted sample formats Level and tier Workload and coded-rate constraints libaom, SVT-AV1, hardware encoder Implementations choosing an AV1 representation Grain parameters An optional output-synthesis description An encoder's search and rate-control decisions determine which valid representation is produced. A decoder follows its AV1 syntax and reconstruction rules; it does not need to be the implementation that created the stream. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility VP9 Video Film Grain in Compressed Video Video Codec Levels and Tiers References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP8 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP8 Video A web recording can contain a changing foreground over a mostly stable background. If every new picture used only the immediately preceding one, the best view of an uncovered background region might have disappeared behind the foreground. VP8 provides three logical reference roles so its predictor can use more than that immediately preceding view. Reference role Purpose in reconstruction Last A retained recent reconstructed picture Golden A picture retained separately for later reuse Altref An alternate retained picture available for prediction These are decoder reference roles, not three independently selectable video tracks. Retain a useful view Suppose a decoded picture shows the whole wall. The encoder can preserve it in a golden reference while later displayed pictures show a person crossing in front of it. When a wall region becomes visible again, a predictor can use the retained wall samples instead of the recently obscured region. The bitstream tells the decoder which available reference to select for each relevant block and which motion information locates its samples. A coded residual supplies the changes needed for the current picture. VP8 divides picture work into 16 × 16 macroblocks with smaller block operations. Its common reconstructed sample representation is 8-bit 4:2:0 . Integer reconstruction rules, transforms, quantization, and filtering define the result that later prediction will reuse. Refresh the reference state A decoded frame can replace the last, golden, or alternate reference according to the stream's update instructions. A picture retained as golden need not be replaced just because another picture has been shown. A keyframe establishes independently reconstructed content and refreshes the relevant reference state. Initially several logical roles can refer to the same newly reconstructed picture. Their later updates create the differing views used for prediction. This makes reference updating part of decoding. A picture is not simply forgotten after display; the next blocks may still need its samples. Decode a frame without showing it VP8 has a show_frame flag. A coded frame can reconstruct useful reference content while not becoming a displayed picture at that point. The decoder still performs its work and can retain the result. Later visible frames can predict from that state. Counting coded frames and counting displayed pictures therefore answer different questions. An output timeline is supplied by the surrounding media system. WebM is a common wrapper for VP8, carrying timestamps and other tracks. The coded reference operations and the container's scheduling cooperate to produce the recording. RFC 6386 documents the format and decoding process as an informational publication. It also says the supplied reference decoder takes precedence over conflicting narrative. This is the appropriate specification context when following the technical details. See Also VP9 Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Inter-Frame Video Prediction Containers and Codecs References RFC 6386: VP8 data format and decoding guide

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP9 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP9 Video VP9 organizes video reconstruction around flexible picture regions and retained reference pictures. It is often found in web-origin media and is commonly carried by WebM. Build the picture in regions The coded picture is organized into 64 × 64 superblocks , with smaller blocks selected for local content. A broad predictable area can use a larger region while a changing edge can be split more finely. The decoder constructs the selected intra or inter predictor, decodes the transformed correction, and applies the specified reconstruction and loop filtering. Prediction divisions and transform choices let different parts of a picture use different descriptions. Tiles organize groups of coded blocks and provide processing boundaries useful for parallel decoding. The picture header and the required references supply state beyond an individual block's local bytes. Choose from retained views A VP9 decoder maintains eight reference slots . The frame header selects at most three of those reference pictures for its prediction choices. Blocks then choose the applicable reference or permitted compound pair. This separates two decisions: Decision Scope Which decoded pictures are retained? Reference-slot state across frames Which references are available for this frame? Frame-header selection Which available reference prediction is used? Block-level coding choice A frame can refresh selected slots with its reconstructed picture. A useful older view can remain in another slot while newer views are decoded. For compound prediction , the decoder forms predictions from two references and combines them. If they describe the scene from useful neighboring views, their combination can leave a smaller residual than either alone. The coded residual still defines the necessary correction. VP9 also permits reference pictures of different dimensions under its scaling and format constraints. Prediction can include the specified reference rescaling rather than assuming every stored view has the current picture's grid. Reconstruction and display are separate instructions A coded frame can be hidden : decoded and retained without being shown as the next visible picture. The format can also instruct the decoder to show an existing retained picture rather than send a complete new reconstruction. These choices explain why coded-frame count and visible-picture count can differ. They are part of the representation, not evidence that a camera necessarily recorded an additional moment. The container timeline schedules visible output, while the VP9 header and block syntax rebuild the reference state and picture content needed for it. Identify the sample format precisely VP9 profile Sample depth Color sampling 0 8-bit 4:2:0 1 8-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 2 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:0 3 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 The depth and sampling determine the sample arrays those operations reconstruct. Color and transfer information then establish their display interpretation, including an appropriate HDR path for HDR content. A decoder target is consequently described by the actual profile, sample format and resource limits, rather than just “VP9.” In an Emby conversion, those source arrays are reconstructed before processing creates the output representation. The WebM Project labels its linked bitstream/decoding description a draft . Its published profile definition and implementation provide the accompanying reference context; the draft's status should remain explicit when using its detailed coding rules. See Also VP8 Video AV1 Video Video Codec Profiles What HDR Video Adds to SDR References WebM Project: VP9 bitstream and decoding specification (draft) WebM Project: VP9 coding profiles

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.title: Color Gamut | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.keywords: Color Gamut The points at the corners of an RGB gamut identify its red, green, and blue primaries. Mixing their light produces the colors between them. A wider gamut gives a system coordinates for more saturated colors, such as greens or reds that lie beyond a smaller gamut's boundary. Primary coordinates in CIE 1931 xy. The colored lines identify the standards; they do not reproduce the extreme colors. Luminance is omitted, and distances on this diagram are not perceptually uniform. Read the triangle as a set of possibilities A point inside a triangle can be formed from nonnegative mixtures of that triangle's primaries. On an edge, one primary contributes nothing; at a corner, only that primary contributes. The white point is the mixture that the system treats as its neutral reference. The same physical color generally has different RGB values in different spaces. The values describe amounts of particular primaries. For example, a green made from a mixture in BT.709 can be represented within BT.2020 by another mixture of its wider primaries. Keeping the numbers unchanged while changing the primaries would ask for a different color. This distinction explains a useful question about a film: does it use very saturated colors, or can its signal merely represent them? A BT.2020-encoded scene of a gray wall and a face need not use the outer part of the BT.2020 gamut. The encoding defines the available coordinates, while the picture determines which coordinates are occupied. Three gamuts can appear in one playback session Consider a movie graded with colors that fit within P3, stored using BT.2020 signal primaries, and played on a television with its own measured gamut. The grading range, encoding space, and display capability describe different stages. The player first interprets the encoded values in their declared space. It then needs a color-management path to produce those colors on the display. Colors within the display's capabilities can be reproduced using suitable mixtures of its primaries. A color outside those capabilities needs gamut mapping : a choice of an achievable replacement that maintains useful relationships with neighboring colors. An Emby Direct Play session preserves the delivered encoded video, but the player and screen still perform this interpretation. A larger native display gamut is beneficial when the output path also reproduces smaller encoded gamuts correctly. Stretching a conventional BT.709 image to the screen's outermost primaries would change the intended colors. What to keep separate when reading specifications Property Question it answers Encoding gamut Which color coordinates can the signal describe? Measured display gamut Which chromaticities can this screen reproduce under the test conditions? Bit depth How finely can values be represented? Color volume Which colors are available at different light levels? A gamut boundary describes the reach of the primaries. Smooth gradients also need adequate precision and processing; bright saturated colors need an adequate color volume . When comparing two systems, keep those questions separate so that a large triangle is interpreted as a color-range property, rather than a complete picture-quality score. See Also Color Volume ITU-R BT.2020 P3 Color Gamuts References ITU-R BT.2407: Color gamut conversion ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.title: Color Volume | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.keywords: Color Volume A red light and a white reflection can ask very different things of a screen. The reflection can use all three RGB components. A saturated red uses mostly the red component, so it can run out of available output well before the screen reaches its maximum white brightness. Color volume describes colors together with their light levels. It extends the two-dimensional idea of color gamut into the brightness dimension: which colors can be reproduced near black, at middle levels, and near the brightest output? Why the volume is not a straight stack of gamut triangles Imagine an ideal additive RGB display using BT.709 primaries, with linear component values limited to zero through one and 100-nit white. Its neutral white is R = G = B = 1. In this example, luminance is: Y = 100 × (0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B) nits The coefficient sum is one. Setting all components to one produces 100 nits, but setting just one component to one gives different results: Linear RGB setting Color Calculated luminance 1, 0, 0 Red primary 21.26 nits 0, 1, 0 Green primary 71.52 nits 0, 0, 1 Blue primary 7.22 nits 1, 1, 0 Red plus green 92.78 nits 1, 1, 1 White 100 nits An idealized calculation with fixed primaries and component limits. It is not a measurement of a television. To make that pure red brighter while retaining the same chromaticity would require increasing its red component beyond one. The display has already reached the limit. Adding green and blue can raise luminance, but moves the color toward a less saturated mixture. This is the brightness/saturation tradeoff the word “volume” helps describe. Near the top of this ideal volume, fewer saturated colors remain available. At the very highest white level, all components are already at their maxima. Real displays add other limits: their primaries and channel behavior vary, their black floor affects dark colors, and power or thermal control can change output during a bright scene. Follow a bright colored object to the display Consider an HDR picture containing a bright orange flame. Its encoded RGB values describe both its color and light level. The display may have sufficient reach toward orange at a moderate luminance but insufficient output to reproduce that particular orange at the requested high luminance. A conversion can reduce the flame's brightness, reduce its saturation, or combine adjustments. Keeping only the brightness target and clipping individual color components can shift hue. Keeping only the hue and saturation target can require a larger luminance reduction. A useful mapping balances the relationships that make the flame look convincing alongside the rest of the scene. This is why tone mapping and gamut mapping interact. Their jobs can be integrated into one color-volume mapping. Treating the output as a brightness ceiling plus an independent fixed triangle misses part of the problem. Read measurements with their conditions A color-volume percentage needs a reference volume and a specified measurement method. Different coordinate systems weight color differences differently; a percentage relative to one reference cannot be compared directly with an unrelated percentage. Test conditions also matter. A brief small white patch, a large bright area, and a sustained colored patch can produce different output limits on the same screen. Measurements across luminance and color give more information than one peak-white number. Near black, useful separation between dark colors matters even when the high-brightness result is impressive. Mastering-display metadata records properties of the mastering reference. During Emby playback, the receiving screen can have a different volume. The renderer adapts the produced image to the output; retaining the original source allows that adaptation to be chosen again for another display. See Also Color Gamut Why Tone Mapping Is Needed ITU-R BT.2100 References SMPTE study group report: HDR ecosystem ITU-T H.274: Supplemental enhancement information ITU-R BT.709: Primary coordinates and luminance weights

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2020 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2020 BT.2020 defines a set of wide-gamut RGB primaries for UHD television. Their coordinates identify the colors from which mixtures are formed: Primary CIE 1931 x CIE 1931 y Red 0.708 0.292 Green 0.170 0.797 Blue 0.131 0.046 Reference white, D65 0.3127 0.3290 Coordinates show the encoding gamut. The diagram omits luminance; its line colors identify the triangles. An encoding space can be larger than the colors in the movie Suppose a film is graded with colors that fit in P3 , then represented with BT.2020 coordinates for delivery. The converter finds BT.2020 RGB mixtures for those existing colors. The film does not acquire more saturated objects simply because the available coordinate space grew. This is similar to choosing a larger map for a journey: the map has room for more places, while the route still visits its actual locations. In video, the important operation is converting coordinates correctly. Reusing P3 numbers and merely changing the primary label would describe different colors. The standard also defines UHD image sizes of 3840 × 2160 and 7680 × 4320 and 10- or 12-bit signal precision. The color-primary label in a media report identifies only the primary-coordinate part of that system. A renderer still needs the rest of the signal description. Read the other fields beside the primaries Transfer characteristics: BT.2020 includes a conventional nonlinear transfer characteristic. HDR television systems in BT.2100 reuse these primaries with PQ or HLG. Consequently, the transfer field tells a player which light interpretation applies. Matrix coefficients: The standard defines constant-luminance and non-constant-luminance component representations. A report of BT.2020 non-constant describes the nonlinear RGB-to-luma/chroma arrangement; it is not another set of primaries. Reconstructing RGB needs the corresponding matrix interpretation. Range and precision: These establish how code values carry the signal. Ten bits give the number of levels; numerical range establishes the code positions for nominal black and white. Neither replaces the transfer characteristic. For an Emby source with BT.2020 primaries and PQ, the playback path needs the PQ interpretation, then appropriate rendering for the output display. A BT.2020 SDR signal follows a different light relationship. Comparing the fields together lets two apparently similar 4K files be distinguished before choosing color or tone-mapping processing. See Also ITU-R BT.2100 P3 Color Gamuts Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2100 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2100 BT.2100 is the HDR television system specification that joins image geometry, wide color, signal precision, and HDR transfer relationships. A file usually exposes those pieces in separate fields rather than carrying a single “BT.2100” badge. System part Defined relationship Primaries The wide-gamut coordinates also used by BT.2020 HDR transfer systems PQ and HLG Image sizes 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160, 7680 × 4320 Scanning Progressive Precision 10 or 12 bits per component The current recommendation is BT.2100-3, approved in February 2025. Its transfer-system definitions connect scene light, the encoded signal, reference display light, and viewing conditions. Recognize the system in a media report An HDR recording can identify BT.2020 primaries, a PQ transfer characteristic, and a compatible component matrix. Those fields provide the instructions for interpreting the decoded pictures. A different recording can use the same primaries with HLG, changing the light relationship while retaining the color coordinates. The decoder first reconstructs samples from the compressed video. HDR-aware presentation then interprets those samples and prepares the picture for the output. Being able to decode HEVC, for example, answers a coding question; handling the resulting HDR signal answers a rendering question. Emby playback needs both parts of the selected path to work. Can 1080p be HDR? Yes. HD geometry is part of the BT.2100 system. A 1920 × 1080 HDR picture has fewer spatial samples than UHD, while its brightness and color interpretation can still require HDR-aware presentation. Reducing the grid to a smaller delivery size changes spatial detail. It does not automatically replace the transfer function. An SDR destination needs an actual HDR-to-SDR conversion , including the appropriate brightness and color operations, rather than a resolution change alone. Where do HDR formats fit? Formats such as HDR10 combine defined signal characteristics with delivery conventions and metadata. BT.2100 supplies the underlying television image parameters; the format describes how a particular presentation is carried and identified. Reading an HDR label becomes more useful when those layers are kept visible: compressed coding, television signal interpretation, format metadata, and the intended display output. See Also ITU-R BT.2020 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.601 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.601 An archived SD recording is enlarged to 1080p, and its colored objects change slightly even though neutral gray still looks sensible. One possibility is a disagreement about the luma/color-difference matrix: an image represented using BT.601 values is being reconstructed as if those values used BT.709. BT.601, or Rec. 601, defines digital component-video encoding for standard-definition television. Its matrix remains relevant after a picture is resized, because enlarging the sample grid does not automatically change what the samples mean. Follow the color through an upscale Start with nonlinear RGB components R′, G′, and B′. The familiar BT.601 luma weighting is: Y′ = 0.299R′ + 0.587G′ + 0.114B′ Two color-difference components describe the color around that luma value. A playback stage uses the matching inverse relationship to recover RGB. The weights operate on nonlinear signal components; this luma is different from a direct measurement of emitted light. For a neutral signal with R′ = G′ = B′, any weighting whose coefficients sum to one gives the same luma value, and the color differences are neutral. That explains why a matrix mismatch can leave a gray patch plausible. Colored patches exercise the different weights and reveal the disagreement. Resizing the luma/chroma grids can retain the BT.601 interpretation. Alternatively, a processing path can reconstruct color and perform an appropriate conversion to a destination representation, such as BT.709. The delivered values and their signaling must then describe that destination. These are actual processing choices, rather than consequences of the output resolution alone. When comparing an Emby Direct Play and transcoded session , inspect the source and delivered matrix information. An SD-to-HD conversion can change more than geometry, so comparing only the resolution leaves the color conversion unexplained. Useful reference details Detail BT.601 role Standard 4:2:2 family Full horizontal luma sampling with half-rate color-difference sampling Luma sampling rate 13.5 MHz for the standard 525-line and 625-line 4:2:2 systems Corresponding chroma sampling rate 6.75 MHz for each color-difference component Nominal 8-bit luma black/white Code values 16 and 235 Familiar nonlinear luma weights 0.299 red, 0.587 green, 0.114 blue The numerical range must also be interpreted correctly. Nominal black at 16 and white at 235 are not the same code positions as full-range black and white. A range mismatch affects contrast, while a matrix mismatch mainly changes the reconstructed colors. BT.601-era material can have differing primary and transfer descriptions depending on its television system and history. Read those fields individually when available. The matrix answers how component signals relate; it does not replace the rest of the source's color description.
