See Also ITU-R BT.709 Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.601-7: Digital television studio encoding ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.709 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.709 A media inspector can show “BT.709” in several fields. Each occurrence answers a different question about the same signal: Field Meaning of BT.709 there Color primaries The red, green, blue, and D65 reference-white coordinates Transfer characteristics The source's nonlinear light-to-signal relationship Matrix coefficients The conversion between nonlinear RGB and luma/color-difference signals BT.709 , or Rec. 709, specifies HDTV image and signal parameters. It is the familiar color system for conventional SDR HD video, but those parameters continue to matter when the same signal is carried at another resolution. Why one field cannot stand in for the others The primaries define what RGB mixtures mean. The transfer characteristic defines how the signal represents light. The matrix describes how nonlinear RGB becomes Y′CbCr. A processing stage can change one of these representations while retaining another, so a reader needs the complete description. The nonlinear luma weights are 0.2126R′ + 0.7152G′ + 0.0722B′ . Green contributes most strongly to luma under this relationship. These weights differ from BT.601 , which explains why using the wrong matrix can shift colored objects. Neutral RGB values produce neutral color differences in both systems, so a gray-only test can miss the error. The source OETF and the display response have different roles. BT.1886 supplies a reference SDR display EOTF, including the effect of display black and white. A BT.709 transfer tag identifies the source characteristic; it does not instruct a reader to treat the picture as linear light. Put an SDR signal on a wide-gamut screen Suppose a television's native primaries reach farther toward saturated red and green than BT.709. The intended BT.709 colors still need to be reproduced as BT.709 colors. The output path can mix the display's primaries to obtain those colors inside its larger gamut. Driving the screen's most saturated red for a BT.709 red value would stretch the source gamut, changing the produced image. Correct color management lets the larger panel serve both smaller and wider gamuts. This is relevant to Emby playback even when the server delivers the original file unchanged: the app and display must agree on signal interpretation. A 4K file can carry SDR BT.709 video, and an HD file can carry HDR. Resolution identifies the grid; the color fields identify its interpretation. For an HDR-to-SDR conversion , the brightness and color processing must actually produce suitable SDR values, then describe those values using coherent output signaling. When recording a playback comparison, keep the source's primaries, transfer, matrix, and range alongside the delivered stream's fields. That makes an apparent “BT.709 mismatch” a specific question about the part of the representation that changed. See Also ITU-R BT.601 ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: P3 Color Gamuts | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: P3 Color Gamuts The name P3 turns up on cinema standards, photographs, mastering reports, and television specifications. Resolve the context before treating those uses as the same color encoding: Name or use Primaries White/transfer information Cinema DCI-P3 P3 Cinema white point and 2.6 display gamma P3-D65 P3 D65 white; specify the transfer characteristic separately Display P3 P3 D65 white with the sRGB transfer curve “P3 coverage” on a screen A measured capability relative to P3 Depends on the stated measurement method All three named spaces use the same primary coordinates: red (0.680, 0.320), green (0.265, 0.690), and blue (0.150, 0.060) in CIE 1931 xy. P3 reaches farther than BT.709 toward saturated red and green. The coordinates determine the gamut; the white and transfer choices complete the interpretation. Two uses that are easy to confuse An image in Display P3. Its RGB values use P3 primaries, D65 white, and the defined nonlinear transfer curve. A color-managed image viewer can convert those values to the destination screen while preserving their intended colors. Display P3 provides a wider gamut than sRGB without, by itself, defining a PQ HDR presentation. A movie graded within P3 and delivered using BT.2020. The movie can fit within the grading display's P3 capabilities while its encoded video uses BT.2020 coordinate values. The conversion expresses the same intended colors as mixtures of different primaries. The player's input interpretation follows the delivered video fields. In the second case, choosing a P3 input mode merely because the film was graded on a P3-capable display would assign the wrong meaning to the delivered numbers. The mastering range and encoding space have separate places in the production chain. Use a coverage claim for the question it answers A percentage of P3 describes a screen's measured reach relative to a reference gamut under particular conditions. Different area or volume methods can give different numbers, so compare measurements that state the same reference and method. For an Emby video, record the signal's primaries and transfer characteristic independently of the display's P3 coverage. The signal tells the renderer what colors were requested; measured capability tells it what can be reproduced. For bright colored highlights, color volume extends that second question across light levels. See Also Color Gamut ITU-R BT.2020 Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References SMPTE EG 432-1: Color processing for digital cinema ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3 W3C CSS Color 4: Display P3 ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: ITU-R BT.1886 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: ITU-R BT.1886 A reference SDR display response needs more than a gamma number: its black floor and white level determine the light available at the endpoints. BT.1886 defines an EOTF for HDTV reference displays using those measured endpoint luminances and an exponent of 2.4. Calculated reference responses. The shadow panel shows the effect of the black floor; these are selected display parameters, not measurements of a television. Calculate the response from its endpoints Let Lw be white luminance, Lb black luminance, and V the normalized signal. With gamma = 2.4: a = (Lw^(1/gamma) − Lb^(1/gamma))^gamma b = Lb^(1/gamma) / (Lw^(1/gamma) − Lb^(1/gamma)) L = a × max(V + b, 0)^gamma The coefficients make V = 0 reach the specified black and V = 1 reach the specified white. If black is zero, b becomes zero and a becomes Lw, leaving the familiar pure power response L = Lw × V^2.4. For 100-nit white, compare zero black with 0.1-nit black: Signal V Light at zero black Light at 0.1-nit black 0 0 nits 0.1 nit 0.1 0.398 nit 1.064 nits 0.5 18.946 nits 21.605 nits 1 100 nits 100 nits The second response reaches the higher black floor and redistributes the lower tones to meet the same white. It is not obtained simply by adding 0.1 nit to every output of the zero-black curve. Use the shadow panel to interpret a dark scene A dark jacket can contain several distinct low-level folds. Their encoded values have a display-light relationship; the black floor and response determine how much separation is produced. Room reflections and the viewer's adaptation can further affect whether that separation is visible. BT.1886 gives a reference response for this part of the system. It is distinct from the BT.709 source transfer characteristic , so a conventional BT.709 file is not retagged BT.1886 to describe reference display behavior. In a playback comparison, use the same SDR source and inspect the app's output and screen mode. A difference in shadow appearance can arise after decoding. Keeping the response's endpoints and middle-tone behavior visible makes the investigation more precise than comparing a single “gamma” label. See Also ITU-R BT.709 Video Gamma Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) What light should a screen produce for a signal value of 0.5? An electro-optical transfer function , or EOTF, supplies the relationship needed to answer. The signal is electrical or numerical; the result is light. For an ideal SDR display with zero black, 100-nit white, and a 2.4 power response, use L = 100 × V^2.4 . V is the normalized signal and L is neutral-gray luminance: Signal V Calculated light 0.25 3.6 nits 0.50 18.9 nits 0.75 50.1 nits 1.00 100 nits Halfway through the signal range therefore produces about 19% of white's light in this example. Equal signal steps do not create equal light steps. These are the zero-black conditions of BT.1886 ; another EOTF gives another relationship. Apply the function to the right input The stored video code first needs the correct numerical-range interpretation. Nominal black and white may occupy only part of the available integer range. Interpreting those endpoints produces a normalized signal; the EOTF then supplies its light meaning. The order is significant. If nominal black is mistakenly normalized to a positive signal, the EOTF produces light for a sample that was meant to be black. If a nonlinear sample is treated as already linear, later arithmetic also begins from the wrong light value. A color-processing path applies the relevant component relationships and transfer interpretation to obtain a suitable working representation. A neutral-gray calculation keeps the example above simple; colored pictures additionally need their primaries and component matrix interpreted correctly. Reconstruct light, then choose what the output can show PQ gives HDR samples an absolute reference-light interpretation. Recovering that interpretation can reveal a 1,000-nit highlight, but a destination with a smaller usable range still needs a mapping decision. The EOTF identifies the requested light. Tone mapping adapts it. After a light-domain operation, the output needs an encoding appropriate to its own display relationship. In the ideal SDR example, a desired 50-nit gray requires V = (50/100)^(1/2.4), approximately 0.749. Writing 0.5 instead would request 18.9 nits. That inverse operation explains why light values and final video signal values cannot be interchanged. An Emby Direct Play session identifies how the server delivers the file. The app and display still render the samples using their output path. Comparing displayed brightness therefore requires the source interpretation and the destination response alongside the delivery mode. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) ITU-R BT.1886 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) A camera measures light, but the video signal usually represents it nonlinearly. An opto-electronic transfer function , or OETF, supplies that light-to-signal relationship. The BT.709 reference below assigns more signal space to low scene-light levels than a straight linear encoding would. Normalized scene light becomes a normalized video signal. Neither axis is a raw sensor code or an absolute number of nits. Follow one scene-light value For normalized scene-light E, the BT.709 curve uses 4.5E below 0.018 and 1.099E^0.45 − 0.099 at or above that point. The lower straight segment avoids the behavior of a bare power near zero. The full function is more precise than calling it simply “gamma 0.45.” At E = 0.18, the signal is approximately 0.409 . The encoded value has increased numerically, but that does not mean the camera recorded more light. It is another representation of the same input. To return from the upper segment's signal value V to scene light, use E = ((V + 0.099) / 1.099)^(1/0.45) . That inverse is what a light-domain processing stage needs when its input uses this encoding. An averaging example shows why the distinction is useful Suppose an operation is intended to average two light contributions: black at E = 0 and white at E = 1. Their light average is E = 0.5. Applying the OETF gives a signal of approximately 0.706 . Averaging their encoded values instead gives V = 0.5, because black and white encode to zero and one. Inverting that signal gives scene light of only about 0.260 . The two computations therefore describe different results: Operation Resulting scene-light value Average light, then encode 0.500 Average encoded signals, then interpret About 0.260 The nonlinear relationship is the cause. This matters for operations whose purpose is to combine light contributions, such as a physically motivated blend. Other processing can deliberately choose a perceptual working space; its intended effect determines the right arithmetic. Capture encoding and display appearance are separate stages An OETF is not automatically the exact inverse of the eventual display EOTF . The full imaging system also chooses an appropriate relationship between scene light and reproduced light for the viewing environment. The OOTF describes that overall relationship. For camera footage stored in an Emby library, preserve the actual transfer description through editing and export. A conventional camera signal, a camera-specific log representation, and HDR can use different light relationships even if they share a codec. Correctly converting footage requires interpreting the source, performing the intended rendering, and encoding the destination—not merely assigning it a familiar transfer label. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) ITU-R BT.709 References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) A camera points at a scene, and a screen later produces light for the viewer. The opto-optical transfer function , or OOTF, describes the relationship between those two kinds of light across the complete imaging system. The OOTF spans scene light to reproduced light. A real chain can include exposure, grading, tone mapping, and viewing adjustments in addition to the illustrated transfer stages. Compose the functions rather than cancel their names The OETF describes light becoming a signal. The EOTF describes a signal becoming light. Combining those operations determines the overall scene-to-display relationship. Use a deliberately simple model. Suppose capture encodes relative scene light E as E^0.5, and display produces relative light V^2.4 from the encoded signal V. For E = 0.25: Capture gives V = 0.25^0.5 = 0.5 . Display gives L = 0.5^2.4, approximately 0.189 . The combined relationship is L = E^1.2, since 0.5 × 2.4 = 1.2. The result is not the original relative light 0.25. The system's overall rendering has changed the relationship. This is a constructed demonstration of function composition; specified video functions can include linear segments, offsets, and luminance-dependent operations, so their complete equations must be combined. Why a useful reproduction can change scene contrast Looking at a screen in a room differs from standing in front of the photographed scene. The screen has a limited light range, the image occupies part of the field of view, and the viewer adapts to a particular surround. Reproducing the scene's light numerically, without accounting for those conditions, need not produce the intended appearance. An imaging system can therefore include an overall rendering that adjusts contrast for its reference viewing environment. Camera encoding and display behavior are parts of that design. An exponent greater than one in the simplified overall model darkens middle relative levels while leaving zero and one unchanged. This is an appearance relationship, not an instruction to use one fixed extra filter on every produced movie. A colorist may already have established the intended display image during grading. Locate the rendering in the source you have A scene-referred representation retains a relationship to captured scene light. A display-referred representation describes an intended produced image. The same named operations cannot be added indiscriminately to both: applying a scene-to-display rendering twice can alter a picture that was already rendered. For HLG , the system relationship includes adaptation to display and viewing conditions. PQ provides an absolute reference-display interpretation. These systems place parts of the rendering relationship differently. Emby normally begins with already authored media. The playback path needs to know which interpretation it receives and adapt that produced picture to the output. The diagram is useful for locating an operation: did it occur in capture, in production, in the app's presentation, or in the display? That location determines whether the required overall rendering is being completed or applied again. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 A PQ signal assigns picture samples an absolute reference-display light meaning. A normalized signal of 0.5 requests approximately 92.2 nits for neutral gray; it does not request half of an arbitrary television's brightest output. Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) is standardized in SMPTE ST 2084. Its nonlinear function distributes precision across a reference-light range extending to 10,000 nits, taking human visual sensitivity into account. ST 2084 neutral-gray reference EOTF. The logarithmic panel reveals shadows; zero cannot be plotted on its logarithmic luminance axis. Follow a light request into a stored sample A 100-nit neutral gray has a normalized PQ signal of approximately 0.508078 . That value is a signal coordinate, not a luminance percentage. Encoding into a numerical format comes next. For an illustrative 10-bit narrow-range neutral-gray component, nominal black is code 64 and the top nominal signal is code 940. There are 876 intervals between those endpoints. Rounding 64 + 876 × 0.508078 gives code 509 . On interpretation, (509 − 64) / 876 gives approximately 0.507991. Applying PQ recovers about 99.913 nits . The slight difference from 100 is the finite-precision rounding in this example. That chain connects three representations: Representation Example Intended neutral-gray light 100 nits Normalized nonlinear PQ signal About 0.508078 Stored 10-bit narrow-range component 509 A player needs the correct range before applying PQ. Treating the integer 509 as a full-range value would produce a different normalized signal and therefore another light request. For colored video, component and primary interpretation also participate in recovering the intended picture. Read the curve's unequal spacing Light level Normalized PQ signal, rounded 1 nit 0.150 100 nits 0.508 1,000 nits 0.752 10,000 nits 1.000 The large light changes in the table occupy uneven signal intervals. This lets a finite set of signal values serve a much wider luminance range than a simple linear allocation would. Bit depth then determines how finely those signal intervals are divided. The 10,000-nit endpoint defines the reference range of the function. An actual movie uses its own distribution of light levels; its brightest encoded content can be far below that endpoint. Content-light metadata and measured picture statistics describe aspects of that content. The equation, for reproducing the values For normalized signal V, use p = V^(1/m2), then: L = 10,000 × [max(p − c1, 0) / (c2 − c3p)]^(1/m1) The exact constants are m1 = 2610/16384, m2 = 2523/32, c1 = 3424/4096, c2 = 2413/128, and c3 = 2392/128. L is luminance in nits for neutral gray at the reference white chromaticity. The inverse function finds the PQ signal for a desired light level. Adapt the interpreted picture to the destination Suppose a highlight requests 1,000 nits and the output's usable peak is 400. PQ identifies the request; it cannot expand the screen's light capability. A subsequent tone-mapping decision fits that highlight alongside the rest of the picture. A capable renderer can retain PQ's intended light relationship over a supported range and adapt the regions beyond the display's useful output. An SDR conversion instead prepares values with an SDR transfer meaning after brightness and color processing. For Emby playback, these operations can happen in a server conversion or in local presentation. The Windows app documentation describes presentation-stage tone mapping. The source transfer, actual content range, and destination are each inputs to understanding the delivered appearance. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Video Gamma | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Video Gamma Both curves below reach the same black and white. Their difference is in the tones between those endpoints: Zero-black display models with white normalized to one. The dotted diagonal is a linear reference. Gamma is the exponent in a power relationship. For a display model written as L = V^gamma, a higher exponent gives less light at intermediate normalized signal values. At V = 0.5, gamma 2.2 gives about 0.218 of white , while gamma 2.4 gives about 0.189 . With a hypothetical 100-nit white, that is 21.8 versus 18.9 nits. The darker middle tone does not require a change in peak white. State the direction of the relationship Use of a gamma number What the exponent acts on Capture or encoding shorthand Light values becoming a nonlinear signal Display response Signal values becoming light Image adjustment An existing image representation changed by another power For values between zero and one, a power below one raises the number; a power above one lowers it. That mathematical direction is why “increase gamma” can mean different visual changes in controls that apply different conventions. Real transfer functions can use more than a power. The BT.709 OETF has a straight segment near black; BT.1886 includes display black and white; PQ uses a different nonlinear function. When comparing an Emby picture across playback paths, keep the output and display modes consistent. Then distinguish a deliberate tone adjustment from the transfer relationship the signal expects. The graph gives a concrete check: a pure power adjustment chiefly redistributes intermediate tones, while a range error can move the black and white endpoints too. See Also ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.title: Lossless Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.keywords: Lossless Video Compression The samples 40, 42, 43, 43 can be stored in four 8-bit words, requiring 32 payload bits. They can also be stored as a starting sample plus differences: 40; +2, +1, 0. Nothing has been rounded. Knowing the starting value, the decoder can reverse every addition and recover all four samples exactly. A complete small coding rule Give common differences short prefix codes: Difference Code 0 0 +1 10 +2 110 Anything else 111 , followed by a signed 9-bit difference No complete prefix is the start of another. The decoder can distinguish the short codes and knows to read nine more bits after the escape prefix. Nine signed bits cover differences between arbitrary 8-bit sample values. For the four-sample example, store: starting sample 40 +2 +1 0 00101000 110 10 0 The payload is 8 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 14 bits , instead of 32. Real byte storage can add padding, and a real format must communicate length and coding rules. This is an original toy codec, not FFV1's entropy coding. Decode it: Read the first eight bits: 40. Read 110 : add 2, giving 42. Read 10 : add 1, giving 43. Read 0 : add zero, giving 43. The values and their order are identical. That is lossless sample compression . A good predictor saves space without taking a risk A predictor tries to make differences small and statistically common. In the toy rule, zero needs only one bit. An unpredictable sequence uses the escape code more often and can become larger. The decoder still recovers the exact values because every difference is retained. A poor prediction hurts compression efficiency, not correctness. Real lossless codecs use more capable predictors and coding methods to exploit picture structure. FFV1 is a specified video format built for this kind of exact reconstruction. Some delivery codecs also have lossless modes, with their own format and decoder requirements. Place the guarantee around the encoder Imagine decoding an existing lossy film, resizing it, then losslessly encoding the result. The lossless decoder recovers the resized samples exactly. It does not recover the earlier camera samples, because the losses and resize happened before that codec received its input. This identifies a practical verification boundary: compare the samples immediately supplied to the lossless encoder with the samples restored by its decoder, in the same sample format and order. A file checksum answers a different question. Repackaging or changing tags can change file bytes while leaving decoded video identical. Conversely, an intact file can faithfully preserve an input that already contained damage. For an Emby preservation master, the exact sample representation can be retained separately from a smaller delivery version. The master supplies the stable input for future derivatives; the playback copy supplies the representation appropriate for its viewing route. See Also Lossy Video Compression How Video Compression Works Intra-Frame Video Compression References RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.title: Lossy Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.keywords: Lossy Video Compression Lossy video coding saves data by allowing a reconstructed picture to differ from the encoder's input. The useful question is which information was approximated, and what did that change in the picture? Follow three corrections through the codec Suppose a predictor supplies values 100, 100, 100 for three positions. The actual input is 117, 97, 139 , so the differences needed to reproduce it are 17, −3, 39 . Now use a deliberately simple quantizer that rounds those corrections to the nearest multiple of eight: Position Input Predictor Exact correction Rounded correction Decoded result 1 117 100 17 16 116 2 97 100 −3 0 100 3 139 100 39 40 140 The decoder adds the rounded correction to the predictor. Its errors relative to the input are −1, +3, +1 . Original scalar example. It omits transform coding and uses arbitrary sample values to isolate quantization; it is not the exact quantizer of a named video codec. The compressed representation says “zero correction” for position 2. That could have arisen from −3, +2, or zero. Several different inputs map to the same coded result, so the decoder has no information with which to choose the original one. This many-to-one mapping is the irreversible step. Why approximation can reduce data Small corrections often occur where a predictor already describes the picture well. Rounding more of them to zero leaves fewer significant values to transmit. Coarser quantization can also reduce the precision required to describe the remaining values. In block-transform codecs, quantization operates on coefficients representing patterns across a region, rather than directly on the simple scalar corrections above. Removing or coarsening a coefficient changes the corresponding pattern when the block is reconstructed. A fine texture can weaken, or an edge can gain a faint oscillating outline. The complete compression walkthrough connects prediction, transform, quantization, and reconstruction. Lossy behavior comes from the permitted approximation, rather than from the fact that prediction was used. Allocate the compromise within a scene A stationary wall may have predictable regions and small corrections. Grainy foliage in motion can have more changing information. Preserving the latter at the same fidelity needs a different allocation of bits. An encoder makes decisions about predictors, block divisions, and quantization strength. With a constrained bitrate, difficult regions compete for that budget. With a quality target, the encoder can let size grow as the source becomes harder. The visible consequences follow the information affected. Simplified texture looks smoother; disagreeing neighboring regions can reveal block boundaries; coarse gradients can lose distinct levels. Some differences remain invisible at the intended display size, while others affect details the viewer notices quickly. Identify the stage being compared For a library file that is played directly, the decoder reconstructs the representation already stored. During video transcoding, Emby Server reconstructs that source and supplies its decoded pictures to another encoder. The second encoder's input already contains the first encode's changes. Giving the second stage more bits can preserve that input more closely; it cannot reverse the first stage's many-to-one decisions. Generation loss follows what happens when such stages are repeated. A useful comparison keeps the same source pictures, timing, and presentation and examines the converted reconstruction against them. That reveals the additional change caused by this encode, which is the quantity its quality settings can control. See Also How Video Compression Works Lossless Video Compression Intra-Frame Video Compression References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Inter-Frame Video Prediction | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Inter-Frame Video Prediction A new video picture often contains much of the scene already visible in another one. Inter-frame prediction describes a useful part of that decoded scene, then sends the information needed to correct it into the new picture. The decoder is not asked to identify the object or guess its true movement. The encoded stream tells it which reference to use, where to sample it, and which correction to apply. Conceptual motion prediction plus residual reconstruction, not a measured codec result. Find a useful reference region Suppose a reconstructed reference row is: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. The current four-sample region needs values 31, 39, 53, 60 . The reference region starting two positions to the right of the current block's coordinate is 30, 40, 50, 60 , already a close match. The encoder can select that reference and transmit an offset corresponding to +2 reference-sample positions in this declared convention. A motion vector locates the predictor. Its sign describes that coordinate relationship, rather than directly declaring a person's real-world velocity. A camera pan, object movement, or a repetitive texture can all make a shifted region useful. The encoder searches among permitted predictors and balances their fit against the cost of describing them. Add the residual The required difference between the current input and predictor is: Position Input Predictor Residual 1 31 30 +1 2 39 40 −1 3 53 50 +3 4 60 60 0 These are the residual values. A real codec can transform and quantize them before entropy coding. In a lossless representation they can be retained exactly. In a lossy representation the reconstructed corrections can differ. For a toy quantizer rounding these corrections to multiples of four, none of the values are half-step ties: +1, −1, +3, 0 → 0, 0, +4, 0. Add those decoded corrections to the predictor and the result is 30, 40, 54, 60 . Its errors relative to the input are −1, +1, +1, 0 . The sample arithmetic isolates prediction and approximation. It omits the named codecs' transform, quantization, and filtering details. A well-matched predictor leaves a small correction. A region containing a new object, an uncovered background, or different lighting can need larger corrections. The encoder can select another reference or use intra prediction for that region instead. Reconstruct the same reference on both sides Now imagine using this reconstructed picture to predict the next one. The decoder has 30, 40, 54, 60 , not the encoder's original 31, 39, 53, 60 . The encoder must build the next predictor from the reconstructed picture too. It therefore contains a local reconstruction loop that follows the decoder's operations. If it predicted from the original input instead, its transmitted residual would assume values the decoder does not have, causing a mismatch that could propagate into later pictures. This is why decoded reference pictures are part of the coding process. They are not merely pictures the player happened to retain for display. The vector can point between samples Movement need not be an exact number of sample positions. A codec can specify fractional-position prediction, using defined interpolation rules to construct reference values between the stored grid points. For example, a requested reference position halfway between two samples needs a calculated predictor rather than an integer array lookup. Each codec specifies its filters and rounding so compatible decoders construct the expected values. The residual then corrects this calculated predictor just as it corrects an integer-position one. This interpolation forms a predictor for a coded picture. It does not add new video presentation times. Combine available references A predictor can also combine information from two decoded references. For a scalar illustration, reference predictions of 40 and 44 average to 42. A residual of +1 reconstructs 43. A full picture can have different reference choices and coding modes in different regions. The picture's “P” or “B” description does not mean every sample uses one identical operation. One reference may be earlier and another later in display order . A decoder can process the later-displayed anchor first, retain it, then decode pictures scheduled before it on screen. The coded order satisfies the dependencies; presentation timestamps and the picture order then restore the viewing sequence. GOP structure and reference storage follow those relationships in more detail. When seeking into an Emby film, reconstruction starts from a suitable access point and rebuilds the needed reference state before the requested picture can be shown. Motion interpolation performs a different job: it estimates an extra picture at a time never supplied by the original coded sequence. Inter-frame coding instead has a represented target picture and transmitted corrections that define its reconstructed result. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Reference Frames Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Motion Interpolation References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Intra-Frame Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Intra-Frame Video Compression A picture can be compressed efficiently even when no earlier picture is available. Intra-frame compression finds useful structure within that picture: similar neighboring samples, continuing edges, and patterns that can be represented compactly. Predict a block from its boundary In a common block-based codec, some regions have already been reconstructed while the next block is still being decoded. Suppose the samples immediately above a four-column block are: 10, 20, 30, 40. A simple vertical predictor extends those values downward: 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 10 20 30 40 If the input block's first row is 12, 21, 30, 38 , its correction from that prediction is +2, +1, 0, −2 . The encoder can describe the predictor choice and those relatively small corrections. The decoder constructs the same prediction from its available upper boundary, adds the decoded corrections, and obtains the reconstructed block. Original numerical illustration of a directional predictor. It does not specify every mode or coding step of a particular codec. A horizontal predictor could instead extend samples from the left boundary. Other modes continue diagonal structures or form a flatter estimate. The encoder chooses a suitable description; the decoder follows the transmitted choice rather than searching for the original camera image. Why reconstructed neighbors matter The encoder's original boundary samples can differ from the decoded boundary after lossy coding. To keep prediction consistent, the encoder builds its predictor from the reconstruction the decoder will have. Both sides then start from the same known samples. Any approximation occurs in the coded correction and related reconstruction operations, rather than through a hidden disagreement about the boundary. This creates dependencies within the picture. Intra coding removes sample prediction from other pictures, but it does not imply that every block is decoded in arbitrary order or that a raw block is independently meaningful. Not every intra-frame codec uses this exact predictor style. Motion JPEG, for example, emphasizes independent JPEG picture coding. The general property is that picture samples are represented without temporal prediction from another picture. Work with independent pictures An all-intra video avoids chains that require reconstructing earlier picture samples before a chosen picture. An editor can seek to a picture, read its coded representation, and decode it using the stream's configuration and same-picture rules. That is useful for scrubbing, cutting, and assigning complete frames to processing jobs. The source's own picture content is available without a long temporal reconstruction chain. The cost is that a nearly unchanged wall has to be described within each new picture again. Temporal prediction can reuse an earlier decoded wall and transmit mainly its changes. Intra-only formats allocate the coding budget differently. An intra-coded picture inside an otherwise inter-predicted stream still needs the surrounding access rules interpreted. It can reconstruct its own samples independently, while reordered or following pictures may use references from before it. Random access therefore considers more than the picture's intra coding alone. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Video Keyframes and Random Access How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Reference Frames | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Reference Frames A decoder reconstructs pictures into memory. Some are kept because another picture will use their samples for prediction; these are reference pictures . Others are kept because their display time has not yet arrived. One picture can have both roles. The decoded picture buffer tracks these uses so a surface is not released while either job still needs it. A displayed picture can remain a reference Consider a GOP where I0 is displayed first and P3 later predicts from it. Displaying I0 does not make its samples dispensable: P3's reconstruction still needs them. After decoding P3, the decoder can retain both I0 and P3 for B1 and B2, which use the anchors around them. Once every required dependent has been decoded and the stream no longer retains I0 as a reference, that reference role can end. A picture's lifetime is therefore set by the actual dependency instructions, not simply by whether the user has already seen it. A reference can also wait for display P3 may be decoded before B1 and B2 because they need it. Its samples already exist, but showing it immediately would put the film out of order. Picture state Why memory remains occupied Already displayed, still a reference Future decoding needs its samples Decoded ahead of display Its presentation time has not arrived Both reference and pending output Both requirements apply to one picture Neither role remains The surface can become available for reuse These roles can overlap, so adding a reported reference count to a reported reorder count does not automatically give the number of distinct stored pictures. Some reference pictures remain useful for longer stretches, such as an older view of a background temporarily covered by a foreground object. Codecs provide explicit rules for retaining and releasing the available references. Count the samples in a surface For an even-sized, tightly packed 8-bit 4:2:0 example, the main plane has width × height samples. Each of the two color-difference planes has half the width and half the height: W × H + 2 × (W/2 × H/2) = 1.5 × W × H samples. With one byte per sample: Grid One picture's sample payload Four pictures' payload 1920 × 1080 3,110,400 bytes, 3.1104 MB 12.4416 MB 3840 × 2160 12,441,600 bytes, 12.4416 MB 49.7664 MB The bytes are decoded sample payloads , not compressed packet sizes. A low-bitrate UHD stream still reconstructs a UHD surface. If the same sampling grid uses 16-bit containers for its samples, one FHD picture requires 6,220,800 payload bytes and four require 24,883,200 bytes . A 10-bit sample can occupy such a 16-bit container, so valid precision and allocated storage width are different quantities. Actual decoder allocations can add row alignment, a larger coded raster, additional working surfaces, and an output queue. The calculation isolates the visible-grid payload rather than estimating every implementation's total memory. Connect lifetime to decoder capacity More retained pictures need more surface storage. Larger pictures increase each surface's footprint. Codec level constraints describe relevant buffer resources along with picture size and throughput. In Emby playback, this helps explain why recognizing the codec is only one part of source decoding. The active decoder must hold the pictures required by that bitstream's dependencies and presentation order. When inspecting a reference count, establish whether it is a declared maximum, an encoder setting, or observed use. Individual blocks can choose among a smaller set at a particular moment. The dependency graph determines which decoded surfaces must actually stay alive. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) A group of pictures (GOP) is easiest to understand by following which decoded pictures other pictures use. The visible sequence below contains seven pictures: I0, B1, B2, P3, B4, B5, P6. In this example, I0 is intra-coded; P3 uses I0; P6 uses P3. B1 and B2 use I0 and P3, while B4 and B5 use P3 and P6. Declared dependency example. Its B-pictures are not references. Other legal structures use different dependencies and orders. Decode the anchors before the pictures that need them The decoder can begin with I0 . It creates that picture's samples and retains them as a reference. Next it decodes P3 , using I0 and P3's coded corrections. P3 appears later on screen, but it must exist before B1 or B2 can use its samples. The decoder now has both anchors and can reconstruct B1 and B2 . It can then present the initial sequence in viewing order: I0, B1, B2, P3. The next anchor is P6 . Decode it from P3, then use P3 and P6 to reconstruct B4 and B5. The remaining viewing order is B4, B5, P6. One valid coded order is therefore: I0, P3, B1, B2, P6, B4, B5. Decoding follows dependencies. Display follows the picture timeline. The decoder needs picture storage to bridge those two orders. What the letters tell you Letter in this example How its samples are predicted I Within the picture, without another picture as a sample reference P From an available reference picture, with coded corrections B From the permitted reference choices, including the two anchors used here The letters describe coding possibilities and picture/slice types, not a universal lifecycle. A modern B-picture can itself become a reference. A picture can also mix prediction choices across its regions. For example, a hierarchical structure might decode a B-picture between two distant anchors, then use that intermediate picture to predict other B-pictures. The dependency graph becomes deeper even if the visible I/P/B sequence looks similar. “B” therefore does not mean that the decoder can always discard it immediately. Follow the references' lifetimes I0 can already have been shown when P3 and the early B-pictures use it. It remains in memory because prediction still needs it. P3 may first be held because it was decoded ahead of display. After it has been displayed, it still remains a reference for P6, B4, and B5. Being displayed and being safe to release are separate events. In this declared graph, I0 can cease being a reference after its last dependent picture is reconstructed. P3 lasts longer. These decisions affect the decoded picture buffer , while output reordering decides when each finished picture is shown. GOP length in pictures and seconds An encoder's maximum keyframe interval is often expressed as a picture count. At 24 fps, 48 pictures span two seconds . At 24000/1001 fps they span 2.002 seconds ; at 60 fps they span 0.8 seconds . The same picture count therefore gives different time spacing in different sources. Scene-change decisions can also create an entry earlier than the configured maximum. More frequent independently usable pictures provide closer starting places for seeking or joining playback. Longer prediction runs can reuse more scene information before a reset. Their benefit depends on how well the scene remains predictable; a cut replaces much of that useful relationship. Closed and open boundaries A closed GOP can reconstruct its pictures without sample references from an earlier group. The illustrated seven-picture graph is closed because all its references are inside the group beginning at I0. An open GOP allows dependencies across a nominal boundary. As a conceptual example, leading pictures displayed before a new intra anchor can use both that anchor and an older one from the preceding group. The new anchor is independent, but those leading pictures are not. A random start needs the codec's rules for those relationships: which pictures can be reconstructed, which must be skipped, and where valid presentation begins. Starting continuously with the previous group already decoded is a different situation from starting with an empty reference buffer. This is why access-point type matters alongside a GOP length. A run of “48 frames” does not by itself describe the boundary dependencies. In an Emby seek or transcode start, the decoder reconstructs the required graph before it can deliver the requested pictures. Understanding that graph explains why picture order, access spacing, and reference storage work together.
