articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Keyframes and Random Access | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Keyframes and Random Access You seek to 11.3 seconds in a film, but the picture you want is predicted from earlier decoded pictures. Jumping directly to its compressed bytes would leave the decoder without those references. A random-access point , commonly marked as a keyframe , provides a place from which the required state can be rebuilt. Follow one seek request Assume a constant 24 fps stream with clean entry points every two seconds. For this example, the player selects the first picture at or after the requested time. 11.3 × 24 = 271.2 , so that picture is frame 272 , at 11.3333 seconds . The preceding entry point is frame 240 , at 10 seconds . Stage Work performed Locate an entry Find the coded access point at 10 seconds Configure decoding Supply the codec's required stream parameters Rebuild pictures Decode from frame 240 toward the target Begin requested presentation Show the selected picture at its assigned time For a deliberately simple I/P-only chain where each picture depends on its predecessor, frames 240 through 272 require 33 picture decodes , including both endpoints. The earlier output pictures are not necessarily shown; they supply reference state and are discarded from the requested presentation. The selection policy and dependency chain are declared examples. Reordered structures can need additional anchors or different preroll handling. The container index helps locate byte positions associated with access points. The codec determines whether the decoder can actually begin there. Both pieces are needed for a useful seek. Supply the configuration An independently reconstructable picture still needs its codec configuration. The decoder must know dimensions, sample format, and the applicable coding parameters. These can be supplied by the container or repeated in the stream, depending on its format. For H.264, sequence and picture parameter sets are part of that configuration. A bare picture payload without the needed parameters is not a complete decoding starting package. An I-picture answers a narrower question An intra-coded picture reconstructs its own samples without temporal prediction from another picture. That says nothing by itself about dependencies of following or reordered pictures. Consider a group that starts with an ordinary I-picture but also contains leading B-pictures using an older reference. Starting with an empty decoder at the I-picture cannot reconstruct those leading pictures just because the I-picture itself is independent. H.264 IDR pictures establish a reference reset: subsequent prediction cannot rely on pictures preceding that reset. HEVC defines IDR and additional access types, including CRA , with specific handling for leading pictures when playback begins at the access point. These rules determine which pictures can validly be presented after a random start. Access spacing changes the work More frequent clean entries can reduce how far the decoder needs to work forward after a seek. In the example, starting at 10 seconds is much closer to the target than starting at the beginning of the film. Encoders also spend data establishing new independently usable pictures. Access-point spacing is therefore a tradeoff between prediction efficiency and convenient starts, with scene changes sometimes creating additional entries. In Emby, the same source reconstruction can precede transcoded output after seeking. Its delay can include storage reads, decoder work, and output initialization; the reference chain explains the part due to picture dependencies. Changing an index flag does not rewrite those dependencies. If a byte location is incorrectly marked as an entry, uninterrupted playback can work because the decoder already has state, while seeking there fails. The useful repair is a correct access description or a newly encoded entry structure, rather than an unsupported “keyframe” label. See Also Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Intra-Frame Video Compression Inter-Frame Video Prediction References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.title: Video Codec Levels and Tiers | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.keywords: Video Codec Levels and Tiers A codec level defines a resource envelope for a bitstream: how large its coded pictures can be, how quickly they must be processed, how much picture state can be retained, and how much coded data must be buffered. A profile selects the kinds of operations. Level limits describe the scale at which those operations are required. Some codecs also define tiers , particularly for bitrate and coded-buffer limits. Work through a 1080p AVC stream H.264 counts several level resources in 16 × 16 macroblocks . For a progressive picture presented as 1920 × 1080, round each coded grid dimension up to a macroblock boundary: Width: 1920/16 = 120 macroblocks . Height: ceil(1080/16) = 68 macroblocks . Picture size: 120 × 68 = 8,160 macroblocks . The coded macroblock grid is 1920 × 1088 . A signaled crop can remove the extra eight rows from presentation. The decoder's coded-picture work still follows the larger macroblock grid. For H.264 Level 4.1, selected limits are: Resource Level 4.1 limit Macroblocks in a coded frame, MaxFS 8,192 Macroblocks processed per second, MaxMBPS 245,760 Decoded-picture-buffer macroblocks, MaxDpbMbs 32,768 These are selected standard constraints, not the whole conformance test. Picture size and throughput give different answers The example's 8,160 macroblocks fit the per-picture limit of 8,192. At 30 fps , processing demand is: 8,160 × 30 = 244,800 macroblocks/s , below 245,760. At 60 fps , demand is: 8,160 × 60 = 489,600 macroblocks/s , above that limit. The dimensions are identical, but the second stream requires a larger throughput envelope. A label assigning “1080p” to one universal level would hide this difference. Other level constraints still need checking, including bitrate, coded buffering, motion limits, and profile-dependent factors. Passing the two calculations above explains one part of the requirement rather than certifying an arbitrary file. The reference-buffer calculation At this coded picture size, the selected DPB limit gives: floor(32,768 ÷ 8,160) = 4 picture slots. References and pictures awaiting output have to satisfy the decoded-buffer rules. A stream requesting more state cannot be made compliant by reducing only its bitrate. Conversely, a small compressed file can still require the full decoded picture surfaces. The reference-buffer article explains those surfaces' lifetimes and sample-memory footprints. A standard's logical DPB constraint and an implementation's total allocated memory are related but distinct measurements. Read a tier with its codec HEVC defines Main and High tiers. Where High tier is defined, it permits higher bitrate and coded-buffer limits within the relevant level. It does not select a different camera resolution or automatically improve the picture. In the description “HEVC Main 10, Level 5.1, Main tier” : Main 10 is the profile's sample/tool permission. 5.1 is the level's resource envelope. Main tier selects the corresponding bitrate/buffer limits. The word “Main” serves two different names in this family. The entire codec-specific description supplies the meaning; H.264 Level 4.1 and HEVC Level 4.1 do not share one interchangeable resource table. Change the demand, or correct an excessive declaration If a source really exceeds a target's throughput, producing a suitable representation can require a lower picture rate, smaller raster, different reference structure, or other encoding changes. Editing its level flag does not reduce the coded work. A file can also be declared at a higher level than its actual demand needs. Correcting such a declaration requires checking the complete applicable constraints, including peak and buffer behavior, rather than looking only at the visible resolution. For an Emby decoder target, these calculations turn a broad resolution claim into questions about the actual stream: its coded grid, picture rate, retained state, profile, tier, and delivery demand. See Also Video Codec Profiles Video Reference Frames Video Resolution Video Frame Rate References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers Android decoder video capabilities

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.title: Video Codec Profiles | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.keywords: Video Codec Profiles A decoder needs to understand every coding operation a stream can ask it to perform. A profile selects a permitted set of those operations and sample formats within a codec. This is useful both for designing a decoder and for creating a file for a known playback target. The encoder can restrict its choices to the target's tool set, rather than asking the decoder to handle every feature in the complete standard. Selected sample-format permissions Profile Sample depth Sampling covered by this row H.264 Baseline 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 Main 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 High 8-bit 4:2:0; monochrome also permitted H.264 High 10 Up to 10-bit 4:2:0; monochrome also permitted HEVC Main 8-bit 4:2:0 HEVC Main 10 8-bit or 10-bit 4:2:0 These rows describe selected format permissions, rather than a complete profile specification. They show why a decoder for an ordinary 8-bit stream may need additional sample-processing capability for a 10-bit stream. The tools can differ even at the same depth H.264 Baseline, Main, and High can all represent 8-bit 4:2:0 pictures, yet their bitstreams can use different operations. Entropy coding: CABAC encodes syntax through context-adaptive binary arithmetic coding. Its decoder follows a probability state and arithmetic decoding process. H.264 Main and High permit it; Baseline uses the permitted non-CABAC coding route. Identical final pixel depth does not make those compressed syntax representations interchangeable. Picture prediction: Main and High permit B-slices. The associated reference choices and possible reordering require the relevant prediction and buffering behavior. Baseline's restrictions exclude that B-slice tool set. Block transforms: High adds permission for an 8×8 transform tool, while Main's transform set is narrower. The decoder must apply the transform described by the stream to reconstruct its corrections. The profile label identifies these restrictions as a package. More tools give an encoder different options for representing the source, but the label itself does not select its quantization strength or measure the finished picture. Make a stream conform to another profile Suppose a target requires H.264 Baseline, while the source uses High with CABAC and 8×8 transforms. Changing the word “High” in metadata leaves the CABAC-coded syntax and transformed blocks in place. The decoder would still encounter operations excluded from the claimed profile. Creating the target requires decoding the source and encoding its pictures using the target's actual permitted tools. The encoder restricts entropy coding, prediction, transforms, and any other relevant choices together. A High 10 source converted to an 8-bit target also needs a change of sample representation. That happens in the processing/encoding path, rather than being accomplished by relabeling a 10-bit payload. A Main 10 HEVC stream can contain SDR or HDR. HDR interpretation comes from the appropriate transfer/color signaling and content; the profile's depth permission describes the sample/tool set. Pair the profile with its resource limits “HEVC Main 10, Level 5.1, Main tier” describes three aspects: a permitted tool/sample set, a workload level, and a bitrate/buffering tier. The level and tier need to accompany the profile when establishing a decoder target. For an Emby playback route, identifying the source profile and the app's usable decoder makes a profile-related conversion understandable. The target encode supplies a representation that conforms to the chosen tool set; it does not improve the source merely by giving it a different profile name. See Also Video Codec Levels and Tiers How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers x264 source: Profile restrictions

articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.title: How Video Compression Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.keywords: How Video Compression Works A camera following a person across a plain wall records much of the same scene again and again. Storing every picture as a fresh list of sample values would spend a large amount of data describing that repetition. Video compression finds a cheaper description from which a decoder can reconstruct the pictures: where to get a useful prediction, how to correct it, and which small differences to retain. That description is what Emby stores and delivers as a compressed video stream. The player reconstructs full pictures for display. To understand the savings—and why quality, encoding speed, and seeking behave as they do—it helps to follow one region through this process. How much data is being replaced? For a 1920 × 1080 picture stored as 8-bit 4:2:0 video, four picture locations use four luma samples and two chroma samples. Luma carries the brightness-related signal; the two chroma components carry color differences. The lower chroma sampling density gives an average of 1.5 bytes per picture location. Ignoring padding and headers: One picture occupies 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes . At 24 pictures per second, that is 74,649,600 bytes per second , about 74.65 MB/s or 597 Mb/s . One minute would occupy about 4.48 GB in decimal units. A hypothetical compressed video stream averaging 6 Mb/s would use about 45 MB for that minute, before audio and container overhead. The raw-to-compressed ratio in this example is roughly 100:1. That calculation describes the data reduction, not a guarantee of what any particular source will look like at 6 Mb/s. The raw baseline already has a defined sample format. Comparing it with full-resolution RGB or with samples of a different bit depth would give a different ratio. Compression operates on the picture representation supplied to the encoder; scaling, reducing bit depth, and changing chroma sampling are additional ways a workflow can change that input. Find a prediction worth describing The encoder divides a picture into regions and looks for useful ways to predict their samples. Region sizes and available prediction tools depend on the codec. A large region can describe a smooth wall efficiently. Around a moving hand or a detailed edge, smaller regions may provide better matches. There is a cost to that flexibility. Dividing a region means describing the divisions and their individual choices. The smallest possible regions do not automatically make the smallest file. The encoder has to weigh improved predictions against the extra instructions. Predict from the same picture With intra-frame prediction , a region can be predicted from neighboring samples that have already been reconstructed. If nearby samples have similar values, extending those values into the new region can be a good starting point. A directional prediction can continue an edge across the region. Both encoder and decoder know those reconstructed neighbors and the selected prediction rule. The encoder sends the choice of rule and a correction, rather than a completely independent value for every sample. “Intra” therefore does not mean “uncompressed.” Even a picture that has no dependencies on other pictures can exploit a great deal of repetition within itself. A broad, evenly lit wall is much easier to describe this way than a field of unrelated random values. Predict from other pictures With inter-frame prediction , the encoder can obtain samples from reconstructed reference pictures. When the person moves to the right, a region at the person's new position may resemble a region farther left in a reference picture. A motion vector tells the decoder where to obtain the selected prediction. The decoder does not need to recognize a person or understand the motion of an arm. It follows sample-location instructions. The encoder does the search; the decoder uses the result. Depending on the codec, predictions can use several reference pictures, interpolated sample positions, or combinations of predictions. Motion prediction is especially useful when a camera pans across a scene. Many sample positions change, but large areas still resemble shifted versions of an earlier picture. Conversely, a small newly revealed strip behind a moving object may have no useful match. The encoder can choose another prediction or code that region using intra prediction. The prediction is often imperfect: illumination changes, an edge moves by a fraction of a sample, or a surface deforms. The remaining difference is the residual . A useful prediction makes that correction easier to describe. Follow the correction through an encode Take four illustrative luma samples. The prediction is close to the source: Stage Four sample values Prediction 100, 102, 104, 106 Source 102, 101, 108, 107 Residual: source minus prediction 2, −1, 4, 1 If the decoder receives that exact residual, adding it to the prediction recovers the source exactly. This subtraction is reversible. Lossy compression enters when the encoder chooses to describe an approximation of the correction. Change the representation before rounding A transform expresses a region as a mixture of patterns. One pattern might represent a constant offset; others describe variations across the region. The resulting numbers are coefficients : how much of each pattern is present. A constant residual of 2, 2, 2, 2 illustrates the attraction. Instead of treating the four equal corrections as unrelated numbers, a suitable transform represents their common component and leaves the variation components at zero. Real picture regions often contain smooth areas and gradual changes that concentrate much of their information in relatively few coefficients. For a transparent numerical example, use a small reversible add-and-subtract transform. This is a teaching example, not the transform prescribed by H.264 or H.265. Given residual samples a, b, c, and d, calculate: c0 = (a + b + c + d) / 2 c1 = (a + b − c − d) / 2 c2 = (a − b + c − d) / 2 c3 = (a − b − c + d) / 2 For 2, −1, 4, 1, the coefficients are 3, −2, 3, 0 . For the constant residual 2, 2, 2, 2, they would be 4, 0, 0, 0 : all the correction is in the common component. The transform has not thrown away information. Applying the corresponding inverse to the unrounded coefficients recovers the original residual. It has put the information into a form that is often cheaper to approximate and code. Quantize the coefficients Quantization reduces the number of coefficient values that need distinct representations. For this example, round to the nearest multiple of two, with halfway cases rounded away from zero: Coefficient values Before rounding 3, −2, 3, 0 After rounding 4, −2, 4, 0 Levels, expressed in units of the step size 2, −1, 2, 0 A decoder given the levels and step size reconstructs 4, −2, 4, 0. It cannot determine whether an original coefficient of 3 or 4 led to the reconstructed value 4. Those distinctions have been merged. Larger quantization steps merge more distinctions and often make more coefficients zero. That can reduce the number of bits substantially, while changing the reconstructed picture more. Actual codecs define their own scaling and quantization rules, and encoders can adjust choices across a picture. The simple step of two here is not a codec QP setting. Code the remaining symbols compactly The bitstream must describe more than coefficients. It also contains prediction choices, region divisions, reference information, motion data, and other syntax. Entropy coding represents those symbols using their statistical patterns. For example, a long region of zero coefficients does not need a separate full-sized integer for every zero. Contexts in which one outcome is very likely can also be represented more economically than contexts with many equally likely outcomes. The exact method depends on the codec. This stage preserves the symbols it is given. It does not decide that a coefficient should become zero; quantization and the encoder's coding decisions have already established what will be represented. A decoded coefficient sequence can be an exact copy of the coded sequence even while the resulting picture differs from the original. Reconstruct the picture the player will get Applying the inverse toy transform to the rounded coefficients produces a residual of 3, −1, 5, 1 . Adding that correction to the same prediction gives: Four sample values Original source 102, 101, 108, 107 Decoded reconstruction 103, 101, 109, 107 Reconstruction minus source 1, 0, 1, 0 Two sample values changed by one. The decoder has done its job correctly: this is the picture specified by the compressed description. It has no access to the discarded distinctions needed to restore the two original values. The example also shows why a compression error need not look like a single missing pixel. Changing a transform coefficient changes a pattern spread over several samples. In real pictures, stronger approximation can soften texture, alter an edge, or produce visible patterns around it. Compression artifacts are the visible consequences of those decisions. The encoder keeps a local reconstruction so later predictions use pictures that the decoder can also obtain. The codec defines the actual transforms, syntax, and reconstruction rules. Why the encoder needs its own reconstruction For later pictures, the encoder must predict using the samples the decoder will have. After the example above, a reference region contains 103, 101, 109, 107, even though the original source contained 102, 101, 108, 107. Suppose the next source picture has a sample value of 104 at the corresponding position. Predicting from the reconstructed value 103 leaves a correction of 1. The decoder can make that same prediction and obtain 104. Predicting instead from the pristine source value 102 would leave a correction of 2; adding it to the decoder's reference value 103 would produce 105. That disagreement is why the encoder reconstructs its chosen approximation and uses the result for future references. Both sides must operate from matching information. A lossy reference does not inevitably make all following pictures worse: later corrections can account for differences, provided the encoder uses the correct reconstructed reference. Reconstruction can also include codec-defined processing such as in-loop filtering. In block-based coding, this processing can reduce some discontinuities or adjust reconstructed samples. When those filtered pictures serve as references, the encoder must account for the same processing. A filter used only for display has a different role because it does not redefine the samples used for subsequent predictions. Lossless video compression retains the information needed to recover the input samples exactly. It can still exploit prediction and statistical coding. It does not have to use this lossy transform-and-rounding path; FFV1, for example, codes sample differences without discarding them. Lossless applies to the samples supplied to that encoder. Any earlier scaling or color conversion remains part of how those samples were produced. Picture dependencies explain decoding order and seeking A reference picture must be reconstructed before a picture that uses it. The order in which pictures are decoded can therefore differ from the order in which they appear on screen. Consider a simplified sequence displayed as A, B, C. Suppose C is predicted from A, and B is predicted using both A and C. The decoder needs this order: Decode A. Decode C using A. Decode B using the two available references. Present A, B, C at their intended times. The player holds the necessary pictures and uses their timing information to restore presentation order. “A later picture” in a prediction description can mean later in display order; it is already available when the dependent picture is decoded. The same dependencies matter when seeking. Jumping directly into a dependent picture may omit references needed to reconstruct it. A player typically starts at a suitable random-access point , then decodes the necessary path to the requested time. Merely having a picture coded without inter prediction does not, for every codec structure, guarantee that all subsequent dependencies have been reset. More frequent independent access points can make entry into the stream easier, but give the encoder fewer opportunities to reuse earlier pictures. This is one reason a seek-friendly or low-latency stream can have different compression characteristics from a stream designed mainly for efficient sequential playback. The encoder chooses between competing descriptions For one region, an encoder may have several plausible descriptions: one large prediction, several smaller predictions, a different reference picture, or an intra prediction. Each produces a different residual and requires a different amount of syntax. A prediction with the smallest raw residual is not necessarily the best final choice. It might require many extra motion instructions. Conversely, accepting a slightly less accurate prediction can be worthwhile if its coded description is much smaller. Rate-distortion optimization expresses this tradeoff. “Rate” is the number of bits needed; “distortion” is a measure of the reconstructed picture's difference from the source. As a constructed example, consider two complete coding choices: Choice Bits for this region Distortion in illustrative units A 120 10 B 70 14 If the cost is distortion + 0.05 × bits, A costs 16 and B costs 17.5, so A wins. If bits are more expensive and the multiplier is 0.2, A costs 34 and B costs 28, so B wins. Nothing about the source changed; the available tradeoff changed. Real encoders use more involved calculations, and a simple sample-error score does not capture every aspect of perceived quality. The example explains why a coding decision can change when a bitrate budget changes. The x265 analysis options expose controls for how thoroughly such alternatives are evaluated. Scene complexity affects those alternatives. A static wall offers predictable samples and often small corrections. Film grain and sensor noise contain variations that are harder to predict. Leaves moving independently, splashing water, or newly revealed detail can require many corrections. Preserving that information costs bits; smoothing it makes the picture cheaper to describe. Rate control manages these choices over time. A quality-oriented encode can allow difficult sections to use more data. A constrained stream has to fit its delivery budget, potentially using stronger approximation in a difficult scene. A full movie's average bitrate hides those local differences. Resolution and frame rate describe the output grid and timing, while the coding decisions determine how faithfully that grid represents the source. Encoding effort and playback effort are different The decoder follows a selected description. The encoder may have tried many descriptions before choosing it. That search is why increasing encoder effort can improve compression without requiring the player to repeat the search. The x265 presets provide a concrete example: slower presets evaluate more possibilities, while faster presets take more shortcuts. Comparing encoders fairly means considering the resulting quality, bitrate, and time together. Identical codec names or nominal quality settings do not establish identical decisions. Playback still has work to do: entropy decoding, reference management, prediction, reconstruction, and any required filters. A device must support the particular codec features and sample format, and perform those operations fast enough for the picture rate. A compact stream can consequently be harder for a device to decode than a larger stream in a simpler supported format. For Emby, these distinctions separate three common paths. During Direct Play, the app decodes the stored compressed video. When the server copies that video into a different container, the compressed picture description remains intact. During a video transcode , the server decodes the source, performs any required processing, and creates a new compressed description for the destination. The new encoder sees the reconstructed source, including any texture or edge changes already present in it. More output bits can preserve that input better; they cannot identify discarded original detail. That is why keeping the original library file gives future playback and conversion paths the best available starting point. See Also Lossy Video Compression Lossless Video Compression Inter-Frame Video Prediction Containers and Codecs References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format x265: Encoder presets and compression efficiency x265: Coding decisions, quantization, and rate control

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Compression Artifacts | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Compression Artifacts A moving fabric texture becomes smooth, an edge gains faint ripples, or a dark sky breaks into steps. Compression artifacts are the visible effects of reconstruction decisions that failed to retain an important part of the source's appearance. Different appearances come from different relationships inside the picture. Boundaries between coded regions Block-based coding gives neighboring regions their own predictions and corrections. If quantization simplifies them differently, their reconstructed edge values may disagree. A smooth surface can then acquire a rectangular boundary that was not in the source. In-loop deblocking can address selected discontinuities, but the reconstructed representation still reflects how the regions were coded. The visible block size need not equal one fixed macroblock size: partitioning, motion, filtering and error propagation can produce larger or less regular patches. Patterns around a sharp edge A sharp transition needs a combination of spatial patterns to represent it. Transform coding describes those patterns with coefficients. Coarsening or dropping coefficients changes their balance when the block is reconstructed. The edge can soften or gain small alternating ripples around it, often called ringing. Similar appearances can also arise from scaling or sharpening filters, so compare where the ripple first appears in the processing path. This is more informative than treating every halo as proof that a particular codec was selected. Follow a smooth ramp through fewer levels Use a simple scalar quantizer that rounds to multiples of four: Source values 100 101 102 103 104 105 106 107 Rounded values 100 100 104 104 104 104 108 108 The source advances one unit at a time. The reconstructed array repeats a few levels and jumps between them. Spread such repeated values over a visible gradient and the smooth transition can appear as bands. Original rounding example with half-step ties upward. Real video transforms and sample processing introduce their own region and precision behavior. Limited source precision or a later display conversion can also create stepped gradients. The calculation demonstrates the loss of distinct levels; locating the responsible stage determines which operation can change it. Texture can change in time Fine detail and grain need many changing correction values. A constrained encoder can simplify them, making a region smoother. When the allocation or prediction changes in later pictures, the amount of retained texture can change too. A surface may then shimmer, pulse, or briefly become sharper at certain picture boundaries. A still frame does not reveal that temporal inconsistency. Observation Relationship worth inspecting Rectangular surface changes Region reconstruction and boundaries Edge ripples Transform approximation and later filters Soft detail Retained high-frequency patterns Pulsing texture Picture-to-picture allocation or prediction Stepped shading Available sample/reconstruction levels Find the first changed representation For an Emby conversion, compare the selected source with the delivered result at the same picture time and presentation scale. If the source already contains the defect, the output is working from that reconstruction. If it appears only in the new stream, examine that encode and any preceding processing. Then view the passage in motion. Grain consistency, flickering outlines and movement-specific breakup can be missed by paused comparisons. A controlled second encode with more available precision or data can test whether the new coding compromise caused the change. A filter can instead conceal it by removing or modifying detail; that is another picture operation, not recovery of the original coefficients. The comparison identifies the actual transformation to improve, while generation lineage identifies which earlier source information is still available. See Also Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Bitrate Film Grain in Compressed Video Video Generation Loss References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding Zhou Wang: SSIM index and reference implementation

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Film Grain in Compressed Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Film Grain in Compressed Video A still wall can be difficult to compress when its scanned film texture changes in every picture. The wall is stable, but the grain is additional varying information the encoder has to represent. Film grain can be part of the intended appearance of a film scan or a deliberately added effect. Its strength, scale and behavior belong to that presentation. A static scene can have a changing residual Take a simplified underlying scene sample of 100: Picture Grain contribution Observed sample A −3 97 B +4 104 Predict B from A without any movement and the residual is 104 −97 =7 . The scene's underlying value did not change; the grain contribution did. Across many samples, that varying texture weakens the usefulness of directly reusing the previous picture. Finer grain can leave many changing coefficients rather than a small predictable scene correction. Original scalar illustration, not a film-grain generator or measured codec result. Direct coding spends data on the visible pattern An encoder can represent the grain as part of the picture samples. Its predictions, transforms and quantization then handle both the underlying scene and the texture. At a tight budget, some grain detail can become smoother or form coarser patches. If the coding decisions change sharply between regions or pictures, the retained texture can also appear uneven: one area has stronger grain, then another frame suppresses it. This can make a film seem to pulse or “breathe,” even when its overall resolution and average bitrate remain unchanged. A grain tuning can prioritize consistency x265's documented tune grain emphasizes avoiding artifacts caused by uneven grain distribution. It restricts selected QP-varying behaviors and biases decisions toward more high-frequency content. Its specialized rate control also tries to limit quantizer fluctuations. That is a specific allocation priority. It is not a promise to reproduce every original grain sample or simply a universal instruction to keep all noise. A whole-scene review should therefore assess whether the texture remains coherent in motion, alongside the resulting data requirement. Model the appearance instead AV1 can encode a cleaner picture and signal parameters for adding modeled grain during output processing. Parameter role What it contributes to the generated appearance Strength versus brightness Grain can behave differently in dark and light areas Relationships between nearby samples Gives the texture structure rather than independent noise alone Generation seed Specifies the generator's repeatable pattern behavior The decoder applies the specified synthesis to the output. The reconstructed scene retained for future prediction is separate from that added grain realization. This can reduce the need to transmit every grain sample in the coded picture while retaining a designed grain-like appearance. It preserves an appearance model, rather than the exact source texture array. Evaluate texture rather than a single paused speck Compare passages at the intended scale and in motion. Look at grain strength, clumping, continuity across regions and stability around picture changes. A paused enlargement can emphasize isolated samples without showing temporal pumping. Pixel-error metrics can also react to a different grain pattern even if its intended texture is similar. A synthesized realization and the original scan need not match sample for sample. Decide whether the comparison aims at exact sample preservation or the intended viewing appearance. For an Emby viewing version, that distinction explains whether a grain change came from simplification, filtering, inconsistent direct coding, or a different modeled texture. Those are different operations on the film's appearance. See Also AV1 Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts Video Generation Loss References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification x265: Presets and tunings

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Generation Loss | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Generation Loss If two viewing copies are made separately from the same retained source, each begins with that source's picture information. If a third copy is made from one of the viewing copies, it begins with an already altered reconstruction. That difference is the useful way to understand generation loss . The diagram shows conversion lineage, not measured visible damage. Separate new encodes from a chain Let M be a retained master. Make A for one playback target and B for another: M →A and M →B . B does not inherit A's encoding errors because A was not its input. Ordinary Emby playback conversions that each read the retained library source have this branching relationship. Repeated viewing does not itself turn the previous delivery stream into the next source. A chain instead looks like M →A →C . A user might create it by converting a small copy and later using that copy for another export. Each stage's encoder receives the samples reconstructed at the preceding stage. Follow the errors at one aligned position For pictures in the same sample representation, let A's error relative to M be A −M , and C's new error relative to A be C −A . Then: C −M =(A −M) +(C −A). Take a scalar example: M is 17, A is 16, and C is 18. The first stage changes the value by −1, the second by +2, and the final error relative to M is +1. This does not mean every encode adds the same visible damage, or that each sample's absolute error must increase. Errors can reinforce or partly cancel at a position. The equation identifies the inputs whose differences are being combined. Original scalar illustration; it is not a prediction of a named codec's multigeneration quality. Why lost distinctions cannot be recovered from size Suppose a first quantizer rounds both 17 and 19 to 16. The stored result no longer identifies which of those two inputs occurred. A later process might produce 18, but it cannot know which original input to recover from the shared 16. More output bits can describe that input reconstruction more accurately; they do not supply the discarded distinction. In a picture, such distinctions can correspond to texture, grain or subtle gradients. A delivery copy can therefore be an adequate viewing source while being a reduced input for later production. Locate the operation that creates a generation Operation Video sample/coding effect Copy the file Existing coded video is retained Repackage the same video packets Existing picture coding is retained Convert audio while copying video No new video encode Decode and encode video with lossy settings A new video reconstruction is created Losslessly encode the decoded samples That stage retains its input exactly Display metadata or timestamps can also change presentation without a new video encode. Cropping/resizing/filtering followed by encoding changes the input array as well as its later coding. Identify those operations before interpreting a difference between copies. A useful source strategy follows from the lineage: keep the best retained input and make needed derivatives from it. When editing requires an intermediate, a suitable lossless or production representation can serve the next stage, while its guarantee remains tied to the samples it actually received. articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video Start with four 8-bit grayscale sample values in a reference picture and the corresponding four values in a test picture: Position Reference Test Difference Squared difference 1 50 52 +2 4 2 100 98 −2 4 3 150 153 +3 9 4 200 196 −4 16 The squared differences total 33 . Dividing by four gives the mean squared error, MSE =8.25 . Its square root is the RMS error , approximately 2.8723 sample units . Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) expresses this error relative to a declared peak using a logarithmic scale. Convert the sample error to decibels For this example, choose peak =255 , the maximum code value of an 8-bit sample: PSNR = 10 × log10(peak² /MSE) So: 10 × log10(255² /8.25) = 38.9663 dB , approximately 38.97 dB. The peak is the declared sample-format convention, not the brightest observed reference value, which happened to be 200. Selecting a different peak changes the score even if every error remains the same. Original paired-sample calculation for one plane. It is not a measured video encode. Read the logarithmic scale Calculated curve for one plane, peak 255, and positive RMS error; no encoder benchmark or perceptual threshold is implied. RMS error in this convention PSNR 1 48.13 dB 2 42.11 dB 4 36.09 dB 8 30.07 dB Doubling RMS error multiplies MSE by four. Its PSNR change is 10 × log10(4) ≈6.02 dB downward . With zero sample error, the mathematical value is infinite. That establishes exact equality of the compared sample arrays. Their file bytes, metadata and earlier source history are separate observations. The statistic records energy, not location One four-sample error pattern could be +2,+2,+2,+2 : a uniform offset. Another could be +4,0,0,0 : a localized error. Both have MSE 4 and the same PSNR. Their distribution differs. In an image, a change on a sharp outline can be noticed differently from error spread across a smooth region. PSNR averages squared magnitudes and does not describe that placement or local structural relationship. SSIM develops a different comparison using local picture statistics. Aggregate the quantity you intend Suppose two equally sized frames have MSE values 1 and 100 , using peak 255. Pool their squared errors first: mean MSE =(1 +100)/2 =50.5. The resulting PSNR is 31.10 dB . Average their separately calculated frame PSNR values instead: (48.13 +28.13)/2 =38.13 dB . These are different calculations because the logarithm is nonlinear. The score's aggregation rule therefore belongs with its reported number. FFmpeg's PSNR filter documents accumulation/averaging of MSE before calculating its aggregate. Prepare corresponding pictures A valid conversion comparison needs corresponding content at corresponding times, with a declared geometry, sample format and peak convention. A shifted crop, a one-picture offset or an unintended range conversion can measure those changes rather than the encoder's reconstruction error. For an Emby derivative, compare the actual delivered reconstruction with the selected retained source after the intended common preparation. Record the compared span and plane handling as well as the aggregate. The calculation then tells you which sample error the reported decibels represent. See Also Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video VMAF Video Quality Metric Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Generation Loss References FFmpeg: PSNR filter Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli: Image quality assessment from error visibility to structural similarity

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video Take a small reference patch with values 40,40,60,60 . It contains a step from a darker region to a lighter one. Now compare two reconstructions: Patch Values Mean squared error from reference A: brightness shifted 50,50,70,70 100 B: step flattened 50,50,50,50 100 Both have the same squared sample error. A retains the step and its contrast, while B removes it. Structural Similarity (SSIM) compares local statistical relationships that distinguish those results. Separate mean, contrast and structure The original SSIM approach uses three relationships: Local mean: the average sample value. This is its luminance comparison; in this grayscale example it refers to code values, not physical display luminance. Local contrast: the spread around that mean, described by variance or standard deviation. The step patch has variation; the flat patch has none. Local structure: how corresponding deviations vary together, described by covariance. When both pictures put their below-mean and above-mean values in the same places, that correspondence is positive. For the reference, the mean is 50 . Its deviations are −10,−10,+10,+10 . Using sample variance with denominator N−1: (100 +100 +100 +100)/3 =133.333… Patch A has mean 60 and the same deviations. Patch B has mean 50 but all its deviations are zero. Calculate the combined comparison For this illustration, use the original combined form: SSIM =((2µxµy +C1)/(µx² +µy² +C1)) ×((2σxy +C2)/(σx² +σy² +C2)) Here µ denotes the local mean, σx² and σy² are variances, and σxy is covariance. Choose an 8-bit peak convention L = 255, with K1 =0.01 and K2 =0.03: C1 =(K1L)² =6.5025 , and C2 =(K2L)² =58.5225 . The constants stabilize comparisons when a mean or variation is small; two identical flat patches should not require dividing zero by zero. Test patch Mean Variance Covariance with reference Calculated SSIM A 60 133.333… 133.333… 0.983624… B 50 0 0 0.305034… A's contrast/structure factor is 1, with a smaller change in its mean factor. B's mean matches, but its variance and covariance describe the missing step. Original four-value arithmetic using uniform local statistics and N−1 variance/covariance. It demonstrates the formula, not the output of a particular video tool's 2D windowing implementation. Reverse the step A third patch, 60,60,40,40 , has the same mean and variance as the reference, but its deviations are opposite at every position. Its covariance is −133.333… . With the declared constants, its SSIM is approximately −0.640071 . Negative covariance can therefore produce a negative index. SSIM is not universally a 0–1 percentage of retained picture quality. Identical local content gives 1 in this original formulation. That identity case and the reversed-pattern example describe what the mathematical comparison is measuring. Move from a patch to a video A real implementation calculates local windows across each picture and combines their results. Window size and weighting, color/plane handling, scale preparation and frame aggregation all affect the number. The author's suggested image scaling is one concrete example. Netflix's VMAF FAQ documents that its included SSIM applies empirical downsampling that differs from FFmpeg's SSIM filter. Equal input filenames do not make those preprocessing choices identical. For a conversion comparison, align the picture content and times and declare the measurement geometry. Then examine local or per-frame results where detail changed, rather than relying only on a whole-film aggregate. See Also Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video VMAF Video Quality Metric Video Compression Artifacts Video Generation Loss References Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli: Image quality assessment from error visibility to structural similarity Zhou Wang: SSIM index and reference implementation Netflix: VMAF frequently asked questions

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: VMAF Video Quality Metric | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: VMAF Video Quality Metric Suppose you are making smaller playback versions of the same retained movie source. Looking at every frame of every candidate is impractical, but file size alone says little about which version preserved the picture better. VMAF supplies one way to measure that comparison. VMAF, Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion, is a full-reference video-quality metric. It receives decoded pictures from a reference and a test sequence, extracts comparison features, and uses a trained model to predict quality in a defined viewing context. What goes into the score The comparison begins with corresponding pictures, not with file extensions or compressed byte sizes. Features capture aspects of the relationship between the reference and test content, such as retained detail and motion-related behavior. A model combines the features using relationships learned from subjective-quality data. The published v0.6.1 model, for example, lists an ADM detail feature, a motion feature, and VIF features at four spatial scales. These give the model several measurements of the picture relationship rather than one overall sample-error value. The selected model defines which measurements it consumes. Training supplies examples for which comparison features and viewer assessments are both available. The fitting process learns a mapping from the feature combinations to those assessments. Evaluation then measures a new reference/test pair and applies the fitted mapping. The training happened before this evaluation; choosing a VMAF model does not train a new model on the movie being tested. That last stage is why the result differs from a direct error formula such as PSNR . VMAF's number is the output of a particular learned model. It is intended to be useful for perceptual comparison; it is not a count of retained bits, pixels, or original information. A score of 95 therefore needs context. Which model produced it? How were the inputs prepared? Is it a mean for a whole film, or the score of one scene? Prepare the comparison before interpreting it Corresponding input pictures must represent the same content at the intended comparison geometry. A frame offset can compare two different moments. A crop difference can compare different regions. A range or color conversion applied on only one side can become part of the measured difference. When comparing a lower-resolution playback version with a larger reference, scaling is an explicit part of the evaluation. Use a consistent preparation that represents the intended viewing situation. A different scaler can change what the metric sees. This is especially relevant to HDR-to-SDR material. A straightforward comparison of incompatible signal representations does not isolate compression quality. Establish which picture representation is being compared and whether the selected model is suitable for it. For repeatable results, keep a small record with each test: The reference source and the tested encode. Model/version and tool settings. Sample format, geometry, scaling, and timing preparation. How per-frame results were aggregated. Read the model's viewing assumptions Artifacts that are visible close to a large screen may be much less visible from farther away. Models calibrated for different viewing conditions can therefore assign different values to the same reconstruction. Netflix's familiar v0 models and the v1 models released in June 2026 have documented viewing assumptions. Common models use a 0–100 scale; the v1 4K model for viewing at three screen heights uses 0–110. These are model conventions, not a universal percentage scale. A score from one model should not be treated as the same quantity as an equal-looking score from another. Even within one model, changing clipping settings or input preparation can change the interpretation of the result. Look past the whole-film average Consider a hypothetical constant-frame-rate, one-minute test: fifty seconds score 95, and ten seconds score 50. The arithmetic mean is 87.5. That single number cannot tell you whether the lower-scoring section is an inconsequential transition or the scene the viewer most cares about. Per-frame and per-scene results help locate the weakness. A low-tail summary can be useful alongside the mean, and a targeted viewing check can show what happened: smeared grain, unstable texture, blurred fine detail, or another visible change. Enhancement processing can complicate the measurement. Sharpening may change measured features while introducing a look that a viewer dislikes. Grain handling can also affect a reference comparison even where a synthetic-grain presentation is intentional. The metric and a viewing check answer related questions, rather than replacing one another. For an Emby library conversion, use VMAF to narrow the candidate encodes and identify passages worth inspecting. After choosing a satisfactory picture reconstruction, test the intended playback path separately for decoding and delivery performance. That preserves a clear meaning for the score: how the tested pictures compare under the stated model and preparation. See Also Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts References Netflix: published v0.6.1 model inputs Netflix: available comparison features Netflix: VMAF project Netflix: VMAF documentation Netflix: VMAF v0 models and viewing conditions Netflix: VMAF v1 model selection, viewing assumptions, and score ranges Netflix: VMAF frequently asked questions

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Bitrate Average video rate Bytes for one second of pictures Video-only size over two hours 4 Mb/s 0.5 MB 3.6 GB 8 Mb/s 1 MB 7.2 GB 16 Mb/s 2 MB 14.4 GB Decimal units. Two hours is 7,200 seconds; the calculation excludes soundtracks and packaging. Video bitrate counts coded picture data against media duration. It is the video's data budget or measured rate, rather than the whole file's rate when that file also contains audio and other tracks. Divide one second among its pictures At 8 Mb/s, one media second contains 1,000,000 video bytes on average. At 24 fps, the average allocation is 1,000,000/24 =41,666.67 bytes per picture . At 60 fps it is 16,666.67 bytes . The same per-second budget is spread among more pictures. Actual pictures need not have those average sizes. Consider a deliberately constructed 24-picture interval: Pictures Bytes per picture Combined bytes One independently coded picture 195,000 195,000 23 predicted pictures 35,000 805,000 Total 1,000,000 The interval still has 8 Mb/s of coded video. The large picture establishes content that the following pictures can reuse. Their sample count is not smaller; their encoded descriptions are. This example explains why a source can contain substantial frame-size variation at a stated average bitrate. Decide what the encoder is trying to hold A target average rate tells rate control to allocate data around an overall budget. It may use more in difficult sections and less elsewhere. A rate/buffer limit constrains local coded demand. Its meaning includes the relevant time and buffering model, not only a maximum number printed beside a file. A quality-based encode lets the resulting average rate emerge from its source and target. The measured bitrate is then an outcome rather than an exact amount selected in advance. CBR , VBR , and CRF develop these policies separately. Connect the budget to the source An encoder can reuse a wall across neighboring pictures with small corrections. Grain, fine texture and changing scenery require more information. Adding more frames also creates additional prediction opportunities, so a simple bits-per-picture division does not by itself determine visible quality. Presets change how thoroughly the encoder searches for a representation; quantization changes what approximation it accepts. The rate budget constrains their result. In an Emby session, compare the source video's measured rate with the delivered video's rate . Video conversion can create a different allocation while the original library file keeps its own rate. A file-wide bitrate can also include unused soundtracks, so keep the measurement's counted streams and duration explicit. See Also Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets References FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding A channel supplying 4 Mb/s can deliver four million bits in one second. Constant bitrate (CBR) encoding controls the video around a selected rate and its buffering requirements so that delivery can be planned predictably. Pictures still require different amounts of data. A keyframe may establish an entire scene; a predicted picture may mainly describe what changed. Supply a large picture over time Suppose one coded picture contains one megabit . At 4 Mb/s, supplying it takes: 1,000,000 ÷4,000,000 =0.25 second. A 30 fps presentation interval is only 33.33 ms. The complete picture therefore cannot be expected to arrive from an empty buffer solely during its own display interval. Its data must have been supplied ahead of its decoding deadline. Smaller surrounding pictures leave more opportunity to build that buffered supply. The model limits both data rate and how much data can be retained. VBV follows the occupancy calculation in detail. The blue series uses equal one-second totals as a simple illustration. Actual CBR control need not make every one-second bucket or individual frame identical. Both plotted allocations contain 32 megabits over eight seconds. Rate control changes the picture description The encoder estimates how many bits a candidate picture description will need. As the available budget tightens, it can increase quantization strength or choose a less expensive coding representation. After encoding, the actual number of produced bits updates its rate-control state. If a difficult scene needs more data than the permitted model allows, that feedback must affect the representation. Fine texture can be simplified or reconstructed less precisely. Easy scenes can meet the same delivery requirements with smaller corrections. This is why CBR places predictability in the data path while allowing picture fidelity to change with the source. It does not assign an equal-quality amount of data to every scene. Strict output can include filler An easy section may not need all the channel's allowed data to reach the intended coding result. Some implementations offer filler or padding to keep strict coded output at the required rate. NVIDIA's NVENC API explicitly documents filler/padding controls for that purpose. Their presence is an implementation and mode choice, rather than a requirement that all encoders calling a mode “CBR” produce identical bytes every instant. Filler occupies data capacity without adding new photographed picture information. Counting it as part of encoded traffic and evaluating picture payload alone are different measurements. Coded rate and transfer speed are separate observations An Emby player can fetch data faster than it consumes it, then pause requests while buffered video plays. Its network graph can show bursts even when the video was encoded under CBR constraints. To interpret the result, use the coded stream's data across media time, its rate-control settings and relevant buffer model. Network arrival across wall-clock time describes how that representation was transported. The buffer bridges those two schedules. See Also Video Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Constant Quality Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Quality Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Quality Video Encoding When preparing a library viewing copy, one possible objective is to preserve an acceptable appearance and let the resulting size follow the source. Constant quality encoding starts with that kind of quality policy instead of requiring the video to spend exactly a chosen amount of data. The policy belongs to the encoder. It guides reconstruction choices; it is not a measurement stamped onto every finished scene. Follow the controller's decisions The encoder analyzes picture structure and predicts how difficult regions will be to represent. It chooses prediction, partition and quantization decisions that serve its quality objective. A largely static region may need only a short correction. Changing fine texture can need many significant coefficients. The same quality policy can therefore produce a small description of one region and a larger description of another. After coding those choices, the number of produced bits is the result. Across a film, varying source difficulty makes bitrate fluctuate and determines the final size. This reverses an average-budget control priority: Objective Held as the main target Allowed to respond to content Average bitrate Overall data budget Reconstruction compromise and local allocation Quality-led encoding Encoder-defined quality policy Overall size and local bitrate Fixed quantizer mode Selected quantizer policy Bits and scene-dependent visible error The last row is related, but not identical to the middle one. Holding one quantizer does not ensure equal perceptual quality across different scenes. Preserve the parts that matter to later pictures A reference region can influence more than its own displayed picture. If later predictions reuse it repeatedly, improving that reconstruction can benefit many dependent pictures. An encoder can incorporate that importance into its quantization decisions. Regional adaptation can also distribute precision differently between smooth areas, detail, and motion according to the chosen model. These operations explain why the same quality setting does not require a single unchanging QP. CRF , hardware target-quality controls, and CQP have different mechanisms and scales. The model need not be an external score such as VMAF. Its internal coding estimates and perceptual priorities guide the encode; a later quality measurement evaluates the resulting pictures using another defined method. A delivery cap adds a competing requirement Suppose the quality-led choices for a difficult section would require more coded data than its permitted rate and buffer deadline. The encoder cannot both transmit that full representation and satisfy the restrictive deadline. It must change the picture description: coarser quantization, another prediction/partition choice, or other permitted rate-control behavior. The desired quality becomes a goal constrained by delivery. VBV provides the buffer model behind that decision. The source and chosen cap determine when this tradeoff occurs. Without the cap, the encode can use more data for that section; with it, the output has another obligation besides the quality policy. Evaluate the policy on the actual source A useful evaluation includes material that exercises the policy differently: static detail, grain, rapid movement and smooth gradients. Compare candidate settings using the same source and encoder configuration, looking at the reconstruction as well as its data demand. For an Emby viewing copy, this establishes both the picture you want to retain and the stream the playback route must supply. Size is then an observed outcome of those decisions, rather than a quality value selected independently of the source. See Also Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Variable Bitrate Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video At one constant rate factor (CRF) setting, a video can produce different bitrates and different picture quantizers from scene to scene. The constant is an encoder model's selected rate-factor control, rather than the number of bytes allocated to each second. x264 and x265 use CRF as quality-led variable rate control. Within a fixed setup, lowering the selected value generally moves toward finer reconstruction and more data; raising it moves toward stronger approximation. For exact sample preservation, use the encoder's documented lossless mode. x265 documents an explicit mode for that purpose; CRF 0 is not a universal lossless convention. This separates quality-led approximation from a different reconstruction guarantee. Separate the control from the quantizer it produces QP selects quantization strength. CRF guides the decisions that produce those quantizers. The controller analyzes the source and applies its quality/importance model. It can choose a different baseline or regional QP as content and picture role change while retaining the same user CRF. Observation at one CRF Reason it can change Frame QP Picture role and rate-control analysis Regional QP Adaptive precision/importance decisions Bits per frame Source information and selected representation Whole-file average The accumulated demands of that source The CRF number therefore does not mean “all frames used QP 23” or “every second received the same rate.” Those would be different control policies. Follow the source into the model An encoder's analysis estimates how well the pictures can be predicted and how much correction their structure leaves. More complicated content can have more significant information to represent. In x265's implementation, a fixed rate factor participates in the conversion from modeled terms into quantizer scale. Additional picture and regional analysis changes the resulting allocation. The full code has separate branches for its enabled analysis tools, rather than one equation directly mapping CRF to visible error. Picture role is important. An independently coded anchor establishes information needed by later pictures. A region reused by many future predictions can be worth reconstructing more carefully than a region that disappears immediately. Adaptive decisions can distribute precision accordingly. The encoder then chooses partitions, predictors and coded corrections at those quantizers. The actual produced bits update its coding estimates. Size emerges from this process instead of being an exact budget requested for the film. What a rate cap changes A CRF encode can also have a maximum rate and buffer constraint . The model's preferred representation must then fit local delivery deadlines. If a demanding section needs more data than the cap allows, the controller changes its reconstruction choices to satisfy the constraint. Its output can depart from the unconstrained quality policy there. The cap is therefore part of the encoding setup, not an invisible accessory to the CRF value. The same CRF with two different caps can create different results in the scene that binds those caps. Evaluate the value with the encoder fixed Choose representative passages that include the important source characteristics: grain or clean animation, motion, fine static detail and smooth shading. Make candidate encodes that differ in the CRF value while keeping the codec implementation, version, preset, sample format and other constraints stable. Then compare the decoded pictures and their observed rate/size. A setting is useful when the reconstruction serves the intended viewing context and its data demand serves the intended delivery. The source's easy passages and difficult ones need to be assessed together. CRF 20 in x264, CRF 20 in x265, and a CRF-like AV1 control belong to different models. Their shared number is not an equal-quality specification. Record the implementation and settings with the result so the comparison can be repeated. See Also Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Video Encoder Presets References x265: Quality and rate-control options FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) A coded correction value of 21 can be reconstructed as 20 with one quantizer and 24 with a coarser one. The choice changes both the value recovered and the amount of detail the encoder needs to describe. A quantization parameter (QP) selects quantizer strength through the particular codec's rules. Original scalar model: output =step ×floor(input/step +0.5), with arbitrary steps 4 and 8. It isolates rounding, not the exact quantization equation of a named codec. Read the rounding operation Input correction Round to multiples of 4 Error Round to multiples of 8 Error 3 4 +1 0 −3 9 8 −1 8 −1 21 20 −1 24 +3 27 28 +1 24 −3 The coarser step has fewer reconstruction levels. Several precise input values share one output, leaving less precision to encode. The error can also change direction, depending on where the input falls between levels. In a transform codec, those quantized values describe patterns across a block. Changing a coefficient changes its contribution to the reconstructed correction, rather than necessarily changing only one visible pixel. A codec maps QP onto its scale For ordinary 8-bit AVC luma coding, QP ranges from 0 to 51. With the same relevant scaling, an increase of six doubles the quantization step. Using QP 20's scale as 1 for a declared relative comparison: QP Relative scale 20 1 26 2 32 4 These are relative factors at six-step separations, not a declaration that QP 20 has an absolute step of one sample unit. The transform/scaling context supplies the absolute meaning. Different codecs and greater sample depths use their own indices and conventions. AVC's higher-depth internal quantizer index includes a depth offset, for example. A reported QP needs that context before being compared to another encode. A mode decides how the parameters are assigned Constant QP is an encoder's quantizer-control policy. It can define a base value and different picture-type settings or offsets. x265 documents its selected base for P-slices and related I/B values. CRF uses an adaptive rate-factor model that can produce varying picture and region quantizers. Bitrate control can also change QP to fit a data/buffer budget. These modes operate at different levels of the decision. A fixed base quantizer does not impose equal frame bytes: one picture can contain far more information to code at that precision than another. Interpret a reported average Imagine two equally weighted regions using QP 20 and QP 32. Their arithmetic mean QP is 26 . In the relative AVC scale above, their scales are 1 and 4, whose mean is 2.5 . A uniform QP 26 region instead uses relative scale 2. The equal mean QP has hidden a different distribution. This is a numerical illustration with equal weights and unchanged scaling, not a reconstruction-quality prediction. A log can also average over picture types, region sizes or other weights. Its number summarizes those assignments, while the actual bitstream reconstructs each region with its applicable quantizer. See Also Lossy Video Compression Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Compression Artifacts References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Two-Pass Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Two-Pass Video Encoding Suppose an offline conversion must fit 40 seconds of video into an average 4 Mb/s . Its video budget is: 40 ×4 =160 megabits , or 20 decimal MB. The encoder can spend that budget differently in different scenes. Two-pass encoding first analyzes the source so its final allocation can use knowledge of the complete sequence. The final pass reads the original source again; statistics guide its choices. Analyze before making the final allocation A first pass evaluates picture difficulty and coding relationships. Its statistics can describe prediction costs, picture types, bits produced or estimated, and information useful for allocating precision later. Suppose four ten-second scenes receive illustrative difficulty weights 1,1,4,2 . A deliberately simple planner assigns budget proportional to these weights: Scene Declared weight Allocated data Rate across ten seconds A 1 20 Mb 2 Mb/s B 1 20 Mb 2 Mb/s C 4 80 Mb 8 Mb/s D 2 40 Mb 4 Mb/s Total 8 160 Mb 4 Mb/s overall This is an original proportional-planning example, not x265's rate-control formula or a measured encode. Real allocation models and local buffer constraints are more involved. Knowing that C is difficult lets the planner reserve more data for it while keeping the whole budget. A controller making decisions with only a short lookahead has less information about the complete video's later demands. Encode the source with the plan The second pass decodes or reads the same source pictures , uses the statistics to guide its quantizers and other choices, then produces the final bitstream. Actual coded sizes can differ from an estimate, so rate control updates its decisions as the encode proceeds. A local rate/buffer limit can also prevent spending the planned 80 megabits evenly or freely in C. The complete-file objective and the local deadline constraints both need to be satisfied. The first pass's compressed pictures are not ordinarily the second pass's source. Its useful output is the statistics. That is why analyzing and then encoding do not automatically create two successive lossy generations. Keep the statistics attached to their source The analysis describes a particular picture sequence. Changing its trims, picture order, scale, filtering or other relevant processing before the final pass can make those statistics describe the wrong input. The two passes therefore need consistent source and processing context. If a first pass uses faster analysis settings, those are deliberately chosen as part of the encoder's documented process, while the source relationship remains intact. Audio and packaging also occupy space if the objective is a complete-file size. The 160-megabit example is a video-only budget; reserve those other contributions separately when planning a full output. Hardware multipass has a smaller scope An encoder such as NVENC can analyze a frame in an internal pass, then use the result when encoding that frame. Its analysis can improve the distribution within the picture. That is not a first scan of the entire 40-second clip followed by a second reading. Both are called “passes,” but the amount of future source information available differs. Whole-source two-pass preparation suits an offline library derivative whose final budget matters. An immediate Emby playback transcode needs to begin output without waiting for a whole-film analysis. Its controller instead works with the information available at that stage of delivery. See Also Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets Video Bitrate References x265: Quality and rate-control options NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding The variable-rate allocation in this figure uses 2, 3, 6, 7, 2, 3, 5 and 4 Mb/s across eight one-second intervals. Original allocation example, not encoder measurements. Each column represents one media second. The total is 32 megabits , giving an average of 32/8 =4 Mb/s . An equal 4 Mb/s allocation also contains 32 megabits. The two have the same total data, distributed differently through time. Variable bitrate (VBR) permits that changing allocation. Simple content can use less data and difficult content more, under the encoder's selected overall or local constraints. Supply the plotted sequence Use a simplified delivery model: the connection supplies 4 megabits per second continuously, and the video consumes each plotted interval's amount evenly within that second. Begin with 2 megabits already buffered. Interval Video demand Supplied Buffer at interval end 1 2 Mb 4 Mb 4 Mb 2 3 Mb 4 Mb 5 Mb 3 6 Mb 4 Mb 3 Mb 4 7 Mb 4 Mb 0 Mb 5 2 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb 6 3 Mb 4 Mb 3 Mb 7 5 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb 8 4 Mb 4 Mb 2 Mb The quiet first two intervals build supply for the demanding third and fourth. With an empty initial buffer, the same accounting would fall 2 megabits below zero by the end of interval 4. Matching the average rate would not be enough to start this simplified sequence without advance data. The assumptions deliberately isolate the arithmetic. Real frame removals, request timing, overhead and network interruptions require their own scheduling; this is not a decoder-buffer conformance test. A seek beginning near interval 4 also starts with a different buffer state. Earlier quiet content cannot supply a surplus unless it was actually fetched for that playback start. Two objectives can produce variable output An average-budget encode tries to fit the complete video into an overall amount of data. It can transfer allocation from easier sections to harder ones. Two-pass analysis provides additional knowledge of where those sections occur. A quality-led encode allows the size to follow the source at a chosen quality policy. The final average can be different for two films, or for a clean and grainy version of the same scene. CRF is one implementation of that kind of control. Both produce variable rates, but they are solving different optimization problems. “VBR” by itself does not identify which objective was used. Add a local limit deliberately A whole-film data budget says little about a short burst's deadline. A maximum-rate/buffer constraint adds local delivery requirements. The encoder may need to accept a less detailed picture when a difficult section reaches those limits.
