In an Emby session, original delivery retains the source's local variation; a video transcode creates another allocation with its own constraints. The plotted calculation shows which parts of that rate description explain total size, and which explain the supply needed during playback. See Also Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Two-Pass Video Encoding Bitrate Variation References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) A film can average 4 Mb/s and still contain a short section that needs data faster than a decoder can accept it. Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) constraints address that problem by asking whether the encoded pictures can pass through a defined rate-and-buffer model. The model has three essential ingredients: how data arrives, how much coded data can be stored, and when each picture removes its required data. An average for the whole film leaves the last two questions unanswered. Rate, capacity, and occupancy Suppose a simplified model accepts data at 4 Mb/s , has a capacity of 8 megabits , and starts with 4 megabits already available . The input rate describes how quickly the buffer can refill. Capacity is its maximum stored amount. Occupancy is how much it contains at a particular moment. A large picture can use data accumulated during easier pictures. It can require more than one frame interval's worth of arriving data without exceeding the model, provided that enough has arrived before its removal time. A picture fails the model if it needs bits that are not available when it must be decoded. The opposite limit matters too: arrivals and removals must follow rules that keep stored data within the permitted capacity. Codec models specify these details more precisely than this simplified illustration. Follow a burst through the buffer The following calculation groups picture removals into one-second intervals to make the arithmetic visible. Real bitstream conformance checks operate at the codec's specified removal times. Interval Starting occupancy Data arrives Pictures use Ending occupancy 1 4 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb 2 2 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 0 Mb 3, same demand continues 0 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb short The first two demanding intervals succeed because the buffer had a reserve. Continuing the burst exhausts it. An easier interval using 2 Mb could rebuild the reserve by 2 Mb under the same arrival rate. The film might still average 4 Mb/s overall. That would not repair the shortage in interval 3: data from a later easy scene cannot travel backward in time. Buffer capacity divided by arrival rate gives a useful scale. Here, 8 Mb / 4 Mb/s is two seconds. It is a description of the model's capacity relative to the rate, not an automatic two-second player startup setting. What the encoder changes An encoder enforcing VBV has to fit its choices to the available budget at each point. During a difficult scene it may increase quantization, simplifying the residual information and reducing the number of coded bits. The result can be a local loss of texture or visible artifacts even when a quality setting stays unchanged. In x265, vbv-maxrate supplies the rate constraint and vbv-bufsize supplies the capacity. Their documented units differ: kilobits per second for the former, kilobits for the latter. Initial fullness is another setting because starting with a larger reserve changes what an early burst can use. Combining CRF with these constraints lets the encoder pursue its quality target while the model permits it. When the two conflict, the delivery constraint can take priority. A smaller buffer or lower rate leaves less room to accommodate a difficult sequence at that quality. VBV is also not a synonym for CBR . A variable-rate encode can obey a bounded-buffer model. The buffer is exactly what allows some variation in picture sizes and short-term demand. Coding buffer versus playback buffer The coding model describes a constrained decoder's coded-data supply. An app's downloaded-data buffer deals with the actual network: requests, bandwidth variation, latency, and stalls. They are related in use but are different quantities. A player can accumulate data before starting, yet still have a decoder with limits on coded-picture size, timing, or buffering. Conversely, a conforming bitstream can stall over a connection that delivers less data than it needs. For an Emby transcode whose picture becomes softer during a busy scene, bitrate and buffering constraints provide a possible causal explanation: the encoder had to reduce that scene's data demand. For a stream whose picture is fine but playback pauses, examine delivery as well. The two observations lead to different parts of the playback path. See Also Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.262: MPEG-2 Video ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/Video-En.title: Video Encoder Presets | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/Video-En.keywords: Video Encoder Presets An encoder can describe the same picture region in several valid ways. It must decide how much time to spend searching for a useful representation. An encoder preset packages those search and coding-effort choices. Search another candidate Use a toy decision cost J =D +0.1R , where D is a declared distortion measure and R is the number of coded bits. Candidate Distortion D Bits R Cost J A, found early 16 100 26 B, found after more search 4 120 16 Under this cost, B is better even though it uses more bits. Its lower distortion outweighs that cost. If the search stops after A, the encoder never gets the chance to select B. Original arithmetic illustration of a decision objective, not an encoder benchmark, preset score or exact x265 configuration. A different candidate could improve both size and reconstruction. More search creates opportunities to find a better tradeoff; it does not define “better” as the smallest possible file regardless of picture damage. Which decisions take time? Motion search evaluates possible reference positions. Partition search evaluates ways to divide a region. Transform and quantization decisions assess alternative corrections. Lookahead examines later pictures to plan relationships and resource allocation. Faster presets take shortcuts or limit these choices. Slower presets can evaluate more candidates or use more detailed decision procedures. The resulting stream contains the choices selected, rather than the entire search history. This explains why encoder computation and decoder computation are different quantities. A costly search can produce a relatively straightforward predictor. Some enabled tools also change decoder work, so the final tool/profile structure remains part of the output description. Read an implementation's actual preset The published x265 table gives these selected examples: Setting medium slow What the difference affects Lookahead pictures 20 25 Amount of later picture analysis Reference setting 3 4 Candidate retained views for prediction These are selected settings from that documented implementation, not all the changes or a portable comparison with another encoder. Its presets also vary motion/partition and decision options. The rate or quality target supplies the allocation objective. The preset supplies the effort used to serve it. A tuning changes priorities for a source/use case, such as grain or low latency. Keep these controls distinct when evaluating an encode. Supply pictures fast enough for playback Suppose an encoder can sustainably produce 20 output pictures per wall-clock second while the requested playback needs 30 per media second. Encoding one second of media takes 30/20 =1.5 seconds . Under this model, the playback reservoir shrinks by 30 −20 =10 pictures per wall-clock second . A 300-picture prefill lasts 30 seconds of that continuing deficit. A short finite clip can finish within an adequate prefill; a continuous session cannot rely on a finite reservoir indefinitely. This is a declared throughput example, not the speed of any named preset or hardware. Processing can have multiple frames in flight. The relevant requirement is sustained output throughput, rather than insisting that each individual frame's processing latency be shorter than 1/30 second. For an Emby transcode, input decoding and required filters also share the processing job. A preset's useful additional search has to fit that complete supply path. An offline derivative can instead spend more time before the file is played, making a different effort tradeoff practical. See Also Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Bitrate Two-Pass Video Encoding How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References x265: Presets and tunings NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/frame-timing/Frame-Rate-C.title: Frame-Rate Conversion | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/Frame-Rate-C.keywords: Frame-Rate Conversion A 24 fps source provides pictures every 41.667 ms. A 30 fps output needs one every 33.333 ms. Frame-rate conversion decides what picture to put at each new output time. There are two separate questions: should the programme retain its duration, and should the additional output pictures be copies or newly constructed images? Answering them leads to different results. Place existing pictures on the new timeline Take four consecutive 24 fps pictures: Source picture Start time A 0 ms B 41.667 ms C 83.333 ms D 125 ms The four-picture span ends at 166.667 ms. Five 30 fps intervals fit the same duration. One illustrative policy selects whichever source picture was already visible at the requested output instant: 30 fps output time Selected source picture 0 ms A 33.333 ms A 66.667 ms B 100 ms C 133.333 ms D The output is A, A, B, C, D . Its duration is unchanged, but A receives two output intervals while the others receive one. For steady movement, the object pauses longer at A's position, then advances through the others more quickly. This table is a declared hold-latest policy, not a claim that every converter chooses that phase. Nearest-time selection or other timestamp rules can repeat a different picture. The unequal allocation remains a property of fitting these rates together with existing pictures. Converting to a lower rate has the corresponding selection problem. Some source pictures have no output slot and are omitted. The programme can remain the same length while containing fewer motion observations. Construct a picture for the requested time Instead of copying A at an intermediate time, a converter can combine or estimate the scene between A and B. Blending combines sample values from neighboring pictures. It can make the transition less abrupt, but a moving object may appear at both positions with partial opacity. Motion interpolation estimates correspondence and movement, then constructs an intermediate position. It can make the output motion more evenly sampled, while adding pictures inferred from the source. The interpolation article follows that reconstruction in detail. These methods preserve the intended programme timeline when their output timestamps remain tied to it. They change the images used at those times. Retiming the source changes duration A different operation plays every original picture once, but at another speed. A one-hour, exact 24 fps sequence has 86,400 pictures . Present those pictures at 25 fps: 86,400 ÷ 25 = 3,456 seconds = 57 minutes 36 seconds. The playback speed increases by 25/24 , about 4.167%. Duration is multiplied by 24/25 = 0.96 , a reduction of 4%. No extra picture has been created and no original one need be dropped. Audio events and subtitles must follow the new timeline. An event at 120 seconds in the original belongs at 115.2 seconds in this speed-changed version. Audio processing then needs to decide how to handle pitch as well as duration. This is why changing an fps description can be consequential if it changes timestamps, while merely displaying a rounded rate label is harmless. A screen can change the holds without changing the file A 24 fps film fits a 120 Hz display with five refreshes per picture. At 60 Hz, a common presentation alternates two and three refreshes. One illustrative display-hold phase for exact 24 fps and 60 Hz. Ten refresh intervals present four film pictures; these are not newly captured frames. Selecting a compatible display mode can retain the encoded picture sequence while making its display holds uniform. Creating a 60 fps file by repetition instead stores an output schedule that a 60 Hz display can follow, but does not remove the underlying uneven hold of the film pictures. Follow the operations in playback order For an interlaced recording, identify and reconstruct the field times before treating a reported pair rate as a progressive rate. A 25-frame-pair source can contain 50 motion times. Converting those pairs as if they were 25 complete camera moments can omit motion before later processing gets a chance to preserve it. For an Emby conversion, compare source timestamps, output timestamps and pictures, programme duration, and display refresh. A rate change with the same duration indicates picture allocation or synthesis; a proportional duration change indicates retiming. The visible result follows the operation performed, rather than the fps number alone. See Also Video Frame Rate Motion Interpolation Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown References FFmpeg command-line documentation FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Familiar label Exact rate Exact picture duration Duration in milliseconds, rounded 23.976 fps 24000/1001 fps 1001/24000 s 41.7083 29.97 fps 30000/1001 fps 1001/30000 s 33.3667 59.94 fps 60000/1001 fps 1001/60000 s 16.6833 These familiar decimals name precise rational frame rates . Each is its corresponding integer rate multiplied by 1000/1001 . The displayed decimal is rounded; use the fraction for timing calculations. The picture duration is the reciprocal of the rate. At 24000/1001 fps, every constant-rate picture occupies 1001/24000 second. Its spacing can be perfectly regular: “fractional” refers to the rate's value, while variable describes spacing that changes. Calculate a whole sequence Take exactly 86,400 pictures . At 24 fps: 86,400 ÷ 24 = 3,600 seconds. At 24000/1001 fps: 86,400 × 1001 ÷ 24,000 = 3,603.6 seconds. The same picture count lasts 3.6 seconds longer. Its duration increases by exactly 0.1%; its playback rate is multiplied by 1000/1001. This calculation explains a subtitle or audio version that starts aligned but gradually diverges after the picture sequence is retimed. Moving the start by a fixed offset does not change the duration difference. Retiming a fixed sequence and converting its picture allocation while preserving duration are different operations. The film-to-television ratio Fractional film and field rates retain the same useful ratio: (60000/1001) ÷ (24000/1001) = 2.5 fields per film picture. Four film pictures therefore span ten field intervals. That is the basis of the repeating 3:2 pulldown relationship at these rates. The 1001 denominator cancels exactly; rounding the rates to decimals is unnecessary for the calculation. See Also Video Frame Rate Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Variable Frame Rate References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Variable Frame Rate | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Variable Frame Rate The four pictures below begin at 0, 40, 60, and 120 ms . Let the last picture remain visible until 160 ms . Picture Starts at Ends at Duration A 0 ms 40 ms 40 ms B 40 ms 60 ms 20 ms C 60 ms 120 ms 60 ms D 120 ms 160 ms 40 ms Their intervals vary. This is variable frame rate (VFR) : the timeline carries the presentation schedule rather than describing every picture with one common duration. The variable picture starts match the table. The added 160 ms endpoint defines the complete example's final hold. What the player does The player shows A until 40 ms, B for the next 20 ms, then C for 60 ms. Audio continues along the same timeline. A new video picture need not arrive on every screen refresh; the current picture can remain visible until the next timestamp. A screen recording can exploit this to retain a picture longer while the screen is static. A camera or edited sequence can produce VFR for other reasons. The timestamp schedule, rather than an assumed capture strategy, defines the representation. The average hides the intervals There are four pictures across 0.160 second: 4 ÷ 0.160 = 25 pictures/s on average. Four equal 40 ms pictures over the same interval also average 25 fps. One sequence is variable and one is constant, even though their count, duration, and average match. A stream inspector can consequently show a reasonable average while picture-level timestamps reveal uneven intervals. This is useful for an Emby home video whose timing changes during conversion: compare the actual starts and durations, rather than only the rate field in a summary. Convert to a constant schedule A 25 fps output needs starts at 0, 40, 80, and 120 ms. One illustrative policy chooses the source picture currently visible at each output instant: Output instant Source picture selected 0 ms A 40 ms B 80 ms C 120 ms D The output still lasts 160 ms, but the transition to C now occurs at 80 ms instead of 60 ms. In a longer sequence, some source pictures may be repeated or omitted. A converter can use a different selection policy or interpolation, so its exact visible changes depend on that policy. The important point is that output pictures are chosen against the existing timeline . Duration and audio timing can remain intact even though the picture allocation changes. Retiming every picture is another operation If those same four pictures are instead each assigned 1/30 second, the sequence lasts 133.33 ms . The old presentation schedule has been replaced. Audio and subtitles following the original 160 ms timeline will no longer match without related retiming. Even assigning 40 ms to every picture, which preserves this example's total duration, moves its internal transitions. VFR carries those internal intervals as information. Preserving or changing them is a deliberate part of making a new video representation. See Also Video Frame Rate Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Frame-Rate Conversion References FFmpeg command-line documentation FFprobe media inspection documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Video Frame Rate | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Video Frame Rate At 24 frames per second, a video supplies a new picture every 1/24 second , or about 41.67 ms . At 60 fps, the interval is 16.67 ms . Frame rate describes this temporal sampling: how frequently the scene is represented by a new picture. Imagine an object moving steadily across the image at 600 picture positions per second. At 24 fps, it moves 25 positions between captures. At 60 fps, it moves 10. The second recording supplies more intermediate positions, so motion can be followed in smaller steps. Constant picture rate Interval between pictures Object movement at 600 positions/s 24 fps 41.67 ms 25 positions 25 fps 40 ms 24 positions 30 fps 33.33 ms 20 positions 50 fps 20 ms 12 positions 60 fps 16.67 ms 10 positions An ideal steady-motion example, not a measurement of a camera. Exposure happens inside that timing The camera also integrates light for an exposure. If this moving object is exposed for 1/48 second, it travels 12.5 positions during the exposure . Its image can therefore cover more than one sharply defined position in a single frame. Frame interval and exposure duration do different jobs. More frames provide more recorded motion steps. A shorter exposure can make each step crisper; a longer one can blur the movement within it. A recording can have frequent but blurred pictures, or infrequent but sharply edged ones. The player's task is then to present these existing pictures at their assigned times. Simply repeating them more often does not change the recorded exposure. Put a 24 fps film on a 120 Hz screen A screen's refresh rate is how often it updates. At exactly 120 Hz, the screen has five refresh intervals for each 24 fps picture: 120 ÷ 24 = 5. It can hold A for five refreshes, B for five, then C for five. Each picture remains visible for 5/120 second = 1/24 second. The display refreshes frequently, but the video still supplies 24 different pictures per second. At 60 Hz, the ratio is 2.5 . A common cadence alternates two and three refreshes. Some pictures remain for 33.33 ms and others for 50 ms, rather than a uniform 41.67 ms. During a steady pan, this alternating hold can produce judder. Frame-rate conversion can allocate pictures to another schedule; interpolation can estimate additional pictures. Choosing a display mode with an evenly divisible refresh rate is a separate route that preserves the existing picture sequence. Read the rate at the right stage In an Emby session, the source rate describes the library track. A video transcode has an output picture rate, and the display has an active refresh rate. Observing each stage explains whether a motion change came from the source, picture conversion, or screen cadence. Interlaced sources need their unit named as well. A stream reported as 25 frame pairs per second can contain 50 field capture times; its fields are not 25 complete progressive motion samples. Short labels may also round 24000/1001 to “24.” Exact timing calculations use the rational rate and the actual presentation timestamps. The interval between recorded pictures and the interval between screen refreshes remain separate quantities. See Also Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Variable Frame Rate Frame-Rate Conversion References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Deinterlacing | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Deinterlacing A progressive screen needs a complete picture for each presentation time. A native interlaced field supplies only alternating rows at that time. Deinterlacing solves the resulting reconstruction problem: keep the known rows and produce the rows needed between them. The difficult part is that the other field's existing rows come from a different moment. They may be ideal for a stationary background and wrong for a moving object. Original reduced-line schematic. It shows the principle of selecting one field's time and estimating its missing rows, rather than measured output from a named filter. Choose the time of the output picture Take a top-first 50-field/s recording: The top field describes the scene at 0 ms. The bottom field describes it at 20 ms. The next top field describes it at 40 ms. To make a complete progressive picture at 0 ms , the top-field rows are observations from the correct time. The bottom-field rows are later observations. If an object moved during those 20 ms, directly inserting its later rows puts two positions into one picture. A deinterlacer therefore needs more than the frame's height. It needs the field times, their order , and a rule for reconstructing the absent rows at the selected time. The simplest reconstruction: estimate between known rows Suppose one column in the top field contains these three brightness values at 0 ms: Row Known value at 0 ms Simple complete-picture estimate 0 10 10 1 Missing 20 2 30 30 3 Missing 50 4 70 70 A simple vertical interpolator estimates row 1 as (10 + 30)/2 = 20 and row 3 as (30 + 70)/2 = 50 . It retains the known rows and constructs the missing ones from nearby spatial information. These are arbitrary sample values demonstrating interior-row interpolation. They are not a named filter's output or a claim that the estimates equal the unavailable camera samples. Frame-edge handling requires an additional rule. This basic “bob” idea can produce one complete picture for each field time. It avoids weaving a later moving edge into the earlier picture. However, fine vertical patterns have been observed only on alternating rows, so their absent samples must be inferred. Thin horizontal details can soften or shimmer. A more sophisticated spatial method can interpolate along a diagonal edge instead of only between the values immediately above and below. Following an edge's direction can keep it sharper, provided the direction estimate is sound. Use the other field where time does not matter For a stationary area, both fields describe the same scene. Weaving their existing rows retains more direct line information than reconstructing half the rows from one field. The result changes with movement. Suppose the bottom field at 20 ms gives values 80 and 90 in rows 1 and 3 because a bright object has crossed the column. Weaving them into the 0 ms top field gives 10, 80, 30, 90, 70 . The added rows are real observations, but of a later scene. A moving outline can then alternate between its old and new positions on successive rows, producing combing. This is a time mismatch, not necessarily damage in the compressed file. Blending tries a different compromise by combining information from both times. It can reduce the stark row alternation, but a moving object may leave two partially visible outlines. The picture has integrated two scene states rather than reconstructed one sharply. Motion adaptation combines decisions within a picture A motion-adaptive approach asks where temporal information agrees and where it changes. It can use neighboring fields or frames to compare the relevant regions. In an area judged stationary, it can retain existing rows from both fields. In an area judged moving, it reconstructs the missing rows using spatial information and carefully selected temporal evidence. One frame can therefore contain different reconstruction decisions for its background and its moving foreground. Detection matters because a change in sample values can come from motion, noise, lighting, or a scene cut. Repeated textures can also make matches ambiguous. A wrong stationary decision leaves combing; a wrong moving decision can unnecessarily soften a static pattern. Switching decisions around an uncertain boundary can create flicker. FFmpeg's bwdif is documented as motion-adaptive, based on yadif with additional interpolation methods. These names identify particular implementations. The principles explain their task without assuming that every Emby server or client uses that implementation. Preserve the field cadence At 50 fields/s, the source has 50 native motion times. One-output-per-field reconstruction can make: Output time Field providing the known rows 0 ms Top at 0 ms 20 ms Bottom at 20 ms 40 ms Top at 40 ms 60 ms Bottom at 60 ms The result is 50p , with complete estimated pictures 20 ms apart. One-output-per-pair processing instead makes 25p , with pictures 40 ms apart. For example, retaining the earlier time in each pair keeps 0, 40, 80 ms and omits the intervening field times. Another algorithm may blend or otherwise combine them, but it still supplies fewer distinct output moments. Both outputs can have 1080 rows and the same programme duration. The 50p representation retains the source's more frequent motion sampling. The corresponding fractional-rate pair is approximately 59.94p versus 29.97p. Establish what the fields actually contain The reconstruction choice begins with the source: Native interlaced movement: each field has a new camera moment. Reconstruct complete pictures while retaining the desired field cadence. Progressive segmented frame: both segments belong to one captured progressive frame. Pairing the correct segments recovers it; treating them as different moving moments introduces unnecessary estimation. Telecined film: fields repeat parts of a progressive film sequence. Field matching and cadence recovery can reconstruct the film pictures from existing rows and remove their repeated presentations. A recording can contain more than one of these structures, especially around edits and graphics. Its scan flag describes part of the format, while moving picture content reveals the capture relationship. In an Emby playback route, reconstruction may happen in the client or during server video conversion. To understand the resulting motion, compare the source fields with the delivered progressive rate and a moving passage. A filter can need a later field before it finishes an earlier picture, adding processing latency. The output timestamps still describe the original programme moments. Correctly scheduled audio and reconstructed pictures remain aligned even though processing took time to produce them. See Also Interlaced Video Video Field Order Inverse Telecine References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Interlaced Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Interlaced Video In a native interlaced recording, the camera represents movement with alternating sets of picture rows called fields . The first field supplies one row set; the next supplies the rows between them at a later capture time. For a simplified zero-based grid, the top set contains rows 0, 2, 4, and so on. The bottom set contains rows 1, 3, 5, and so on. Each set spans the full height of the image. It is not the upper or lower half of the scene. Capture a moving edge twice In a 50-field/s sequence, a new field time occurs every 20 ms . Suppose a moving vertical edge is at horizontal position 20 in the top field at 0 ms, then at position 30 in the bottom field at 20 ms. Weave the row sets together: Displayed row Field's capture time Edge position 0, top 0 ms 20 1, bottom 20 ms 30 2, top 0 ms 20 3, bottom 20 ms 30 The alternating edge positions create a comb-shaped outline. Both fields can be correctly recorded and decoded: the error is treating their two times as one complete moving picture. Original reduced-line schematic. Green lines belong to the earlier top field and blue lines to the later bottom field. A static background can weave cleanly because it has not changed between field times. The same frame can therefore contain a sharp stationary region and a combed moving object. Count fields and pairs separately System timing Distinct field times per second Pairs of fields per second 50-field system 50 25 60000/1001-field system Approximately 59.94 Approximately 29.97 A media inspector reporting 25 frame pairs/s and a television description using 50 fields/s can be describing the same recording. The pair combines enough rows for the full raster, but native capture supplied those rows at two different times. Field order says which row set came first. Reversing it swaps the temporal order within each pair, producing backward steps in otherwise steady movement. Why interlacing was a useful tradeoff A 1920 × 1080 interlaced raster has 540 main-grid rows in each field. At 50 fields/s: 1920 × 540 × 50 = 51,840,000 sample positions/s. A 1920 × 1080 progressive sequence at 25 frames/s has the same main-grid count per second: 1920 × 1080 × 25 = 51,840,000. The interlaced representation allocates that sample count to more frequent motion times, with only alternating rows available at each one. A 1080p50 sequence supplies the complete raster at all 50 times and doubles this particular sample count. These are uncompressed grid counts, not encoded bitrate predictions. They expose the spatial-versus-temporal allocation that explains the format. Present it on a progressive screen Deinterlacing builds complete output pictures from the available fields. For native 50-field movement, producing one progressive picture for each field gives 50 output times. Each picture must reconstruct the rows missing at its own time. Producing only one picture per pair gives 25 output times. It can preserve the programme's duration while retaining fewer of its original motion moments. This is why a converted broadcast recording can keep its 1080-line height yet become less fluid. Finally, inspect what the fields represent. Telecine distributes existing progressive film pictures over repeated field intervals, while PsF divides one progressive frame into two segments. Those sources call for matching existing picture rows rather than treating every field as a new camera moment. See Also Video Field Order Deinterlacing Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Progressive Video References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Inverse Telecine | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Inverse Telecine A film transfer can store five television field pairs for every four original film pictures. Inverse telecine (IVTC) recovers those original pictures and removes the redundant presentation created by pulldown . The recovery has two distinct operations: field matching reconstructs complete pictures; decimation removes duplicate presentations. Keeping them separate makes the process understandable. Start with the stored cycle Use the two-field-phase sequence from the telecine example: Pair Top field Bottom field Woven result 0 A, field 0 A, field 1 A 1 B, field 2 B, field 3 B 2 B, field 4 C, field 5 Mixed B/C 3 C, field 6 D, field 7 Mixed C/D 4 D, field 8 D, field 9 D The mixed pairs have enough data in their neighborhood to recover film pictures, but their own top and bottom fields do not belong together. Match rows from the same film picture A suitable matching phase can construct: Reconstructed picture Fields selected Why they match A Top 0 + bottom 1 Both came from A B Top 2 + bottom 3 Both came from B C Top 6 + bottom 5 Both came from C, across a pair boundary D Top 8 + bottom 7 Both came from D, across a pair boundary D again Top 8 + bottom 9 Another presentation of D The candidate result is A, B, C, D, D . Another matching phase can put the duplicate elsewhere. The desired result is the same four source pictures. This is reconstruction from existing rows. Ordinary deinterlacing would instead estimate rows missing at a selected field time. For this clean film sequence, matching can retain the source picture's line detail because both row sets actually exist. In real compressed transfers, repeated fields can differ slightly after encoding or processing. Duplicate detection may therefore use similarity measurements rather than expecting identical file bytes or perfect pixel checksums. Remove redundancy and rebuild the timeline Drop the redundant D, leaving A, B, C, D . At 30000/1001 frame pairs/s, the five-pair cycle lasts: 5 × 1001/30000 = 0.166833… seconds. At 24000/1001 progressive pictures/s, four pictures last: 4 × 1001/24000 = 0.166833… seconds. The picture count falls, but the programme's duration stays the same. Each recovered picture is now assigned its proper film duration instead of retaining the five-slot television schedule. Audio can remain on the original programme timeline. The operation is therefore more than deleting every fifth frame. Matching fixes the picture content; appropriate timestamps fix its presentation. What an edit changes An edit can begin a new cadence phase. A field matcher needs to examine neighboring candidates rather than assuming one phase for the whole file. A mismatched pair near a cut can combine two entirely different scenes, so the transition itself needs attention. FFmpeg's fieldmatch and decimate illustrate these separate stages. Field matching reconstructs pictures but does not drop duplicates. A deinterlacing fallback can handle pictures that remain combed before a later allocation stage. Mixed material introduces another decision. A programme may have telecined film plus a native video insert or a moving graphic. In the native section, successive fields contain new motion, not repeated film rows. Forcing a film-rate removal pattern there throws away temporal information. A recovery workflow can treat sections separately, retain variable picture timing, or choose an output schedule capable of representing both. What matters is following the capture relationships and the timeline of each section, rather than requiring every part of the programme to fit one cadence. When reviewing a restored Emby source, check clean moving frames across edits and the programme's duration. Those observations show whether both matching and presentation have been recovered. See Also Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Deinterlacing Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Progressive Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Progressive Video Read 1080p50 as a 1080-line progressive picture sequence with 50 complete pictures per second. Every output frame contains all its picture rows. The next complete frame begins 20 ms later. Example Complete pictures per second Interval between pictures 1080p24 24 41.667 ms 1080p50 50 20 ms 2160p60 60 16.667 ms Integer-rate examples. Their 1000/1001 alternatives are separate exact timing values. The temporal unit is a complete captured frame. A moving edge can appear at one position in frame A and another in frame B, rather than occupying alternating rows from two successive field captures inside one displayed picture. This makes each progressive frame a direct input to scaling and display processing. Its rows do not first need to be reconstructed from two native interlaced motion times. Progressive pictures in segmented transport Some studio systems carry a progressive picture as progressive segmented frame (PsF) . They divide frame A's alternating rows into a top-shaped segment and a bottom-shaped segment: Transport segment Where its rows came from A-top Alternating rows of captured frame A A-bottom Remaining rows of captured frame A B-top Alternating rows of captured frame B B-bottom Remaining rows of captured frame B Joining A-top and A-bottom reconstructs A. Both segments belong to the same progressive frame, so weaving them does not combine two different field motion times. Native interlaced capture differs: successive fields describe successive moments. Joining them without motion handling can put an object's old position on one set of rows and its new position on the other. That distinction determines the appropriate reconstruction. PsF segments are paired to recover a complete frame; native interlaced fields need temporal handling for progressive output. The transport's field-shaped appearance alone does not tell those two jobs apart. See Also Interlaced Video Video Frame Rate Video Field Order References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.2020: Ultra-high-definition picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Film and television can require different presentation schedules. Four pictures at 24 fps span 1/6 second . A 60-field/s television schedule has ten field intervals in that same time. Ten cannot be divided evenly between four film pictures. 3:2 pulldown solves the scheduling problem by holding successive pictures for alternating three and two field intervals. Starting at a two-field phase, one cycle is: A A B B B C C D D D. The extra field intervals repeat parts of existing film pictures. They do not contain newly photographed moments. Original cycle starting at the two-field phase. A different starting phase shifts the pattern. Follow the fields into stored pairs Top and bottom field parity alternate even while the source picture is repeated: Field interval Parity Source picture 0 Top A 1 Bottom A 2 Top B 3 Bottom B 4 Top B 5 Bottom C 6 Top C 7 Bottom D 8 Top D 9 Bottom D Pair neighboring fields into five television frames and the sequence becomes: AA, BB, BC, CD, DD. AA, BB, and DD combine rows from one film picture. BC and CD combine rows from different pictures. A moving object can therefore show combing in two pairs even though the original film frames were progressive. This pattern is useful when inspecting older film transfers in an Emby library. The stored interlaced-looking pairs can be evidence of a film-to-television cadence rather than native interlaced camera capture. The fractional version fits exactly too Common film transfers use 24000/1001 pictures/s and 60000/1001 fields/s . Their ratio is still 2.5 fields per film picture. Four source picture durations: 4 × 1001/24000 = 0.166833… seconds. Ten field durations: 10 × 1001/60000 = 0.166833… seconds. The whole cycle retains its duration. Within the cycle, however, a two-field hold lasts 33.3667 ms and a three-field hold 50.05 ms , instead of the film's uniform 41.7083 ms picture spacing. A steady pan is presented with unequal holds, which is the source of pulldown judder. Store the repetitions, or describe them In hard telecine , the stored picture/field sequence already contains the repetitions and mixed pairs. Recovering the film sequence requires identifying which row sets belong together and which presentations are redundant. In soft telecine , a format can retain the underlying coded film pictures and signal field repeats for presentation. The display schedule has more intervals than the coded picture count. Different inspection stages can consequently report the coded-picture rate or the intended repeated-field presentation. Modern playback can sometimes use the underlying film sequence directly with a suitable progressive display cadence. The old television scheduling problem and the display's current refresh schedule are separate stages. Inverse telecine reverses a recoverable film cadence. In the illustrated hard-telecine cycle, it must join B's or C's matching rows across pair boundaries before removing redundancy. Simply throwing away one of the five existing pairs would leave BC or CD incomplete as film pictures. See Also Inverse Telecine Interlaced Video Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Video Field Order | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Video Field Order An interlaced pan can look as if it moves backward briefly, then jumps forward. One possible cause is reversed field order : the player has presented the two fields in each pair in the wrong temporal sequence. Top field first (TFF) means the top line set was captured before the bottom line set. Bottom field first (BFF) means the opposite. “Top” and “bottom” identify alternating rows across the whole picture, rather than its upper and lower halves. Follow one moving object Take a native 50-field/s, top-first sequence. An object moves 10 horizontal positions between each 20 ms capture: Field Capture time Object position Top 0 0 ms 0 Bottom 0 20 ms 10 Top 1 40 ms 20 Bottom 1 60 ms 30 The correct reconstructed order is 0 → 10 → 20 → 30 . Each movement is +10. If each pair is interpreted bottom-first, the order becomes 10 → 0 → 30 → 20 . Its displacements are −10, +30, −10 : backward, a larger forward jump, then backward again. Original schematic of this timing reversal. It illustrates steady movement, not the output of a named deinterlacer. A still picture cannot expose this temporal reversal clearly. A slow pan, moving text, or a steadily traveling object is more informative. In an Emby recording, comparing the two parity interpretations on that moving passage can identify the mismatch. Correct the description or the arrangement A wrongly tagged TFF sequence can have correct samples and incorrect metadata. Correcting the description lets processing use the existing top-before-bottom capture order. A genuine field-order conversion changes the relationship between the line sets and their temporal arrangement. It must preserve which rows represent which capture moment, rather than simply renaming the stream. Processing filters may shift or reconstruct line positions to produce the requested arrangement. The relevant boundary is the input to field reconstruction . It needs the earlier field's actual time and parity to build a forward-moving output sequence. For film-cadence recovery , that information instead guides the selection of fields belonging to the same source film picture. See Also Interlaced Video Deinterlacing Inverse Telecine References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/Motion-Inter.title: Motion Interpolation | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/Motion-Inter.keywords: Motion Interpolation Suppose a ball is at position 20 in a picture at 0 ms and at position 60 in the next picture at 40 ms. A display wants another picture at 20 ms. Holding the first frame leaves the ball at 20. Blending the two frames can show faint balls at both 20 and 60. Motion interpolation instead tries to put the ball at a plausible intermediate position. The middle picture is inferred from the two recorded pictures, rather than captured by the camera. Compute the requested point in time The requested instant is halfway between the source times: α = (20 − 0) ÷ (40 − 0) = 0.5. If the estimated motion is a straight, constant-speed displacement of 40 positions, the intermediate position is: 20 + 0.5 × (60 − 20) = 40. At 10 ms, the same model would put it at position 30; at 30 ms, position 50. This is a trajectory estimate. The two observed endpoints do not reveal whether the real ball accelerated, curved, or briefly disappeared between them. Find correspondence in the pictures The interpolator first needs to decide which regions in the two frames represent the same content. A block-based method can search for a similar patch and record its displacement as a motion vector. Other methods estimate a finer motion field. A whole scene has many such displacements. The camera may pan while a person moves independently, and different depths can shift by different amounts. Treating the complete picture as one translation would not handle all those regions. The image is then warped toward the requested time. For a halfway picture, content from the earlier frame can be moved halfway forward; corresponding content from the later frame can be moved halfway backward. If both mappings are correct, their ball images line up at position 40. The overlapping information can be combined to construct output samples. Spatial interpolation is still needed where a moved position falls between sample locations. Why warping differs from blending Consider a simplified bright object with value 100 on a dark background with value 0. In the first frame it occupies position 20, and in the second position 60. An equal blend gives value 50 at both old positions. It averages the pictures without moving their content into alignment. A correct motion warp aligns both object observations at position 40 before combining them. The combined object can remain value 100 at that intermediate position. This is the difference between a double outline and a reconstructed movement. These scalar values illustrate the operations, not a filter's measured output or a complete image synthesis algorithm. The picture may contain information neither endpoint supplies An object can uncover a background that was hidden in one frame. A moving foreground edge also changes which surface occupies a sample. Forward and backward motion estimates may disagree around those occlusions . The interpolator must decide which observation to use and how to fill a gap. If it uses the wrong surface's motion, a foreground edge can drag background texture along with it, creating a halo or warped outline. Repeated patterns introduce another ambiguity: several fence bars may look equally similar. Thin lettering, a fast ball, motion blur, or a lighting change can also make correspondence unreliable. An incorrect match then becomes a visibly incorrect intermediate picture. A scene cut is more fundamental. There is no continuous trajectory between two unrelated shots. Implementations can detect the cut and repeat an endpoint instead of inventing movement across it. FFmpeg's minterpolate documents that kind of scene-change handling. Where the new motion appears Interpolation can be applied while producing a file, in a player, or in a television after an Emby app delivers its frames. In the television case, the source and server delivery remain unchanged while the display constructs additional presentation pictures. That can make a film look more like frequently sampled live video: the screen now shows more distinct intermediate positions. The source's photographed exposures and their blur still supplied the evidence. Synthesizing more positions does not recreate the actual camera observations between them. Codec prediction has a different purpose. It constructs a predictor for an already encoded source picture, then uses transmitted corrections to reconstruct that picture. Motion interpolation has no transmitted original intermediate picture to correct toward. Its output follows the estimated scene model. See Also Frame-Rate Conversion Video Frame Rate Inter-Frame Video Prediction References FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/fundamentals/Digital-Vide.title: How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures | Emby Learn
articles/video/fundamentals/Digital-Vide.keywords: How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures Pause a video and the moving scene becomes one picture. Advance by one frame and the objects have moved a little; advance again and they move farther. Digital video represents those successive pictures and tells the player when each should appear. Original schematic of three pictures in time order. The drawing simplifies the sample grid. A picture is a grid of values A 1920 × 1080 frame has 1,920 positions across each of 1,080 rows. At each position the picture representation supplies information about brightness and color. The values are numbers, so the decoder and display processing can work on them: reconstructing a compressed picture, enlarging it, applying a display transformation, and eventually making the screen emit light. Different sample formats arrange that information differently. A simple RGB example stores red, green, and blue values at every position. Common video formats instead separate brightness-related information from color-difference information. These are ways of describing a picture; the recognizable scene appears when those values are interpreted together. Resolution counts the positions in the main picture grid. It does not describe how many different moments the recording contains. Timing makes the pictures move Suppose a clip contains 24 frames for each second. The starts of its first three frames are: Frame Presentation time Time until the next frame A 0 ms 41.667 ms B 41.667 ms 41.667 ms C 83.333 ms 41.667 ms An exact 24 fps timeline, with times rounded for display. The player shows A, keeps it on screen until B is due, then replaces it with B. A screen that refreshes more often may show the same video picture several times. That is still one recorded moment, rather than several new frames from the camera. Now imagine that a ball moves 20 picture positions between A and B. Those positions describe how far it moved; the 41.667 ms interval describes how quickly it moved. Keeping the same pictures but assigning different times changes the apparent speed. Keeping the timeline but reducing picture dimensions changes the spatial representation instead. This is why frame rate and resolution describe different parts of a recording. Audio has its own samples and timestamps. Both streams are scheduled on a shared playback timeline so a visible action and its sound occur together. Why the file usually contains compressed instructions Storing every sample independently would be expensive. For a deliberately simple 8-bit RGB example: One frame: 1920 × 1080 × 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes . At 24 frames/s: 149,299,200 bytes/s , about 149.3 MB/s. This is raw picture data only, with no audio or packaging. A compressed movie is usually far smaller because it describes patterns efficiently instead of storing that complete raw array for every moment. A video decoder turns those coded instructions back into picture values. For a region that resembles an earlier picture, the instructions can describe a prediction and the changes needed to correct it. The decoder may therefore need earlier reconstructed pictures before it can build the next one. From a file to the screen The container reader first finds the selected video track and its coded data. The decoder uses the track's codec information to reconstruct pictures. Presentation timestamps then place those pictures in time order for the player. Finally, display processing fits and converts them for the screen. These stages explain familiar observations in an Emby session. A picture can be decoded correctly but shown with the wrong shape if aspect information is mishandled. Motion can be irregular if presentation timing is wrong. During video transcoding, the server reconstructs the source and creates a new coded representation, while the receiving app still performs the final decoding and presentation. The picture grid describes where the scene is sampled, the timeline describes when , and the coded representation tells the decoder how to build the pictures . See Also Video Resolution Video Frame Rate How Video Compression Works References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/An.title: Anamorphic Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/An.keywords: Anamorphic Video An older widescreen recording may report 1440 × 1080 , yet look properly proportioned on a 16:9 television. Its storage is anamorphic : the grid has been allocated fewer horizontal positions than a square-pixel representation of the intended picture would use. The missing width is described by pixel aspect information , rather than supplied by another set of hidden columns. 1440 × 1080 samples with PAR 4:3 have the same display proportions as 1920 × 1080 square pixels. Follow the recording to the display The stored grid's width-to-height ratio is 1440/1080 = 4/3. The file tells the player that each sample interval should appear 4/3 as wide as tall. Applying that factor gives: (4/3) × (4/3) = 16/9. On a square-pixel screen, the player can present the decoded image across a 1920 × 1080 rectangle. It calculates the screen samples needed for that rectangle from the 1440-column source. The people and circles have their intended proportions, while the recorded horizontal detail still originates from 1440 sample positions. This arrangement allowed recording and delivery formats to carry a widescreen field of view in a constrained raster. It describes digital storage. A film need not have been photographed with an anamorphic lens to use this representation. Two ways to make a correctly shaped copy Copy Picture representation Presentation information Preserve the original encoding 1440 × 1080 samples Retain PAR 4:3 Convert to square pixels Resample to 1920 × 1080 Use PAR 1:1 The first route can preserve the compressed video during compatible repackaging. The app applies its aspect information during display. The second route constructs a new sample grid and ordinarily needs video encoding if it is saved as a compressed file. Both routes aim at the same 16:9 composition. A square-pixel copy is a convenient representation of the source, rather than additional camera detail. When the result is squeezed or too wide If the original grid is treated as square, it displays as 4:3 and faces look thin. If it is resampled to 1920 × 1080 and its old PAR 4:3 is retained, its equivalent width becomes 2560 at height 1080: too wide. The processing error is the same presentation transformation being omitted or applied twice. This gives a useful way to examine a converted Emby recording: follow the source dimensions and PAR into the output dimensions and PAR, and calculate the intended ratio at each boundary. Letterboxing solves a different storage problem. It places a wider image inside a frame with border rows. An anamorphic source changes the sample spacing used for presentation. A file can combine both, so the stored frame's aspect information and the active image inside it should be interpreted separately. See Also Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Video Display Aspect Ratio Video Resolution References ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.title: Video Display Aspect Ratio | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.keywords: Video Display Aspect Ratio Display aspect ratio (DAR) is the intended width of a displayed picture divided by its height. A 16:9 picture keeps that shape on a phone, a television, and a projector even though its physical size changes. Both outlines have the same height. The 16:9 outline is wider. For an unrotated rectangular frame, with no additional display crop: DAR = (stored width ÷ stored height) × pixel aspect ratio. A 1440 × 1080 grid has a stored ratio of 4:3. With pixels intended to appear 4:3 as wide as tall, its display ratio is (4/3) × (4/3) = 16/9. A 1920 × 1080 square-pixel grid arrives at the same display shape by a different route. Fit a picture into a window Consider a playback window measuring 900 × 600 , a 3:2 shape. A 16:9 video fitted to its width becomes 900 × 506.25. There are 93.75 unused vertical pixels in the ideal geometry, split into 46.875 above and below. Those spaces are letterbox bars . A 4:3 video fitted to the same window becomes 800 × 600. It uses the full height and leaves 50 pixels on either side: pillarboxing. Source shape Ideal fitted image in a 900 × 600 window Unused space 16:9 900 × 506.25 Above and below 4:3 800 × 600 Left and right These calculations use continuous geometry; an actual pixel display rounds the final placement to its grid. The same fitting rule explains both outcomes. Uniformly scale the picture until one dimension reaches the window boundary. The other dimension follows from the picture's ratio. Fill and stretch change different things To fill the window with the 16:9 video, scale it to 600 pixels high. It becomes approximately 1066.67 pixels wide, so about 83.33 pixels must fall outside each side of the window. The people retain their proportions, but the left and right edges of the composition are lost. To stretch , change width and height independently until the image is exactly 900 × 600. Every part of the frame remains visible, but a circle becomes an oval because the horizontal and vertical scale factors differ. These are presentation choices. The file's DAR supplies the shape that fitting or filling starts from. If an anamorphic file has an incorrect pixel aspect ratio , both operations can faithfully fit the wrongly interpreted shape. The frame and the film inside it DAR describes the frame being presented. A 1920 × 1080 frame can contain a 2.4:1 film plus black rows above and below. Its frame DAR is 16:9, while its active film ratio is 2.4:1. That distinction is useful when a playback window shows unexpected extra borders: establish whether it is fitting the film itself or a larger stored rectangle around the film. The geometry then explains which edges will remain visible under fit, fill, or a deliberate crop. See Also Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Anamorphic Video Letterboxing and Pillarboxing References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.title: Video Pixel Aspect Ratio | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.keywords: Video Pixel Aspect Ratio A 1440 × 1080 picture shown with square pixels is 4:3. To present the same grid as 16:9, each horizontal sample interval must appear wider. The required multiplier is: (16/9) ÷ (1440/1080) = 4/3. That multiplier is the pixel aspect ratio (PAR) : the intended width of a picture sample relative to its height. It describes presentation spacing, rather than a little physical rectangle stored in the file. The two grids contain the same number of samples. Only their presentation spacing differs. At PAR 4:3, the equivalent square-pixel display width is 1440 × 4/3 = 1920 , with the height still 1080. A face that looked too thin when the samples were treated as square takes its intended shape when the spacing is applied. Two equivalent representations The intended picture can be carried in either of these forms: Representation Stored grid PAR Display shape Anamorphic grid 1440 × 1080 4:3 16:9 Resampled square-pixel grid 1920 × 1080 1:1 16:9 The first form keeps 1,440 horizontal sample positions and relies on presentation information. The second calculates 1,920 output samples from those positions. Resampling makes the dimensions convenient for square-pixel display, but the source still supplied only 1,440 independent horizontal observations. A metadata correction changes the interpretation of the existing samples. A resampling operation changes the array of sample values. These operations need to be distinguished during conversion so the intended display shape survives. For example, after resampling this source to 1920 × 1080 square pixels, carrying its old PAR 4:3 into the output would make the picture wider again. The output geometry and output PAR must describe the same representation. Work backward from a known frame shape For a rectangular, unrotated frame without an additional display crop: PAR = intended DAR ÷ (stored width ÷ stored height). If a full 720 × 576 raster is intended as 4:3, the calculation gives (4/3) ÷ (720/576) = 16:15 . This is a full-raster numerical example. Some standard-definition workflows describe a smaller active region instead, so that region must be used in the calculation when it is the signaled display rectangle. PAR often appears as SAR, sample aspect ratio , in FFmpeg and media inspection. Both refer to the sample's presentation proportions in that terminology. The file's dimensions, its aspect signaling, and any crop together define the rectangle whose shape the player presents. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Anamorphic Video ITU-R BT.601 References ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/Letterboxing-Pil.title: Letterboxing and Pillarboxing | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Letterboxing-Pil.keywords: Letterboxing and Pillarboxing A wide film on a taller screen leaves unused space above and below. A narrow picture on a wider screen leaves space at the sides. These are letterboxing and pillarboxing : the player preserves the picture's proportions while fitting the entire rectangle. Original proportional examples on 16:9 screens. Green marks the active image. The geometry comes from uniform scaling. To fit a 2.4:1 film into a 1920 × 1080 screen, use the full width: 1920/2.4 = 800 pixels high . The unused 280 rows divide into 140 above and 140 below . Stretching the picture to 1080 high would make its contents taller. Filling the height without stretching would push its side edges off screen. Two files can produce the same television picture Imagine two copies of that film: Copy Stored frame What happens on a 1920 × 1080 display A 1920 × 800 active picture The player supplies 140 rows of space above/below B 1920 × 1080, including 140 black rows at each edge The player fits the whole frame; the borders are already samples in it On this screen, their visible compositions can be identical. In A, the display space lies outside the video frame. In B, the black borders are part of what the decoder reconstructs. That difference becomes visible when the screen shape changes. Move both copies to a 2560 × 1080 screen Copy A scales by 2560/1920 = 4/3. Its picture becomes approximately 2560 × 1066.67 , nearly filling the ultrawide screen. Only about 6.67 pixels of ideal space remain above and below. Copy B still presents a 16:9 frame , because the coded border rows count toward its shape. Fitting that frame to the same screen uses the full 1080 height and only 1920 width. There are 320 pixels of space on either side , while the film retains its 140 stored border rows above and below. The film now has borders on all four sides, sometimes called windowboxing . The player has correctly fitted the rectangle it received. That rectangle was larger than the active film image. The numerical examples assume square pixels and ideal continuous scaling; final pixel placement can be rounded. Decide which rectangle to retain This distinction helps with an Emby file whose bars persist under a display-size change. Inspect the decoded frame: do its outer rows or columns contain black samples, or does the player add space around a border-free picture? A crop can remove stored border samples. A display zoom can conceal them while playing. Neither is equivalent to stretching the image, and neither automatically identifies which regions are safe to discard. Some films change aspect ratio for selected sequences. A subtitle, credit, or opening title can also occupy a border that is empty in another scene. Establish the largest intended composition before creating a permanently cropped version. For an uncropped source, borders are often the space needed to keep that composition visible. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Cropping Video Video Resolution References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/Video-Cropping.h.title: Cropping Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Cropping.h.keywords: Cropping Video Suppose a 1920 × 1080 frame contains a 1920 × 800 film centered vertically. A crop can make the film rectangle the output picture, removing the black rows around it. First find the top edge: (1080 − 800) ÷ 2 = 140. Then describe the retained rectangle by its upper-left coordinate and its dimensions: Crop property Value Left coordinate, x 0 Top coordinate, y 140 Width 1920 Height 800 With zero-based source rows, the crop keeps rows 140 through 939 , inclusive. Output row 0 comes from source row 140; output row 799 comes from source row 939. There are 140 discarded rows on each side of that retained region. This mapping is the essence of cropping . The samples inside the rectangle remain in their relative positions; the boundary moves inward. Crop and resize have different mappings For square pixels, this crop has a display ratio of 1920/800 = 2.4:1 . If instead the complete 1920 × 1080 frame is resized to 1920 × 800, every row contributes to the compressed vertical extent. The black borders remain in scaled form, and the people become shorter. The output dimensions are the same as the crop's, but the mapping from source samples is different. A crop followed by a proportional resize is another useful operation. It first identifies the composition to retain, then reconstructs it at a chosen output size. Keep the display ratio and pixel aspect information consistent with those choices. Where a crop can happen A player can select a region while displaying the decoded frame. The stored video remains intact, so another viewing mode can show its edges again. A conversion can crop the decoded samples before encoding a new stream. That saved copy contains the smaller picture array. Edges omitted from that copy cannot be recovered from it. A codec or container can also describe a display crop around a larger coded picture. The decoder still handles the coded data, but the signaled visible rectangle excludes selected edges. This is how a picture boundary can change without treating all coded samples as visible content. Why exact coordinates sometimes need format handling Color-subsampled picture formats share color samples between neighboring brightness positions. Crop boundaries can therefore need alignment to that sampling grid. A processing tool may round dimensions or coordinates to supported boundaries, or offer an exact-crop mode with explicit handling of the sample planes. FFmpeg's crop filter documents this distinction in its exact option. It also has a separate option that changes pixel aspect ratio to preserve the original DAR. That is a presentation choice beyond simply retaining the source's existing sample spacing. For a border-removal job, inspect several scenes before choosing the rectangle. A dark image region is not automatically a border; changing film ratios and subtitles can reveal valid content there later. The crop coordinates should follow the composition actually being retained. See Also Letterboxing and Pillarboxing Video Display Aspect Ratio Video Resolution References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/Video-Resolution.title: Video Resolution | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Resolution.keywords: Video Resolution Familiar description Common picture dimensions Main-grid positions per frame 720p HD 1280 × 720 921,600 1080p Full HD 1920 × 1080 2,073,600 2160p Ultra HD 3840 × 2160 8,294,400 DCI 4K full container 4096 × 2160 8,847,360 Resolution is the width and height of the picture's sample grid. The table counts that main grid, rather than all component samples or a file's compressed bytes. The “p” in labels such as 1080p describes progressive timing ; it is additional information about how the picture is formed. “4K” is a family of descriptions. Television UHD commonly uses 3,840 columns, while the full DCI cinema container uses 4,096. Cropped cinema images can have other heights. The explicit width and height are the useful values when calculating or comparing files. The UHD calculation Doubling the width doubles the number of positions in each row. Doubling the height doubles the number of rows. Together: 3840 × 2160 = 4 × (1920 × 1080). This is why UHD contains four times as many main-grid positions as Full HD, rather than twice as many. At 30 frames/s, a 1920 × 1080 stream represents 62,208,000 such positions per second; a 3840 × 2160 stream represents 248,832,000. That count helps explain processing load. Scaling, filters, and picture reconstruction operate on the samples. Frame rate adds another dimension to the work: UHD at 60 fps represents twice as many picture positions per second as UHD at 30 fps. File size has a different calculation. An encoder can represent similar regions and neighboring pictures efficiently, so four times the positions need not mean four times the compressed data. Which rectangle is being described? A media file can contain a 1920 × 1080 frame with a widescreen film occupying only 1920 × 800 positions. The remaining 280 rows are black borders. Its stored resolution is still 1920 × 1080, while the active image contains 1,536,000 positions. A cropped copy can store only that 1920 × 800 rectangle. These two copies can look the same when fitted to a 16:9 television, yet use different stored grids. Bars supplied by the player do not count as stored picture rows. The presented rectangle can differ again. A phone clip stored as 1920 × 1080 may display as 1080 × 1920 after its rotation is applied. An anamorphic 1440 × 1080 grid can display as 16:9 because its samples are intended to appear wider than square. Samples and detail Two files with the same grid can resolve very different detail. A camera's optics, focus, exposure, processing, and compression determine what information reaches those positions. Scaling a 720p picture to a UHD grid calculates additional output samples from the existing ones; it changes the grid available for display, rather than adding new camera observations. When comparing library versions, first identify the stored and active rectangles. Then use frame rate and bitrate to understand processing and delivery needs. That keeps a resolution comparison attached to the pictures actually represented. articles/video/geometry/Video-Rotation-M.title: Video Rotation Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Rotation-M.keywords: Video Rotation Metadata A phone can store each video frame in a 1920 × 1080 landscape grid while recording a portrait scene. The file's display transformation tells the player to turn that grid upright. After a pure quarter-turn, its presented dimensions become 1080 × 1920 . Rotation metadata stores the instruction, rather than a second rotated copy of all the pictures. Turn a small sample grid Here is a 4-column, 3-row grid. The letters stand for sample positions: A B C D E F G H I J K L After a clockwise quarter-turn, the picture has 3 columns and 4 rows: I E A J F B K G C L H D Every position survives. Rows and columns change roles. In zero-based coordinates the mapping is (x, y) → (H − 1 − y, x) , where H is the original height. For a 1920 × 1080 source, its top-left sample moves to output position (1079, 0), and its bottom-left sample moves to (0, 0). A quarter-turn can be described as a position permutation. Arbitrary angles also require constructing output samples between the original grid positions, so their processing is a different resampling problem. The matrix is a presentation instruction QuickTime and related MP4 workflows represent display transformations with a matrix. It can combine a turn with translation, scaling, or mirroring. A media inspector often reduces a simple matrix to an angle for convenience. An angle's sign depends on the tool's convention: clockwise and counterclockwise descriptions use opposite signs for the same physical turn. The useful question is where the picture's positions are presented, rather than whether two tools print the same signed number. Follow one upright playback route When the Emby app receives the original clip, it can decode the stored landscape grid and apply the display transformation as it presents the frame. The coded video remains in its original orientation. A conversion can instead rotate the decoded samples before encoding them. It then produces a 1080 × 1920 picture that is already upright, and the output's display information should describe that upright grid. Output representation What the player needs Original sideways sample grid The original turn instruction Physically rotated upright grid A normalized orientation that does not apply the old turn again Deleting the instruction from the first representation leaves the clip sideways. Keeping the old instruction on the second applies the turn twice. The two outputs need different metadata because their stored pictures differ. A thumbnail and a playback stream can pass through different transformation stages. When they disagree, compare the source matrix, the decoded or converted picture dimensions, and the output orientation information. These observations locate the boundary where the turn was applied.
