articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: How Dolby Vision Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: How Dolby Vision Works A Dolby Vision release carries a produced picture and information for reproducing it on different display targets. To understand what reaches the screen, follow three jobs: prepare the intended image, represent it for delivery, and use the delivered image and metadata during playback. Begin with the authored picture A colorist establishes the HDR master on a reference display. Faces, ordinary surfaces, bright reflections, and dark details receive deliberate relationships. The master can contain a large light range without making every shot use its extremes. Analysis then describes relevant picture characteristics over a shot or frame. A trim pass can review a mapped version for another target and adjust its balance where needed. The resulting information can travel alongside the image rather than requiring a complete independent movie for every possible display. Imagine a dim room followed by a bright exterior. A program-wide peak alone cannot describe the distribution within both shots. Scene-specific information lets the playback mapping use more context, while the creative trims can preserve decisions made during preparation. These are instructions about how an existing produced picture is handled. They do not replace the captured and encoded information that the picture contains. Separate the coded image from its accompanying data Conceptual delivery and reconstruction roles. The selected profile defines the signal interpretation, layers, and packaging. The base layer is the main coded picture. The RPU metadata supplies Dolby Vision information associated with that picture. Some profiles also contain an enhancement layer , which can contribute additional reconstruction information. A report of BL+RPU therefore identifies one picture layer plus metadata. BL+EL+RPU adds enhancement data. These names describe roles within the presentation, while container tracks describe how that data is packaged. One reported video track can carry more than one codec layer. The RPU has a relationship to the actual sequence. Analysis and trims belong to the pictures from which they were prepared. If an edit moves the pictures while leaving the old associations in place, the mapping can receive information for another shot. RPU metadata follows that timing relationship in detail. For dual-layer content, full reconstruction may need both base and enhancement information. A compatible base can sometimes be used independently, but that is another reconstruction path. The layer article explains the roles, and MEL/FEL identifies whether a picture residual is present. A profile defines the delivery arrangement Dolby Vision has several profiles because different applications need different codecs, layer structures, and base interpretations. A profile identifies that feature arrangement; its level specifies processing limits such as pixel rate, width, and bitrate. Some base signals have a defined HDR10 or HLG interpretation for a path that does not process Dolby Vision. Other signals use Dolby Vision-specific reshaping and color representation. In the latter case, a codec decoder can recover samples correctly while an ordinary HDR renderer assigns those samples the wrong color meaning. That distinction separates two kinds of support. Codec support reconstructs the compressed sample description. Dolby Vision profile support supplies the additional signal interpretation and metadata processing for the selected arrangement. Both are relevant to the full route. The profile family can be browsed through its individual pages. A higher profile number denotes another arrangement rather than a higher-quality grade of the movie. Follow a compatible-base session Take a source whose base has a defined HDR10 interpretation. A container reader locates its video and Dolby Vision information. The selected decoder reconstructs the available image data. A Dolby Vision-capable processing route interprets the profile, associates the metadata with the right pictures, and performs the required reconstruction and display management. The mapping also needs a target. The output's useful brightness, color volume, and rendering mode help determine how the produced picture is adapted. Scene information and creative trims can guide that adaptation, while the physical output still supplies its own limits. If the route instead uses the compatible HDR10 base, it can present a valid HDR picture with a different set of adaptation inputs. That outcome differs from full Dolby Vision processing and from a failed decode. The base's correctness is established by its defined signal arrangement, not by the word Dolby Vision alone. An SDR destination requires another operation: interpreting the available image and producing suitable SDR brightness, color, and encoding. Removing Dolby Vision metadata does not carry out that conversion. Fallback compatibility distinguishes those paths. Locate the operations in an Emby session The source record, server delivery, app processing, and display input each describe a stage: Stage Useful evidence Source Profile, base compatibility, codec, layers, detected RPU Server delivery Direct Play, stream copying, or newly encoded video App and decoder Support for the delivered packaging and profile operations Output and display The received presentation and active rendering mode Direct Play reports server delivery of the original file. The app still needs to open the packaging, decode the coded data, interpret the profile, and prepare its output. A video transcode instead creates a new picture presentation, whose output should be examined as that rendition. A display indicator is evidence about an output mode. It does not record every operation upstream. For example, an enhancement residual could be absent from the delivered stream or unused by the decoder while a later path still produces Dolby Vision output. Confirming an original enhancement contribution requires information about reconstruction, not only the final indicator. The same discipline applies to a metadata-present flag. It identifies source data that was detected, while correct timing, supported processing, and coherent output determine whether the intended information reached the picture. Compare the adaptation in the same produced image Use the same release, same scene, and known playback routes. Inspect faces and ordinary surfaces as well as the brightest reflection. A mapping can make the peak fit while redistributing contrast elsewhere; temporal changes can matter across flashes and cuts. A separate HDR10 or SDR release may include another grade or trim. It gives context but is not automatically the required pixel result of this release's Dolby Vision processing. Keeping the produced source and each route identified turns the comparison into a concrete question: which image information and mapping inputs were used, and how did that change the displayed relationships? articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Start with the diagram's reconstruction roles. A Dolby Vision base layer (BL) contains the main coded picture. An optional enhancement layer (EL) supplies additional reconstruction information, while RPU names accompanying metadata. Conceptual roles. The selected profile determines the actual signal, packaging, and decoder operations. Why an enhancement is not a second independent movie In the UHD Blu-ray workflow, the enhancement can code a residual associated with the base and the prepared Dolby Vision source. The composer uses the relevant base, enhancement, and metadata information to reconstruct the intended signal. Watching the enhancement alone would not perform those operations. A useful analogy is a correction associated with another representation: its meaning depends on the thing being corrected. The exact Dolby Vision reconstruction also includes its specified transformations, so the diagram is a role description rather than an instruction to add two decoded photographs numerically. The MEL/FEL distinction identifies whether the enhancement contains a nonzero picture residual. RPU metadata remains another part of the system; enhancement size and metadata presence answer different questions. Separate three levels of packaging Reported item What it names File A stored container Video track A container's selected coded presentation Codec layer and metadata units Roles inside that presentation A muxing arrangement can carry multiple coded layers within one reported video track, while another layout can expose them differently. Counting tracks therefore does not establish the number of reconstruction layers. Inspect the stream's profile and layer indicators. Follow the available picture when a layer is unused Profile 7 provides an HDR10-compatible base. A path using that base can show a valid HDR10 picture while leaving the complete Dolby Vision reconstruction unused. Profile 5 is a single-picture-layer arrangement with Dolby Vision-specific signal interpretation. The presence of a base there does not define the same HDR10 fallback. For an Emby playback comparison, identify which source layers survive delivery and which operations the decoder performs. A stream-copy operation can preserve selected coded bytes, while removing an enhancement can remove information from the original reconstruction. The resulting picture must be described in terms of the layers and interpretation actually used. articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision MEL and FEL | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision MEL and FEL For dual-layer Dolby Vision UHD Blu-ray delivery, ask whether the enhancement adds a picture residual: Type Expanded name Picture residual MEL Minimum enhancement layer Zero FEL Full enhancement layer Nonzero Both remain part of a Dolby Vision presentation with associated metadata. The distinction concerns reconstruction information, rather than the amount of scene-specific guidance. Follow the residual's role The authoring workflow prepares a base representation and an enhancement associated with it. With FEL, the enhancement supplies differences needed for the complete Dolby Vision reconstruction. The decoder/composer uses that information with the base and metadata. Those differences can involve the prepared signal's precision and range. Their significance depends on the authored title. A larger enhancement stream can carry more coded correction data, but its byte size alone does not predict how obvious that correction will be in a scene. With MEL, there is no nonzero picture residual to contribute. The presentation can still use Dolby Vision metadata and its specified base interpretation and mapping. “Minimum” therefore identifies the enhancement's residual role, rather than an absence of Dolby Vision processing. Compare three paths from the same source Full FEL reconstruction: the relevant enhancement residual contributes to the composed picture before display adaptation. Base plus supported Dolby Vision processing: a route may use the base and applicable metadata while omitting that residual contribution. Compatible base presentation: Profile 7 can provide an HDR10 picture through its compatible base. These paths can produce plausible images, but they use different source information. A final Dolby Vision output indicator cannot establish which reconstruction path occurred earlier. For an Emby test, retain the exact source, profile/layer record, delivered stream, and decoder information. Use known content when examining whether enhancement data affects the picture. If a conversion discards an FEL, report that information loss even when the main base video was copied without re-encoding. See Also Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision RPU Metadata References Dolby Vision: Distinguishing MEL and non-MEL bitstreams Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision RPU Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision RPU Metadata Cut the first second from a 24-frame-per-second movie while leaving its metadata associations unchanged. The new first picture is the old picture 24, but it could receive information for old picture 0. Dolby Vision RPU data needs to remain associated with the pictures it describes. New frame Correct source association Wrong association if old metadata starts unchanged 0 Old picture 24 and its metadata Old metadata 0 1 Old picture 25 and its metadata Old metadata 1 2 Old picture 26 and its metadata Old metadata 2 An illustrative frame-alignment problem. Actual metadata can describe a shot or frame, and the packaging determines its association. What the RPU carries RPU is the conventional name used for Dolby Vision metadata in bitstream and media reports. Its information supports the relevant picture interpretation, reconstruction, and display management. It is different from a coded movie image or an audio track. Depending on the profile and metadata version, the workflow can include picture analysis, target-display trims, and active-picture-area information. Analysis describes characteristics of the produced image; trims adjust its mapped appearance; active-area information distinguishes the image from surrounding letterbox regions. For HEVC-based delivery, the data is carried in special units associated with the encoded pictures. Other codecs define another carriage. A report of BL+RPU names a base picture plus metadata; BL+EL+RPU also includes an enhancement layer . Why an edit can affect the result Metadata prepared for a bright exterior should not be used as if it described an adjacent dim shot. An association error can change mapping inputs or creative adjustments at the wrong moment, potentially causing unwanted shifts. A simple offset, reordered frames, a dissolve, or another version of the film can all change that relationship. Picture modifications can matter even with unchanged timing. Cropping can change active-area coordinates. A new grade can change the characteristics that analysis described. A correct operation preserves or deliberately recreates the appropriate relationship rather than merely copying a block with the same title. Inspect presence, association, and use separately For an Emby source, an RPU-present report establishes that metadata was detected. Next inspect whether server delivery retained it or produced a new rendition. Then determine which profile operations the app and output path use. A supported compatible base can sometimes provide another valid presentation if Dolby Vision metadata is unused. A Dolby Vision-specific signal needs the relevant interpretation or conversion. The fallback article explains that difference. To investigate a brightness change across a cut, compare the exact video version, frame timing, metadata associations, and delivery path. That locates the operation that may have detached the instructions from the image. articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility When a Dolby Vision processing route is unavailable, begin with the base signal's defined interpretation. A compatible base can supply another valid presentation; a Dolby Vision-specific base needs its appropriate interpretation or conversion. Make the playback decision in order First, can the path read and decode the available video? Container handling and codec support still apply. A compatible light representation is of little use if the player cannot obtain or decode its coded samples. Second, what does the base represent? The profile and base compatibility identify an HDR10, HLG, SDR, or Dolby Vision-specific arrangement. Third, can the destination present that interpretation? A supporting HDR10 path can use an HDR10 base. An SDR-only destination needs suitable conversion of that HDR source. HLG requires its own system interpretation. Finally, which extra information is being used? Dolby Vision metadata and any enhancement contribution belong to the complete presentation path. Their absence or nonuse changes which source information drives the output. A reference for common base choices Source example Available base interpretation Profile 5 Dolby Vision-specific; no ordinary HDR10/SDR base Profile 7 HDR10 Profile 8.1 HDR10 Profile 8.4 HLG Profile 9 SDR Profile 10 uses AV1 with its defined base variants; Profile 20 can add multiview and other processing requirements. Their codec and structure remain inputs to the first decision. Resolve three plausible sessions An Emby app receives supported Profile 7 data and uses the HDR10 base. The server may have copied the selected coded video, and the app/display presents HDR10. This is compatible-base use, not automatically an SDR conversion or complete Dolby Vision reconstruction. Another app receives an HLG-based Profile 8.4 source and uses its HLG presentation. Assigning a PQ interpretation instead would not be that source's defined fallback. The base field decides which relationship is appropriate. For a Profile 5 source on an incompatible output, simply stripping RPU data leaves the Dolby Vision-specific picture values. A supported converter must interpret those values and prepare another coherent output. If that destination is SDR, HDR-to-SDR processing supplies the brightness, color, and encoding changes. The source record, actual server delivery , and output mode place each of these sessions on the decision path. They distinguish full processing, compatible-base use, and a newly transformed rendition. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision Profile 8 How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Playback device capabilities Dolby: Introduction to Dolby Vision Profile 10 Dolby: Profile 20 FAQ

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 10 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 10 Moving a Dolby Vision presentation from HEVC delivery to AV1 delivery changes the picture codec, not merely the container. Profile 10 supplies the single-picture-layer ten-bit AV1 arrangement, with Dolby Vision data carried in an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU using an EMDF wrapper. Trace the preparation of an AV1 delivery An encoder can use an existing produced Dolby Vision master and its corresponding information to prepare an AV1 stream. The compressed picture needs real AV1 encoding. The associated metadata must be carried and remain consistent with those encoded pictures. At playback, the reader locates AV1 picture data and metadata. The decoder reconstructs the AV1 samples; supported Profile 10 processing supplies the Dolby Vision interpretation; the output route presents the resulting image. This separates three capability jobs: opening the packaging, decoding AV1, and using the selected Dolby Vision arrangement. A device's support for HEVC-based Dolby Vision does not complete the AV1 decoding job. AV1 decode support alone likewise does not supply the profile's metadata processing. Read the base variant Shorthand Available base interpretation 10.0 Dolby Vision-specific 10.1 HDR10-compatible 10.4 HLG-compatible These forms determine the base presentation a supporting fallback path can use. Their numbers identify compatibility choices rather than steps in picture quality. The level remains another field describing processing limits. For an Emby session, retain the AV1 and base-compatibility information beside the complete Dolby Vision record. If the destination uses the base, its light interpretation must match that variant. If video is transcoded, inspect the resulting codec and representation as the new output rather than assuming the source Profile 10 operations remained unchanged. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Profile 8 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby: Introduction to Dolby Vision Profile 10 Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 20 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 20 A stereoscopic presentation needs the correct picture for each eye as well as the intended brightness and color rendering. Dolby Vision Profile 20 combines these requirements using ten-bit Multiview HEVC for its 3D form and additional Dolby Vision metadata processing. Follow the two views to the viewer The 3D stream uses codec layers for distinct views of the scene. The base view and the additional view are decoded with their multiview relationship. The layer-to-eye association identifies which view belongs to the left or right eye; correct assignment is part of producing the intended depth. This arrangement differs from side-by-side packing of two reduced-width views in one ordinary frame. It also differs from Profile 7 's base and enhancement residual. A second eye view represents another viewpoint, while an enhancement residual supplies reconstruction information for a picture. A supporting route therefore has to perform several connected jobs: Read the multiview packaging and configuration. Decode the required HEVC views and their dependencies. Use the signaled eye assignment. Process the required Dolby Vision information. Deliver the views and presentation to the selected output. Each stage can affect the result independently. Successfully showing one ordinary HEVC view is useful codec evidence, but does not establish the complete stereoscopic path. Check the additional presentation information The public profile notes require Profile 20 playback devices to consume display-management version 4 metadata, including L8 target trims. Those requirements extend beyond the mandatory metadata support of some other Dolby Vision profiles. For stereoscopic content, the notes also specify a reference-display information message that associates layers with eyes. The Dolby Vision level applies to each view layer. A source record needs these structural facts alongside its codec and profile to describe the required path. Distinguish the defined forms Form or property Meaning 3D Ten-bit MV-HEVC views for stereoscopic presentation 2D A defined ten-bit HEVC form Base compatibility ID 0 Dolby Vision-specific base interpretation Base compatibility ID 4 HLG-compatible base interpretation The specification describes 2D Profile 20, while its public notes do not require every approved Profile 20 playback device to play that 2D form. Inspect support for the actual content form rather than inferring it from the general profile badge. An HLG-compatible base identifies its light interpretation. It does not resolve multiview packaging, codec dependencies, or eye assignment for an ordinary HLG television. Those are separate jobs in the route above. For an Emby investigation, record whether the selected content is 2D or 3D, its base compatibility, codec, views, and delivered stream. Then identify the exact app, decoder, and output. That turns “Profile 20 fails” into a specific question about reading, view reconstruction, metadata, or presentation. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby: Profile 20 FAQ Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profile 3 is a legacy dual-layer HEVC arrangement. Dolby lists it among profiles not supported for new applications; the record is useful when identifying older material. Legacy property Profile 3 Coded precision Eight-bit HEVC Picture structure Base plus enhancement Layer resolution relationship Equal resolution Base compatibility No standard HDR10 or SDR fallback An archived file using this arrangement needs its own supported interpretation or a real conversion. Current support for another Dolby Vision profile does not establish Profile 3 capability. Because the base has no standard HDR10/SDR interpretation, discarding the additional Dolby Vision information does not create either output. Keep the original and its complete profile record when preparing a supported viewing rendition. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Profiles not supported for new applications

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) Use this record when identifying older Dolby Vision media: Legacy property Profile 4 Coded picture precision Ten-bit HEVC Structure Base plus enhancement Enhancement size One-quarter of the base picture's pixel count Base compatibility SDR New-application status Listed by Dolby as not supported for new applications Why can a ten-bit base be SDR? Precision identifies the available sample levels. The transfer and color interpretation identify what those levels represent. Profile 4's ten-bit base has an SDR-compatible interpretation; a supporting Dolby Vision route uses the complete prepared presentation with its enhancement and metadata. That separates it from Profile 7 , whose compatible base is HDR10. Counting two layers in both files would leave their base-light relationships unresolved. Does SDR output mean Emby Server converted the file? Not necessarily. An app can use the compatible SDR base after receiving supported source data. A server conversion is another route that creates a new delivered stream. The server's playback method and delivered media information locate which operation occurred. The legacy status describes Dolby's direction for new applications. For an existing archived source, identify the actual decoder and presentation path used, then preserve that source record alongside any newly prepared viewing version. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Profiles not supported for new applications Dolby Vision: Distinguishing MEL and non-MEL bitstreams

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 5 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 5 A Profile 5 file can decode as HEVC yet show badly shifted colors if its samples are sent through an ordinary HDR10 interpretation. The compression decoder and the signal renderer have different jobs. Follow the samples past the decoder Profile 5 carries a single ten-bit HEVC picture layer with Dolby Vision RPU metadata. Its signal uses PQ with reshaping and the IPT-PQ-C2 component representation. It does not provide an ordinary HDR10 or SDR-compatible base. The HEVC decoder reconstructs those coded component samples. The Dolby Vision processing path then supplies their required interpretation and associated operations. Treating the decoded components as conventional BT.2020 YCbCr would use a different relationship to reconstruct color. That difference explains why a codec-capable player can produce an image while rendering it incorrectly. The necessary next stage is appropriate interpretation or a real conversion to another coherent representation. Required job Evidence to look for Open the delivery Supported container and configuration Decode the picture Ten-bit HEVC capability Interpret Profile 5 Supported reshaping, color, and metadata operations Present the result A suitable output/rendering path Removing metadata or changing labels leaves the underlying picture representation in place. It does not reconstruct a new HDR10 or SDR picture from those values. During Emby playback, inspect the selected app and delivered rendition as well as the stored source. A server conversion can prepare another output if the path supports the required source interpretation. Direct delivery needs that interpretation later in the route. Profile 8.1 makes a different choice by providing an HDR10-compatible base. The contrast identifies why one source can have a straightforward base fallback while another needs Profile 5-aware processing. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Profile 8 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 7 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 7 The Dolby Vision UHD Blu-ray workflow prepares three related parts of a Profile 7 presentation: Part Role Ten-bit HEVC base A complete HDR10-compatible picture Enhancement Additional reconstruction information according to the authoring mode RPU metadata Dolby Vision information associated with the pictures Base and enhancement must stay aligned. The profile defines a dual-layer delivery arrangement rather than two independently watchable releases. Choose the reconstruction path, not merely the final indicator A supporting Dolby Vision path can use the base, metadata, and relevant enhancement operations. With FEL , the nonzero picture residual supplies information for complete reconstruction. With MEL, no nonzero picture residual needs to contribute, while Dolby Vision interpretation and metadata remain part of the presentation. Another path can use the compatible HDR10 base. That gives a valid HDR10 image if the surrounding container, codec, and output path support it. It can be an intentional fallback rather than damaged content. The two paths use different information. A Dolby Vision output indicator identifies a presentation mode, while confirming an enhancement contribution requires evidence of the decoder/composer operations. An HDR10 indicator can instead describe the compatible-base path. Follow a repackaging or conversion Moving preserved coded data from disc packaging into another container changes the reader's arrangement, not the source's required reconstruction jobs. The destination app needs to locate and process the layers correctly. A disc player and an app receiving a file can consequently choose different available paths. A conversion to a single-picture-layer profile also needs its operation described. Did it keep the base, transform the metadata, or omit enhancement information? Copying the base without re-encoding preserves that coded base, while a discarded FEL can remove information from the original complete presentation. For an Emby comparison, record the source layer type, delivered stream, player support, and output mode. Those observations distinguish preserved Profile 7 delivery, compatible-base playback, and a newly prepared rendition. See Also Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision MEL and FEL Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 8 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 8 A report says Profile 8.1 and dvhe.08.06 . Those fields can agree: one describes base compatibility, while the full string identifies Profile 8 and Level 6. Profile 8 uses one ten-bit HEVC picture layer plus Dolby Vision metadata. It has no Dolby Vision picture enhancement layer. The current public profile definition lists these compatible base forms: Common shorthand Base interpretation 8.1 HDR10-compatible 8.4 HLG-compatible What changes between the two base forms? The HDR10-compatible form has a PQ-based light interpretation. A supported ordinary HDR10 route can use that base without completing the Dolby Vision presentation. The HLG-compatible form has a relative scene-light system relationship. Its appropriate fallback is HLG processing, not reinterpretation as PQ. HLG explains how display adaptation participates in that system. The compatibility number after the point identifies this base arrangement. It does not replace the level, which supplies processing bounds. Keeping both fields matters when selecting a playback path. Follow an HLG-based camera recording A personal-video source can carry an HLG-compatible base with Dolby Vision information. A suitable Dolby Vision route processes the prepared presentation using the applicable metadata. A suitable HLG route can use the defined base interpretation instead. The same decoded signal values do not imply the same absolute light in the two named systems without their respective rendering operations. That is why a broad HDR badge gives less useful diagnostic information than the transfer and compatibility fields. Apple's HDR video metadata guidance describes these relationships in camera-originated content. For an Emby library, inspect the actual recorded stream rather than assuming every Dolby Vision file uses the same base as a UHD Blu-ray title. Keep single-layer delivery separate from conversion history Profile 8's one picture layer differs from Profile 7 's base-plus-enhancement arrangement. A file prepared from Profile 7 can change what reconstruction information remains available, even when its copied base is still a valid picture. During playback, follow the source, server-delivered stream, and app/output interpretation. That record shows whether the session uses Dolby Vision, an HDR10 or HLG base, or a separately converted output. See Also HDR10 Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes Apple TN3145: HDR video metadata

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 9 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 9 Profile 9 pairs an eight-bit AVC/H.264 picture with Dolby Vision metadata and an SDR-compatible base. It is a specific delivery arrangement, with these properties: Property Profile 9 Compression AVC/H.264 High-profile family Coded base precision Eight bits Dolby Vision picture enhancement None Base compatibility SDR Why can playback legitimately appear as SDR? A suitable ordinary AVC/SDR route can decode and interpret the compatible base. It is using an intended available picture rather than necessarily converting the entire presentation on the server. A Dolby Vision route additionally needs Profile 9's metadata and signal processing. The successful AVC decode is the starting picture-reconstruction job, not a record of whether those later operations occurred. What does the eight-bit field describe? It identifies the coded base precision. That says how the compressed picture represents its samples, while the profile's processing establishes how those samples and metadata become the output presentation. Another source release can differ in its grade or retained precision, even if both are eventually shown with a Dolby Vision output mode. For Emby, compare the source profile, actual delivered stream, and app/output path. A source and an SDR display can be connected by compatible-base use or by a real conversion; the delivery evidence distinguishes them. The profile number identifies this arrangement rather than a quality tier above Profile 8 . See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Read dvhe.05.06 as a delivery description: 05 identifies Dolby Vision Profile 5, while 06 identifies Level 6. The two numbers describe different axes of compatibility. Item Question answered Profile Which codec, signal interpretation, layer arrangement, and metadata carriage apply? Level Which pixel-rate, width, and bitrate limits apply within that arrangement? Base compatibility ID Which other defined signal interpretation can the base provide? Estimate the processing dimension Pixel rate connects resolution and frame rate. A 3840 × 2160 picture has 8,294,400 pixel positions. At 24 frames per second, that is 199,065,600 positions per second ; at 60, it is 497,664,000 . The latter rate is 2.5 times the former even though both files are described as 4K. A higher permitted level can accommodate greater processing demand, while width and coded-bitrate limits also have to fit. Comparing only frame size misses those other limits. The Dolby Vision level and the underlying codec's own profile/level constraints both matter. Support needs to cover the delivered combination, not just one isolated label. Resolve two common kinds of notation A complete codec string: profile and level appear as separate fields in a defined syntax. It supplies a compact signal for capability matching. Shorthand such as 8.1: this commonly names Profile 8 with base cross-compatibility ID 1, the HDR10-compatible form. The number after the point is not the level field. A report saying 8.1 and dvhe.08.06 can consequently describe one stream: Profile 8, HDR10-compatible base, Level 6. Profile numbers identify feature arrangements rather than chronological quality tiers. A different profile can change the codec or base interpretation without changing the production master. For an Emby playback report, retain the full codec, profile, compatibility, level, layer, and container information. Then place it beside the delivered stream and actual decoder/output capabilities. The individual profile pages explain the arrangements; fallback describes which other presentation may be available. See Also How Dolby Vision Works Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profile 8 References Dolby Vision: Bitstream levels Dolby Vision: Playback device capabilities Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10.html.title: HDR10 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10.html.keywords: HDR10 An HDR10 delivery combines a ten-bit picture signal with a defined light and color interpretation. Its components have separate jobs: Component What it supplies Ten-bit precision The possible signal levels PQ transfer characteristic Absolute reference-light interpretation BT.2020 primaries The color-coordinate space Static mastering metadata Context about the grading display Content can additionally carry MaxCLL and MaxFALL , which provide reported content-light bounds. The number 10 refers to precision; peak brightness comes from the encoded picture and its interpretation. From the encoded picture to a light request A video decoder reconstructs sample values. The range and component information establish the normalized nonlinear signal, PQ supplies its light meaning, and the primaries establish its colors. These operations turn a compressed picture into an image suitable for rendering. The mastering description gives a renderer context about the source reference. The current picture can use much less of the available range than the mastering display allowed. A restrained night scene and a bright exterior can therefore share one HDR10 mastering record. Fit the source to the output Suppose a reflection in the source requests 1,000 nits and the destination has a lower usable peak. The output path chooses how to fit that reflection alongside the face and background around it. Tone mapping redistributes brightness differences; color adaptation handles the destination gamut and volume. HDR10 supplies a stable signal interpretation and static context rather than a prescribed per-scene appearance for every output. Different implementations can use the available picture and metadata differently while adapting to different screens. In an Emby session, record the source and delivered stream separately. The source can be HDR10 while an SDR destination receives a converted rendition . A Direct Play session can instead deliver the original picture for adaptation in the app or display. Codec, container, audio, and subtitle support determine other parts of playback compatibility . HDR10 describes the image interpretation within that route. HDR10+ adds dynamic information to a compatible base so adaptation can also use scene-specific guidance. See Also What HDR Video Adds to SDR HDR10+ HDR Metadata References SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata HDR10+ Technologies: System white paper

articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10-Plus.ht.title: HDR10+ | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10-Plus.ht.keywords: HDR10+ A movie cuts from a candlelit room to a bright snowfield. A program-wide peak gives a converter a useful bound, but says little about how those two scenes distribute their light. HDR10+ adds scene- or frame-specific information to an HDR10-compatible picture so a supporting renderer can adapt each part with more context. What travels with the picture? The base video retains the HDR10 signal relationship. Dynamic metadata defined by SMPTE ST 2094-40, Application 4 supplies picture characteristics and mapping guidance. These can include brightness-distribution information and parameters for shaping a mapping to a target. The metadata is compact information about the existing picture. It is not a second coded image layer. The decoded image remains the material being adapted, while the additional information helps select how it uses the destination's available brightness and color range. Follow the two scenes through adaptation In the candlelit room, preserving the face and ordinary surfaces may be more valuable than reserving a large part of the output range for a rare high peak elsewhere in the film. The snowfield has a different distribution: much more of the picture is bright, and retaining visible separation among clouds, snow, and reflections may require another mapping balance. Scene-specific metadata can make those differences available without the playback device relying solely on its own picture analysis. The renderer combines the information with its output target. It still has to produce valid colors and maintain sensible transitions as the metadata changes. The destination's physical capabilities remain inputs to this operation. Two displays with different useful peaks can choose different adaptations from the same prepared source information. The question is how the image's relationships survive those limits. Interpret an actual distribution item ST 2094-40 can report a percentile of the scene's linearized maximum RGB component values. For neutral gray, those component-light levels coincide with luminance. Consider median and 90th-percentile items in two illustrative scenes: Scene Percentile Normalized maxRGB value Corresponding gray light Interior 50th 0.002 20 nits Interior 90th 0.008 80 nits Snowfield 50th 0.020 200 nits Snowfield 90th 0.050 500 nits The normalization uses the 10,000-nit reference range. The interior record says at least 90% of the scene's selected sample values are at or below 80 nits. The snowfield's median establishes that at least half its selected samples reach 200 nits or more, while its 90th-percentile level is 500. Both scenes could still have a 1,000-nit peak. For a 100-nit target, at least 90% of the interior samples fit below the ceiling. At least half of the snowfield samples exceed it, so a larger part of that scene's sampled distribution requires fitting. A renderer can use this distribution to decide which tonal intervals need room and where to place a transition or curve anchors. The statistic supplies information for that decision; the implementation and target determine the resulting mapping. The ST 2094-40 curve page works through how anchors change a curve. There are three useful playback outcomes Path Presentation information available Supporting HDR10+ route Compatible picture plus dynamic adaptation metadata HDR10 route that ignores the extension The compatible base image and its HDR10 information SDR conversion A newly prepared SDR rendition, using the converter's supported source information In the middle path, the movie can decode correctly even though scene-specific HDR10+ guidance is unused. That differs from a decoder failing to reconstruct the picture. An Emby source report establishes what was detected in the file. Actual use requires the delivered stream, app, output path, and display to retain and interpret the extension where appropriate. A video transcode creates another presentation, so its output should be inspected as a new rendition rather than assumed to have copied every source operation. For a comparison, use the same release and examine both scenes across a cut. Look at middle tones and texture, and check temporal stability as well as the brightest point. Those observations show what the additional adaptation information changed in this particular picture. See Also HDR10 HDR Metadata Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References HDR10+ Technologies: System white paper SMPTE ST 2094-40: Dynamic metadata, Application 4

articles/video/hdr/formats/HLG.html.title: Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HLG.html.keywords: Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) A broadcaster needs one HDR signal that can be distributed and rendered on displays with different useful brightness ranges. Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) approaches this with a relative scene-light representation and a defined system relationship to the display. The basic rendering does not need a separate content-dependent mastering record for each program. The BBC and NHK developed HLG for television use. Its capture curve combines a lower power segment with an upper logarithmic segment, while its display processing establishes an appropriate scene-to-screen rendering. Calculated BT.2100 examples under reference conditions, with zero black. The display examples use the specified peak-dependent system gamma within the 400–2,000-nit monitoring range. They are not television or Emby measurements. The camera curve assigns scene light to signal values Let E be normalized scene light and V its encoded signal. The reference OETF uses: V = sqrt(3E) for E up to 1/12. V = a × ln(12E − b) + c above 1/12. The constants are a = 0.17883277, b = 1 − 4a, and c = 0.5 − a × ln(4a). The two segments meet at E = 1/12 and V = 0.5. That join divides the lower power portion from the upper logarithmic portion; it is not a physical maximum for the camera. The curve assigns signal positions to relative captured light. An output still needs to decide what light those positions produce on its screen. Camera exposure and production choices establish how the scene is placed within this representation. Rendering adds the scene-to-display relationship A renderer first interprets the signal and recovers the relevant scene-light values using the inverse OETF. It then applies the overall rendering relationship, or OOTF , for the display and environment. For neutral gray, an ideal zero-black reference example can be expressed as L = Lw × E^gamma , where Lw is the nominal peak luminance. At a 1,000-nit reference peak, system gamma is 1.2. Follow V = 0.75 through that example: Inverting the HLG OETF gives E of approximately 0.265 . Applying the reference relationship gives 1,000 × E^1.2. The resulting neutral-gray light is approximately 203 nits . This is a complete system calculation under its stated conditions. Interpreting V = 0.75 as 75% of 1,000 nits would skip both nonlinear operations. For colored pictures, the reference OOTF uses the scene's luminance to determine a common scaling of the linear RGB components. It does not independently raise each colored component to the system-gamma power. That preserves the intended component relationships during this part of rendering. Numerical range, primaries, and component-matrix interpretation are still required before the calculation. The same signal adapts to different peak targets Within the reference monitoring range, BT.2100 specifies gamma = 1.2 + 0.42 × log10(Lw/1,000) . Black-level treatment and viewing conditions also belong to the full system. The zero-black examples isolate the peak-dependent effect: Nominal display peak System gamma Light for neutral V = 0.75 500 nits About 1.074 About 120 nits 1,000 nits 1.200 About 203 nits 2,000 nits About 1.326 About 343 nits Each uses the same encoded value and the same recovered relative scene value. The overall display relationship changes to fit the target. The right-hand plot makes that difference visible across the whole signal range. PQ places an absolute reference-display light meaning on the encoded values. HLG instead includes this display-adapted overall relationship in its system. A PQ/HLG conversion must account for where that relationship is applied; swapping transfer labels would not perform the conversion. Why the metadata model suits television workflows A relative scene-based signal can move through conventional production and playout operations without requiring each program to supply dynamic content analysis for its basic HDR display relationship. The receiving system still needs signaling identifying HLG and the correct color representation. “No content-dependent metadata required” does not mean “no interpretation information needed.” The defined rendering also gives different output targets a common system starting point. Content can still be graded and monitored creatively: scene-referred describes the relationship of the representation, rather than implying that a finished broadcast is an untouched sensor recording. A camera HLG recording can provide a viewing-oriented HDR signal. Camera log footage has another representation and normally needs its production transform. The recording mode identifies which relationship is in the file. What the SDR-compatibility claim means HLG's shape was designed to provide a degree of useful compatibility with suitable conventional television paths. That does not make HLG samples numerically identical to a finished BT.709 SDR master. The wide color representation also has to be addressed when producing a BT.709 output. An HDR-aware conversion can interpret the HLG system and prepare an SDR rendition deliberately. A legacy path that applies a conventional component response can approximate aspects of the picture without completing the specified HLG rendering. These are different presentation paths, which is why compatibility must be tied to actual signal handling. Locate HLG within the delivered stream HLG appears in broadcast recordings and personal videos served by Emby. Inspect the source transfer field, the server's delivered rendition, and the app/display output mode when tracing a result. A source identified as HDR is not necessarily PQ or HDR10. If the server converts an HLG recording to SDR, check the newly produced output interpretation. If it delivers HLG unchanged, the later renderer needs to complete the appropriate system relationship. A change in bitrate alone would not explain or correct a mistaken transfer interpretation. Some Dolby Vision Profile 8 material uses an HLG-compatible base with additional Dolby Vision information. In that case, base signal and dynamic system describe two parts of one presentation. Identify which path is actually being used before comparing the resulting picture. See Also HDR Capture in Cameras HDR10 What HDR Video Adds to SDR References ARIB STD-B67: Hybrid Log-Gamma system parameters ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters BBC R&D: HDR television frequently asked questions

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Camera-Capture.ht.title: HDR Capture in Cameras | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Camera-Capture.ht.keywords: HDR Capture in Cameras A sunlit window and a person inside a dim room place different demands on a camera. The sensor and recording path must retain useful information from both if a later HDR grade is to show their relationship. Capture is where that information first becomes available. Place the exposure inside the usable range A sensor has an upper signal limit and a low-light region increasingly affected by noise. If the window reaches the upper limit, several different bright scene values can produce the same recorded value. Its texture is clipped. If the face falls too far toward the low-light noise floor, later brightening exposes noise alongside the wanted detail. Exposure places the scene within those limits. Reducing exposure can protect a window while reducing the signal available for the interior. Lighting, framing, or another capture choice can change the scene's demands; a wide-range sensor gives more room to balance them. Capture range is often expressed in stops . Each stop doubles the light ratio. A hypothetical 15-stop range corresponds to a ratio of 2^15, or 32,768:1 , under the measurement's noise and clipping criteria. It is a relative capture range, not a declaration that the finished film uses a certain peak number of nits. Choose the recording representation Recording approach Information and next stage Raw Sensor-oriented data developed through an image-processing pipeline Log video Processed picture values encoded to retain grading latitude Delivery-oriented HLG An HDR signal suitable for a compatible presentation path Log encoding allocates values differently from ordinary viewing encodings. It can retain a useful span of captured information in the recording precision, but the intended rendering remains part of production. A flat-looking log image viewed without its appropriate transform can contain good capture data; it has not yet been presented in its intended finished form. Raw development performs the necessary camera-image operations before or during grading. The exact stages depend on the camera and format. Both raw and log workflows can lead to HDR or SDR deliverables, because capture representation and output rendering have different roles. HLG recording can place those roles differently by providing a defined HDR television signal. A compatible renderer knows how to interpret that signal. The recording mode and color descriptions identify which path a personal video needs. Use the preview to judge the picture without confusing it with the recording A camera's display assist or monitoring transform can show a more viewable preview of log material. The preview operation can leave the underlying recorded log values unchanged. ARRI and Sony document these separate monitoring and recording uses. This distinction matters when a camera image looked normal on set but the saved file looks flat in a player. Check which transform was used for monitoring and whether it was incorporated into the exported viewing copy. Repeating the preview's appearance requires the relevant rendering, not a new label on the original values. Carry useful source information into the master Grading and mastering choose the output appearance from the retained source information. A colorist can place faces, windows, and highlights at suitable levels, match shots, and create different delivery versions. The source's captured range gives options for those decisions. For a home-video collection in Emby, keep camera originals and finished viewing copies identified. A log or raw original can need production work before routine playback. A delivery-ready HDR file instead needs a compatible display path or a suitable HDR-to-SDR conversion . Those stages solve different parts of the journey from captured light to the screen. See Also HDR Mastering in the Studio Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) What HDR Video Adds to SDR References ARRI: HDR FAQ Sony: What is S-Log? Sony: Gamma display assist and HDR recording ITU-R BT.2408: HDR television production guidance

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Luminance-Nits.ht.title: Luminance and Nits | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Luminance-Nits.ht.keywords: Luminance and Nits 1 nit = 1 candela per square metre (cd/m²). The unit expresses luminance: light leaving a surface in a specified direction, weighted for human vision. The number is useful only when its object is identified: Stated number Read it as A patch at 500 nits The intended or measured luminance of that patch Mastering maximum of 1,000 nits The mastering display's configured maximum Television peak of 1,000 nits A display result under stated test conditions MaxFALL of 200 nits A reported frame-average content-light bound Patch size makes a practical difference A small 1,000-nit reflection and a large 1,000-nit field have the same local luminance, but ask the screen to illuminate different areas. The screen's power and thermal behavior can make the sustainable result depend on patch size and duration. A peak measurement therefore needs its test conditions beside the number. Signal coordinates and light units are different Video transfer functions establish the relationship between stored signal and light. With PQ, a normalized signal near 0.508 represents approximately 100 nits for neutral gray; doubling that signal would not double the nits. The PQ curve shows the nonlinear relationship. HDR production guidance uses a 203-nit reference white under specified reference conditions, leaving space above ordinary white for highlights. Actual object placement is a grading decision. During playback, tone mapping can change source light levels to fit the output. Keep the source request, metadata field, and measured screen output named separately when comparing an Emby session. See Also What HDR Video Adds to SDR MaxCLL and MaxFALL Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References BIPM: Principles governing photometry ITU-R BT.2408-6: HDR production and reference white SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Mastering.html.title: HDR Mastering in the Studio | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Mastering.html.keywords: HDR Mastering in the Studio The camera records material with a range of available detail. HDR mastering turns that material into a finished image with deliberate light levels, color, contrast, and continuity from shot to shot. The reference display and viewing environment give those judgments a known basis. Consider a scene that cuts between a wide view of a room and a close view of a person's face. Both camera shots can retain bright window detail, yet present the face differently because of exposure, lenses, lighting, and processing. The master has to make those shots feel like the same scene while deciding how much attention the window should attract. Establish a trustworthy viewing basis A grading monitor is configured for a known color representation, white point, luminance range, and response. The signal sent to it must match that configuration. Otherwise, a colorist could compensate for a monitoring mismatch and bake an unwanted correction into the release. The viewing environment also matters: light reflected from the screen and the surround affect perceived contrast and adaptation. Reference conditions make judgments repeatable. They do not describe every home room, but provide the starting point against which the image is authored. Mastering-display metadata records the configured color volume used for that judgment. It gives later reproduction useful context. It is separate from measurements of the actual finished frames. Convert the capture representation into a grading image Camera originals can be raw, log, or another production representation. The workflow interprets that source with the appropriate camera processing and color transforms. An output transform provides the relationship to the grading display. This placement matters when changing a look. A correction made before a rendering transform acts on one representation; the same numerical correction after it can act on another. A production manages that order so color decisions remain meaningful and shots from different cameras can be compared. The work can use a scene-referred or display-referred approach, depending on the production. The purpose is to retain a coherent relationship from source through the chosen rendering to the reference image, rather than relying on the codec or filename to define the look. Place the important objects, then match the shots In the room example, the colorist might keep the face at a restrained light level, retain the window's structure, and let a small reflection reach higher. Increasing the available highlight range makes those choices possible without forcing every ordinary object upward. A close-up should continue the intended placement of the face, even if its captured values differ. Shot matching can adjust exposure relationships, color balance, and local contrast so the cut does not cause an accidental change in the scene's appearance. Dark details receive the same deliberate treatment. Some folds or background objects may remain visible; others may be held low to preserve mood or attention. HDR mastering does not require extracting every captured shadow or placing a bright sample at the display's maximum in every shot. Bright colored objects add a color-volume decision. A flame's saturation and luminance interact. The colorist checks their balance on the reference rather than treating brightness as an independent slider that leaves all colors unchanged. Review how the master maps to other targets A home screen can have a smaller useful range than the grading monitor. A production can inspect mapped versions before release, considering whether ordinary objects, colored highlights, and dark details retain the intended relationships. In a Dolby Vision workflow, image analysis supplies shot or frame characteristics. A trim pass lets the colorist review the mapping to another target and adjust it where needed. The instructions can travel as metadata alongside the main image. They do not need to be a full separately encoded movie for each possible screen. This is a review of a produced image under another set of limits. A trim can affect the balance within a scene, not merely the highest pixel. A window that fits numerically but loses all useful texture, or a face that shifts during the mapping, is visible during that review. Different target versions can also be separately authored. A dedicated SDR master can include grading decisions suited to SDR from the outset. An automatic playback conversion of the HDR master uses the HDR image and its conversion inputs instead. The two paths can reasonably produce different appearances. Prepare the release with consistent descriptions The finished picture is encoded for its delivery representation. A production graded within P3 can deliver values in BT.2020 coordinates; that conversion retains intended colors while changing their numerical description. The chosen transfer characteristic establishes the light meaning of the output. Static metadata can describe the mastering display and content-light bounds. Dynamic metadata, where the format uses it, belongs to the actual edited and graded shots. Editing after analysis can change timing or picture content, so the metadata needs to correspond to the delivered sequence. A final quality check therefore examines both pictures and their descriptions. Can the encoded stream be decoded correctly? Are its color fields consistent with the actual values? Do metadata and shot timing match? Does the mapped target retain the intended visual relationships? These checks cover different kinds of error. Compare releases with the production history in mind Emby presents the retained release through a particular app and output path. For a tone-mapping comparison, start with the same HDR source and inspect whether a change loses detail or creates a shift within that produced image. A separate SDR release is useful context, but it can contain different trims or a separate grade. Treating its pixels as the required numerical result of every HDR conversion would ignore those authored decisions. Keeping the versions and playback paths identified makes the comparison a question about an actual production and rendering choice. See Also HDR Capture in Cameras Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 How Dolby Vision Works References Dolby Vision: Color grading best practices SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata Dolby Vision: Shot analysis and long-play analysis

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.title: What HDR Video Adds to SDR | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.keywords: What HDR Video Adds to SDR Picture a dim room with a face beside a window and a reflection on glass. In the finished image, the face should remain readable, the window should feel brighter, and the reflection can be brighter still. HDR gives the filmmaker more room to separate those light levels in one picture. A conventional SDR rendition has a smaller reference range. Its production or conversion must fit bright areas closer together, choose which differences to compress, and establish a coherent image within that range. HDR can retain more of the separation, so a reflection stands out without requiring the whole room to become bright. What changes in the picture? Part of the scene Use of the additional range Face and ordinary surfaces Can remain at a deliberately chosen comfortable level Bright window Can stay distinct from the interior Small reflection Can stand out above nearby bright surfaces Dark folds and corners Can retain useful low-level distinctions in an appropriate presentation The creative choice comes first. A night scene can remain dark, a gray day can remain muted, and a deliberately flat shot can remain low in contrast. The extra range is available room for the image, rather than an instruction to fill every shot from black to the highest supported light level. Dynamic range has its own place beside resolution and color Resolution determines how many samples describe the scene. Bit depth determines the possible numerical precision of the signal. Gamut determines its color-coordinate reach. HDR's light relationship can improve alongside those properties, but each answers a different question. For example, a 4K SDR video can contain fine spatial detail while still using an SDR light representation. A 1080p HDR picture can use a wider light range with fewer spatial samples. A ten-bit file provides more levels than an eight-bit file, while its transfer characteristic determines whether those levels describe SDR, PQ, HLG, or another representation. BT.2100 specifies HDR television image parameters. PQ and HLG establish different HDR light relationships. Delivery formats add their particular packaging and metadata conventions. Follow the release to the screen The source describes a produced image. A receiving display has a usable light range and color volume of its own, and the room affects the appearance. When source requests exceed the destination, tone mapping fits the picture while deciding where to retain contrast. An Emby server can deliver HDR unchanged for a compatible playback path or produce a converted rendition for the destination. Local presentation can also adapt an unchanged source to the screen. The playback method identifies server delivery, while the app's output and display mode identify the later presentation. To compare HDR results, keep the same source release and scene, then inspect ordinary objects, dark detail, and bright texture together. That evaluates how the image uses its range, rather than judging only the largest brightness number. See Also Why Tone Mapping Is Needed Luminance and Nits HDR10 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function BBC R&D: HDR television frequently asked questions

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 A source report might contain this mastering-display record: Field Illustrative value Primaries P3 coordinates Reference white D65 Minimum luminance 0.005 nit Maximum luminance 1,000 nits SMPTE ST 2086 describes the configured color volume of the display on which the finished image was judged. Read the record as mastering context, not as a measurement of each frame. Interpret the two apparent mismatches The video uses BT.2020 primaries. That can coexist with P3 mastering primaries. The image was graded within one display's capabilities and expressed for delivery using a larger coordinate space. The two records name different stages. Correct coordinate conversion preserves the intended colors. MaxCLL is below 1,000 nits. The mastering display could support a highlight brighter than any used in the actual sequence. Content-light metadata describes that sequence under its definition, while ST 2086 records the configured display range. The numbers need not be equal. The minimum field likewise describes the mastering reference's lower luminance limit. It does not imply that every dark pixel reaches that level, or predict the black floor of the television currently showing the movie. Use the record during adaptation A renderer can use the reference volume as one input when deciding how to fit the produced image to a different output. The metadata supplies primary coordinates, white point, and luminance endpoints. It does not specify a complete transfer function or a sequence of shot-specific creative trims. During an Emby comparison, keep this source record beside the actual delivered signal and display target. A display with another volume can use tone mapping and color adaptation. The record explains the source reference; the playback path determines how that reference is used. See Also HDR Metadata MaxCLL and MaxFALL HDR Mastering in the Studio References SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: MaxCLL and MaxFALL | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: MaxCLL and MaxFALL One small highlight and one broadly bright frame can determine different content-light fields. MaxCLL is the reported maximum content-light bound; MaxFALL is the reported maximum frame-average bound. Both use cd/m², commonly called nits. Calculate the two summaries from three simple frames Use neutral-gray pictures so component-light and luminance values coincide. The constructed sequence contains: Frame Picture contents Highest level Frame average A 1% at 1,000 nits; 99% at 10 nits 1,000 19.9 B 50% at 300 nits; 50% at 20 nits 300 160 C Entire frame at 50 nits 50 50 Frame A's average is 0.01 × 1,000 + 0.99 × 10 = 19.9. Frame B's average is 0.5 × 300 + 0.5 × 20 = 160. Using the measured maxima as the declared bounds gives MaxCLL 1,000 and MaxFALL 160 . A determines the content peak; B determines the largest frame average. No averaging across the three frames is needed to obtain MaxFALL. This explains the distinction physically. A tiny reflection can be intense while most of its frame remains dark. A broadly illuminated scene can have a lower peak while placing a larger average-light demand on the display. What the measurement definition adds for colored pictures The standardized content-light messages describe bounds for linear-light RGB component intensities. A strong colored component can consequently give a value different from true CIE luminance calculated with color-dependent weights. Production measurement methods must be interpreted with their component definitions and picture-area treatment. The neutral-gray table above deliberately avoids that distinction. For a real program, keep the measuring tool and its definition identified when comparing reported values. The field records a declared bound; it is not a live measurement made by the television during playback. Read missing information and mastering context separately In the standardized messages, zero indicates that the corresponding upper bound is not supplied. It does not describe a movie whose light levels are all zero. A media report can also omit fields or carry values that were not correctly measured. Mastering maximum identifies the grading display's configured range. It can exceed the program's content peak, so a 1,000-nit mastering record and a lower MaxCLL can be consistent. A tone mapper may use reported content bounds, mastering context, measured picture statistics, or a combination. When an Emby conversion changes across different source editions, recording these fields beside the exact release helps identify whether the mapper began with different source assumptions. articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: HDR Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: HDR Metadata A media report can show BT.2020 primaries, PQ transfer, a 1,000-nit mastering maximum, content-light fields, and dynamic-metadata information. Those fields describe different parts of the picture's journey. Read them by role before treating them as one HDR quality score. Role Typical information What a renderer learns Signal interpretation Primaries, transfer, matrix, range What the decoded numbers mean Mastering context Display primaries, white point, luminance limits The reference volume used for judgment Content bounds MaxCLL, MaxFALL Reported light-level bounds of the produced sequence Adaptive instructions or statistics Format-specific dynamic metadata Information applicable to a shot or frame Signal interpretation is often called color signaling rather than HDR metadata in the narrower sense. It is essential because a valid compressed stream can reconstruct samples whose meaning still depends on those descriptions. Follow a simple metadata record through playback Suppose a source has BT.2020 primaries and PQ, a mastering maximum of 1,000 nits, and a reported MaxCLL of 600 nits. The first pair specifies color and light coordinates. The mastering number describes a display configuration. The content number supplies a bound for the picture under its measurement definition. A compatible app can interpret the source, read whichever metadata its rendering path supports, and adapt the produced picture to its output. A display with a different range does not have to imitate the mastering monitor's hardware; it needs an appropriate reproduction of the authored image. Some metadata is carried in codec supplemental messages; other signal descriptions can also appear in container structures. The container reader and video decoder make the needed information available to later processing. Correct packaging and interpretation are both parts of preserving it. Static and dynamic describe when information applies Static information applies to the relevant sequence or program. A mastering-display description can remain constant while the movie cuts between a dim room and a bright outdoor scene. Dynamic metadata can vary with a shot or frame. It can describe that image's brightness distribution or carry adjustments intended for a mapping target. A converter can therefore choose different parameters for scenes with different demands, while managing transitions over time. The format defines what those parameters mean. A dynamic block is not a hidden higher-resolution picture, and dynamic metadata from one format cannot simply be assigned to a different one. It needs the corresponding processing that interprets its values. The individual subjects— mastering metadata , content-light bounds , and Dolby Vision RPU —explain their particular roles. When the pixels change, their descriptions need review During Emby video transcoding , a new picture stream is created. Several possible operations have different metadata consequences: Copying the encoded video into another container can preserve its picture values, while requiring correct carriage of their descriptions. Resizing retains or changes the relevant color representation according to the processing path; spatial size alone does not select a new transfer function. HDR-to-SDR conversion changes brightness, color, and transfer representation. The output descriptions must identify that converted SDR picture. Cutting or reordering a sequence changes which pictures correspond to timed dynamic information. The metadata must still match the delivered sequence. Blindly copying a source field after processing can leave a plausible number attached to the wrong output. Conversely, dropping essential color signaling can make the destination assign another interpretation to otherwise valid samples. For a playback investigation, compare the stored source record with the stream actually delivered to the app and the output mode used for presentation. That locates the change: source information, carriage, picture conversion, or final rendering.
