articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Gamut Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Gamut Mapping A neon green can be correctly described in BT.2020 coordinates and still lie outside the colors a BT.709 destination can produce. Gamut mapping chooses a reproducible replacement while managing the relationships among color, brightness, and neighboring detail. Primary-coordinate plot, with luminance omitted. The line colors identify the gamuts rather than displaying their extreme primaries. First convert coordinates without discarding the desired color RGB values specify mixtures of particular primaries. A color conversion finds another set of coordinates for the same requested color. If the requested color lies outside the target triangle, some new coordinates can be negative: the target would need to subtract one of its primary lights to reproduce it exactly. Take the full BT.2020 green primary, with linear RGB 0, 1, 0 and D65 white. Converting to linear BT.709 coordinates using the published primaries gives approximately: Target component Converted value Red −0.588 Green 1.133 Blue −0.101 The coordinate transform is mathematically describing the requested color. The negative components and over-range green show why the target cannot directly reproduce it within zero-to-one component limits. A floating-point intermediate can retain those values until a mapping decision is made. See what independent clipping does Clipping each target component to zero through one changes the triplet to 0, 1, 0 , the BT.709 green primary. That is an achievable color, but it has another chromaticity from the original BT.2020 green. Its location has moved to the smaller triangle's corner. The same operation can merge distinctions. A BT.2020 green at linear level 0.9 converts to approximately −0.529, 1.020, −0.091. Clipping again gives 0, 1, 0. Source levels 0.9 and one have now reached the same target triplet. This example combines gamut reach with a component-output ceiling. It shows why merely transforming coordinates and clipping them can remove both color and light differences. The transformation identifies the problem; the mapping chooses how to resolve it. Compress color relationships deliberately A mapping can reduce chroma toward a neutral color, alter lightness, or use a combined color-volume strategy. In a perceptual hue/chroma representation, a method can try to keep the hue direction while reducing chroma until the target contains the color. Its chosen representation affects how that path behaves. Soft compression can start near the boundary, bringing extreme colors inward more gradually. It can preserve distinctions that hard clipping merged, but may also modify colors near the boundary that already fit. Broad desaturation moves every color inward, including ordinary colors that did not require much adjustment. Decision Image relationship affected Reduce chroma Saturation and separation among vivid colors Change lightness The object's brightness relative to its surroundings Clip components Component proportions and potentially hue/detail Preserve interior colors Limits how much of the image participates in compression A smaller target cannot retain every source color and every difference unchanged. The useful strategy preserves the relationships that matter to the produced scene, rather than just satisfying component bounds at the end. Combine the decision with brightness fitting In HDR-to-SDR conversion, the destination commonly has both a smaller light range and a smaller gamut. Brightness adaptation can change how a saturated color fits within the output color volume . A very bright colored light may need joint brightness/chroma treatment. A neutral-gray curve isolates brightness and cannot show that behavior. Inspect a red stage light, flame, or shop sign alongside gray surfaces when comparing an Emby rendition. Keep the source and output primaries, transfer, matrix, and range correctly interpreted so that a signaling mismatch is not mistaken for a deliberate gamut mapping. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough places the color decision within the complete conversion. The negative-component example explains why an otherwise correct coordinate transform still needs that decision before producing the target's final values. articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping Follow two bright folds in a white shirt. Clipping can give both the same maximum output. A highlight roll-off instead lets the brighter fold receive a little more output, while progressively reducing the room given to further source increases. Qualitative sketch with illustrative axis spacing. It is not a measured display response or the plot of a specified implementation. The relevant property is slope . A smaller slope maps neighboring source levels closer together. A completely flat segment maps them to the same value. A shoulder can therefore retain ordering and some texture while compressing the light differences that made the texture strong in the source. Place the transition while there is room above it The transition is often called a knee. Starting earlier changes more ordinary levels but leaves a larger output interval for the highest values. Starting later preserves more of the lower range while squeezing highlights into less remaining room. For one numerical example, the smooth mapping in the curve overview takes inputs 4 and 8 to 0.9 and one. It retains a distinction, but only 0.1 of the output separates a four-unit source difference. Keeping different numbers is one part of retaining visibly useful texture. The whole response matters in an Emby comparison: inspect the folds alongside faces and nearby ordinary surfaces, so an improved highlight is judged together with any changed lower tones. Saturated colored highlights also need color fitting . Roll-off describes the brightness response's shoulder; it does not specify the complete color conversion. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 Gamut Mapping References ITU-R BT.2390-6: HDR television and display adaptation FFmpeg 8.1: tone-mapping implementation

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping A mapper needs a source-range estimate. Peak detection obtains one by examining the decoded picture, rather than using only a mastering record or a configured assumption. Define the statistic before taking its maximum Stored video values need their range, transfer, and color interpretation. Taking a raw integer maximum does not by itself give a light level. A detector analyzes a defined quantity, such as a light-domain component statistic or a perceptual representation, then supplies it in the units its mapper expects. For a neutral PQ-gray example, recovered light levels can be expressed in nits. Colored pictures need the statistic's component/luminance definition too: a maximum RGB component and weighted luminance are different quantities. Test a frame with a few extreme samples Suppose 10,000 neutral-gray samples consist of 9,990 at 100 nits and ten at 1,000 nits: Estimate Result in this constructed frame Absolute maximum 1,000 nits 99.9th percentile, nearest-rank method 100 nits Average 100.9 nits The maximum sees the ten intense samples. The percentile selects the 9,990th sorted sample, at 100. The average is (9,990 × 100 + 10 × 1,000)/10,000 = 100.9. These statistics describe the same frame differently. Using the absolute maximum can reserve mapping range for a tiny sparkle. Discounting a small upper tail can give the rest of the scene more room but may compress or clip those rare highlights more strongly. The selected policy establishes that tradeoff. A practical detector can use sampled pixels or a histogram rather than sorting every value. Bin precision, selected picture area, and the treatment of exceptional values then affect the estimate. The example demonstrates percentile reasoning, not a particular library's binning or default setting. Keep source information in its proper role Input to a mapping Role Mastering-display maximum Context about the grading reference MaxCLL A reported sequence-level content bound Dynamic scene statistics Prepared information for the current content interval Runtime detected peak The detector's estimate from analyzed pictures Destination peak The output range to fit These values can be combined or selected according to the implementation. Missing metadata can make picture analysis especially useful, while a detector still needs an appropriate interpretation of the source. Finally, the estimate should be managed across time. A single flash can otherwise change a global curve for an unchanged face. Scene-adaptive mapping develops that stability problem. For an Emby comparison, record the source information and actual processing path, then watch a dim scene with isolated lights as well as a broadly bright one. Those scenes exercise the estimator's real decision. See Also Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References FFmpeg 8.1: mastering-display and content-light metadata libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection parameters

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping A tiny flash enters the window beside an otherwise stationary face. The source face stays at the same values, but the picture's detected peak rises. If a global mapper immediately changes its curve for that peak, the face can change brightness too. Scene adaptation needs to react to content without making that reaction distractingly visible. Conceptual responsibilities, not a description of one Emby implementation. Watch a simple smoothing model respond Let the estimated peak begin at 200 nits. In an illustrative model, update it as new estimate = 0.75 × previous estimate + 0.25 × new measurement . A single measured jump to 1,000 followed by a return to 200 produces: Frame event Measured value Smoothed estimate Initial stable scene 200 200 Flash 1,000 400 Next ordinary frame 200 350 Following ordinary frame 200 312.5 The model reduces the abrupt peak change, but its memory also leaves a smaller change after the flash. If those estimates control a global curve, they can still move the face's output over several frames. This arithmetic isolates temporal lag. Actual detectors can smooth other representations, use different time constants, and discount exceptional samples through percentiles . The model is not a product setting or a claim that a library uses these coefficients. A cut and a flash need different responses Now replace the flash with a real cut to a bright scene. A slowly smoothed estimate can keep applying the previous scene's assumptions for too long. Scene-change handling can reset or accelerate adaptation when the measured change warrants it. The tension is between stability inside a continuing scene and responsiveness to another scene. Brightness statistics are useful evidence but cannot always identify an edit unambiguously: camera motion, exposure changes, and flashes can also move them. Implementations choose detection and response policies for that ambiguity. Prepared dynamic metadata supplies another source of changing information. It can describe a shot from production; runtime analysis instead estimates from the pictures received. Both still need coherent timing and appropriate transitions. Keep temporal adaptation separate from spatial adaptation A curve can change over time while remaining the same across one entire frame. Local processing varies by region within a frame and is another choice. Calling a mapper adaptive does not specify which dimension varies. During an Emby test, let the picture move. Examine a stationary face when a bright object enters, then the first frames after a cut. Identify the processing location so the observed change can be attributed to the source, app, converter, or display. The temporal example explains why one attractive paused frame cannot establish stable adaptation. See Also Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection and scene-change handling FFmpeg 8.1: OpenCL tone-mapping kernels

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable Hable's filmic curve shapes the darker and middle region as well as rolling bright values toward white. The lower-range panel makes that whole-image behavior visible: FFmpeg 8.1 scalar Hable mapping, source peak 8 and output white 1, neutral gray in relative linear light. Dashed gray is clipping. Follow the ordinary values as well as the highlight Input Output in this plotted example 0.18 About 0.0731 0.3 About 0.1183 1 About 0.3315 4 About 0.7769 8 1 Lower values do not pass through unchanged. The curve allocates its output range across the whole input, so an ordinary object can become darker while bright regions retain gradations. The shoulder supplies less additional output as the input rises, compressing highlight separation. John Hable developed the original response for Uncharted 2 and explains its filmic construction in the referenced articles. A toe shapes the transition out of black, the middle controls much of the apparent brightness, and the shoulder approaches the upper range gradually. Reproduce the stated implementation For FFmpeg's fixed coefficients, the unnormalized function is: H(x) = [x(0.15x + 0.05) + 0.004] / [x(0.15x + 0.50) + 0.06] − 0.02/0.30 With source peak P, the plotted mapping is T(x) = H(x) / H(P) . This normalization makes the assumed source peak land at output white. It also affects other points: at x = 1, P = 8 produces about 0.3315, while P = 4 produces about 0.4266. The peak assumption is thus part of the image transformation, not merely a label on its brightest point. If an Emby route uses this mapping, comparing the source peak and surrounding conversion explains why two runs can differ with the same curve name. The HDR-to-SDR example shows where brightness mapping sits between source interpretation and output encoding. Use the lower panel here to inspect the ordinary objects whose brightness that mapping changes. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius Mobius leaves a lower interval unchanged, then joins it to a curved upper section. The knee is where the mapping begins reducing the extra output assigned to brighter inputs. FFmpeg 8.1 scalar mapping, knee 0.3, source peak 8, output white 1, neutral gray in relative linear light. Dashed gray shows clipping. Move the knee and follow the same input Input Knee 0.3 Knee 0.6 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.6 About 0.516 0.6 1 About 0.667 About 0.806 4 About 0.937 About 0.976 8 1 1 The plot shows the first column's mapping. Raising the knee keeps more inputs on the unchanged line, but leaves less output range above that point. For example, the knee-0.6 version places input 4 at about 0.976, leaving only 0.024 before the peak. The knee-0.3 version leaves about 0.063 there. These numbers make the tradeoff visible: more preservation in the lower region means stronger compression of the remaining highlight interval. The knee uses the input working units; 0.3 is not 30% of a source peak of eight. The join is constrained, not an arbitrary corner The upper part uses a rational Möbius relationship, a scaled ratio of two linear functions. Its coefficients are chosen so it meets three conditions: output equals input at the knee, the slope there is one, and the source peak maps to output white. Matching both value and slope makes the transition continuous without a sharp first-derivative corner. Above it, the curve gradually becomes shallower. The unchanged portion and the compressed portion therefore form one coherent response. In an HDR-to-SDR path , surrounding color and output operations also act on the picture. An Emby comparison can use this plot to separate the curve's lower-interval behavior from those other stages: inspect an ordinary object below the knee and bright texture above it under the same conversion conditions. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard Start with the simple relationship T(x) = x/(1+x) for an already scaled linear-light input. At small x, the denominator is near one. As x grows, the denominator grows too, making further input increases contribute less output. Input x Basic output Output after normalization to peak 8 0.1 0.0909 0.1023 1 0.5000 0.5625 4 0.8000 0.9000 8 0.8889 1.0000 The basic function approaches one gradually. At a finite source peak of eight, its endpoint is eight-ninths. Multiplying by nine-eighths makes that known peak reach one and also raises the other mapped values. FFmpeg 8.1, public parameter 0.5, source peak 8, output white 1, relative linear light for neutral gray. Dashed gray shows clipping. Read the compressed separation Inputs 4 and 8 are four units apart, but the normalized outputs differ by only 0.1. The values remain ordered and distinct; much less output contrast separates them. An input of one moves to 0.5625, showing that this mapping also changes ordinary levels. Uniform division by eight would put the same input of one at 0.125. The nonlinear relationship spends more of the output on the lower region and compresses the top more strongly. That is the actual compromise visible in the plot. Distinguish the curve from the complete photographic operator Reinhard and coauthors' original photographic tone-reproduction work also includes exposure scaling and a spatially varying method. A global function called Reinhard in a video filter represents one part of that family, with its own parameter and peak convention. FFmpeg's stated parameter corresponds to the normalized function in the table. In general its scalar form is x/(x+k) × (P+k)/P, with k derived from the public parameter. Changing k or P changes the mapping even before surrounding color operations. When comparing an Emby conversion, identify the actual curve implementation and normalization, then inspect both ordinary objects and highlight texture. The arithmetic here explains their relative placement rather than assuming the historical photographic method and a video option produce identical pictures. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Clip | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Clip Clipping puts a hard ceiling on a value. Below the ceiling it keeps the value unchanged; above it, every input becomes the same maximum. FFmpeg 8.1 clip mapping with scale parameter 1. Both axes use relative linear light for neutral gray; output white is 1. The flat section is the important part. Three parts of a bright cloud with inputs of 2, 4, and 8 all become 1. The cloud's positions remain, but the brightness differences that made its texture visible disappear. Input Output 0.2 0.2 1 1 2 1 8 1 A highlight roll-off bends toward the limit gradually, leaving output space for some of those differences. It starts changing the values before they reach the ceiling. Clipping preserves the in-range part exactly and spends none of that range on brighter values. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Gamma | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Gamma A power mapping can give lower values more output room than uniform scaling. In the plotted FFmpeg example, most of the curve uses T(x) = (x/8)^(1/1.8) , fitting a source peak of eight into output white one. FFmpeg 8.1 scalar CPU function, relative linear light for neutral gray. Its very dark region uses the implementation's linear extension. Input Mapped output Uniform division by eight 1 About 0.315 0.125 4 About 0.680 0.500 8 1 1 The endpoint fits in both cases. The power function assigns more output to the lower and middle inputs, changing the contrast distribution. Follow the darkest part separately A bare power with exponent below one becomes very steep near zero. FFmpeg replaces the part below input 0.05 with a straight extension that meets the power value there: T(x) = x × (0.05/8)^(1/1.8) / 0.05 for x up to 0.05. Input 0.01 therefore produces about 0.01193, and 0.05 produces about 0.05963. The plotted function includes that treatment; using the power expression down to zero would describe a different shadow response. Resolve the parameter's meaning before reproducing a result libplacebo's mapper also uses the name gamma, but preserves an unchanged lower interval and chooses a power above its knee. Its knee parameter has a different role from FFmpeg's gamma parameter. Neither is simply the display gamma . This function remaps a brightness range. Display gamma participates in a signal-to-light response. During an Emby comparison, locating that operation within the playback path keeps the mapping arithmetic separate from output interpretation. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Linear | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Linear Divide each linear-light input by the peak ratio, and the source range fits proportionally. For a ratio of eight, T(x) = x/8 : Input Output 0.8 0.1 1 0.125 4 0.5 8 1 The output preserves the ratios of these light values. It also darkens every lower value by the same factor, which can spend too little brightness on ordinary objects when the source has only a small very bright highlight. Peak ratio 8:1. Green scales linear light; blue follows libplacebo's PQ-space stretch with output white 203 nits. Both axes show relative linear light; gain is one and black is zero. Why the blue proportional mapping bends PQ coordinates are nonlinear with respect to light. The blue operation proportionally changes those coordinates, then the figure converts its result back to linear light. The operation is linear in its selected representation, while its plotted light relationship is curved. This distinction occurs in software: FFmpeg's CPU linear mapper operates on linear-light samples; libplacebo distinguishes its PQ-space linear option from linearlight. The selected space is part of the method, not a minor naming detail. A useful Emby comparison therefore starts with the implementation, source range, target, and working space. For the green example, input 4 and input 8 stay distinct at 0.5 and one. Clipping would merge both at one. That retained separation is what proportional fitting buys, and the lower-value arithmetic shows what it costs. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Spline | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Spline A spline lets the mapper shape two parts of a brightness relationship around a selected pivot. In the plotted libplacebo implementation, a quadratic lower segment and a cubic upper segment meet with the same value and slope. libplacebo 7.360.1 defaults, zero black, 1,000-nit input peak, 100-nit output peak, and no scene-average value. The function operates in PQ coordinates; the axes show light levels. What is fixed and what can move? The source and target endpoints set the range to fit. The pivot sets an input/output pair inside that range. A contrast control adjusts the slope at the pivot, while the polynomial coefficients make both segments meet their remaining constraints. Changing the pivot's output moves that part of the scene to another brightness. Changing its input moves where the two pieces meet. Changing the slope alters nearby contrast. These are different controls over the shape, even when its endpoints remain unchanged. Input light Output in the displayed example 10 nits About 5.98 nits 100 nits About 36.16 nits 500 nits About 76.78 nits 1,000 nits 100 nits The function distributes much of the available output below the highest input. A 500-nit difference from 500 to 1,000 nits becomes about 23.22 nits. Those values belong to the stated default selection, not to every spline. Feed the pivot meaningful information The library can select its pivot using range and scene-brightness information. A dim interior and a bright exterior can consequently receive different curves. With scene average absent, a defined fallback selection still produces a curve, as in the figure. Scene adaptation provides and stabilizes changing information; the spline provides a form that responds to it. The mathematical join itself addresses spatial value continuity, while temporal stability depends on how its parameters change between pictures. For an Emby comparison, identify the actual mapper and its source/target inputs. The Windows rendering path is one place where presentation can adapt the picture. The graph here explains the spline's selected brightness function within such a path. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A BT.2446 Method A is an HDR/SDR conversion method. A renderer option called BT.2446A can use its brightness function within a larger conversion pipeline; the complete report also defines associated color processing. Follow the brightness calculation's stages The plotted library function normalizes source light to the source range and applies a power representation. It then compresses that coordinate through a logarithmic relationship whose scale depends on the peak. A piecewise function treats three coordinate regions differently: a scaled lower segment, a quadratic middle segment, and a linear upper segment. Finally, the calculation converts back through the destination relationship to obtain output light. The changing slope is what distributes contrast across the range. libplacebo 7.360.1 brightness function, zero black at both ends. The plot isolates this scalar stage of Method A. Source light Output light in this example 10 nits About 3.13 nits 100 nits About 22.66 nits 500 nits About 73.15 nits 1,000 nits 100 nits The peak fits, while the hundred-nit region uses less than a quarter of the target peak. The function has chosen a particular contrast distribution; it is not simply source light divided by ten. For example, 500 nits would become 50 under that proportional scaling, rather than 73.15 here. Work one 100-nit point through those coordinates For the stated 1,000-nit source and 100-nit target, define h = 1 + 32 × (1,000/10,000)^(1/2.4), about 13.260, and s = 1 + 32 × (100/10,000)^(1/2.4), about 5.697. These peak-dependent factors set the two logarithmic ranges. Normalize the source point and take the power: (100/1,000)^(1/2.4) ≈ 0.3831. Form q = ln[1 + (h−1) × 0.3831] / ln(h), about 0.6732. This q is in the lower piecewise region, q ≤ 0.7399. Apply 1.077q, giving about 0.7250. Return through the target logarithmic relationship: V = (s^(1.077q) − 1)/(s − 1), about 0.5387. The zero-black target response gives 100 × V^2.4 ≈ 22.66 nits . The upper regions use a quadratic and then another linear expression instead of the lower 1.077q rule. The branch is selected in the intermediate coordinate, so its breakpoints are not direct input-nit thresholds. Put the function back into the complete conversion For a neutral gray, brightness can be followed with a scalar. For colored objects, changing light also changes color appearance, and the target can have another gamut or volume. Method A's color operations address that relationship; a renderer using only the named brightness stage combines it with its own surrounding color path. Output transfer encoding is another required job. The mapped light value is a processing result, not automatically a final YCbCr code. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough explains that handoff. In an Emby comparison, locate whether the complete method or a scalar stage is being used, then retain the same source and target assumptions. That identifies why two results with the same Method A name can use different color processing around the brightness curve. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-40 in libplacebo The ST 2094-40 mapper in libplacebo can use a content-supplied knee and Bézier curve anchors. It then adapts that prepared relationship to the actual output range. When those anchors are absent, the implementation constructs a fallback curve. How an anchor changes the curved section A knee specifies the transition into the upper mapping, with input and output coordinates. The section above it is normalized between that transition and its endpoint. Bézier controls shape how the output travels between those ends. For a simple mathematical illustration, a quadratic section with endpoint controls zero and one and middle control a is: B(t) = 2a × t(1−t) + t² At t = 0.5, a = 0.25 gives output 0.375, while a = 0.75 gives 0.625. Both sections still start at zero and end at one. Moving a control changes the middle shape rather than changing those endpoints. The controls shape the curve; they are not ordinary measured image samples that the curve must pass through. Actual metadata defines its knee, anchor set, and target under the standard's conventions. A real metadata-defined relationship can select another shape. Follow the available information Information reaching the mapper Operation available Knee, anchors, and their target Adapt the prepared content curve Source statistics Use them in brightness matching or curve construction No complete anchor set Use the implementation's fallback construction HDR10+ supplies its prepared dynamic information through the delivery path. articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.title: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.keywords: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Choose an input on the horizontal axis, trace upward to a curve, then trace across to the vertical axis. The point answers: what output brightness does this mapping assign to that input? Calculated examples in relative linear light. Clipping is min(x,1), straight scaling is x/8, and the smooth curve is (9/8) × x/(1+x). These are illustrative relationships, not Emby presets. Read a pair of points to see contrast On the clipping curve, inputs 2 and 4 both map to 1. Their separation has gone. On the scaling curve, they become 0.25 and 0.5. On the smooth curve, they become 0.75 and 0.9. Inputs 2 and 4 Output difference Clipping 0 Scaling 0.25 Smooth example 0.15 The difference is part of the available output contrast. A flatter segment gives less separation to neighboring inputs; a steep segment gives more. Smooth compression can retain distinct highlight values while reducing their spacing substantially. Now check a lower input, x = 1. Scaling produces 0.125; the smooth curve produces 0.5625. A curve that makes the peak fit can consequently place an ordinary object very differently. The highest endpoint alone does not describe the picture. Look across the shape The lower part controls separation near black. The middle affects a large amount of scene content. A shoulder gradually reduces the extra output assigned to very bright inputs. A knee marks a transition in behavior; its numerical meaning depends on the curve's working representation. The axes are therefore essential. A function that is straight in PQ coordinates can bend when plotted against linear light. Physical-nit axes, normalized-light axes, and signal-coordinate axes show different relationships. State the source peak, target, and parameters before comparing two plots. Use curve names to find a specific relationship The individual pages show Hable , Reinhard , Mobius , and other curves. Each page identifies the plotted implementation and its assumptions. The curve is one part of a conversion. Input interpretation, color handling, adaptation over time, and output encoding affect the final picture too. In an Emby comparison, hold those conditions steady while examining how ordinary objects and bright texture move along the selected relationship. The conversion walkthrough puts the curve into that full path. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: CUDA Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: CUDA Tone Mapping NVIDIA video processing can involve three separate engines or execution roles. Follow a possible decoded-picture route: Stage Work NVDEC Reconstruct compressed video into decoded surfaces CUDA program Perform programmable picture calculations, such as tone mapping NVENC Encode the prepared pictures into another video stream The decoder and encoder are hardware video engines. CUDA supplies programmable parallel computation. A tone mapper's kernel defines the brightness and color calculations; those decisions do not come from choosing the NVIDIA brand for decoding or encoding. Keep a decoded surface accessible to the next stage NVIDIA's NVDEC API supports decoding to video memory and making the resulting surfaces available for CUDA processing. The application can use those decoded samples as the input to its kernel, then hand the processed result onward through a supported route. This is a memory and synchronization relationship. The filter must understand the surface's format and layout, wait until decoding has produced it, and ensure its output is ready for the next consumer. Shared access avoids a needless trip through system memory when the complete path supports it. Now insert a software-only operation between the stages. The application may need to download a representation to system memory, process it there, then upload the result again. The tone kernel can still be fast while those transfers add cost. CPU mapping gives raw-frame storage arithmetic that explains the scale of such traffic. Read activity by the job it represents An Emby session can use an accelerated encoder while another stage handles tone mapping. Video-encode activity then describes NVENC's job, not the location of every preceding calculation. Different monitoring views can aggregate or separate video and compute activity. To understand the session, identify its decoder, filter, frame transfers, and encoder. The hardware overview supplies the product's platform context; the actual application implementation chooses which supported operations use CUDA. The kernel's chosen curve, input peak, color interpretation, and output target determine the prepared picture. Comparing these inputs alongside the memory route explains both the image result and the execution cost without treating one activity percentage as a description of the entire conversion. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: OpenCL Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: OpenCL Tone Mapping An OpenCL filter is selected, but processing fails before a picture is delivered. Locating that failure requires three distinct pieces: the application's filter, the runtime's selected device, and the frame representation passed between stages. Piece Responsibility Application/filter Supplies the mapping program and accepted formats OpenCL platform/runtime Discovers devices and compiles or loads programs Device/context/queue Executes the work and provides accessible frame resources OpenCL can target supported CPUs or GPUs. The interface name alone does not identify which device was selected or which curve the application implements. Follow initialization into picture processing The application chooses a platform and device, creates the relevant context, and obtains a command queue for submitted work. It supplies a kernel program: a function executed across many work items so regions of a picture can be processed in parallel. Decoded pictures must be made accessible in the filter's expected hardware-frame arrangement. The filter then supplies its color descriptions, range and mapping parameters, launches the program, and makes the result available to the next stage after the required synchronization. FFmpeg 8.1's OpenCL tone mapper provides a concrete implementation. It checks supported source transfer and component information, prepares the corresponding color/transfer operations, and uses the selected mapping function in its OpenCL program. Its accepted hardware formats constrain that filter's path rather than defining all OpenCL devices' possible formats. Resolve two different failure cases No usable OpenCL device appears. Check the runtime and device access in the application's environment. A hardware video decoder can work while a separate compute runtime is absent. A container also needs the applicable runtime and device resources, not only a device visible to the host. A device is selected but the frame format cannot reach the filter. Inspect the preceding decoder's frame format, the required mapping or upload, and any supported sharing between APIs. Successful device discovery does not supply the missing representation or interoperability operation. In Emby logs, those stage failures differ from an inability to decode the source codec. Hardware-acceleration documentation describes the surrounding platform options; the bundled implementation and session specify the actual filter route. Once the path works, frame transfers and synchronization remain part of its cost. Keeping accessible frames across decoding, filtering, and encoding can avoid unnecessary copies. A faster kernel alone may leave the surrounding traffic or another stage as the limiting operation. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: Vulkan Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: Vulkan Tone Mapping A renderer can use Vulkan to submit shader work on a GPU. The shader supplies the picture calculations; Vulkan provides the device, resources, command submission, and synchronization used to execute them. Follow a picture through a renderer A decoded picture becomes accessible as the required GPU image or buffer. A rendering library can assemble operations such as source interpretation, color conversion, tone mapping, scaling, and output preparation into shader processing. The application submits the work and manages when resources can be read or written. A following presentation or encoding operation must wait for the prepared result. These relationships matter when frames are shared with another API or transferred from a decoder using a different memory arrangement. libplacebo is a rendering-library example with a Vulkan backend. Its image-processing controls sit above Vulkan's lower-level interface. The source/target descriptions, selected curve, and adaptation inputs determine the brightness relationship that its programs perform. Use the result in either of two contexts Consumer of the processed picture Purpose Display presentation Prepare the image for an output surface and screen Video encoder Produce another compressed rendition from processed frames FFmpeg's libplacebo filter demonstrates the second use. GPU rendering calculations can be part of a conversion pipeline even when their immediate result is not being drawn to a window. Vulkan Video decoding is another capability. Running a tone-mapping shader does not imply that the source was decoded using Vulkan Video; an application can support another decoder and the needed upload or resource sharing. The representation and synchronization at that boundary decide whether the pieces can connect efficiently. Locate a Vulkan message in the Emby path A renderer's Vulkan-related message describes that renderer's execution route. A separate server transcode can use another filter and API. Start with the playback-path diagram , then identify the application and stage producing the message. Two routes using Vulkan can choose different image-processing programs, target descriptions, or library versions. Holding those inputs steady is what makes an image comparison meaningful; following the resource handoffs is what makes an execution comparison meaningful. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: CPU Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: CPU Tone Mapping A CPU tone mapper processes reconstructed pictures in system memory. Its work follows the picture grid and processing representation, even if the source's compressed file is small. Count the picture work before the compressed bytes Grid and rate Picture positions per second 1920 × 1080 at 24 fps 49,766,400 3840 × 2160 at 24 fps 199,065,600 3840 × 2160 at 60 fps 497,664,000 These are input sizes, not measured CPU throughput. Each position can require component conversion, transfer-function calculations, curve evaluation, and output preparation. The chosen implementation determines how those operations are combined or accelerated with vector instructions and threads. Follow a software-filter representation FFmpeg's CPU tonemap filter operates on floating-point RGB in linear light. A suitable surrounding path interprets the incoming HDR signal, supplies that working representation, runs the mapping, and prepares the final output format. For a 3840 × 2160 picture with three 32-bit float components, the logical sample storage is: 3840 × 2160 × 3 × 4 = 99,532,800 bytes , about 99.53 MB per picture before padding. At 24 fps, one full read and one full write of that representation account for approximately 4.78 GB/s of logical traffic . Additional passes can require more; cache reuse and implementation choices change the physical traffic. This is a storage calculation, not a benchmark or a required network bitrate. The example explains why an operation's cost includes memory access as well as the scalar curve formula. A decoded working picture can be much larger than the compressed data used to deliver it. Keep the other CPU jobs visible An Emby transcode can also decode, rescale, render subtitles, convert audio, and encode. A high total CPU reading covers those jobs together. To locate a bottleneck, inspect the actual stages and whether their completed-picture rate keeps up with the source. A hardware encoder at the end does not move all earlier filtering to the GPU. Conversely, software decoding can feed GPU presentation; the Windows FAQ describes that combination. A transfer between system and device memory may be needed at that boundary. When frames already occupy system memory and the required software path is supported, CPU mapping avoids introducing an additional device-transfer stage solely for the curve. When a supported GPU path can keep frames accessible across several operations, its residency changes the traffic picture. The playback-path article locates those choices within the session. articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session Two sessions can show the same HDR library file yet perform brightness adaptation in different places. Follow the delivered video before attributing the displayed result to a server setting. Conceptual routes. A particular app's supported signal and processing path determines which route it can use. Session A: the server prepares SDR The server decodes the HDR picture, interprets its light and color representation, and performs HDR-to-SDR conversion . It encodes the resulting picture with matching SDR descriptions. The app receives that SDR rendition and presents it through an SDR output path. The mapping has occurred before delivery. The library source remains HDR, while the delivered video describes the processed SDR image. Source metadata and final stream metadata consequently answer different questions. Session B: unchanged HDR reaches a local renderer With Direct Play , the server supplies the original file. Direct Stream can change packaging or other tracks while retaining the coded video. A supported app then decodes and interprets the delivered picture. If its presentation adapts HDR to the selected output, the pixel change occurs after delivery. The Windows app FAQ describes GPU-shader tone mapping during presentation, including a path with software decoding. Decoding location and mapping location can therefore differ. Session C: the display fits an HDR signal An HDR signal reaches an HDR display whose useful range is smaller than the source request. The display can perform HDR-to-HDR adaptation . Its HDR indicator identifies the signal mode, while its internal mapping determines the reproduced light. Other device or operating-system stages can participate in the output chain. The relevant evidence is the actual signal and processing at each boundary rather than the library's HDR badge alone. Record a comparison by boundary Boundary Useful observation File to server Exact source release, HDR format and color fields Server to app Video copied or re-encoded; delivered HDR/SDR representation App to output Decoder, renderer, selected presentation mode Output to screen Received signal mode and display processing Video transcoding can be required for reasons other than tone mapping, so it should be inspected for the actual picture processing. Likewise, copied video locates any later pixel adaptation downstream. This boundary record makes two Emby sessions comparable: it identifies which stage could have changed the image and which conversion inputs belonged to that stage. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping A source contains 2,000-nit highlights, while the intended HDR output has a usable peak of 600 nits. The source and destination are both HDR, but their available light ranges differ. HDR-to-HDR tone mapping fits that image to the smaller range while keeping an HDR output representation. Establish the actual source and destination For PQ material, the transfer function supplies absolute reference-light requests. A source's mastering maximum describes the grading display, while content bounds and picture analysis describe what the produced sequence uses. These are different inputs to selecting the range that needs fitting. The destination is also a rendering target. Its useful peak depends on the relevant area and duration, and its black floor and color volume constrain the reproduced picture. A supported HDR signal format does not define all those physical limits. The worked example below chooses zero black, a source peak of 2,000, and a target peak of 600. It is a constructed brightness relationship that makes the decisions visible. Preserve a lower interval and fit the highlights Let L be source light in nits. Leave values through 200 unchanged. Above 200, define d = L − 200 and use: T(L) = 200 + d / (1 + 7d/3,600) At the transition, d is zero and the output is 200. The initial upper slope is one, matching the lower unchanged segment. As d grows, the denominator grows and the response flattens. At L = 2,000, d = 1,800, the denominator is 4.5 and output is 200 + 400 = 600 nits . Original neutral-gray example for the stated ranges. It is not a measured Emby preset or the specified BT.2390 function. Source light Smooth-knee output Uniform scaling by 0.3 100 nits 100 nits 30 nits 200 nits 200 nits 60 nits 500 nits About 389.47 nits 150 nits 1,000 nits About 513.04 nits 300 nits 2,000 nits 600 nits 600 nits All source values in the declared range fit. Compared with uniform scaling, the constructed function devotes more light to the lower region. Compared with clipping, it retains differences above the destination ceiling instead of merging them. Those differences are compressed: a 1,000-nit separation between the last two source rows becomes about 86.96 nits. The lower interval is preserved because it was a deliberate constraint; another mapper can choose a different transition and redistribute ordinary tones too. Prepare an HDR output with the new light meaning Interpreting the input, applying the mapping, and encoding the result are separate operations. In the example, a 2,000-nit PQ neutral has a normalized input signal of about 0.827. After mapping to 600 nits, the corresponding PQ output signal is about 0.696. Both numbers use PQ, but they describe different light requests. Keeping the original sample and only changing a peak metadata field would not perform the calculated brightness adaptation. A renderer can make the change in its presentation pipeline; a newly encoded HDR rendition needs values and signaling consistent with the prepared output. Colored pictures add another operation. Scaling brightness can preserve linear component ratios within one color system, while the destination volume may require further saturation or hue handling. A small bright saturated light can exceed a colored-output limit even when neutral white fits. Gamut mapping explains that fitting problem. Black-level adaptation has its own effect near the bottom. The zero-black diagram intentionally isolates highlight fitting. A screen with a higher useful black floor needs a response that accounts for lower-level separation, as discussed in the BT.2390 report. Locate the adaptation in the playback session With an Emby Direct Play session, the original coded video can reach the app, while the app or display still maps it to the selected output. A server transcode can instead prepare another rendition before delivery. The playback-path diagram separates those locations. Two HDR screens can therefore produce different pictures from the same delivered file. To assess the actual fitting, inspect ordinary objects, dark separation, and bright texture in the same moving scene. The curve's source range, target, and temporal inputs explain the differences more precisely than the common HDR signal badge. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Imagine a scene with a person beside a window: the face has ordinary indoor brightness, the outdoor sky is much brighter, and a reflection on glass is brighter still. An HDR picture can keep those regions distinct across a large range of light. An SDR conversion has less brightness range available, yet still needs to show a convincing face, a bright window, and some structure in the reflection. Tone mapping decides how to redistribute that brightness. The complete HDR-to-SDR conversion also has to interpret the original signal, fit its colors into the output color system, and produce correctly encoded SDR samples. Each part affects the result. A well-chosen highlight curve cannot repair incorrectly interpreted input values. For Emby playback, this conversion can happen in a server transcode or during presentation by a playback renderer. Both paths need to solve the same underlying problem, even though their implementations and output targets can differ. These are the jobs in the conversion. An implementation can combine operations or perform parts in different working spaces. Decoding gives samples; their meaning still matters A video decoder reconstructs numerical picture samples from the compressed stream. The converter then needs to know what those numbers represent. Many video sources store luma and color-difference components rather than directly storing red, green, and blue. Their matrix coefficients describe the relationship to color components. Signal range describes how stored code values represent nominal black, white, and color differences. Color primaries establish the meaning of the RGB color coordinates. Transfer characteristics relate nonlinear signal values to light. Those properties work together. If limited-range values are interpreted as full-range values, nominal black and white are assigned the wrong positions. The picture can have raised blacks or altered contrast before tone mapping starts. If the wrong matrix is used, reconstructing the color components can introduce a different error. Changing the tone curve would then adjust an already misinterpreted picture. Bit depth has a separate role. Ten bits provide more possible sample values than eight bits. They do not identify which color system or transfer function those values use. A ten-bit source can be SDR. For a PQ source, the signal has an absolute reference-display light meaning. A normalized PQ value of 0.5 corresponds to approximately 92.2 nits for neutral gray. It does not mean half of a television's peak brightness or half of PQ's 10,000-nit reference range. The nonlinear transfer function is what establishes that relationship. Before applying a curve defined in linear light, the converter must obtain linear-light values. For a neutral PQ gray, applying the PQ electro-optical transfer function gives its reference luminance. In a common linear-RGB processing path, the converter first restores nonlinear RGB from the luma/chroma samples using the appropriate range and matrix. It then applies the PQ transfer interpretation to those components to obtain linear RGB. Encoded luma and linear-light luminance are different quantities, so applying the PQ equation to luma alone would not perform this full color reconstruction. A method designed for a perceptual working space performs a different set of transformations. The conversion of HLG also needs to account for its system relationship to the intended display. Assigning PQ's absolute-light interpretation to HLG samples would skip that relationship. The important question at this stage is which representation the particular mapping expects. For example, FFmpeg's CPU tone-mapping filter expects linear-light input. Decide which brightness range to fit There are two ends to the decision: the useful brightness range in the source and the intended brightness behavior of the destination. A source can provide several kinds of information: Mastering-display metadata describes the display used during mastering, including its luminance capabilities. That is information about the mastering environment. Content-light metadata can summarize properties such as the maximum content light level. That is a description of the content under the metadata's measurement definition. Measured picture statistics come from inspecting the actual decoded pictures. A renderer can use them to adapt its mapping to the material being shown. A mastering display capable of 1,000 nits does not require every picture to contain a 1,000-nit highlight. Similarly, a whole-program maximum describes the brightest relevant content, not the brightness of each scene. These distinctions matter because reserving output range for a peak that is absent from the current scene can change how much brightness is available to its ordinary objects. The mapper may use a fixed source assumption, trustworthy metadata, peak detection , or a combination. If its assumed peak is too low, brighter source values can reach a part of the mapping that was never intended to preserve their distinctions. If the assumed peak is unnecessarily high, more compression may be applied than the scene needs. The destination also needs a defined target. A conventional SDR reference-display example can use 100 nits for white and a specified display transfer function. An actual television may show SDR white more brightly, particularly in a bright room. The largest brightness number on its product sheet does not, by itself, establish the intended SDR rendering. Reference white, black level, and viewing conditions influence the relationship between the converted picture and its appearance. The converter can prepare a conventional SDR signal for later display adjustment, or a renderer can adapt directly to a particular output. Those are different targets for the mapping. For the worked example below, choose an 800-nit source peak and a 100-nit SDR output peak . Use 100 nits as one unit on both sides solely to make the arithmetic easy: input values run from zero to eight, and output values from zero to one. This normalization does not assign a 100-nit reference white to all HDR material. Work through what the brightness curve does Three simple mappings show the tradeoff clearly. Let x be the input light level in the relative units just defined. Straight scaling uses x / 8. It fits the entire range, with the same scaling factor everywhere. An 800-nit highlight becomes 100 nits, but a 100-nit object becomes only 12.5 nits. If most of the scene sits well below its brightest highlight, the picture can become unnecessarily dark. Clipping uses the smaller of x and one. Inputs up to 100 nits retain their light levels in this example; every higher input becomes 100 nits. A 200-nit cloud and an 800-nit reflection then have the same output value. Their original brightness separation has disappeared. A smooth nonlinear mapping can devote more output range to ordinary brightness levels and compress the highlights more strongly. For an easily calculated example, use: T(x) = (9/8) × x / (1 + x) This function maps zero to zero and eight to one. For an input of one, its result is (9/8) × 1/2 = 0.5625. With the chosen output reference, that means 56.25 nits. Illustrative neutral-gray mappings. For this example, multiply either axis by 100 to express its light level in nits. The green curve is T(x) above; these are calculated relationships, not measured Emby presets. Source light level Straight scaling Clipping Smooth mapping T(x) 20 nits 2.5 nits 20 nits 18.75 nits 80 nits 10 nits 80 nits 50 nits 100 nits 12.5 nits 100 nits 56.25 nits 200 nits 25 nits 100 nits 75 nits 400 nits 50 nits 100 nits 90 nits 800 nits 100 nits 100 nits 100 nits All three make the 800-nit peak fit. They produce very different pictures everywhere else. The smooth example keeps substantially more brightness in the 80-nit region than straight scaling does, while retaining some separation among the highlights that clipping merges. That separation is still compressed. Under the smooth curve, a 600-nit region becomes about 96.43 nits, while an 800-nit region becomes 100. A source difference of 200 nits has become about 3.57 nits. The converter has preserved an ordering and a distinction, but has greatly reduced their spacing. Curve slope explains the contrast redistribution The slope of the curve describes how a small change in input light affects the output. A flat segment gives no separation to neighboring inputs. A shallow segment gives little separation; a steeper segment gives more. The green curve gradually becomes shallower toward its top. This is a highlight roll-off : extra source brightness has progressively less effect on output brightness. Fine texture in a very bright region can consequently become difficult to see even while its values remain mathematically distinct. A practical mapper has to choose how much separation to retain in shadows, middle brightness levels, and highlights. Preserving more of one region's brightness differences spends part of the finite output range. A curve's midpoint and any transition into highlight compression matter as much as its endpoint. The example's 100-nit object becomes 56.25 nits. That makes the effect on ordinary objects explicit: mapping is not confined to the few pixels above the SDR ceiling. Other curves can preserve a selected lower interval more closely or place the transition differently. The curve overview links to individual shapes and their behavior. Keep brightness changes from distorting the colors A neutral-gray example has equal RGB components, so a scalar curve is easy to interpret. Color introduces another choice: which quantity drives that curve, and how is the resulting brightness change applied to the components? Consider a linear RGB color with components 2, 1, 0.5 in one fixed set of primaries. Applying the example curve independently to each component gives 0.75, 0.5625, 0.375 . The original red-to-green ratio was 2; it is now about 1.33. The component proportions have changed, so the operation changes the color's chromaticity as well as its brightness. An alternative is to derive a single brightness-related quantity, calculate a scale factor, and apply that same factor to all three components. If the maximum component 2 drives the example curve, it maps to 0.75. The factor is 0.75 / 2 = 0.375 , producing 0.75, 0.375, 0.1875 . The original component ratio of 4:2:1 is retained. This calculation illustrates why a tone mapper needs a color strategy. A luminance-driven method can use a different driving quantity from a maximum-component method. Preserving linear RGB proportions retains chromaticity in that fixed color system, while perceived saturation can still change with brightness and viewing conditions. There is also the question of which colors the destination can represent. HDR material commonly uses a wider color gamut than a BT.709 SDR destination. Conversion between their primaries changes the RGB coordinates needed to describe a color. For a color outside the destination gamut, those coordinates can include a negative component or a component beyond the output range. Scaling the brightness alone does not necessarily bring that color into gamut. Independently clipping offending components changes their proportions and can cause hue shifts or merge distinct colors. Gamut mapping instead provides a strategy for fitting the color—for example, reducing its distance from a neutral color while trying to preserve hue. Brightness and saturation limits interact through the destination's color volume . A strongly saturated color cannot necessarily reach the same luminance as neutral white. A conversion may therefore adjust both brightness and chroma to obtain a useful result. The different methods in ITU-R BT.2446 show why HDR-to-SDR conversion includes color processing alongside tone mapping. A movie also needs stable decisions over time A fixed mapping produces the same output for the same input throughout the program. That consistency can be useful, but a single curve chosen for the brightest scene may use the available range less effectively in a much dimmer scene. Scene-adaptive tone mapping changes parameters based on the content. It can make better use of the output range, but the parameter changes themselves become visible if they are too abrupt. Imagine a stationary face beside a window. A tiny flash in the window raises the measured peak for one picture. If that peak immediately changes the mapping for the whole picture, the face can darken for that instant, although its source values did not change. When the flash ends, it brightens again. The viewer sees pumping caused by the adaptation. A method can moderate that response by considering the distribution of bright samples, smoothing parameter changes over time, or distinguishing a scene cut from a brief highlight. Those choices balance responsiveness against stability. Looking at one still frame will not reveal whether the conversion maintains a consistent appearance through movement, flashes, and cuts. Turn the mapped light back into an SDR signal After brightness and color processing, the converter has to produce samples whose encoding matches the intended SDR interpretation. Linear-light values cannot simply be written into a nonlinear video signal without the appropriate transfer operation. Continue the neutral-gray example. An original 100-nit PQ gray has a normalized PQ signal of about 0.508 . Interpreting PQ recovers 100 nits, which is x = 1 in the chosen working units. Applying T(x) produces y = 0.5625, meaning 56.25 nits in the chosen SDR display model. For an ideal SDR reference display with zero black, 100-nit white, and the BT.1886 exponent of 2.4, the nonlinear signal needed to obtain that light is: signal = 0.5625^(1/2.4) ≈ 0.787 The sequence is therefore: Representation Value for this neutral gray Normalized input PQ signal About 0.508 Interpreted HDR light 100 nits Linear mapping input x 1 Linear mapping output T(x) 0.5625 Intended output light 56.25 nits Normalized SDR signal for the stated ideal display About 0.787 The input and output signal numbers differ because they have different transfer meanings. Writing 0.5625 directly as that nonlinear SDR signal would produce only about 25.14 nits under the same display model. The tone-mapping calculation could be correct while the displayed brightness was wrong because the output encoding step was skipped. The real output process also accounts for black level and the selected conversion method. BT.2446 describes several methods; their processing spaces and transfer operations differ. The calculation above isolates one display-referred example so that the distinction between light values and signal values is visible. For a conventional video output, the converter prepares the required luma/chroma representation, numerical range, bit depth, and matching color signaling. Retagging original HDR samples as SDR performs none of the brightness or color calculations. Correct labels describe the converted values; they do not create those values. Precision matters during this work. Intermediate calculations can retain more precision than the final video format. When values are reduced to the output bit depth, rounding can make smooth gradients form visible steps. Dithering can make those steps less conspicuous by distributing rounding error. It helps represent the converted gradient; it cannot restore highlight differences that the mapping has already merged. Relate the conversion to the playback path During an Emby video transcode , the server decodes the HDR source, processes the pictures for the selected output, and encodes the resulting stream. Tone mapping is a picture-processing operation within that path. It changes the delivered rendition while the library file remains available as the source. During local presentation, a playback renderer can perform adaptation as it prepares pictures for the screen. The Windows app documentation describes tone mapping at this stage. Direct Play therefore identifies the server's delivery behavior; it does not, on its own, describe every color or brightness operation performed by the app, operating system, and display. To investigate an unexpected result, first establish where conversion happens and what output is intended. Then use the appearance to narrow the stage worth examining: Raised black or incorrect contrast throughout the picture: check input and output range interpretation, transfer characteristics, and display mode before adjusting highlight compression. Ordinary objects look sensible but bright texture disappears: examine the assumed source peak and highlight mapping. Check several frames to distinguish strong compression from time-dependent adaptation. Brightness looks plausible but vivid colors shift: examine primary conversion, gamut handling, and chroma processing. A stationary object brightens and darkens when another area flashes: examine how the mapping adapts over time. These observations connect a visible change to the operations that can cause it. Comparing the same scene along known playback paths—using both moving pictures and representative stills—makes that investigation much more informative than judging the brightest highlight alone. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: Why Tone Mapping Is Needed An HDR source asks for a 1,000-nit reflection beside a 100-nit surface. A destination with a 100-nit output peak has room for the surface, but cannot reproduce the reflection at its requested absolute light level. Tone mapping chooses how both parts fit into the available picture. There are two simple solutions with visibly different costs: Choice in this example Surface Reflection Result Clip at 100 nits 100 100 Brightness separation is lost Divide all light by ten 10 100 The whole lower range is darkened A nonlinear mapping can give ordinary levels more room while compressing highlights more strongly. It redistributes contrast according to the source and destination instead of making only an all-or-nothing cutoff decision. Why this is an image operation Changing resolution alters the spatial sample grid. Changing bitrate alters how the encoder describes the picture. Neither operation, on its own, changes the light interpretation enough to solve this range mismatch. A transfer-function label describes the meaning of the samples. Relabeling HDR as SDR would ask the player to apply another meaning to the existing values. Correct conversion first interprets the source, adapts its brightness and colors, then prepares suitable output values and signaling. The HDR-to-SDR walkthrough follows those steps. Curves show the brightness relationship; gamut and color-volume handling also matter for a bright colored object. Place the mapping in the playback path Emby Server can process pictures during a video transcode. A renderer can also adapt them locally; the Windows app documentation describes presentation-stage tone mapping. Direct Play identifies delivery from the server, while later app and display processing still determines the light produced. Mapping can also be needed between two HDR ranges, not only from HDR to SDR. A source peak above an HDR display's usable output presents the same fitting problem, even when the destination remains HDR. The useful comparison is the relationship among objects in the same scene: ordinary surfaces, dark detail, and bright texture. A good peak fit is one part of that relationship. The mapping's available range and its chosen distribution explain the rest.
